AGENCY:
Nuclear Regulatory Commission.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC, agency, or Commission) is revising the agency's rules of practice and procedure to streamline contested adjudications in NRC licensing proceedings in response to the Accelerating Deployment of Versatile, Advanced Nuclear for Clean Energy Act of 2024 (ADVANCE Act) and
Executive Order 14300
, Ordering the Reform of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.
DATES:
This final rule is effective on December 3, 2026, and applies to contested adjudicatory proceedings noticed on or after the effective date.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Executive Summary
A. Need for the Regulatory Action
The Accelerating Deployment of Versatile, Advanced Nuclear for Clean Energy Act of 2024 (ADVANCE Act) was signed into law in July of 2024. The ADVANCE Act establishes requirements to enhance the NRC's timeliness and efficiency, including a broad requirement for efficiency through an updated Mission Statement.
[
1
]
As directly relevant to the hearing process, ADVANCE Act § 505(b) requires the NRC to provide “efficient and timely . . . proceedings” for a broad category of licensing actions, and ADVANCE Act § 207(c) requires the NRC (for certain reactor combined license applications) to, among other things, complete “any necessary public licensing hearings and related processes” not later than two years after docketing the application, to the maximum extent practicable.
Subsequently, the President directed a series of reforms to improve the agency's efficiency and effectiveness in the May 23, 2025, Executive Order (E.O.) 14300, “Ordering the Reform of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission” (
90 FR 22587
, May 29, 2025). As relevant to this final rule, section 5(j) of
E.O. 14300
directs the NRC to streamline its public hearing process. Relatedly,
E.O. 14300
section 5(a) directs the NRC to establish fixed deadlines for its evaluation and approval of specified licensing actions and requests, section 5(d) directs the NRC to establish an expedited approval pathway for reactor designs tested and demonstrated by the Department of Defense (also referred to as the Department of War (DOW))
[
2
]
or the Department of Energy (DOE), and section 5(e) directs the NRC to “[e]stablish a process for high-volume licensing of microreactors and modular reactors[.]”
In response to Congressional and Executive action, the NRC has developed this final rule focused on streamlining the agency's rules of practice and procedure. The changes to the contested hearing process will reduce burden, increase clarity, and promote efficiencies in line with deadlines established in accordance with the ADVANCE Act and
E.O. 14300
.
B. Major Provisions
Major provisions of this final rule include the following:
Revisions to the contested hearing process that will enable the NRC to generally complete adjudications within 11 to 13.5 months or faster for expedited proceedings.
A requirement for evidentiary hearings to begin as soon as practicable upon admission of contentions.
Strict deadlines for the completion of hearings.
Tailored hearing schedules that correspond to the staff's review schedule to the maximum extent practicable, considering the complexity of the application.
A reduction in discovery burden on all parties to focus on information of highest value and reflect the greater availability of information due to technological developments.
Revisions to accelerate Commission review of appeals.
Elimination, refinement, or addition of provisions that will accommodate the schedule directives of the ADVANCE Act and
E.O. 14300
.
C. Costs and Benefits
This final rule is considered to be a deregulatory action and will reduce burden for both the government and hearing participants by streamlining contested hearing proceedings. Over the five-year analysis period (2026-2030), the revisions to the contested hearing procedures are projected to yield savings for the public, the industry, and government. The combined net savings would generate cumulative undiscounted savings of $67.4 million. Using 2025 as the base year, the net present value (NPV) of these net savings is $61.7 million, discounted at 3 percent, or $55.2 million, discounted at 7 percent. The projected annualized cost savings would be $13.5 million
(
printed page 69447)
discounted at 3 percent, or $13.5 million discounted at 7 percent. These values represent net savings, as implementation and transition costs are expected to be minimal.
For more information, please see the regulatory analysis included later in this notice.

I.
Executive Order 14300
: Ordering the Reform of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission
On May 23, 2025, the President signed
E.O. 14300
, “Ordering the Reform of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.” Section 5, “Reforming and Modernizing the NRC's Regulations,” directs the NRC to undertake a review and wholesale revision of its regulations and guidance documents as guided by the policies set forth in section 2 of the E.O. This rulemaking addresses section 5(j), which directs the NRC to “[s]treamline the public hearings process,” and also supports meeting the objectives of sections 5(a), 5(d), and 5(e) of
E.O. 14300
, as discussed below.
II. Background
Since its inception, the Commission has periodically taken steps to assess and improve the efficiency of its adjudicatory process, as discussed in a 2004 rule (
69 FR 2182
, pages 2182 through 2186, January 14, 2004) (hereafter “2004 Adjudications Rule”). Generally, these reforms have yielded less formal adjudications intended to reduce the burden of litigation costs for all parties and remove procedural mechanisms that are not essential to developing an adequate hearing record. The Commission last finalized a major reformation of its hearing processes in 2004 in anticipation of a significant volume of new proceedings to consider applications for new facilities, to renew operating licenses, to reflect restructuring in the electric utility industry, and to license waste storage facilities.
The Commission now expects a similar increase in licensing applications in the coming years, and Congress and the President have directed the NRC to prepare to review and process these applications as expeditiously as possible. In 2024, Congress passed the ADVANCE Act, which established requirements to enhance the NRC's timeliness and efficiency, such as the direction to update the NRC's mission statement to provide that the NRC's licensing and regulation of the civilian use of radioactive materials and nuclear energy be conducted in a manner that is efficient and does not unnecessarily limit—(1) the civilian use of radioactive materials and deployment of nuclear energy; or (2) the benefits of civilian use of radioactive materials and nuclear energy technology to society. The ADVANCE Act also addresses the hearing process, with section 505(b) amending the Atomic Energy Act of 1954, as amended (AEA) section 181 to require the NRC to provide “efficient and timely . . . proceedings” for a broad category of licensing actions. Also, for certain reactor combined license applications, section 207(c) of the ADVANCE Act requires the NRC, to the maximum extent practicable, to (1) complete safety and environmental reviews not later than 18 months of docketing, (2) complete “any necessary public licensing hearings and related processes” not later than two years after docketing, and (3) make a final decision on whether to issue the combined license not later than 25 months after docketing.
[
3
]
Building on the ADVANCE Act, the President signed
E.O. 14300
“Ordering the Reform of the Nuclear Regulatory Commission,” on May 23, 2025 (
90 FR 22587
, May 29, 2025). Section 3 of
E.O. 14300
directs the NRC to consider the benefits of increased availability of, and innovation in, nuclear power to the nation's economic and national security in addition to safety, health, and environmental considerations, when the NRC carries out its licensing and related regulatory functions. In furtherance of the President's directive,
E.O. 14300
tasked the NRC with streamlining its public hearing process. As relevant here, section 5 of
E.O. 14300
directs the NRC to undertake a review and wholesale revision of its regulations and guidance documents and establishes specific tasks this effort must encompass, including streamlining the public hearings process, as directed by section 5(j).
Relatedly, section 5(a) of the E.O. directs the NRC to establish fixed deadlines for its evaluation and approval of specified licensing actions and other requests from a licensee or potential licensee rather than nonbinding generic milestone schedule guidelines. These deadlines include taking no more than 18 months to make a final decision on an application to construct and operate a new reactor of any type and taking no more than one year to make a final decision on an application to continue operating an existing reactor of any type. Section 5(a) also directs the NRC to adopt shorter deadlines tailored to particular reactor types or licensing pathways as appropriate. In addition, section 5(e) of the E.O. directs the NRC to establish a process for high-volume licensing of microreactors and modular reactors, and section 5(d) of the E.O. directs the NRC to establish an expedited pathway to approve reactor designs that the DOW or the DOE have tested and that have demonstrated the ability to function safely.
In some cases, completing licensing decisions within the E.O.-directed timeframes could turn on timely completion of a contested adjudication. However, the Commission's existing hearing procedures in title 10 of the
Code of Federal Regulations
(10 CFR) part 2, “Agency Rules of Practice and Procedure,” provide model milestones that would collectively exceed the timeframes specified in
E.O. 14300
. And these milestones, which are not binding, are sometimes exceeded in practice. Therefore, the Commission is revising its hearing procedures to support faster adjudications that will enable the agency to meet the licensing timelines contemplated by the ADVANCE Act and
E.O. 14300
. The NRC believes that the revised adjudicatory deadlines will provide reasonable timeframes for parties to meaningfully raise, and the presiding officer to resolve, disputed issues. These revisions will continue the overall trend, described previously, of reducing the formality in NRC adjudications to enhance efficiency.
The NRC's predecessor agency, the Atomic Energy Commission, at one time believed that the AEA required formal adjudicatory hearings in all cases (2004 Adjudications Rule,
69 FR 2182
, page 2183, January 14, 2004). Now the prevailing view is that, with the exception of hearings on applications for licenses to construct and operate
(
printed page 69448)
uranium enrichment facilities, informal hearings will also satisfy the AEA. (2004 Adjudications Rule,
69 FR 2182
, pages 2183 through 2186, January 14, 2004). On balance, these amendments generally use simpler, more informal processes and shorter schedules to complete adjudications within the timeframes contemplated in the ADVANCE Act and
E.O. 14300
.While the final rule establishes three primary pathways for hearings (a “Standard Proceeding” for 18-month reviews, a “Focused Proceeding” for 12-month proceedings, and an “Expedited Proceeding” for faster reviews), the Commission does not intend for these designations to be rigid. Rather, in light of the direction in
E.O. 14300
to “adopt shorter deadlines tailored to particular reactor types or licensing pathways as appropriate,” the rule does not preclude reliance on the Commission's authority to move a proceeding to a faster pathway when warranted. Additionally, within the pathways, the final rule directs the presiding officer to ensure the hearing schedule does not exceed the staff review schedule to the greatest extent practicable. Collectively, these provisions should ensure that the hearing procedures for each adjudication appropriately reflect the complexity of the issues raised by the underlying application.
The Commission has chosen to use a Licensing Board as the default presiding officer for contested licensing proceedings, including license transfers, because Boards are independent and statutorily established, possess legal and technical expertise, and are well placed to efficiently conduct NRC licensing proceedings given their experience and ability to focus exclusively on adjudicatory matters. Considering the wide variety of situations a Board could face after a contention is admitted, the presiding officer will have considerable flexibility to select the appropriate procedures for resolving disputed issues within the strict timeframes imposed by this rulemaking. For example, these procedures will continue to rely primarily on written pleadings and statements to maintain clarity and precision in the record, although the presiding officer will have the flexibility to convene oral proceedings when necessary.
These revisions will require evidentiary hearings to be held as soon as practicable after a decision admitting contentions. Nonetheless, to support more efficient and timely resolution of admitted contentions in certain circumstances, the procedures and practice will still provide for motions to dismiss contentions and motions for summary disposition prior to an evidentiary hearing.
These procedures also address new or amended contentions filed later in the NRC's review process to ensure that the NRC is still able to complete adjudications in a timely manner. The Commission is making three significant revisions to accomplish this goal.
First, in light of the dynamic nature of our licensing process, parties frequently file new or amended contentions throughout NRC adjudications, often in response to amended applications or other new information. To accommodate these filings within the 18-month and 1-year
E.O. 14300
timelines, the revisions establish deadlines the presiding officer must use in setting hearing schedules that will provide sufficient time to (1) fully litigate an initial round of contentions (including an evidentiary hearing on any admitted contentions) and (2) fully litigate a second round of new or amended contentions through an evidentiary hearing on those contentions, even if there is no overlap between the rounds of litigation.
Second, the Commission recognizes that, in rare instances, critical issues could arise sufficiently late in a proceeding to challenge the
E.O. 14300
timelines for a decision on the application. To ensure that only critical issues have the potential to be admitted late in the proceeding, these revisions establish that the NRC's standards for reopening the record will apply to contentions raising new issues that are submitted after the date by which the presiding officer would be expected to enter an initial decision after an evidentiary hearing on the initial round of contentions, assuming that the evidentiary hearing phase immediately commences upon the admission of the contention and there are no delays along the way.
Third, these revisions establish that new or amended contentions would not be considered pending before the agency until the presiding officer finds there is good cause for submitting these contentions after the prescribed initial filing deadline for contentions (
i.e.,
that they have been timely submitted based on new, materially different information). This change will, as discussed later in this notice, eliminate the possibility of parties delaying licensing in certain proceedings simply by filing an untimely new or amended contention.
As stated previously, the Commission is establishing hearing schedules that would allow for two non-overlapping hearings to be conducted within the 18-month and 1-year
E.O. 14300
timelines—one hearing for contentions submitted by the initial filing deadline for contentions and a second hearing held thereafter on a new or amended contention arising later in the review. The revisions to
10 CFR part 2
primarily accomplish this acceleration by requiring the presiding officer to commence the evidentiary hearing as soon as practicable after admitting contentions. In contrast, evidentiary hearings generally do not begin under the existing rules until after the staff completes its review.
This change also reflects the Commission's understanding that the E.O.'s discussion of fixed deadlines for the NRC's evaluation to support a final decision on the application refers to the agency's approval of the licensing action or other request if the NRC's evaluation determines that applicable requirements are met. Given this understanding, the changes in this final rule focus on ensuring that there is a final presiding officer decision on all contested issues within the
E.O. 14300
timelines as these decisions have immediate effect by default, regardless of the pendency of appeals. As such, the presiding officer's decision would allow the licensing decision to be made even in circumstances where the AEA requires a hearing to be completed before the issuance and effectiveness of a license. Consequently, in this final rule, the appeals process occurs outside of the scope of the fixed deadlines outlined in section 5(a) of
E.O. 14300
. Nonetheless, the NRC is streamlining the appeals process to support the overarching goals of the ADVANCE Act and
E.O. 14300
. First, this final rule makes small changes to the filing deadlines for appeals, shortening the process. Second, the Commission recognizes the importance of issuing its adjudicatory decisions in a timely manner and will use milestones in its internal procedures to effectuate this goal.
While the Commission expects these revisions will substantially improve the efficiency of NRC contested licensing adjudications, they do not constitute a wholesale rewrite of
10 CFR part 2
, and many proceedings such as enforcement proceedings, proceedings on denials of applications, or proceedings for construction or operation of a high-level waste geological repository are only minimally impacted. Proceedings under § 52.103 or 53.1452 are also minimally impacted by the changes because the procedures for such hearings are established by case-specific order, and the NRC will consider modifications to the existing standard procedures for these proceedings in a separate process. Further, a final rule published April 15,
(
printed page 69449)
2026 (
91 FR 20063
) increased flexibility in the mandatory hearing process, and a policy statement published June 8, 2026 (
91 FR 34661
) made changes to the agency's mandatory hearing process for reactors to increase efficiency and timeliness while also enhancing public participation. Additionally, in a separate rulemaking, the NRC proposed changes to the agency's implementation of the National Environmental Policy Act (
91 FR 42086
, July 7, 2026), which could impact the scope of issues that may be permissible for adjudication in contested hearings. The changes in this final rule are a series of targeted amendments intended to ensure timely and efficient contested adjudication for most NRC licensing actions.
This final rule reflects changes to the proposed rule made in response to public comments, as documented in the “NRC Response to Public Comments: Streamlining Contested Adjudications in Licensing Proceedings” (hereafter, Comment Response Document). This final rule also accounts for changes made to the regulations since publication of the proposed rule, including a final rule adding a new
10 CFR part 53
, “Risk-Informed, Technology-Inclusive Regulatory Framework for Advanced Reactors” (
91 FR 15696
, March 30, 2026), which generally revised
10 CFR part 2
to apply the same processes to applications under
10 CFR part 53
, “Risk-Informed, Technology-Inclusive Regulatory Framework for Commercial Nuclear Plants,” as would apply to corresponding applications under
10 CFR part 50
, “Domestic Licensing of Production and Utilization Facilities,” or
10 CFR part 52
, “Licenses, Certifications, and Approvals for Nuclear Power Plants.” This final contested hearings rule includes these changes and consistently treats
10 CFR part 53
applications and licenses the same as the corresponding applications and licenses under
10 CFR parts 50
and
52
. This final rule also accounts for changes made by the rule, mentioned previously, that increased flexibility in the mandatory hearing process (
91 FR 20063
, April 15, 2026). In addition, this final rule makes certain corrections, clarifications, and other minor changes that were not in response to comments but that the NRC identified during the development of the final rule. All changes made in the final rule logically grow out of the proposed rule provisions.
III. Discussion
To achieve the objectives described previously, the Commission is amending
10 CFR part 2
in the following areas:
Hearing Schedule Framework and New Definitions in
10 CFR 2.4
In this rule, the NRC is taking a tailored approach to timeframes for hearing requests and evidentiary hearings to account for specific types of applications rather than the one-size-fits-all approach in the existing regulations, where the same time is generally provided for hearing requests and evidentiary hearings on shorter or simpler applications as on longer or complex applications. The tailored timeframes in this final rule provide sufficient time for the parties to meaningfully raise and litigate disputed issues in the type of proceeding at issue and for the presiding officer to make accurate determinations on these disputed issues. Using tailored hearing timelines is consistent with direction in the Nuclear Energy Innovation and Modernization Act section 102(c), ADVANCE Act section 504, and
E.O. 14300
section 5 regarding specified timelines for different types of NRC reviews.
To accomplish this objective, the NRC is establishing three basic timeframes for most licensing proceedings so that the NRC's hearing regulations are clear and manageable and provide greater flexibility, while recognizing that it would be impractical to establish a multitude of timeframes for every type of proceeding and constantly modify hearing processes and regulations to account for the different NRC decision-making schedules as they are updated over time. Nonetheless, as discussed later, the NRC is accounting for potential variability in NRC decision-making schedules by requiring the presiding officer in each proceeding to establish a hearing schedule that, to the greatest extent practicable, will not extend past the NRC staff's scheduled date for completing its review of the application. This provision could, for example, address an expedited NRC review under
E.O. 14300
section 5(d) of a reactor design tested and demonstrated by DOE or DOW.
The NRC is adding new definitions in § 2.4 to account for the three basic timeframes established by this rule. The new definitions are “Standard Proceeding,” “Focused Proceeding,” and “Expedited Proceeding,” where Standard Proceedings have the longest hearing schedules, Expedited Proceedings have the shortest hearing schedules, and Focused Proceedings have hearing schedules in between these two categories. The proposed rule followed the same basic scheduling construct as this final rule but did not establish formal labels for Standard Proceedings or Focused Proceedings.
[
4
]
The NRC has determined that the clarity of
10 CFR part 2
will be enhanced by formal labels for each basic type of proceeding, and the final rule is accordingly adding definitions for Standard Proceedings and Focused Proceedings. Also, in establishing the basic hearing timeframes in this rule, the NRC has followed the general approach taken in the proposed rule by specifying the applications that are in the Standard Proceeding category and the applications that are in the Expedited Proceeding, with the Focused Proceeding category including, with certain limited exceptions, all other licensing proceedings.
The new definition for “Standard Proceeding” captures those applications that generally present more complex technical issues than those applications that fall into the other categories. While the applications in this category are not all equally complex, they are currently subject to the longer 18-month standard NRC review schedules and warrant longer hearing schedules because of the anticipated complexity of material on which contentions could be based, as well as the potential complexity of the technical issues that could be the subject of admitted contentions. As discussed later in this notice, the hearing schedules established for Standard Proceedings support the potential completion of two non-overlapping evidentiary hearings within 13.5 months and allow for Commission consideration of any associated appeals within 18 months.
Reactor applications falling under the Standard Proceeding category are those for the grant of a construction permit, an operating license, or a combined license under
10 CFR part 50
,
52
, or
53
for a commercial production or utilization facility (other than a non-power production or utilization facility (NPUF)), where the application does not reference an NRC approval providing finality in the adjudicatory proceeding on design matters (
e.g.,
a design certification or manufacturing license).
5
(
printed page 69450)
For materials licenses, the proposed rule applied the Standard hearing schedules to the following licenses: (1) a license to construct and operate a uranium enrichment facility, and (2) a license to construct or operate a uranium recovery or fuel cycle facility under
10 CFR part 40
, “Domestic Licensing of Source Material,” or part 70, “Domestic Licensing of Special Nuclear Material.” The NRC is retaining these categories in the final rule but in response to comments is clarifying what constitutes a “fuel cycle facility” in this category. Specifically, licenses for new fuel cycle facilities that are subject to the Standard hearing schedules are those that are subject to subpart H of
10 CFR part 70
, “Additional Requirements for Certain Licensees Authorized To Possess a Critical Mass of Special Nuclear Material,”
i.e.,
a facility with a critical mass of special nuclear material that necessitates an integrated safety analysis and other requirements in subpart H because of the facility's safety significance. In addition, in this final rule, the NRC has determined that an application for a new low-level-waste disposal facility under
10 CFR part 61
, “Licensing Requirements for Land Disposal of Radioactive Waste,” should be included in the Standard Proceeding category. The currently operating low-level waste disposal facilities are licensed by agreement states rather than the NRC, but it is possible that an application for a new facility might be filed with the NRC. If such an application were to be filed, the NRC has determined that the application should be included in the Standard Proceeding category given the types of technical issues that would be involved.
The new definition for “Focused Proceeding” covers those applications that are subject to more focused NRC reviews because they are generally less complex than applications within the Standard Proceeding category. As such, Focused Proceedings are amenable to faster NRC reviews and hearing schedules than those reserved for Standard Proceedings. Many applications in the Focused Proceeding category are currently subject to a 12-month standard NRC review schedule. Several others are subject to an 18-month standard NRC review schedule, but the NRC would aim to complete the review of these applications more quickly than 18 months if practical since they would generally be less complex and narrower in scope than other applications subject to an 18-month standard review schedule (
e.g.,
10 CFR part 52
combined license applications referencing a design certification). Appropriately accelerating hearing schedules, when warranted, for limited scope applications responds to direction in
E.O. 14300
, section 5(a), which states that the
E.O. 14300
deadlines are “maximum time periods,” and that “the NRC shall adopt shorter deadlines tailored to particular reactor types or licensing pathways as appropriate.” As discussed later in this notice, the hearing schedules established for Focused Proceedings support the potential completion of two non-overlapping evidentiary hearings within 12 months.
Following the approach taken in the proposed rule, the Focused Proceeding category has been defined to include all proceedings for the grant, renewal, licensee-initiated amendment, or termination of licenses or permits subject to
10 CFR parts 30
,
32
through
36
,
39
,
40
,
50
,
52
,
53
,
54
,
55
,
61
,
70
, and
72
, except for a Standard Proceeding, an Expedited Proceeding, a proceeding for the construction or operation of a high-level waste geological repository, or a proceeding on a denial of an application. Applications in the Focused Proceeding category include, but are not limited to, operating reactor license renewal applications under
10 CFR part 53
or
54
; applications for new
10 CFR part 50
,
52
, or
53
licenses referencing an NRC approval providing finality in the adjudicatory proceeding on design matters (
e.g.,
a design certification or manufacturing license);
10 CFR part 52
or
53
early site permit applications; materials license renewal applications; applications to construct or operate new facilities under
10 CFR part 70
that are not subject to the requirements of subpart H of
10 CFR part 70
; license amendment requests; NPUF license applications; and limited work authorization applications. Moreover, several commenters proposed accelerating Nth-of-a-kind proceedings. The Commission expects that the agency will seek to complete these proceedings significantly in advance of the
E.O. 14300
timeframe because the staff will have previously resolved the majority of technical issues. Moreover, the NRC recently finalized a new reactor generic environmental impact statement, which will resolve a significant number of environmental issues in most Nth-of-a-kind proceedings. Therefore, the NRC has also added these proceedings to the Focused Proceedings hearing track. Additionally, commenters noted that faster proceedings would be appropriate for uranium enrichment facilities that employ technologies that have been licensed and operated. The NRC agrees. Given the limited set of technical and environmental contentions these proceedings are expected to raise, the NRC has also added these proceedings to the definition of Focused Proceedings.
Similarly, several commenters suggested providing faster procedures for limited work authorizations. Generally, these proceedings only resolve a limited set of technical and siting issues. Moreover, while in the past a limited work authorization may have occasioned a more detailed environmental review, the NRC recently finalized a generic environmental impact statement for new reactors that would resolve the majority of these issues in most cases. Consequently, the NRC has also included proceedings on these applications within the definition of “Focused Proceedings.”
The new definition of “Expedited Proceeding” captures those applications that are particularly simple or narrow in scope and should be subject to significantly expedited hearing schedules because they will be reviewed on a more expedited basis than the other reviews the NRC would typically handle. As reflected in the standard review schedules on the NRC website at
https://www.nrc.gov/​about-nrc/​generic-schedules.html
,
the NRC currently intends to apply an 18-month or 12-month review schedule to most types of applications it receives. However, some applications have a significantly shorter anticipated review schedule. For example, measurement uncertainty recapture uprate license amendments currently have a six-month review schedule, stretch power uprates have a nine-month review schedule, and amendments adopting a Technical Specifications Task Force traveler using the Consolidated Line-Item Improvement Process currently have a seven-month review schedule. To support expedited decision-making on these applications, the NRC is including these three types of applications within the definition of “Expedited Proceeding,” and applying significantly expedited hearing schedules to these proceedings to reflect the shorter review schedules and focused nature of these reviews. Additionally, several commenters noted that licensing applications that reference prior NRC approvals providing issue finality are not likely to spark complex litigation.
(

The NRC agrees that these proceedings would present a sufficiently narrowed set of issues, particularly when the application references a categorical exclusion, that Expedited Proceedings would be warranted in all cases. Applications taking advantage of issue finality and categorical exclusions will have the vast majority of technical and environmental issues resolved for the facility, and the remaining issues are unlikely to present complex contentions requiring extended litigation. Therefore, the NRC has revised the definition “Expedited Proceedings” to always include these types of applications. As discussed later in this notice, the hearing schedules established for Expedited Proceedings support the potential completion of an evidentiary hearing within 5 to 5.5 months.

The definitions of “Standard Proceeding,” “Focused Proceeding,” and “Expedited Proceeding” cover most, but not all, license-related proceedings before the NRC. These definitions do not include enforcement proceedings, proceedings on denials of applications, proceedings for construction or operation of a high-level waste geological repository, or proceedings under § 52.103 or 53.1452 because this rule is not intended to establish schedules for such proceedings. In addition, these definitions do not cover license transfer proceedings because the NRC is taking a more nuanced approach to transfer proceeding schedules, as explained later in this notice, while remaining generally consistent with the schedule timeframes established by this rule.
In sum, these changes would support hearing schedules that align with the overall timeliness goals of
E.O. 14300

Finally, the NRC is adding a new definition of “Standard Hearing Completion Date” to § 2.4 to support changes elsewhere in this notice regarding standards and schedules for late-stage challenges after the deadline. As discussed later, the NRC considers it appropriate in certain cases to apply a faster evidentiary hearing schedule to such challenges if the associated contention is admitted for hearing. In addition, the NRC considers it appropriate to apply the reopening criteria to such challenges that raise new issues not within the scope of existing admitted or proposed contentions. The NRC is applying these provisions after the point in the proceeding in which the NRC could have completed an evidentiary hearing in the situation where a contention filed by the hearing request deadline is both admitted for hearing and proceeds to the evidentiary hearing phase immediately after the admission of the contention, consistent with the NRC's policy of holding evidentiary hearings as early as practicable. Because the revised regulations define the time (1) in which contentions, answers, and replies are to be filed, (2) when decisions on contention admissibility are due, and (3) when initial decisions after an evidentiary hearing are to be issued, the NRC is able to compute the Standard Hearing Completion Date for different types of proceedings. The proposed rule used the term “Standard Record Closure Date” rather than “Standard Hearing Completion Date,” but the NRC changed the terminology in this final rule to reflect that the “Date” is used for two independent purposes: to identify a time after which certain evidentiary hearing schedules are accelerated and to define a time when proposed contentions raising new issues must meet the standards for reopening the record. The NRC also revised the proposed rule definition so that it focuses solely on how the Standard Hearing Completion Date is calculated, with provisions on reopening appearing solely in § 2.326.

The NRC is also changing the definitions of “contested proceeding” and “potential party” in § 2.4, which are related to matters discussed in more detail later in this notice. Nonetheless, while the challenge after the deadline is not pending before the NRC, the motion for leave to file would still be considered within the scope of the contested proceeding since the purpose of the motion is to seek permission to file a challenge after the deadline to contest the application. For the reasons given in the Comment Response Document, the NRC has not adopted the limitations on non-attorney representation that were included in the proposed rule. Also, as discussed in a 2020 decision in the Vogtle proceeding (CLI-20-6, 91 NRC 225), the Commission has given greater latitude to hearing requests submitted by non-attorney intervenors while acknowledging that non-attorney petitioners are still expected to comply with our procedural rules. The exception pertains to notices of proposed action subject to the requirements of § 50.91 or 53.1515. Notices under § 50.91 or 53.1515 are for proposed amendments to specified production and utilization facility licenses. Historically, such notices have generally been published on a periodic basis given their volume. Given the high volume, it would not be practical to require individual
Federal Register
notices for these licensing actions. Also, only a small number of these amendments are challenged in the hearing process, and the associated licensing actions may be taken during the pendency of a hearing if the NRC makes a final no significant hazards consideration determination.

Federal Register

Consistent with current practice,

While the agency recognizes this practice as helpful, in that it provides sufficient time to create an electronic hearing docket for a proceeding to facilitate compliance with electronic filing requirements and identify applicant and NRC staff contacts, imposing the practice as an additional requirement, as requested by one commenter on the rule, is not necessary. Outside the rulemaking process, the NRC will look to clarify notice templates to highlight the importance of meeting the requirements for electronic filing, including a timely request to establish a docket.
Good Cause for Extensions of Time
Meeting the licensing deadlines contemplated in the ADVANCE Act and
E.O. 14300
will require strict adherence to the schedules described in the rule. Under existing § 2.307(a), time periods in
10 CFR part 2
may be extended either upon a showing of good cause or by stipulation of the parties. An extension of time by stipulation of the parties usually does not result in significant delay as the applicant and NRC staff have an interest in timely adjudication, and such extensions sometimes lead to more efficient resolution of issues (
e.g.,
an extension to complete consultation on a motion). However, contested extensions are more likely to lead to delay, and in recent years the NRC has sometimes found good cause for extensions based on requests detailing ordinary circumstances, such as general resource planning challenges.
The NRC has determined that no changes must be made to § 2.307(a), but in order to ensure that extension requests do not undermine timely adjudications, the NRC is reiterating the need for parties to clearly demonstrate good cause under § 2.307. Good cause is necessarily context specific, and the Commission has previously explained in its 2012 rule (
77 FR 46562
, August 3, 2012) that good cause in the context of § 2.307 should include “extraordinary circumstances.” Extraordinary circumstances are those events that are not within the parties' control, such as sickness or weather. Major holidays could similarly be an extraordinary circumstance. Thus, in normal circumstances the presiding officer should only grant an extension when a circumstance outside of the ordinary occurs that is not brought on by the movant's actions or inactions. In addition, under the ADVANCE Act and
E.O. 14300
, efficient and timely decision-making on license applications is a key focus area for the agency. Therefore, in circumstances where an extension request has the potential to extend an adjudicatory proceeding past the NRC staff's scheduled date to complete its review, the presiding officer should take into account schedule needs when making its determination and minimize the amount of time necessary to accommodate the circumstances giving rise to good cause.

E.O. 14300

However, as discussed in the Comment Response Document, this final rule is not adopting a provision in the proposed rule that would have
(

As such, this final rule will not change current practice on these two matters: litigants will continue to address standing and contention admissibility in the same filings, the presiding officer will address both matters in the same decision, and litigants will not be required to file additional information on the merits of proposed contentions.
The NRC is also refining the contention admissibility criteria in two ways. First, the NRC is augmenting the requirement in § 2.309(f)(1)(iv) to demonstrate that a contention is material by requiring the petitioner to specify the legal requirement on which the contention is based. Specifying the pertinent legal requirement is important for demonstrating the materiality of the contention, and clarity in this regard can avoid needless confusion about the legal basis for a contention (
e.g.,
safety versus environmental requirements) and the inefficiencies that accompany efforts to resolve such confusion. Second, the NRC is revising § 2.309(f)(1)(vi) to require the petitioner to clearly indicate whether a contention is one of omission or adequacy. Different requirements apply to contentions of omission versus contentions of adequacy, and a lack of clarity regarding the nature of the contention requires additional resources from the NRC staff, applicant, and presiding officers to address.

These tailored timeframes provide sufficient time for petitioners to meaningfully raise disputed issues in their hearing requests, for the applicant and NRC staff to file answers to hearing requests, and for the presiding officer to determine whether the standing and contention requirements are met.

Timeline for Motions Submitted in Expedited Proceedings
Consistent with the overall streamlining approach of this final rule, the agency is amending § 2.323 to reduce the timelines for submittal of motions and corresponding answers in Expedited Proceedings. As previously discussed, Expedited Proceedings are simpler or narrower in scope and on a shorter timeline than typical proceedings covered under
10 CFR part 2
. To achieve timelines commensurate with the substance and pace of Expedited Proceedings, § 2.323(a)(2) is changed to require that motions filed in these proceedings must be made no later than seven (7) days after the occurrence or circumstance from which the motion arises. Further, § 2.323(c) is amended to state that answers to motions in Expedited Proceedings must be submitted within seven (7) days after service of the motion. The agency is also instituting a simple restructuring of § 2.323(c) into three subparagraphs (1)-(3), introducing additional clarity and improving readability of the applicable requirements. Finally, in this final rule, the NRC is making an administrative correction to § 2.323(c) to change the title “Assistant Secretary” to the current title “Deputy Secretary.” The NRC is also making this correction in §§ 2.346 and 2.808.
Reopening Standards
The NRC intends to complete contested hearings on a schedule that supports licensing within the timelines contemplated by the ADVANCE Act and
E.O. 14300
. Consequently, to ensure that the adjudicatory process concludes within these timelines, the revised adjudicatory procedures have been constructed so as to generally accommodate an evidentiary hearing on admitted contentions filed by the § 2.309(b) deadline for filing contentions and a hearing on admitted contentions filed after that deadline, even if there is essentially no overlap between the filing and decision schedules for the two. To help accomplish this, the rule introduces a mechanism referred to as the Standard Hearing Completion Date, which facilitates the timely disposition of issues during the contested hearing process. The Standard Hearing Completion Date serves an important dual purpose in maintaining efficiency by identifying a time after which certain evidentiary hearing schedules are accelerated and, as discussed in the following paragraphs, defining a time when proposed contentions raising new issues must meet the standards for reopening the record.
The NRC acknowledges that in rare cases critical issues may arise late in a proceeding that might require the adjudication to exceed the NRC staff review timelines established in accordance with the ADVANCE Act and
E.O. 14300
. However, only critical issues should lead to such delays. Existing § 2.326 addresses this in part by requiring contentions filed after the record closes for an adjudicatory proceeding to meet the heightened reopening standards in § 2.326, which require the contention to be timely in accordance with § 2.309(c), address a significant safety or environmental issue, and demonstrate that it would likely materially affect the outcome of the proceeding. Under existing case law, the reopening standards would apply after the last live contention in the proceeding is resolved.
However, it is possible under existing precedent for a chain of periodically
(
printed page 69457)
filed new or amended contentions, none of them admissible, to hold open the record of the proceeding even to the end of the NRC's review of an application. To avoid this anomalous result and to provide a standard time for when the record would close to new issues for a proceeding, the revisions to § 2.326 add a new paragraph (e)(1) stating that the record for the proceeding will automatically close at the Standard Hearing Completion Date, a date providing sufficient time to hold an evidentiary hearing on admitted contentions submitted by the original deadline. The Standard Hearing Completion Date is based on the timeline structure of a particular proceeding, and applying the reopening standards to new issues raised after this date balances the rights of potential intervenors with the need for efficiency and predictability in a proceeding. The imposition of the reopening standards at this juncture in the timeline is intended to ensure that
new
issues submitted late in the proceeding are only admitted if shown to be critical, and would not affect litigation of issues already raised in a previously filed contention, as explained in subsequent paragraphs.
There may be instances in which an evidentiary hearing is completed before the Standard Hearing Completion Date. Consistent with existing practice, the presiding officer is expected to issue an order closing the record after the evidentiary hearing and before issuing the initial decision. In keeping with existing practice and consistent with themes underlying existing agency case law, § 2.326(e)(1) also provides that the record closes for the adjudicatory proceeding if the presiding officer enters an order closing the record following an evidentiary hearing but before the Standard Hearing Completion Date.
These revisions to § 2.326 comport with existing NRC precedent and are not intended to supersede the concepts already enshrined in case law. The Commission has routinely emphasized that the adjudicatory record for a proceeding closes at the conclusion of an evidentiary hearing, for example, in a 2012 decision in the Pilgrim proceeding (CLI-12-3, 75 NRC 132). Also, the Commission has applied the reopening provisions even earlier in a proceeding (
e.g.,
when a proceeding terminates once all contentions have been decided), such as in the Commission's 2012 decision in the North Anna proceeding (CLI-12-14, 75 NRC 692). Therefore, under existing precedent, the proceeding would terminate and the reopening provisions would apply in a situation when a presiding officer denies all hearing requests filed by the deadline in § 2.309(b) and there are no pending contentions in the proceeding.
The Commission has also recognized that if some issues are pending once the record closes, the record may remain open on those limited issues; an example is the Commission's decision in the Pilgrim proceeding (CLI-12-3, 75 NRC 132). This practice of keeping the record open for particular issues while closing the overall record for the proceeding has been supported in federal court in a 2013 decision in
Massachusetts
v.
NRC
(708 F.3d 63, footnote 18). Therefore, the new § 2.326(e)(1) also clarifies that if other contentions either remain pending or are subject to a motion for leave to file at the time the record closes, the record will remain open only with respect to the particular issues raised by those contentions. As a result, petitioners could continue to litigate live contentions filed prior to closure of the record under final § 2.326(e)(1) without having to meet the reopening standards. This would include (in certain narrow cases) filing proposed amendments of contentions on issues within the scope of the existing contention. For example, a petitioner may adjust an environmental contention filed on the application to address an NRC environmental document's discussion of the same particular issue, given that the NRC has the ultimate responsibility to comply with environmental laws and (when the NRC environmental document has been issued) the hearing on the issue would concern the adequacy of the NRC environmental document. Similarly, the reopening standards under final § 2.326(e)(1) would not apply to a contention of adequacy arising from new information mooting a contention of omission, where the contention of adequacy remains within the bounds of the bases set forth in support of the original contention. This aligns with well-established scope principles outlined in existing caselaw, such as the McGuire/Catawba proceeding (CLI-02-28, 56 NRC 373). However, reopening would apply to a new or amended contention filed after the record closure date under § 2.326(e)(1) that is not squarely within the confines of a live contention filed before that date (
e.g.,
if the pre-record-closure contention raised a particular environmental qualification concern for a component, a post-record-closure contention would have to meet the reopening standards if it raised a different type of environmental qualification concern for the component).
By providing the public with an opportunity to request a hearing prior to closing the record, this change comports with applicable Federal case law considering challenges to the NRC's reopening standards. In the 1984 decision
Deukmejian
v.
NRC
(751 F.2d 1287), the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit addressed a challenge to the NRC requiring an intervenor to meet the reopening standards to participate in a proceeding on a
full power
operating license in order to challenge an applicant's application to amend a
low power
license by extending the license term. The court determined the two actions were separate proceedings. By requiring the petitioner to meet the heightened pleading requirements in the reopening standard, the NRC improperly abridged the petitioner's hearing rights under section 189a. of the Atomic Energy Act. Thus, under
Deukmejian,
the NRC must provide petitioners with at least one opportunity to participate in an adjudication prior to closing the record. The revisions to § 2.326 meet this standard because they would not close the record until well after the opportunity to request a hearing expires.
Also, because the revisions to § 2.326 close the record in the specified circumstances, the NRC is revising §§ 2.104, 2.105, and 2.309(b)(5) to require
Federal Register
notices announcing opportunities to request hearings to state the Standard Hearing Completion Date for the proceeding. This will put the public on notice and provide additional clarity on record closure.
Further, to avoid any implication that final § 2.326(e)(1) overrides or otherwise annuls existing case law, the NRC is adding in response to comments a new § 2.326(e)(2) clarifying that, if the presiding officer enters an order closing the record following resolution of all live contentions in the proceeding, the record for the adjudicatory proceeding will close on the date specified in the order.
Finally, in addition to the adjustments described previously to address the scheduling directives of the ADVANCE Act and
E.O. 14300
, the agency is modifying the criteria included in § 2.326(a)(2) to state that a significant environmental issue under the National Environmental Policy Act can only be identified in a proceeding where a categorical exclusion listed in
10 CFR part 51
does not apply. The final rule language clarifies that categorical exclusions specifically pertain to the agency's obligations under the National Environmental Policy Act. In circumstances where a categorical
(
printed page 69458)
exclusion is used to comply with the National Environmental Policy Act, by definition, there are no significant environmental issues associated with the proposed Federal action under that statute. The agency considers this to be a clarity change responsive to the potential for increased use of categorical exclusions in future reviews. In another clarity change, the final rule specifically refers to categorical exclusions listed in
10 CFR part 51
because categorical exclusions in the regulations have issue preclusive effect in NRC proceedings.
Discovery
The NRC is making several changes to reduce burdens to the parties from their obligations to make certain disclosures after contentions are admitted in most licensing proceedings and is also expediting the production of initial disclosures to support the accelerated evidentiary hearing timeframes in subpart L of
10 CFR part 2
.
[
10
]
The NRC staff's hearing file obligations are being entirely eliminated by this rule. Experience shows the hearing file currently required by § 2.1203 is burdensome and provides little value to the litigation because it covers the entire application under review instead of focusing on the admitted contentions. Moreover, the hearing file was established before the NRC required electronic filing of applications, regularly posted the entirety of applications and related documents on its website, and developed robust search functions in public-facing ADAMS. To the extent members of the public face difficulties in searching ADAMS, NRC Public Document Room staff are available to assist during business hours. Thus, the rationale supporting the hearing file obligation has become outdated. While the NRC is eliminating the hearing file requirements in § 2.1203, it is retaining paragraph (d) of this section, which specifies that no additional forms of discovery are authorized beyond what is permitted by subpart C of
10 CFR part 2
.
In a change from the proposed rule, the NRC is retaining the NRC staff's § 2.336(b) disclosure obligations. While the staff's disclosures largely replicate the applicant's required disclosures or otherwise concern internal documents that are typically not produced to the other parties, there could be cases where the staff would disclose relevant information that would not otherwise be produced.
To effectuate the elimination of the hearing file requirement, the NRC is changing the scope of case-specific orders issued under § 2.307(c) for access to sensitive unclassified information. Under existing Commission precedent, these orders no longer apply to a petitioner if its hearing request is granted, as discussed in a 2010 decision in the South Texas Project combined license proceeding (CLI-10-24; 72 NRC 451, 461-63). That precedent, however, was issued when regulations required the NRC staff to disclose documents unrelated to the admitted contentions. Since the NRC staff would no longer produce a hearing file under § 2.1203, a change is needed so that a petitioner who is admitted as a party could continue to make requests for access under the § 2.307(c) access order on matters outside the scope of disclosures under § 2.336. The NRC intends to revise its templates for § 2.307(c) access orders to reflect this change; no change to the regulations is needed for this purpose.
The NRC is modifying the § 2.336(b) disclosures obligation in proceedings on denials of applications. In these types of proceedings, the staff is required to be a party and is in opposition to the applicant. The NRC is modifying § 2.336(b) to tailor the required document disclosures to the circumstances associated with a proceeding on a denial of an application (
e.g.,
the document categories associated with the application and NRC correspondence with the applicant would not apply because the applicant already would be in possession of this material). Finally, the NRC is making conforming changes to § 2.336(a) to reflect applicant disclosures in a proceeding on a denial of an application.
Second, the NRC is further modifying § 2.336 to reduce the burdens of other participants. Parties commonly agree to exclude from disclosures non-public draft documents that have not been circulated among the parties; the NRC is codifying this practice in the NRC's regulations in new subparagraphs (a)(4) and (b)(2). Moreover, in response to comments, the NRC is adding new subparagraphs (a)(5) and (b)(3) to exclude internal instant messages, text messages, and voice messages from mandatory disclosure absent a showing of exceptional circumstances. This exclusion only applies to communications that are internal to a party, its litigation team, and its contractors; if a single external person or entity is included in a communication, the communication would not be subject to this exclusion. These internal communications are generally high-volume, but low-value, and similar to non-public drafts that reveal a party's internal thinking. Generally, NRC licensing proceedings involve admitted contentions from qualified intervenors and focus on the technical conclusions on safety and environmental issues and how they are supported,
[
11
]
rather than on intent or motive that could be revealed through a party's internal thinking. Therefore, the NRC finds it appropriate to focus disclosures on technical documents that will reach the ultimate issues in dispute. However, to avoid inadvertently excluding relevant technical documents merely because they are attached to an excluded internal communication, the NRC is not excluding any documents attached to those excluded internal communications. These attachments would need to be included within the scope of mandatory disclosures if they are relevant to the admitted contentions. Also, in exceptional circumstances, such as when an admitted contention or license denial proceeding relates to a party's intent or motive and these types of internal communications would be relevant to the specific issue in the proceeding, the presiding officer may require that these communications be included.
Under existing rules, the duty to update disclosures relevant to an admitted contention ends when the presiding officer issues a decision resolving the contention. In this final rule, the NRC is also providing that the duty to update ends upon the initiation of the evidentiary hearing phase for the contention as delineated in an order from the presiding officer. This change serves to avoid requiring updates during the evidentiary hearing phase, as the relevant documents should have been disclosed by this point, and the evidentiary hearing is the most resource-intensive phase of the process.
[
12
]
Notably, this does not relieve
(
printed page 69459)
litigants from their ongoing general obligation to keep the presiding officer and litigants informed of relevant new developments in a proceeding, as the Commission emphasized in its 2006 decision in the USEC proceeding (CLI-06-10, 63 NRC 451).
Finally, the NRC is revising § 2.336(a) and (b) for added clarity and to require parties to produce their initial disclosures within 20 days of a presiding officer order admitting contested issues into the proceeding when the proceeding is immediately moving to the evidentiary hearing phase under § 2.332(d), while continuing to allow a 30-day period if the proceeding is not immediately moving to the evidentiary hearing phase or for an order granting a demand for hearing upon a denial of an application. Twenty days should be sufficient for diligent litigants to prepare their § 2.336 disclosures given the reduced scope of disclosures and modern discovery and file management tools, including artificial intelligence. Also, an accelerated initial disclosures schedule is necessary to support the expedited evidentiary hearing timeframes that are in the revised subpart L of
10 CFR part 2
when the proceeding is continuing to the evidentiary hearing phase immediately. In proceedings that are not moving immediately to the evidentiary hearing phase,
i.e.,
when the expedited discovery schedule is not needed, the extra 10 days will allow parties additional time to meet their disclosure obligations.
The 20 or 30 days would generally run from the date of an order admitting contentions to account for new or amended contentions that might be admitted after the § 2.309(b) initial filing deadline for contentions. However, in a proceeding on a denial of an application, the 30-day period would run from the order granting a demand for hearing.
Conforming Changes to Scheduling Regulations
To accommodate the shorter timeframes for completing adjudications contemplated by this final rule, the NRC is making a number of conforming amendments to other sections in
10 CFR part 2
, which pertain to scheduling. Specifically, the NRC is revising paragraph (b) in § 2.312, “Notice of hearing,” to reflect the Commission's expectation that considerations informing the selection of a time and place for a hearing should not override the overall timeframes established for timely adjudications by this rule or by any proceeding-specific Commission order. To provide additional flexibilities that may facilitate meeting those timeframes, the NRC is also revising § 2.329, “Prehearing conference,” to give the presiding officer or Commission discretion on whether to hold a prehearing conference.
Next, the NRC is making a number of edits to § 2.332, “General case scheduling and management,” to conform to the streamlined procedures and shortened timeframes elsewhere in this rule. Because the timeframes in this rule are mandatory, the NRC is revising paragraph (a) to reflect the presiding officer's obligation to develop a schedule that would meet the licensing timeframes in this rule. Likewise, the NRC is amending paragraph (d) to conform to the Commission's expectations that hearings under subpart L of
10 CFR part 2
would ordinarily begin once the presiding officer admits contentions, not when the staff issues its review documents. Specifically, the presiding officer would immediately proceed to an evidentiary hearing after the admission of a contention unless either (i) the NRC staff or applicant intend to seek dismissal or summary disposition of the admitted contention or (ii) the NRC staff decides to participate as a party but is not yet able to take final positions on the matters in controversy. Section 2.332(d) includes notification requirements to effectuate this provision—the proposed rule required these notifications within seven days of admission of the contention, but to avoid unnecessary delay, this final rule requires the notifications to be filed as soon as possible and no later than seven days after admission of the contention. The commencement of the evidentiary hearing phase would be delayed in cases where the NRC staff or applicant seek to resolve a contention through a motion to dismiss or a motion for summary disposition because the process for seeking dismissal or summary disposition is quicker and less resource-intensive than an evidentiary hearing; thus, the dismissal or summary disposition process may be a more efficient way of resolving a contention if the presiding officer decides that the standards for dismissing the contention are satisfied.
[
13
]
The other reason for delaying the commencement of the evidentiary hearing—when the NRC staff seeks to participate as a party but is not able to take a final position on the matters in controversy—reflects the special role the NRC staff has in the licensing process and the Commission's desire to ensure that the presiding officer is aware of the NRC staff's considered position on the contested issues in those cases where the staff chooses to participate as a party. The NRC staff may not always be in the position (particularly early in its review of an application-specific or first-of-a-kind issue) to take a final position on the matters in controversy (
e.g.,
the NRC staff is seeking further information from the applicant or further considering information already provided). In this regard, the NRC staff is in a different position from the petitioner (who formulated and supported the proposed contention and should be in a position to commence the evidentiary hearing upon admission of the contention) and the applicant (who developed the application and should have the wherewithal to promptly address challenges to it). In the interest of prompt adjudication, revised § 2.332(d) further requires the NRC staff, in cases where it decides to participate as a party but is not yet able to take a final position on the admitted contention, to prioritize its resources to put itself in a position to provide testimony on the contention at the earliest practicable time and notify the presiding officer and the other parties when the staff is ready to do so.
Because the evidentiary hearing phase would, with certain exceptions, immediately commence after admission of a contention, litigants should ensure they are prepared to move immediately to an evidentiary hearing posture if a proposed contention is admitted. Thus, the NRC expects that litigants will consider their potential strategies and resource needs to litigate contentions at an evidentiary hearing before a presiding officer issues its decision on contention admissibility.
Section 2.332(d) is further revised to require the presiding officer, to the greatest extent practicable, to establish a schedule that will not extend past the
(
printed page 69460)
NRC staff's scheduled date for completing its review of the particular application. This provision has the purpose of ensuring timely NRC decision-making when it is practicable to do so and is intended to address both individual NRC reviews that are on a more expedited review schedule as well as the resolution of admitted contentions submitted later during an NRC review. In establishing a schedule under this provision, the presiding officer must ensure, as stated later in this rule, that the process still supports accurate decision-making and the development of a sound record, while giving parties a fair and equal opportunity to make their cases.
As a conforming change, the NRC is revising § 51.104(a) to remove the prohibition, in proceedings where a final environmental impact statement (EIS) has been prepared in connection with a proposed action, on the NRC staff either presenting a position on matters within the scope of the National Environmental Policy Act or offering the final EIS into evidence until the final EIS is made available. There is no statutory basis for this prohibition. Also, delaying the commencement of evidentiary hearings on environmental contentions until a final EIS has been completed, which might occur near the end of the NRC's review period, does not support the timeliness and efficiency goals of the ADVANCE Act and
E.O. 14300
. With the removal of this prohibition, the operative provisions of § 51.104(a) and (b) would be essentially identical, so the NRC is further consolidating § 51.104(a) and (b) into § 51.104(a) and removing and reserving § 51.104(b).
In another conforming change, the NRC is revising § 2.332(b) to reflect that only enforcement proceedings, not licensing proceedings, would be subject to the model milestones in appendix B to 10 CFR part 2. As discussed later, strict deadlines would be imposed in licensing proceedings rather than model milestones.
Finally, the NRC is amending § 2.334, “Implementing hearing schedule for proceeding,” by clarifying paragraph (a) to directly state the presiding officer's obligation to take necessary measures to ensure timely adjudication, by revising paragraph (b) to incorporate the standard in § 2.307(a) for extending a schedule and to incorporate an “extraordinary circumstances” standard for extending the deadline for completing an evidentiary hearing under subpart L of part 2, and by revising paragraph (c) to require the presiding officer to notify the Commission of any delays beyond the timeframes established by this rule.

10 CFR Part 2
and Conforming Changes Elsewhere in Part 2
As explained previously, the NRC is making a number of significant changes to subpart L of
10 CFR part 2
to streamline and accelerate the hearing process for proceedings for the grant, renewal, licensee-initiated amendment, termination, or transfer of licenses or permits subject to
10 CFR parts 30
,
32
through
36
,
39
,
40
,
50
,
52
,
53
,
54
,
55
,
61
,
70
and
72
. The two most significant changes are (1) to establish strict deadlines for the issuance of initial decisions in most licensing proceedings and (2) to provide greater flexibility to the presiding officer to decide which components of the subpart L hearing process are needed to support the presiding officer's decision-making. The NRC is also making other changes to streamline proceedings and ensure prompt and accurate decision-making, as discussed in the following paragraphs.
The NRC is establishing strict deadlines for the issuance of an initial decision to ensure that adjudicatory proceedings are promptly conducted to support the efficiency goals of the ADVANCE Act and
E.O. 14300
. These deadlines are tailored to different types of proceedings to account for the varying complexity of different license applications as well as the greater need for expedited decision-making in certain proceedings (
e.g.,
in Expedited Proceedings). These deadlines may only be extended if extraordinary circumstances necessitate a delay.
The NRC is also providing presiding officers greater flexibility in structuring the subpart L of
10 CFR part 2
evidentiary hearing phase because admitted contentions could take a wide variety of forms, and the presiding officer in an individual proceeding is better placed to decide what information is needed for the admitted contentions before it to support accurate decision-making and the development of a sound record, while ensuring that the parties are given a fair and equal opportunity to make their cases (
e.g.,
if one party may file written testimony and a position statement, all other parties would have the same opportunity). The presiding officer would also tailor the hearing schedule to the particular circumstances of a proceeding while complying with requirements for decision-making deadlines.
The specific changes to subpart L of
10 CFR part 2
and conforming changes elsewhere in this part are detailed in the following subsections for clarity and completeness.
A. Changes to Scope Provisions in § 2.1200
The NRC is revising § 2.1200 to reflect the modified scope of subpart L of
10 CFR part 2
, as discussed previously in the context of changes to §§ 2.310 and 2.700. As stated before, license transfer proceedings will now be conducted under subpart L, as well as contested proceedings on the grant of licenses to construct and operate uranium enrichment facilities. The NRC is also clarifying § 2.1200 to reflect the existing provision in § 2.310(b) providing that enforcement proceedings may be held under subpart L if all parties agree.
B. Changes to § 2.1202 Regarding the NRC Staff's Authority and Role
The NRC is making several modifications to the provisions in § 2.1202 regarding the NRC staff's authority to take licensing actions and its role in the adjudicatory proceeding. First, the NRC is modifying provisions on the issuance and effectiveness of licensing decisions during the pendency of a hearing. Currently, § 2.1202(a) provides that the NRC staff is expected to promptly issue its approval or denial of the application, or take other appropriate action on the underlying regulatory matter for which a hearing was provided, and that the NRC staff's action is effective upon issuance except for several listed licensing actions. The NRC is revising the list of exceptions in § 2.1202(a) as follows:
Currently, the listed exceptions include all applications to construct and/or operate a production or utilization facility (including limited work authorizations and combined licenses). However, the pre-effectiveness hearing requirements in AEA section 189a. apply to production and utilization facilities licensed under AEA sections 103 and 104b. (corresponding to facilities under §§ 50.21(b) and 50.22 and
10 CFR part 53
) or testing facilities licensed under AEA section104c. (corresponding to a facility under § 50.21(c) that meets the definition of “testing facility” in § 50.2). The AEA's pre-effectiveness hearing requirements do not apply to production and utilization facilities licensed under AEA section104a. (
i.e.,
medical therapy facilities under § 50.21(a)) or to production and utilization facilities licensed under AEA section 104c. that are not testing facilities (
i.e.,
non-testing facilities under § 50.21(c)). The NRC is revising § 2.1202(a)(1) to reflect the scope of the AEA's pre-effectiveness
(
printed page 69461)
hearing requirements and in recognition of the lower safety significance of medical therapy facilities under § 50.21(a) and non-testing facilities under § 50.21(c).
The NRC is revising § 2.1202(a)(3) to remove the existing exception for
10 CFR part 52
or
53
manufacturing licenses and put in its place an exception for licenses to construct and operate uranium enrichment facilities. In the 2007 rule adding the exception for manufacturing licenses (
72 FR 49352
, page 49420, August 28, 2007), the Commission acknowledged that there is no statutory requirement for including an exception for manufacturing licenses, but stated, “Nonetheless, as a matter of discretion, the NRC has decided to treat manufacturing licenses similar to construction permits in this regard, although the NRC reserves the right to change its practice in the future.” The NRC is removing the exception for manufacturing licenses because such licenses are not subject to the AEA's pre-effectiveness hearing requirements, a manufacturing license authorizes only the manufacture (not operation) of a facility, and vendors may fabricate major portions of a facility without a manufacturing license so long as those portions do not constitute a production or utilization facility. In these circumstances, there is no substantial reason to delay the issuance and effectiveness of a manufacturing license because of a pending hearing on the license application. The NRC is including an exception for applications for licenses to construct and operate uranium enrichment facilities. Such applications are currently subject to hearings under subpart G of
10 CFR part 2
, but the NRC will now conduct contested hearings on these applications under subpart L of

. As stated previously, licenses to construct and operate uranium enrichment facilities are subject to a statutory pre-effectiveness hearing requirement, so it is appropriate to include them in the list of exceptions in § 2.1202(a).
The NRC is also modifying § 2.1202(b), regarding the role of the NRC staff in the hearing process, to accelerate the time in which the NRC staff is required to notify the presiding officer and the other parties of whether it will participate as a party in the proceeding, consistent with changes being made to § 2.332(d).
C. Changes to § 2.1203 Regarding Elimination of Hearing File
As discussed previously, the NRC is eliminating the hearing file requirements in paragraphs (a) to (c) of § 2.1203, while retaining the prohibition on additional discovery currently in paragraph (d) of § 2.1203.
D. Changes to § 2.1205 Regarding Summary Disposition
The NRC is making several changes regarding the schedule for summary disposition motions. First, to avoid unduly burdening parties as they undertake evidentiary hearing activities, the NRC is modifying § 2.1205(a) so that summary disposition motions are not permitted later than 30 days before the scheduled date for filing initial written testimony, absent permission from the Commission or presiding officer. Summary disposition may be a useful tool to avoid the resource expenditures associated with an evidentiary hearing, but after evidentiary hearing activities are underway, the filing of summary disposition motions risks distracting parties from their hearing preparations and burdening them unnecessarily.
Second, consistent with other changes in this final rule, the NRC is reducing the time for filing answers to summary disposition motions from 20 days to 15 days after service of the motion. The NRC also is providing a 20-day period from the filing of answers for a decision on the motion. Fifteen days should be sufficient for parties to address the pertinent standards for summary disposition motions, and a 20-day period for decisions is consistent with the overall hearing schedule and other timeframes for decisions in this final rule.
E. Changes to § 2.1206 to § 2.1210 Regarding the Hearing Process and Schedule
Currently, § 2.1206 to § 2.1210 provide the principal requirements for the subpart L evidentiary hearing process and schedule, including prescriptive requirements for which written filings are permitted and when, and whether an oral hearing must be held. For the reasons discussed earlier, the NRC is replacing these detailed requirements with simpler, more flexible, and more informal provisions for most proceedings. However, as reflected in an amended § 2.1206(a)(2), a hearing in a proceeding expressly required by the AEA to be determined on the record after opportunity for an agency hearing (
i.e.,
