Under revised § 2.1206(a), the presiding officer would issue a scheduling order that would include the presiding officer's determinations on which written filings are permitted, the schedule for these filings, whether to hold an oral hearing, and the schedule for issuing an initial decision. Motions for cross-examination under § 2.1204 would be permitted (consistent with the existing regulations). Otherwise, the presiding officer would largely have flexibility to decide which written filings the parties would be permitted to make to provide the information necessary to support the presiding officer's decision. These potential written filings, which are listed in § 2.1206(b)(1), are (1) initial testimony, position statements, and supporting exhibits; (2) rebuttal testimony, position statements, and supporting exhibits; (3) motions in limine and motions to strike; (4) written briefing and/or written responses to questions from the presiding officer; (5) proposed questions for the presiding officer to ask the witnesses; and (6) proposed findings of fact and conclusions of law. 10 CFR part 2

Similarly, the presiding officer would generally have flexibility to determine whether an oral hearing is needed to support the presiding officer's decision—currently, an oral hearing is required unless all parties agree to a hearing based solely on written presentations, but the NRC sees no need to require that an oral hearing be held as a default matter in all proceedings.
The initial decision is the culmination of the evidentiary hearing process, and the NRC is requiring that the scheduling order include the schedule for an initial decision, which must comply with the requirements of §§ 2.332 and (if applicable) 2.1207. Section 2.1206(b)(2) also provides that if statements of position and proposed findings of fact and conclusions of law are both permitted, parties would be allowed to file statements of position in the form of proposed findings and conclusions to facilitate the prompt preparation of proposed findings and conclusions after the hearing. Appeals
As discussed previously, in this final rule, the appeals process occurs outside of the scope of the fixed deadlines outlined in section 5(a) of
E.O. 14300
because the appeals process does not itself delay the issuance or effectiveness of a license. Nonetheless, the NRC is promulgating broad changes to its contested hearing process, including revisions associated with appeals, in response to the ADVANCE Act and the general direction to streamline the public hearings process in section 5(j) of E.O.14300. To streamline the overall process, the changes to the appeals process primarily implement shortened timelines. Further, simple structural changes were made in § 2.311 to streamline the requirements and add clarity. These changes involve consolidation of the requirements in the section into paragraph (a),
Types of appeals covered under this section;
paragraph (b),
Timing of appeals and associated filings under this section;
and paragraph (c),
Scope of appeals under this section.
These structural changes primarily involve consolidating existing § 2.311(d) into § 2.311(c) and consolidating existing § 2.311(e) into § 2.311(a), (b), and (c). The following paragraphs discuss the NRC's streamlining of the appeals process.
Specifically, the agency is amending § 2.341(b)(1) to reduce the time for filing a petition for review of an agency decision with the Commission from 25 days to within 20 days after service of a full or partial initial decision by a presiding officer, and within 20 days after service of any other decision or action by a presiding officer with respect to which a petition for review is authorized. Sections 2.311 and 2.341(b)(3) are amended to allow any other party to the proceeding to file an answer supporting or opposing Commission review within 20 days after service of a petition for review and reduce the period of time the petitioning party has to file a 5-page reply brief from 10 days to 7 days. In response to public comments, the page limit count for answers to appeals in § 2.341(b)(3) is adjusted from 25 pages to 30 pages. This adjustment matches the page limit count allowed for petitions for review, promoting equity and consistency in the regulations. The modest reductions in filing times described previously are in keeping with the ADVANCE Act and the direction of
E.O. 14300
to streamline processes. For interlocutory appeals under § 2.311(a)(1)-(3), the agency is limiting the time for filing the appeal or petition from 25 days to 20 days, consistent with the other appeals.
For interlocutory appeals under § 2.311(a)(1)-(3) and petitions for interlocutory review under § 2.341(f)(2), the agency makes no procedural distinction between them and other appeals because, in many cases, the complexity of an interlocutory appeal is similar to other appeals. Also, this final rule modifies § 2.311 to add a reply brief opportunity for interlocutory appeals under § 2.311(a)(1)-(3).
The agency is modifying § 2.311(b)(2), which addresses interlocutory appeals of an order under § 2.310 selecting hearing procedures, to require the moving party to file an appeal with the Commission no later than seven days after the order—this should be sufficient time to address the comparatively simple matter of selection of hearing procedures. The NRC similarly allots seven days after service of the appeal for any party to file a brief in opposition. The regulatory language further clarifies that a reply brief in response to a brief in opposition is not permitted.
The proposed rule had proposed changes to § 2.311 to address interlocutory appeals of decisions on contentions submitted by the deadline in § 2.309(b) but separately from the hearing request to account for the proposed rule's bifurcation of standing and contention admissibility. Since the final rule does not adopt the proposed rule's bifurcation scheme, these changes have not been included in the final rule.
Referred Rulings and Certified Questions
In cases where the presiding officer identifies significant and novel legal or policy issues, or where prompt decision by the Commission is necessary to materially advance the orderly disposition of the proceeding, the presiding officer has the discretion to refer its ruling to the Commission or certify a question to the Commission for disposition. To ensure efficiency in this process, the agency is including language in § 2.323(f)(1) clarifying that where practicable, the presiding officer should first rule on the matter in question and then seek Commission input in the form of a referred ruling, rather than certify a question to the Commission without issuing a ruling. This change aims to minimize delays in the proceeding during the pendency of the Commission's review. Section 2.323(g) is adapted to clarify that unless otherwise ordered, the referral of a ruling to the Commission does not stay the proceeding or extend the time for performance of any act.

To shorten the process for motions for reconsideration in keeping with the streamlining and burden reduction efforts of the ADVANCE Act and
E.O. 14300

This change is accompanied by a conforming change to § 2.323(a)(2) clarifying that motions for reconsideration are not subject to the general 10-day timeline for motions. Further changes are also carried forward in § 2.345(a)(1) to reflect a seven-day deadline for filing a petition for reconsideration and a seven-day answer period. Similarly, changes to § 2.341(d) reduce the filing timeline for petitions for reconsideration before the Commission to seven days, with a seven-day answer period.
(

The agency anticipates these changes will provide clarity for the parties and serve overall efficiency efforts. Also, seven-day filing periods should be sufficient because reconsideration is only warranted when the existing regulatory standard of compelling circumstances applies, such as in cases of a clear, material error that could not be reasonably anticipated.
Stays of Decisions and Application for a Stay
Consistent with the streamlining efforts throughout
10 CFR part 2
, the NRC is changing the § 2.342(a) timeline for an application for a stay of the effectiveness of the decision or action pending filing of and a decision on a petition for review; the NRC is reducing the filing deadline from 10 days after service of a decision or action of a presiding officer to 7 days. This change is paired with a revision to § 2.342(d) to clarify that the period for any party to file an answer supporting or opposing the granting of a stay is seven days after service of an application for a stay.
Under existing § 2.1213, any application for a stay of the effectiveness of the NRC staff's action on a matter involved in a hearing must be filed with the presiding officer within seven days of the issuance of the notice of the NRC staff's action under § 2.1202(a). While the agency is not altering this timeline, the agency is reducing the corresponding timeline in § 2.1213(c) for any party or the NRC staff to file an answer supporting or opposing the granting of a stay from 10 days to 7 days after service of an application for a stay of the NRC staff's action.
These modest timeline reductions should not significantly impact the burden on the parties to address the limited requirements and capped length of stay applications and associated answers. Further, these timeline changes are consistent with changes in this rule for similar filings while advancing the directives of the ADVANCE Act and
E.O. 14300
.
Further, in response to a public comment on the proposed rule, the NRC is amending § 2.1213(a) to clarify that the Commission will make decisions on applications to stay the effectiveness of an NRC staff order in a license transfer proceeding. Rulings on such applications require speed and stability, which may be more readily afforded if the Commission maintains its authority for deciding stay applications during license transfer proceedings.
Delivery of Hard Copy Documents
Under existing § 2.302, litigants must generally utilize the NRC's electronic filing system unless they (1) obtain an exemption from that requirement by demonstrating good cause to use a nonelectronic means of transmission for electronic documents on optical storage media or to file paper documents, or else (2) file without an exemption a document containing electronic portions that may not be transmitted via the E-Filing system for reasons of security or electronic format. In recent years these circumstances have been rare, and the NRC anticipates they will arise even less frequently going forward. When an alternative to electronic transmission is used, however, § 2.306 automatically extends the timeframes in
10 CFR part 2
to account for the additional time it will take for nonelectronic transmission of the document. Collectively, these extensions could considerably delay a proceeding. Therefore, the NRC is amending § 2.306(b) to direct the presiding officer to establish whether, and how long, the timeframes in
10 CFR part 2
should be extended in cases when nonelectronic transmission is allowed. Prior to this presiding officer order, the NRC is retaining the existing extensions of time in § 2.306. In considering the need to extend the timeframes to account for nonelectronic service of documents, the presiding officer should ensure that the extensions will not cumulatively challenge timely completion of the adjudication.

VII. Regulatory Analysis
The NRC has prepared a final regulatory analysis for this rule in accordance with Office of Management and Budget (OMB) Circular A-4. The analysis examines the costs and benefits of the alternatives considered by the NRC. The NRC has determined that the actions in this rule are expected to reduce regulatory burden and generate cost savings for both the government and hearing participants by streamlining contested hearing proceedings.
As part of the proposed rule, the NRC requested public comment on the draft regulatory analysis, and a few comments were received that were relevant to the regulatory analysis. In response to these comments, the NRC added clarifying text to describe the qualitative assessment of certain impacts. Also, the NRC revised the regulatory analysis to reflect changes made from the proposed
(
printed page 69469)
rule to the final rule in response to other comments (
e.g.,
changes eliminating proposed § 2.309(k) and the proposed bifurcation of standing and contention admissibility, changes to exclude certain internal communications from mandatory disclosures). In addition to these comment-related updates, the NRC made an update to the wage rates from 2024 to 2025, the most recent year for which data were available. Taken together, these updates result in revised impact estimates. The final regulatory analysis is detailed in the following paragraphs.
This analysis uses current contested hearing procedures for licensing proceedings under
10 CFR part 2
as the baseline and evaluates the changes in this rule as the regulatory alternative and estimates the final rule's costs and cost savings for the first five years of implementation of the rule.
[
21
]
The final rule addresses many different types of applications, from applications to construct or operate reactors, to applications to construct or operate significant materials facilities, to applications for license renewals, amendments, and transfers, as well as applications associated with the proposed restart of reactors in decommissioning. Past experience suggests that, depending on the type of application, there is a greater or lesser probability that a hearing request will be filed or that a hearing request, if granted, will proceed to an evidentiary hearing. For example, previous
10 CFR part 52
early site permit and combined license applications for large reactors were nearly always the subject of a hearing request, while reactor license amendment applications are rarely challenged. Power reactor license renewal applications are often contested. Regarding the likelihood that an evidentiary hearing will be held, of the eight combined license applications for large reactors that were granted, an evidentiary hearing was held on four of these applications. There is a lower rate of holding evidentiary hearings for early site permit and reactor license renewal applications, but contested uranium recovery applications have led to a number of evidentiary hearings in the past 10 years. Past experience is to some degree informative, but any effort to extrapolate from this experience will be subject to substantial uncertainty. In addition, there is uncertainty in predicting how many applications of various types will be submitted or how many will be challenged.
Recognizing this uncertainty, the NRC has attempted to develop numerical estimates for this regulatory analysis. The NRC expects an increase in the number of applications that are the subject of a hearing request because of an expected increase in the number of new reactor applications, up to nine applications per year for the next five years based on pre-application engagements. In addition, 20 power reactor license renewal applications are expected between 2026-2030.
[
22
]
Based on this information, the NRC has developed a rough estimate that 15 license proceedings per year will be the subject of a hearing request over the next five years. Based on data from the last 20 years, hearing requests have been granted in 60 percent of the proceedings in which they have been filed, so the NRC estimates that hearing requests will be granted in 9 of these 15 proceedings. Based, in part, on the number of new reactor applications expected and the relative frequency of evidentiary hearings for such applications, the NRC estimates that about 33 percent of the proceedings will lead to an evidentiary hearing (5 evidentiary hearings on average per 15 proceedings with hearing requests).
Resource Projections for Next Five Years Based on Existing Requirements
Combining the previous estimated probabilities for the granting of hearing requests and holding of evidentiary hearings, with the available, albeit limited, internal data on resources expended on NRC hearings, the NRC anticipates that, on average, the NRC staff participating as a party in a contested proceeding would expend 4,150 hours per proceeding on average under the existing requirements—this average accounts for proceedings where hearing requests are denied, those that proceed to an evidentiary hearing, and those where hearing requests are granted but do not proceed to an evidentiary hearing because the admitted contentions are resolved prior to hearing.
The NRC does not possess data on applicant resource expenditures in contested hearings, but the NRC expects an applicant's resources (in terms of hours) to generally be similar to the NRC staff's under the existing rules because the applicant and NRC staff use similar personnel to accomplish similar tasks (answering hearing requests, developing § 2.336 document disclosures, writing testimony, etc.). However, an applicant is not subject to a hearing file requirement like the staff is. Therefore, the NRC projects that applicant resources under existing requirements are 3,925 hours per proceeding in which a hearing request is filed, a bit less than the NRC staff.
The NRC also does not possess data on petitioner resource expenditures in contested hearings. Petitioners vary widely in terms of their level of resources and how many contested issues they raise, but the NRC roughly estimates that, on average, a petitioner would expend about half the applicant's resources (1,975 hours) in a proceeding in which a hearing request is filed.
The NRC would also expend resources for presiding officers to conduct adjudicatory proceedings, where the presiding officer would be a three-member Licensing Board with support staff. In addition, the Office of Commission Appellate Adjudication would draft opinions for Commission consideration that address appeals of presiding officer decisions. In the absence of informative internal data, the NRC estimates (with substantial uncertainty) that there would be 4,700 hours of total NRC adjudicatory decision-making staff resources expended per proceeding in which a hearing request is submitted. This estimate is based on timeframes for adjudicatory decision-making under the existing rules and the following additional assumptions:
As stated above, the NRC assumes that evidentiary hearings are held in 33 percent of the proceedings in which a hearing request is filed.
There would likely be one or more rounds of new or amended contentions submitted after a hearing request is filed.
Presiding officer decisions on an initial hearing request and presiding officer decisions after an evidentiary hearing would likely be appealed, and there may be other petitions for review submitted during a proceeding.
Given the higher volume of applications expected in the next five years, there would likely be overlap in Licensing Board member service for different proceedings given the longer timeframes in the existing process (
i.e.,
(
printed page 69470)
over these longer timeframes, a member of one Licensing Board in active litigation would likely serve on multiple other Licensing Boards in active litigation).
Resource Projections for Next Five Years Based on the Final Rule
The final rule makes a number of changes that affect the resources of litigants:
For the initial filings (hearing requests/contentions, answers, and replies), the final rule accelerates the schedule for filings and decisions thereon, which could save a modest amount of resources. However, participants might compensate for this to some degree by concentrating their resources during the shorter filing and decision periods.
The final rule saves substantial resources during the intermediate phase, between admission of contentions and the evidentiary hearing. Currently, evidentiary hearings are not held until the staff completes its review. This has led to lengthy intermediate periods where parties periodically update their document disclosures (and for the staff, the hearing file) and engage in other litigation activities. The NRC staff will no longer have to produce a hearing file, and the much shorter intermediate period would limit the disclosure burdens of the other parties, as well as limit burdens from other litigation activities during the intermediate period. Further, this final rule excludes some high-volume, low value internal electronic communications from disclosure, which should alleviate burdens on parties making document disclosures.
The final rule will also save substantial resources during the evidentiary hearing phase. The existing model milestones in subpart L of
10 CFR part 2
envision an evidentiary hearing phase of about nine months from a triggering event to an initial decision, and in practice the evidentiary hearing phase has on average taken substantially longer than this. Under the final rule, the evidentiary hearing phase will generally be limited to between 2 to 4.5 months, with 3.5 to 4.5 months being the set period for most proceedings. Also, the schedule could only be extended if extraordinary circumstances necessitate a delay. A much shorter evidentiary hearing phase will inherently limit the number of filings and other litigation activities and otherwise limit the resources that can be expended. Nonetheless, these resource savings would only accrue if an evidentiary hearing is held.
Considering these factors together, the NRC estimates that the NRC staff's resource burdens will drop from 4,150 hours to 3,025 hours per proceeding in which a hearing request is filed. Applicants are expected to see a drop in resource burden from 3,925 hours per contested proceeding to 3,025 hours. The NRC staff will see a larger resource savings than the applicant because of the elimination of the staff's hearing file obligations. Finally, the NRC estimates a modest drop in petitioner resource expenditures from 1,975 hours per contested proceeding to about 1,525 hours (about half of the applicant's resource expenditures).
In this final rule, the NRC estimates a greater per-proceeding resources savings for litigants than it estimated in the proposed rule. This difference generally results from two changes from the proposed to final rule. First, in most licensing proceedings, the proposed rule would have required litigants to provide more information on the merits of proposed contentions in their initial filings, which would have increased resource burdens somewhat at the initial filing stage. Accelerating the resolution of contested issues by including more information on the merits in initial filings was intended to bring about a compensating burden reduction for those contentions that are admitted, but this reduction would have been limited to contentions that were admitted and proceeded to an evidentiary hearing (whereas most proposed contentions are not admitted and some admitted contentions are resolved before an evidentiary hearing is held). In total, the proposed rule provision was expected to increase resource burdens on participants to save some time in the overall schedule—this proposal has not been adopted in this final rule. Second, the proposed rule would have accelerated filings and decisions on standing to save some litigant resources associated with the filing of contentions in circumstances where standing is not demonstrated. Estimated resource savings here would have been limited because presiding officers usually find that petitioners demonstrate standing, and a substantial amount of litigant resources would have been expended on litigation of contentions by the time a decision on standing would have been issued. However, the proposal to accelerate the consideration of standing has been eliminated in this final rule for reasons discussed in this notice and in response to comments. Ultimately, eliminating both of these proposed rule provisions results in a modest resource savings for litigants in comparison to the proposed rule.
For NRC adjudicatory decision-making staff, the NRC estimates that the resource burdens in proceedings where a hearing request is filed will drop from 4,700 hours per proceeding to 3,900 hours per proceeding. This estimated resource savings accounts for the following factors:
Significantly reduced periods for presiding officer decision-making limit the resources that would be employed. For example, currently, there is about a 3.5-month period, on average, between submission of a contention and a ruling thereon. However, under the new final rule, this period is reduced to about 1.5 to 2.5 months. In addition, as stated above, evidentiary hearings take 9 months or longer under existing regulations, while most evidentiary hearings under the new final rule will take about 3.5 to 4.5 months total.
However, savings from the reduced time periods will be limited by the following factors: (1) presiding officers might compensate for shorter periods to some degree by concentrating their resources during the shorter decision periods, (2) there will less likely be overlap in time spent by Licensing Board members on multiple proceedings in active litigation at the same time because the litigation period for each proceeding will be shorter, leading to less overlap in active litigation, and (3) evidentiary hearings are expected in only 33 percent of proceedings in which a hearing request is submitted, thereby diluting the average savings from a shorter evidentiary hearing period in the per-proceeding average.
In this final rule, the NRC estimates a smaller per-proceeding resources savings for NRC adjudicatory decision-making staff than it estimated in the proposed rule. That is because the final rule does not include the proposed rule's provision on accelerating the consideration of standing, which was assumed to save some resources for adjudicatory decision-making staff on contentions in those cases where the presiding officer concluded that standing was not demonstrated, and because the final rule does not include milestones for Commission decisions on appeal, which was assumed to save resources through reduced periods for adjudicatory decision making.
It is difficult to make accurate predictions regarding these factors, so the estimate of resource savings under the new requirements is subject to uncertainty.
(

Monetized Projections for Next Five Years Based on Existing and New Requirements
Building on the time-resources analysis discussed above, the NRC monetizes the time spent by the government staff, applicants, and petitioners on proceedings by applying fully loaded hourly wage rates.
For the government staff, the NRC uses its own internal labor rate of $164 per hour.
[
23
]
For the applicants, who typically include utilities or corporate entities seeking licenses or related proceedings, the NRC bases the hourly rates on two data sources. For outside legal services, the NRC used the Fitzpatrick Matrix, which serves as a proxy for market rates for attorneys and paralegals doing complex federal litigation in the Washington, DC, area.
[
24
]
Since hearing proceedings will involve the use of outside legal counsel, the Fitzpatrick Matrix is used to estimate the hourly cost of attorney and paralegal time. For 2025, the hourly rates for attorneys of varying experience levels ranged from $540 to $933, with a simple average of $793. The matrix also lists a single hourly rate for paralegals of $255. For non-legal labor categories, the NRC used wage data from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS).
[
25
]
The estimated BLS mean hourly wage for relevant positions in 2025 are $66.66 for health and safety engineers, $63.13 for compliance officers, $67.26 for nuclear engineers, $67.01 for engineers, all others, and $43.10 for legal support workers. The NRC applied a multiplier of 2.4 to this BLS wage data to arrive at a fully loaded rate (
e.g.,
$159.98 per hour for health and safety engineers);
[
26
]
no such adjustment was made to the Fitzpatrick Matrix rates as these already reflect market-based rates. For the purposes of this analysis, the NRC assumes a staffing distribution for applicants of 50 percent for lawyers, 20 percent for nuclear engineers, 15 percent for paralegals, 5 percent for health and safety engineers, 5 percent for engineers, all others, and 5 percent for compliance staff. Applying these percentages to the Fitzpatrick Matrix data and the adjusted BLS data yields a blended applicant rate of about $491 per hour.
For petitioners, which also include public-interest organizations and community groups, their wage rates are also derived from the two data sources mentioned previously, with a staffing distribution under the existing regulations of 25 percent for lawyers, 20 percent for nuclear engineers, 20 percent for engineers, all others, 20 percent for legal support staff, 10 percent for health and safety engineers, and 5 percent for paralegals. This estimated staffing distribution accounts for the fact that some petitioners under existing regulations employ non-attorneys as representatives (typically, officers of the petitioning non-governmental organization (NGO)) while other petitioners do employ attorneys, although these may be assisted by officers of petitioning NGOs. NGO officers supporting litigation activities are represented by the legal support staff portion of the staffing distribution. Applying fully loaded hourly rates to the BLS wage data only, this yields a blended and weighted petitioner rate of about $312 per hour.
Using these wage rates, the time spent on proceedings is monetized by multiplying the hours per proceeding by the applicable wage rate and then by 15 proceedings annually. If the existing regulations were to remain in place, the applicants will spend about $28.9 million (3,925 × $491 × 15 proceedings) on proceedings per year, the NRC adjudicatory staff will spend about $11.6 million annually (4,700 hours × $164 × 15), the NRC technical staff and attorneys will spend about $10.2 million annually (4,150 hours × $164 × 15), and petitioners will spend about $9.2 million annually (1,975 × $312 × 15). The combined spending on anticipated proceedings is about $59.9 million annually, undiscounted, if this rule is not implemented.
[
27
]
With this final rule, the applicants will spend about $22.3 million annually on proceedings (3,025 × $491 × 15 proceedings), the NRC adjudicatory staff about $9.6 million annually (3,900 hours × $164 × 15), the NRC technical staff and attorneys about $7.4 million annually (3,025 hours × $164 × 15), and petitioners about $7.1 million annually (1,525 × $312 × 15). The applicants, government, and petitioners will spend about $46.5 million annually, undiscounted, if this rule is implemented.
Cost Savings and Regulatory Accounting Presented in 2025 Base Year Dollars
Over the five-year analysis period (2026-2030), the final rule revisions are projected to yield net savings for the public, the industry, and government. The combined net savings will generate cumulative undiscounted savings of $67.4 million (savings minus costs). Using 2025 as the base year, the net present value (NPV) of these net savings is $61.7 million, discounted at 3 percent, or $55.2 million, discounted at 7 percent. The projected annualized cost savings will be $13.5 million discounted at 3 percent, or $13.5 million discounted at 7 percent.
Because the final rule streamlines existing hearing procedures, the cost of implementing this rule for the hearing participants is expected to be minimal. The NRC does not currently have empirical data to quantify incremental implementation or transition-related effects associated with the accelerated filing schedules and the revised hearing provisions. Consistent with OMB Circular A-4, when impacts cannot be reliably monetized, agencies provide a qualitative assessment. Accordingly, the agency has examined potential implementation and transition effects and determined them to be minimal since the rule streamlines internal agency proceedings without significantly changing the basic adjudicatory framework.
This final rule retains the existing approach to hearing requests by noticing opportunities for hearing after docketing and requiring a demonstration of standing and contention admissibility for a hearing request to be granted. The criteria for standing are unchanged, and the contention admissibility standards have been refined, without being raised. If a hearing request is granted, the agency still generally employs the same types of procedural mechanisms for evidentiary hearings as under the existing rules (
e.g.,
written testimony and position statements, oral hearings, proposed findings of fact and conclusions of law), although the
(
printed page 69472)
presiding officer will have greater flexibility to determine which procedural mechanisms to use in a particular hearing. Adjudicatory schedules have been significantly changed, which will require greater discipline on the part of participants to meet those schedules, but participants will still face the same basic task of managing time and resources. The NRC also retains other procedural mechanisms, such as motions, summary disposition, standards for reopening the record, discovery, appeals, stay requests, and requests for reconsideration. Participants will have to familiarize themselves with changes to some of these procedural mechanisms (
e.g.,
application of reopening standards after the Standard Hearing Completion Date, exclusions of certain documents from discovery), but the costs of doing so are expected to be minimal.
The regulatory analysis embedded in the
Federal Register
notice for the proposed rule included rulemaking costs for developing the final rule, but these costs have been removed from table 6 in this final rule. The costs associated with developing this final rule have already occurred; they are treated as sunk and are not included in this analysis. These costs sunset at the time the final rule is issued.
The applicants, accounting for the largest share of cost savings, will save about $33.1 million over 5 years, undiscounted, with an NPV of $30.4 million discounted at 3 percent, or $27.2 million discounted at 7 percent.
Additionally, the NRC adjudicatory staff will realize savings of about $9.8 million over 5 years, undiscounted, with an NPV of $9.0 million discounted at 3 percent, or $8.1 million discounted at 7 percent.
(
printed page 69473)
During the same period, the NRC technical staff and attorneys will save about $13.8 million over 5 years, undiscounted, with an NPV of $12.7 million discounted at 3 percent, or $11.3 million discounted at 7 percent.
The petitioners' savings total about $10.5 million, undiscounted, with an NPV of $9.6 million discounted at 3 percent, or $8.6 million discounted at 7 percent.
(
printed page 69474)
Overall, this final rule is considered to be a deregulatory action and will reduce burden for both the agency and hearing participants by streamlining the hearing process. These deregulatory actions translate into net savings with an NPV of $55.2 million over the five-year analysis horizon, or $13.5 million annually in 2025 dollars at a 7 percent discount rate.
In addition to this analysis, the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs directs agencies to report results as a perpetual stream (perpetuity) once a rule is implemented. The perpetual stream has annualized savings of about $13.5 million.

XV. Severability
This final rule makes changes to the requirements for contested hearings in NRC licensing proceedings. For the reasons described previously and in response to comments, the NRC has determined that its authority to promulgate these changes is well-supported in law and practice and should be upheld in any legal challenge. However, in the event that any portion of this rule is declared invalid, the NRC intends that the remaining portions be severable and continue in effect. Specifically, the NRC has independently considered each of those provisions in this rule, and intends that, if any of the provisions of this rule (or the application thereof to any person or circumstance) is held to be invalid by a court, such invalidity would not affect other provisions or application of such provisions to other persons or circumstances that can be given effect without the invalid provision or application. For example:
This rule includes provisions for different types of applications. If the provisions for one type of application are held to be invalid, the provisions for other types of applications should continue in effect since these other provisions are not intertwined with the provisions held to be invalid and were independently considered, with their own supporting basis and analysis.
This rule provides scheduling provisions for several procedural categories, including hearing requests, intervention petitions, contentions, motions, discovery, petitions for review, interlocutory appeals, requests for interlocutory review, stay requests, requests for reconsideration, and evidentiary hearings. If the schedule requirements for one procedural category are held to be invalid, the schedule requirements for other procedural categories should remain in effect because the schedules for each procedural category are not intertwined and were independently considered, with their own supporting basis and analysis.
In addition to schedule provisions, the rule includes changes to various procedural categories, including changes to definitions,
Federal Register
notices, contention standards, the reopening standards, discovery requirements, selection of hearing procedures, actions the staff can take during the pendency of a hearing, evidentiary hearings, additional procedures in § 2.1214 for license transfer proceedings, procedures for referred rulings and certified questions, and provisions for computation of time associated with delivery of hard copy documents. If the provisions for one type of procedural category are held to be invalid, the provisions for other types of procedural categories should continue in effect since these other provisions are not intertwined with the provisions held to be invalid and were independently considered, with their own supporting basis and analysis.
In addition, to the extent there are multiple changes in a category, if one of the changes in the category is held to be invalid, the other changes in the category should continue in effect because these changes were independently considered, with their own supporting basis and analysis. Examples include the various definitional changes; the two refinements to the contention admissibility criteria; the different reopening changes (
e.g.,
the § 2.326(a) change, the provisions in each sentence of § 2.326(e)(1), and the change in § 2.326(e)(2)); the various discovery changes (
e.g.,
elimination of subpart L hearing file, limitation on NRC staff's § 2.336 disclosures, exclusion of draft documents from § 2.336 disclosures, exclusion of certain internal communications from § 2.336 disclosures, changes to discovery schedules); the evidentiary hearing procedure changes; and the changes in each paragraph of § 2.1214.
Finally, for all of the matters described in the previous paragraphs, the agency's purpose in making its proceedings timely and efficient would best be effectuated by applying the provisions in this final rule to the maximum practicable extent.

Interlocutory review of rulings on requests for hearings/petitions to intervene, selection of hearing procedures, and requests by potential parties for access to sensitive unclassified non-safeguards information and safeguards information.
(a)
Types of appeals covered under this section.
An order of the presiding officer, or if a presiding officer has not been designated, of the Chief Administrative Judge, or if he or she is unavailable, of another administrative
(

judge, or of an administrative law judge with jurisdiction under § 2.318(a), may be appealed to the Commission with respect to:
(1) A request for hearing;
(2) A petition to intervene;
(3) A request for access to sensitive unclassified non-safeguards information (SUNSI), including, but not limited to, proprietary, confidential commercial, and security-related information, and Safeguards Information (SGI). An appeal to the Commission may also be taken from an order of an officer designated to rule on information access issues; or
(4) An order selecting a hearing procedure.
(b)
Timing of appeals and associated filings under this section.
(1) Appeals under paragraphs (a)(1) through (3) of this section must be made as specified by the provisions of this section, within 20 days after the service of the order. The appeal must be initiated by the filing of a notice of appeal and accompanying supporting brief. Any party who opposes the appeal may file a brief in opposition to the appeal within 20 days after service of the appeal. The supporting brief and any answer must conform to the requirements of § 2.341(c)(3). The appellant may file a reply brief within seven (7) days of service of any answer. This reply brief may not be longer than 5 pages.
(2) Appeals under paragraph (a)(4) of this section must be filed with the Commission no later than seven (7) days after issuance of the order selecting a hearing procedure. Any party who opposes the appeal may file a brief in opposition to the appeal within seven (7) days after service of the appeal. No reply briefs will be permitted.
(c)
Scope of appeals under this section.
(1) An order described in paragraphs (a)(1) through (3) of this section is appealable:
(i) By the requestor/petitioner on the question as to whether the request or petition should have been granted.
(ii) By a party other than the requestor/petitioner on the question as to whether the request for hearing or petition to intervene should have been wholly denied; or
(iii) By a party other than the requestor/petitioner on the question as to whether the request for access to the information described in paragraph (a)(3) of this section should have been denied in whole or in part. However, such a question with respect to SGI may only be appealed by the NRC staff, and such a question with respect to SUNSI may be appealed only by the NRC staff or by a party whose interest independent of the proceeding would be harmed by the release of the information.
(iv) No other appeals from rulings on requests for hearing are allowed under this section.
(2) An order described in paragraph (a)(4) of this section may be appealed by any party on the question as to whether the selection of the particular hearing procedures was in clear contravention of the criteria set forth in § 2.310.

§ 2.323
Motions.
(a)
Scope and general requirements—
(1)
Applicability to § 2.309(c).
Section 2.309 motions for leave to file hearing requests, intervention petitions, or new or amended contentions after the deadline in § 2.309(b) (including motions to reopen the record that relate to such filings after the deadline) are not subject to the requirements of this section. For the purposes of this section, the term “all motions” includes any motion except § 2.309 motions for leave to file hearing requests, intervention petitions, or new or amended contentions after the deadline in § 2.309(b) (and motions to reopen the record that relate to such filings after the deadline).
(2)
Presentation and disposition.
All motions must be addressed to the Commission or other designated presiding officer. All motions, other than motions submitted in Expedited Proceedings as discussed in this paragraph, motions for summary disposition as discussed in § 2.1205, or motions for reconsideration as discussed in paragraph (e) of this section, must be made no later than ten (10) days after the occurrence or circumstance from which the motion arises. Motions submitted in Expedited Proceedings must be made no later than seven (7) days after the occurrence or circumstance from which the motion arises. All written motions must be filed with the Secretary and served on all parties to the proceeding.
(b)
Form and content.
Unless made orally on-the-record during a hearing, or the presiding officer directs otherwise, or under the provisions of subpart N of this part, a motion must be in writing, state with particularity the grounds and the relief sought, be accompanied by any affidavits or other evidence relied on, and, as appropriate, a proposed form of order. A motion must be rejected if it does not include a certification by the attorney or representative of the moving party that the movant has made a sincere effort to contact other parties in the proceeding and resolve the issue(s) raised in the motion, and that the movant's efforts to resolve the issue(s) have been unsuccessful.
(c)
Answers to motions.
(1) For all written motions, other than motions submitted in Expedited Proceedings, motions for summary disposition, or motions for reconsideration, a party may file an answer in support of or in opposition to the motion within ten (10) days after service of the motion, or other period as determined by the Secretary, the Deputy Secretary, or the presiding officer. Answers to motions in Expedited Proceedings must be submitted within seven (7) days after service of the motion.

(2) These comments should be submitted within 30 days after public notice of receipt of the application and addressed to the Secretary, U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission, Washington, DC 20555-0001, Attention: Rulemakings and Adjudications Staff.
(3) The Commission will provide the applicant with a copy of the comments. Any response the applicant chooses to make to the comments must be submitted within 10 days of service of the comments on the applicant. Such responses do not constitute part of the decisional record.
(c)
Generic determination regarding license amendments to reflect transfers.
(1) Unless otherwise determined by the Commission with regard to a specific application, the Commission has determined that any amendment to the license of a utilization facility or the license of an Independent Spent Fuel Storage Installation which does no more than conform the license to reflect the transfer action, involves respectively, “no significant hazards consideration,” or “no genuine issue as to whether the health and safety of the public will be significantly affected.”
(2) Where administrative license amendments are necessary to reflect an approved transfer, such amendments will be included in the order that approves the transfer. Any challenge to the administrative license amendment is limited to the question of whether the license amendment accurately reflects the approved transfer.
(d)
Role of NRC staff.
Except as otherwise directed in accordance with § 2.1202(b)(1), the NRC staff is not required to be a party to proceedings under this subpart but will offer into evidence its safety evaluation report associated with the transfer application and provide one or more sponsoring witnesses, if this safety evaluation report is available at the time a hearing is conducted.

Background
The Normalizing Unmanned Aircraft Systems (UAS) Beyond Visual Line of Sight (BVLOS) Operations final rule was issued under the authority of 49 United States Code (U.S.C.). Section 106. The associated rulemaking was issued under the authority described in
49 U.S.C. 44807
,
Special authority for certain UAS,
which permitted the FAA Administrator
[
1
]
to use a risk-based approach to determine if certain UAS may operate safely in the NAS. Furthermore, the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 (section 930 of
Pub. L. 118-63
) amended
49 U.S.C. chapter 448
by adding § 44811 to require the FAA to establish performance-based regulations for UAS to be used for BVLOS operations. The UAS operations BVLOS regulations established acceptable risk levels for BVLOS operations; standards for remote pilots or UAS operators; an approval or acceptance process for UAS which leveraged special airworthiness certificates (SAC) or a manufacturer declaration of compliance (DOC); operating rules for UAS that were approved or accepted; protocols of networked information; and safety of manned aircraft operating in the NAS. Furthermore, section 932 of the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024 required procedures, including rulemaking, to approve third-party service suppliers. This included suppliers of UAS Traffic Management (UTM) services to support the safe integration and commercial operations of UAS. The rulemaking and subsequent regulations that are covered by this system of records are within the scope of these authorities.
This rulemaking established parts 108
Operations of Unmanned Aircraft Systems Beyond Visual Line of Sight,
and 146
Automated Data Service Providers.
Part 108 established a comprehensive framework enabling routine UAS Operations BVLOS without the need for case-by-case waivers, setting standards for aircraft design, operators, and operational safety. The operators and manufacturers covered by this part can be individuals or businesses. Part 146 established a certification structure for Automated Data Service Providers (ADSPs) that supply the digital traffic management and safety data necessary to support scalable BVLOS activity, including UTM. Like the other groups, ADSPs can be individuals or businesses.
Part 108 introduced two tiers of operating authority: permits for lower-risk, smaller-scale UAS operations and certificates for higher-risk or enterprise UAS operations. To administer this system, the FAA developed an information portal for manufacturers, operators, and ADSPs. Operators must obtain permits or certificates based on operational complexity and report certain data; manufacturers may be required to submit compliance data, including noise and cybersecurity information; and ADSPs must secure both organizational certificates and service-specific authorizations. As a result, the FAA collects identifying and technical data from all the aforementioned participants within the BVLOS ecosystem.
To issue permits/certificates of authorization to conduct certain BVLOS operations in the NAS, the FAA collects contact information (names, physical addresses, email addresses, and telephone numbers) from operators, as well as UAS serial numbers and UAS registration numbers. For a small subset of operators—those who perform package delivery operations—citizenship information is collected and could include birth certificate, passport, or naturalization document, which could include name, parents' names, place of birth, date of birth, certificate of naturalization number/passport number, marital status and photograph. Once submitted, an application identification number (ID) is generated for tracking purposes. If the FAA approves the request, a permit/certificate is generated and includes a permit/certificate number.
The application data for airworthiness acceptance from UAS manufacturers submitting declarations of compliance to the FAA includes manufacturers' contact information (names, physical addresses, email addresses and telephone numbers) and aircraft information (serial number and registration number), among other details. Once an application is submitted, an application ID is generated for tracking purposes. If the FAA approves the request, a waiver number is issued for approved waiver applications. Airworthiness acceptance is tracked by aircraft serial number, while registered manufacturers are tracked by manufacturer's name.
Finally, part 146 introduces the mechanisms and requirements to certify ADSPs and their automated data services. This process requires ADSPs to obtain organizational-level certificates and subsequently obtain authorizations for the individual services they provide. These applicants would also provide their contact information (names, physical addresses, email addresses and telephone numbers). When the applicant initiates an application, an application ID is generated to track it. If the FAA approves the application, a certification number is generated.
(

Privacy Act
The Privacy Act (
5 U.S.C. 552a
) governs how the Federal Government collects, maintains, and uses personally identifiable information (PII) in a System of Records. A “System of Records” is a group of any records under the control of a federal agency from which information about individuals is retrieved by name or other personal identifier. The Privacy Act requires each agency to publish in the
Federal Register
a System of Records Notice (SORN) identifying and describing each System of Records the agency maintains, including the purposes for which the agency uses PII in the system, the routine uses for which the agency discloses such information outside the agency, and how individuals to whom a Privacy Act record pertains can exercise their rights under the Privacy Act (
e.g.,
to determine if the system contains information about them and to contest inaccurate information). In accordance with
5 U.S.C. 552a(r)
, DOT has provided a report of this system of records to the Office of Management and Budget and to Congress.

PURPOSE(S) OF THE SYSTEM:
To allow the FAA to collect, use, and maintain information from individuals acting as or representing operators, manufacturers, and ADSPs when they request authorizations to conduct or support certain BVLOS operations in the NAS and/or airworthiness acceptance to manufacture compliant UAS.
CATEGORIES OF INDIVIDUALS COVERED BY THE SYSTEM:
For part 108, records cover individuals acting as or representing UAS operators requesting a permit or certificate to conduct operations, and individuals acting as or representing manufacturers seeking airworthiness acceptance for UAS. For part 146, records cover individuals acting as or representing the ADSPs, corporate stockholders who own 5% or more of the corporation's total voting stock, non-corporate persons with a financial interest in the entity, and accountable executives.
CATEGORIES OF RECORDS IN THE SYSTEM:
Categories of records in this system apply to individuals acting as or representing operators, manufacturers, and ADSPs as follows:
Operators
These records include name, physical address, email address, and telephone number, the address of the principal base of operations, if different from the address provided for contact information, name of the individual who serves as operations supervisor, application ID, permit/certificate number, UAS serial number and UAS registration number. For a small subset of operators who perform package delivery operations, citizenship information is collected and could include birth certificate, passport, or naturalization document, which could include name, parents' names, place of birth, date of birth, certificate of naturalization number/passport number, marital status and photograph.
Manufacturers
These records include the manufacturer's name, physical address, telephone number, email address, application ID, and waiver number; the unmanned aircraft make, model, series, serial number, and date of manufacture.
Automated Data Service Providers
These records include name, physical address, mailing address, telephone number, email address, application ID, certification number and service authorization number; for corporate applicants: name and physical address of each stockholder who owns 5% or more of the total voting stock of the corporation; for non-corporate applicants: name and physical address of each person having a financial interest in the entity; name, mailing address, telephone number and email address of each accountable executive.
RECORD SOURCE CATEGORIES:
Records are obtained from individuals authorized to operate UAS, manufacture UAS, or offer automated data services to UAS operators, as well as FAA personnel logging actions associated with various activities, including, but not limited to, certification, authorization, oversight, and enforcement.
ROUTINE USES OF RECORDS MAINTAINED IN THE SYSTEM, INCLUDING CATEGORIES OF USERS AND THE PURPOSES OF SUCH USES:
In addition to other disclosures generally permitted under
5 U.S.C. 552a(b)
of the Privacy Act, all or a portion of the records or information contained in this system may be disclosed outside DOT as a routine use pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 552a(b)(3)
as follows:
System-Specific Routine Uses:
1. To the public, in the case of part 108, waiver applications and decisions, including any history of previous, pending, existing, or denied requests for waivers applicable to the UAS at issue for purposes of the waiver, and special provisions applicable to the UAS operation that is the subject of the request. Individual or business names will be shared as needed. Email addresses and telephone numbers will not be disclosed pursuant to this Routine Use. Airspace authorizations that the FAA issues will also not be disclosed pursuant to this Routine Use, except to the extent that an airspace authorization is listed or summarized in the terms of a waiver.
2. To the public, in the case of part 146, the FAA manages a public-facing web page that provides the following information associated with each part 146 certification: (1) the service provider name, (2) the service type of the certification, and (3) the service type and category for each authorized part 146 service associated with the certification.
3. To law enforcement, when necessary and relevant to an FAA enforcement activity.
4. To the National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) in connection with its investigation responsibilities.
5. To government agencies, whether Federal, State, Tribal, local or foreign, information necessary or relevant to an investigation of a violation or potential violation of law, whether civil, criminal, or regulatory, that the agency is charged with investigating or enforcing; as well as, to government agencies responsible for threat detection in connection with critical infrastructure protection.
6. To the Transportation Security Administration (TSA), when necessary
(
printed page 69308)
and relevant to the execution of TSA's duty to impose security measures on related operations, assess security risks, enforce compliance, conduct security threat assessments, and for the purpose of vetting individuals and operators.
Departmental Routine Uses:
7. In the event that a system of records maintained by DOT to carry out its functions indicates a violation or potential violation of law, whether civil, criminal or regulatory in nature, and whether arising by general statute or particular program pursuant thereto, the relevant records in the system of records may be referred, as a routine use, to the appropriate agency, whether Federal, State, local or foreign, charged with the responsibility of investigating or prosecuting such violation or charged with enforcing or implementing the statute, or rule, regulation, or order issued pursuant thereto.
8. A record from this system of records may be disclosed, as a routine use, to a Federal, State, or local agency maintaining civil, criminal, or other relevant enforcement information or other pertinent information, such as current licenses, if necessary to obtain information relevant to a DOT decision concerning the hiring or retention of an employee, the issuance of a security clearance, the letting of a contract, or the issuance of a license, grant or other benefit.
9. A record from this system of records may be disclosed, as a routine use, to a Federal agency, in response to its request, in connection with the hiring or retention of an employee, the issuance of a security clearance, the reporting of an investigation of an employee, the letting of a contract, or the issuance of a license, grant, or other benefit by the requesting agency, to the extent that the information is relevant and necessary to the requesting agency's decision on the matter.
10a. Routine Use for Disclosure for Use in Litigation. It shall be a routine use of the records in this system of records to disclose them to the Department of Justice or other Federal agency conducting litigation when (a) DOT, or any agency thereof, or (b) Any employee of DOT or any agency thereof (including a member of the Coast Guard), in his/her official capacity, or (c) Any employee of DOT or any agency thereof (including a member of the Coast Guard), in his/her individual capacity where the Department of Justice has agreed to represent the employee, or (d) The United States or any agency thereof, where DOT determines that litigation is likely to affect the United States, is a party to litigation or has an interest in such litigation, and the use of such records by the Department of Justice or other Federal agency conducting the litigation is deemed by DOT to be relevant and necessary in the litigation, provided, however, that in each case, DOT determines that disclosure of the records in the litigation is a use of the information contained in the records that is compatible with the purpose for which the records were collected.

It shall be a routine use of records in this system to disclose them in proceedings before any court or adjudicative or administrative body before which DOT or any agency thereof, appears, when (a) DOT, or any agency thereof, or (b) Any employee of DOT or any agency thereof in his/her official capacity, or (c) Any employee of DOT or any agency thereof in his/her individual capacity where DOT has agreed to represent the employee, or (d) The United States or any agency thereof, where DOT determines that the proceeding is likely to affect the United States, is a party to the proceeding or has an interest in such proceeding, and DOT determines that use of such records is relevant and necessary in the proceeding, provided, however, that in each case, DOT determines that disclosure of the records in the proceeding is a use of the information contained in the records that is compatible with the purpose for which the records were collected.
12. Disclosure may be made to a Congressional office from the record of an individual in response to an inquiry from the Congressional office made at the request of that individual. In such cases, however, the Congressional office does not have greater rights to records than the individual. Thus, the disclosure may be withheld from delivery to the individual where the file contains investigative or actual information or other materials which are being used, or are expected to be used, to support prosecution or fines against the individual for alleged violations of a statute, or of regulations of the Department based on statutory authority. No such limitations apply to records requested for Congressional oversight or legislative purposes; release is authorized under

.
13. One or more records from a system of records may be disclosed routinely to the National Archives and Records Administration in records management inspections being conducted under the authority of
44 U.S.C. 2904
and
2906
.
14. It shall be a routine use of the information in any DOT system of records to provide to the Attorney General of the United States, or his/her designee, information indicating that a person meets any of the disqualifications for receipt, possession, shipment, or transport of a firearm under the Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act. In case of a dispute concerning the validity of the information provided by DOT to the Attorney General, or his/her designee, it shall be a routine use of the information in any DOT system of records to make any disclosures of such information to the National Background Information Check System, established by the Brady Handgun Violence Prevention Act, as may be necessary to resolve such dispute.
15a. To appropriate agencies, entities, and persons when (1) DOT suspects or has confirmed that there has been a breach of the system of records; (2) DOT has determined that as a result of the suspected or confirmed breach there is a risk of harm to individuals, DOT (including its information systems, programs, and operations), the Federal Government, or national security; and (3) the disclosure made to such agencies, entities, and persons is reasonably necessary to assist in connection with DOT's efforts to respond to the suspected or confirmed breach or to prevent, minimize, or remedy such harm.
15b. To another Federal agency or Federal entity, when DOT determines that information from this system of records is reasonably necessary to assist the recipient agency or entity in (1) responding to a suspected or confirmed breach or (2) preventing, minimizing, or remedying the risk of harm to individuals, the recipient agency or entity (including its information systems, programs, and operations), the Federal Government, or national security, resulting from a suspected or confirmed breach.

DOT may disclose records from this system, as a routine use, to the Office of Government Information Services for the purpose of (a) resolving disputes between FOIA requesters and Federal agencies and (b) reviewing agencies' policies, procedures, and compliance in order to recommend policy changes to Congress and the President.
17. DOT may disclose records from this system, as a routine use, to contractors and their agents, experts, consultants, and others performing or working on a contract, service, cooperative agreement, or other assignment for DOT, when necessary to accomplish an agency function related to this system of records.

POLICIES AND PRACTICES FOR STORAGE OF RECORDS:
Records in this system are stored in electronic form. Electronic records are stored in a database with appropriate security and access limitation.
POLICIES AND PRACTICES FOR RETRIEVAL OF RECORDS:
Records can be accessed by both internal and external users to the FAA upon authentication into the system. Based on their business need, users can retrieve records by application ID, service authorization number, waiver number, certificate/certification number, permit number, name, and email address.
POLICIES AND PRACTICES FOR RETENTION AND DISPOSAL OF RECORDS:
FAA is actively working on drafting the appropriate records retention schedule(s) to be submitted to NARA by the latter part of fiscal year 2027. Until these schedules are approved by NARA, all records in this system will be treated as permanent.
ADMINISTRATIVE, TECHNICAL, AND PHYSICAL SAFEGUARDS:
Records in this system are safeguarded in accordance with applicable rules and policies, including all applicable DOT and FAA automated systems security and access policies. Strict controls have been imposed to minimize the risk of compromising the information that is being stored. Access to the computer system containing the records in this system is limited to individuals who have a need to know the information for the performance of their official duties and who have appropriate clearances or permissions.
RECORD ACCESS PROCEDURES:
Individuals seeking notification of whether this system of records contains information about them may contact the System Manager at the address provided in the section “System Manager”. When seeking records about yourself from this system of records or any other Departmental system of records, your request must conform to the Privacy Act regulations set forth in
49 CFR part 10
. You must sign your request, and your signature must either be notarized or submitted under

, a law that permits statements to be made under penalty of perjury as a substitute for notarization. If your request is seeking records pertaining to another living individual, you must include a statement from that individual certifying his/her agreement for you to access his/her records.

Individuals seeking to contest the content of any record pertaining to them in the system of records may contact the System Manager and follow the Privacy Act procedures in
49 CFR part 10, subpart E

SUMMARY:
On October 19, 2026, the North American Free Trade Agreement (NAFTA) Secretariat issued a Notice of Final Panel Action. The U.S. Department of Commerce (Commerce) is notifying the public that the NAFTA Binational Panel's final judgment is not in harmony with Commerce's final determination in the countervailing duty (CVD) investigation of certain softwood lumber products (lumber) from Canada, and that Commerce is amending the final determination and the resulting CVD order with respect to the countervailable subsidy rate assigned to Canfor Corporation (Canfor); J.D. Background
On November 8, 2017, Commerce published its
Final Determination
in the CVD investigation of lumber from Canada.
[
1

The
Final Determination

[

Respondent parties subsequently challenged Commerce's final determination before the NAFTA Binational Panel, pursuant to Article 1904 of NAFTA. The parties briefed and argued the case before the Panel and, on March 6, 2024, the Panel issued its decision, affirming in part and remanding in part Commerce's determination.
[
3
]
On December 17, 2024, Commerce issued its
First Remand Determination.
[
4
]
On March 6, 2026, the Panel issued its decision on remand, affirming in part and remanding in part Commerce's
First Remand Determination.
[
5

On June 17, 2026, Commerce issued its
Second Remand Determination.

6

[

On October 19, 2026, the Panel directed the NAFTA Secretariat to issue a Notice of Final Panel Action; the NAFTA Secretariat subsequently issued the Notice of Final Panel Action on October 19, 2026.
Timken Notice
In its decision in
Timken,
[
8
]
as clarified by
Diamond Sawblades,
[
9
]
the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Federal Circuit held that, pursuant to sections 516A(c) and (e) of the Tariff Act of 1930, as amended (the Act), Commerce must publish a notice of court decision that is not “in harmony” with a Commerce determination and must suspend liquidation of entries pending a “conclusive” court decision. Because NAFTA panels step into the shoes of the courts they are replacing, they must apply the law of the national court that would otherwise review the administrative determination. Therefore, we are publishing notice that the NAFTA Panel's Panel Decision on Second Remand, as memorialized by the NAFTA Secretariat's October 19, 2026, Notice of Final Panel Action, is “not in harmony” with the
Final Determination.
[
10
]
Publication of this notice fulfills the obligation imposed upon Commerce by the decision in
Timken.

FDA is recommending a comprehensive approach to potency assurance of CGT products that is grounded in quality risk management. For investigational products, we describe how to progressively implement a strategy for potency assurance during product development and provide additional considerations to help assure the potency of products that are undergoing rapid clinical development. SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Background
FDA is announcing the availability of a document titled “Potency Assurance for Cellular and Gene Therapy Products.” This guidance provides recommendations to help assure the potency of human CGT products that are regulated as biological products under section 351 of the Public Health Service Act (
42 U.S.C. 262
).
This final guidance provides recommendations for developing a science- and risk-based strategy to help assure the potency of human CGT products. A potency assurance strategy is a multifaceted approach that reduces risks to the potency of a product through: (1) manufacturing process design, (2) manufacturing process control, (3) material control, (4) in-process testing, and (5) potency lot release assays. The goal of a potency assurance strategy is to ensure that every lot of a product released will have the specific ability or capacity to achieve the intended therapeutic effect.
The guidance emphasizes that potency assays and their corresponding acceptance criteria should be designed to make meaningful contributions to potency assurance by reducing risks to product potency. We provide illustrative examples of approaches to potency assay development that are grounded in quality risk management. Due to the diversity of CGT products and the product-specific nature of potency assays, the recommendations in this final guidance regarding the selection and design of potency assays are necessarily general.
In the
Federal Register
of December 28, 2023 (
88 FR 89707
), FDA announced the availability of the draft guidance of the same title dated December 28, 2023. FDA received several comments on the draft guidance and those comments were considered as the guidance was finalized. A summary of changes includes: advice on integration of potency assurance into existing quality systems, expanded risk assessment guidance, advice on regulatory engagement pathways, and additional practical examples with refined terminology throughout. In addition, editorial changes were made to improve clarity. The guidance announced in this notice finalizes the draft guidance dated December 28, 2023.
This guidance is being issued consistent with FDA's good guidance practices regulation (
21 CFR 10.115
). The guidance represents the current thinking of FDA on “Potency Assurance for Cellular and Gene Therapy Products.” It does not establish any rights for any person and is not binding on FDA or the public. You can use an alternative approach if it satisfies the requirements of the applicable statutes and regulations.

SUMMARY:

Hearing Locations—NMFS will hold two online webinars and three in-person public hearings:
1.
Tuesday, November 17, 2026, 4 p.m. to 6 p.m.;
Hilton Garden Inn Boston Logan Airport, 100 Boardman St., Boston, MA 02128; phone (617) 567-6789. Note: The Scoping Meeting will begin 30 minutes after the conclusion of the Joint Scallop Committee and Advisory Panel Meeting.
2.
Monday, November 23, 2026, 11 a.m. to 1 p.m.;
This meeting will be conducted via webinar accessible via the internet from
https://noaanmfs-meets.webex.com/​noaanmfs-meets/​j.php?​MTID=​medf57ebff82a5b2f8eba37822902afaf
.

4.

This meeting will be conducted via webinar accessible via the internet from
https://noaanmfs-meets.webex.com/​noaanmfs-meets/​j.php?​MTID=​mb0a2a4828a3a66f98fecf5e467c73a44
.
5.
Monday, December 14, 2026, 1 p.m. to 3 p.m.;
University of Massachusetts Dartmouth School for Marine Science and Technology East, 836 South Rodney French Blvd., New Bedford, MA 02744; phone: (508) 999-8193.
Background
Based on comments received in response to
Executive Order 14276
, the Secretary of Commerce is considering whether to develop an amendment to the Atlantic Scallop Fishery Management Plan (FMP) to allow permit stacking in the limited access scallop fishery. The publication of this
Federal Register
notice does not commit the Secretary to take action at this time, but is intended to notify the public of the opportunity to be heard and that NMFS, on behalf of the Secretary, is soliciting feedback to inform the Secretary's decision whether to develop an amendment for permit stacking.
The New England Fishery Management Council (Council) established the Limited Access component of the sea scallop fishery through Amendment 4 (1994) to the Atlantic Sea Scallop FMP. This action was part of an effort control program designed to reduce fishing mortality and rebuild the scallop resource in what was, at that time, an overfished stock. Amendment 4 included measures designed to limit increases in a vessel's fishing power and reduce fishing pressure, such as limiting fishing time through days-at-sea (DAS) management, crew restrictions, gear restrictions, reporting requirements, and vessel upgrade restrictions.
Excess capacity remains in the limited access scallop fishery; that is, the capacity of individual vessels and the fleet as a whole is greater than what is needed to efficiently harvest sustainable levels of catch. Since the limited access program was implemented in 1994, the annual allocation of DAS has reduced steadily. Due to effort reductions in Amendment 4 (1994) and Amendment 7 (1999), DAS allocations were reduced almost by half from 204 DAS in 1994 to 120 DAS in 1999. Since 1999, the number of open area DAS has continued
(
printed page 69244)
to decline, although more effort has been allocated to fish in access areas, which served to offset that reduction. In fishing year 2026, a full-time vessel was allocated 36 open area DAS and no access area trips.
Some members of the industry have commented that the current low allocations, paired with increasing costs, are reducing profits and suggesting the reconsideration of certain management approaches may be timely. Some crews routinely work on multiple vessels in one fishing year. Further, reports suggest that some ports are congested with vessels tied to the dock for the majority of the year causing safety and space issues.
The Secretary is considering addressing excess capacity in the limited access scallop fishing by allowing up to two limited access scallop permits to be combined on a single vessel. The vessel would be permitted to fish the allocations for both permits, which would reduce business expenses associated with maintaining multiple vessels with low DAS allocations.
To mitigate risks of fleet consolidation, job loss, and effort spillover into other fisheries, any potential Secretarial amendment under consideration would evaluate specific protective management measures, including but not limited to:
Limiting stacked permits to those within the same Limited Access category (
i.e.,
full-time, part-time, occasional);
Requiring stacking to be a one-time, permanent, and irreversible action (
i.e.,
prohibiting de-stacking);
Whether to restrict permit stacking to strictly respect existing vessel length, tonnage, and horsepower baseline restrictions (
i.e.,
disallowing a permit carrying a smaller baseline specification to stack onto a vessel with larger baselines and to ensure stacking is not used to bypass vessel replacement limits);
Narrowing allowable permit stacking exclusively to vessels under common ownership or common control in order to avoid fleet concentration and accommodate the needs of active owner-operators; and
Maintaining the ownership cap of no more than 5 percent of the total number of limited access permits.
NMFS is seeking public input on all aspects of a potential action to allow permit stacking. Additional details are available in the public hearing document, available at
https://www.fisheries.noaa.gov/​new-england-mid-atlantic/​commercial-fishing/​scoping-potential-secretarial-action-implement-permit
.
Special Accommodations
These hearings are physically accessible to people with disabilities. Requests for sign language interpretation or other auxiliary aid should be directed to Emily Keiley, (978) 281-9116 at least 5 days prior to any meeting date.
