AGENCY:
Nuclear Regulatory Commission.
ACTION:
Direct final rule; confirmation of effective date.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) is confirming the effective date of November 9, 2026, for the direct final rule that was published in the
Federal Register
on August 26, 2026. This direct final rule amended the TN Americas, LLC Standardized NUHOMS® Horizontal Modular Storage System for Irradiated Nuclear Fuel listing within the “List of approved spent fuel storage casks” to include Amendment No. 19 to Certificate of Compliance No. 1004. Amendment No. 19 revises the certificate of compliance to provide for a 61BTH improved basket design using staggered plates similar the 24PTH Type 3 basket approved in CoC 1004 Amendment 18 and similar to the EOS 37PTH and 89BTH baskets approved in CoC 1042. This will simplify construction, reduce weight and improve fabricability. Additional changes are proposed to address editorial corrections, consistency, and terminology clarifications.
DATES:
The effective date of November 9, 2026, for the direct final rule published August 26, 2026 (
91 FR 54941
), is confirmed.

.
The proposed amendment to the certificate of compliance, the proposed changes to the technical specifications, and the preliminary safety evaluation report are available in ADAMS under Accession No. ML26103A250 (package). The final amendment to the certificate of compliance, final changes to the technical specifications, and final safety evaluation report can also be viewed in ADAMS under Accession No. ML26282A009 (package).
NRC's PDR:
The PDR, where you may examine and order copies of publicly available documents, is open by appointment. To make an appointment to visit the PDR, please send an email to

FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Heath Stroud, Office of Nuclear Material Safety and Safeguards, telephone: 301-287-3664, email:
Heath.Stroud@nrc.gov
;
and Tim Mossman, Office of Nuclear Material Safety and Safeguards, telephone: 301-287-9100, email:
Timothy.Mossman@nrc.gov
.
Both are staff of the U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission, Washington, DC 20555-0001.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
On August 26, 2026 (
91 FR 54941
), the NRC published a direct final rule amending its regulations in part 72 of title 10 of the
Code of Federal Regulations
to revise the TN Americas, LLC Standardized NUHOMS® Horizontal Modular Storage System for Irradiated Nuclear Fuel, Certificate of Compliance No. 1004 within the “List of approved spent fuel storage casks” to include Amendment No. 19.
In the direct final rule, the NRC stated that if no significant adverse comments were received, the direct final rule would become effective on November 9, 2026. The NRC received and docketed three comment submissions on the companion proposed rule (
91 FR 55028
; August 26, 2026). An electronic copy of the comments can be obtained from the Federal Rulemaking website at
https://www.regulations.gov
under Docket ID NRC-2026-2806 and is also available in ADAMS under Accession No. ML26286A192. The NRC evaluated the comments against the criteria described in the direct final rule and determined that the comments were not significant and adverse. Specifically, one commenter mentions higher heat load as a significant change. This higher heat load was reviewed by the NRC and is documented in section 5.1.1 of the safety evaluation report (SER) and determined to be acceptable. Another commenter questioned the lack of site-specific analyses. However, specific environmental assessments are not required as
10 CFR 51.22(a)(12)
contains a categorical exclusion. The same commenter challenged that the changes would create appreciable differences in performance of the cask; however, the staff evaluated all proposed changes and documented the results in the SER.
Other comments were outside the scope of this rulemaking and did not oppose the rule; propose a change or an addition to the rule; or cause the NRC to make a change to the rule, the certificate of compliance, or the technical specifications. Therefore, this direct final rule will become effective as scheduled.
Dated: October 30, 2026.
For the Nuclear Regulatory Commission.

abstract: The National Center of Excellence for Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) Safety (National LNG Center) will host a series of informational workshops on best practices for LNG safety titled, "LNG Safety Best Practices Workshop." The workshops are free; will be hosted in-person with select hybrid sessions offered virtually; and will require advance registration. Each workshop will be a full day and will cover a variety of best practices each session. PHMSA established the National LNG Center in 2023 pursuant to section 111 of the Protecting Our Infrastructure of Pipelines and Enhancing Safety (PIPES) Act of 2020 (Pub. L. 116-260), which directs the National LNG Center to advance Federal LNG expertise, serve as a repository of best practices, and facilitate collaboration among LNG stakeholders. Consistent with this mandate, the workshop series will bring together representatives from industry, government, academia, emergency response organizations, and other stakeholders to promote information sharing and continuous improvement in LNG safety.
dates: The inaugural LNG Safety Best Practices Workshop will be held December 2, 2026 from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. CST. Subsequent workshop dates will be announced and posted as they become available at https:// primis-meetings.phmsa.dot.gov/. Online pre-registration for the LNG Safety Best Practices Workshop opens on Monday, November 2, 2026 and will close on Friday, November 27, 2026.

AGENCY:
Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration (PHMSA), U.S. Department of Transportation (DOT).
ACTION:
Notice of public workshop.
SUMMARY:
The National Center of Excellence for Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG) Safety (National LNG Center) will host a series of informational workshops on best practices for LNG safety titled, “LNG Safety Best Practices Workshop.” The workshops are free; will be hosted in-person with select hybrid sessions offered virtually; and will require advance registration. Each workshop will be a full day and will cover a variety of best practices each session. PHMSA established the National LNG Center in 2023 pursuant to section 111 of the Protecting Our Infrastructure of Pipelines and Enhancing Safety (PIPES) Act of 2020 (
Pub. L. 116-260
), which directs the National LNG Center to advance Federal LNG expertise, serve as a repository of best practices, and facilitate collaboration among LNG stakeholders. Consistent with this mandate, the workshop series will bring together representatives from industry, government, academia, emergency response organizations, and other stakeholders to promote information sharing and continuous improvement in LNG safety.
DATES:
The inaugural LNG Safety Best Practices Workshop will be held
(
printed page 69305)
December 2, 2026 from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m. CST. Subsequent workshop dates will be announced and posted as they become available at
https://primis-meetings.phmsa.dot.gov/​
.
Online pre-registration for the LNG Safety Best Practices Workshop opens on Monday, November 2, 2026 and will close on Friday, November 27, 2026.
Individuals requiring accommodations, such as sign language interpretation or other ancillary aids, for the workshop should notify Luciano Vera by phone at 771-233-3278 or by email at
LNGCenter@dot.gov
no later than November 16, 2026. For additional information, see the
ADDRESSES
section of this notice.
ADDRESSES:
The LNG Safety Best Practices Workshop will be held in person at the National LNG Center in Lake Charles, Louisiana. The hotel reservation link, workshop agenda, and instructions on how to attend will be published on the public meeting registration page at
https://primis-meetings.phmsa.dot.gov/​
.
Presentations:
Presentations will be available on the meeting website and on the E-Gov website at
https://regulations.gov
under docket number PHMSA-2026-3004 no later than 30 days following the meeting.
Submitting Comments:
You may submit general questions and comments, identified by Docket No. PHMSA-2026-3004 (LNG Safety Best Practices Workshop Series Presented by the National Center of Excellence for LNG Safety), by any of the following methods:
E-Gov Website:
https://www.regulations.gov
.
This site allows the public to enter comments on any
Federal Register
notice issued by any agency. Follow the online instructions for submitting comments.
Mail:
Docket Management System, U.S. Department of Transportation, 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, West Building Ground Floor, Room W12-140, Washington, DC 20590-0001.
Hand Delivery:
DOT Docket Management System: 1200 New Jersey Avenue SE, West Building Ground Floor, Room W12-140, Washington, DC 20590-0001, between 9:00 a.m. and 5:00 p.m. EST, Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays.
Fax:
202-493-2251. Docket Management Facility. DOT will not issue confirmation notices for faxed comments.
Instructions:
Identify Docket No. PHMSA-2026-3004 at the beginning of your comments. If you submit your comments by mail, please submit two copies. If you wish to receive confirmation that PHMSA received your comments, you must include a self-addressed stamped postcard. Internet users may submit comments at
http://www.regulations.gov
.
Privacy Act:
DOT may solicit comments from the public regarding certain general notices. DOT posts these comments, without edits, including any personal information the commenter provides, to
www.regulations.gov
,
as described in the system of records notice (DOT/ALL-14 FDMS), which can be reviewed at
www.dot.gov/​privacy
.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Luciano Vera, Outreach Coordinator, by telephone at 771-233-3278 or by email at
LNGCenter@dot.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Building upon the National LNG Center's “Prioritizing Safety: Best Practices in LNG” webinar series, the workshops will provide practical learning and direct engagement with subject matter experts on process safety management and best practices at LNG facilities. Hybrid morning sessions will allow both in-person and virtual participation, followed by in-person case studies in the afternoon. Planned agenda topics and the full schedule will be posted to the meeting website.
The workshop directly supports the National LNG Center's congressionally established mission by sharing safety knowledge and best practices, strengthening stakeholder collaboration, and advancing understanding of safe LNG facility operations.
The National LNG Center will use the LNG Safety Best Practices Workshop series to promote information-sharing between LNG industry stakeholders, supporting continuous improvements in LNG facility safety and operational performance while complementing minimum regulatory requirements. The best practices include, but are not limited to, LNG facility management, fire protection and safety, operations, maintenance, system/process design, and other leading industry practices. The best practices may be implemented by various LNG facility types, including, but not limited to, baseload facilities (import/export terminals), peak shavers, satellite, temporary/mobile, transportation fuel, and bunkering.
Identified best practices can be applied in the form of a procedure, technique, process, program, consensus standard, or recommended practice, and may merit consideration by organizations for implementation because they have demonstrated value in improving safety or reliability, in offering superior performance beyond compliance, or in introducing innovative methods to enhance effectiveness. Delivering these practices via workshops enables a formal process of sharing information with LNG stakeholders.
[
1
]
Workshops also facilitate broad outreach, interactive questions and answers, and subsequent measurement of impact.
Public Participation:
The LNG Safety Best Practices Workshop series will be open to the public via registration. Members of the public who wish to attend must register on the meeting website(s), including their names and organizational affiliation. PHMSA is committed to providing all participants with equal access to these meetings. If you need disability accommodations for the workshop, please contact Luciano Vera by email at
LNGCenter@dot.gov
.
PHMSA is not always able to publish a notice in the
Federal Register
quickly enough to provide timely notification of last-minute changes that impact scheduled meetings. Therefore, individuals should check the meeting website listed in the
ADDRESSES
section of this notice or contact Luciano Vera regarding any possible changes to the LNG Safety Best Practices Workshop.
Issued in Washington, DC, under authority delegated in
49 CFR 1.97
.
Thomas Correll,
Associate Administrator for Pipeline Safety.

                         LNG sector stakeholders, as defined in section 111 of the PIPES Act of 2020, are Federal regulatory agencies of jurisdiction, LNG facilities operating in the United States, State governments, Native American Tribes, units of local government, post-secondary educational institutions, labor organizations, and safety organizations.

ACTION:
Notice of waiver.
SUMMARY:
This notice announces a waiver, granted by the Secretary, through the Deputy Secretary, of the minimum 30-day application period required under section 102(a) of the HUD Reform Act for the FY2026 Continuum of Care Program (CoC) notice of funding opportunity (NOFO), which was re-opened for application submission on September 18, 2026 (CPD-2600-DC-0025).
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
For information regarding this notice, contact Claudette Fernandez, General Deputy Assistant Secretary for the Office of Community Planning and Development, Department of Housing and Urban Development, 451 7th Street SW, Washington, DC 20410; telephone number (202) 402-6009 (this is not a toll-free number); email
CoCNOFO@HUD.gov
.
HUD welcomes and is prepared to receive calls from individuals who are deaf or hard of hearing, as well as individuals with speech and communication disabilities. To learn more about how to make an accessible telephone call, please visit
https://www.fcc.gov/​consumers/​guides/​telecommunications-relay-service-trs
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Section 102(a) of the HUD Reform Act (42 U.S.C.
(
printed page 69268)
3545(a)) sets out the requirements for notice to the public regarding assistance available from HUD. Section 102(a)(3) requires publication of selection criteria not less than 30 days before the deadline for applications or requests for assistance. HUD may waive this requirement if “the Secretary determines that the waiver is required for appropriate response to an emergency.” If HUD makes an emergency waiver, then it must publish “the Secretary's reasons for doing so” in the
Federal Register
within 30 days. HUD does not believe that it must seek an emergency waiver for the FY2026 CoC NOFO, but is doing so out of an abundance of caution for the reasons below.
Due to litigation, the FY2026 CoC NOFO has been published, vacated, and restored over recent months.
On June 1, 2026, HUD published the FY2026 CoC NOFO with an August 26, 2026, application deadline, which gave applicants 87 days to review the NOFO and submit applications. HUD subsequently published a modified NOFO on July 24, 2026, which maintained an August 26, 2026, application deadline and made no substantive changes apart from adding a mechanism for direct-to-HUD funding for areas with no collaborative applicant, as spelled out in Appendix III of the NOFO.
In early July, two groups of plaintiffs sued to challenge the NOFO in the United States District Court for the District of Rhode Island. On August 7, the district court vacated the FY26 NOFO. ECF 41,
State of Washington
v.
HUD,
1:26-cv-439 (D.R.I.); ECF 34,
Nat'l All. To End Homelessness
v.
HUD,
1:26-cv-436 (D.R.I.). The NOFO was thus rendered null and void less than 20 days before the original deadline. HUD appealed the ruling. During the appeal, HUD maintained a copy of the NOFO on its website [
https://www.hud.gov/​hud-partners/​coc-program-competition
] and sent a listserv message to applicants notifying them of the same.
And on September 16, 2026, the United States Court of Appeals for the First Circuit stayed the lower court's judgment while the Plaintiffs' challenge to the NOFO proceeds.
State of Washington
v.
HUD,
__F.4th__, 2026 WL 2730937 (1st Cir. 2026). As a result, the NOFO was automatically restored.
See
NOFO at 111.
On September 18, 2026, the Department re-opened the FY2026 CoC NOFO (CPD-2600-DC-0025), with a funding application deadline of 8:00 p.m. ET on September 30, 2026, which created an additional 12-day application window to resume the competition that was paused 68 days after publication of the June 1 NOFO. The additional period was less than the 30-day minimum application requirement under section 102(a)(3). But it is part of the larger application period of 80 days, so HUD does not believe that the NOFO requires an emergency waiver under section 102(a)(3). Still, the Secretary has determined that it is nevertheless prudent to issue a waiver.
It was necessary for the Department to establish a short application reopening period for this NOFO to address certain exigent and emergency circumstances. Specifically, HUD is required by Congress to make awards under the NOFO by December 1, 2026. HUD also endeavors to make timely awards to ensure ongoing funding for successful and meritorious projects, and for other projects that the CoCs or Congress may lawfully protect from competition.
HUD established the original August 26 application deadline to build in the necessary amount of time it reasonably expected it would need to review several thousands of applications and make awards. But the District Court ruling, which is now vacated, eliminated part of the approximately 90-day application period HUD originally provided. HUD must now process all applications and make awards within 62 days, which would be the quickest that the program has ever processed applications. It has received close to 8,000 individual project applications, including 3,500 new project applications, and almost 400 CoC applications. Historically, application reviews have required over 90 days to complete, so it cannot afford to lengthen the general application deadline any further.
Applicants have had nearly four months to review the NOFO and prepare applications, so an additional 12-day application period is sufficient time for applicants to finalize and submit their applications while also reserving for HUD time needed to meet the congressionally mandated December 1 deadline. As such, the circumstances demonstrated that an emergency existed that justified the granting of a waiver of the 30-day application period required under section 102(a) of the HUD Reform Act.
Andrew Hughes,
Deputy Secretary.

This action will set specifications for fishing year 2027 and fishing year 2028 (default) including the overfishing limit, acceptable biological catch/annual catch limit, days-at-sea, access area allocations for Limited Access vessels, quota and access area trip allocation to the Limited Access General Category (LAGC) Individual Fishing Quota component, Total Allowable Landings for the Northern Gulf of Maine management area, a target-Total Allowable Catch for LAGC incidental catch and set-asides for the observer and research programs. Other business will be discussed, if necessary.
Although non-emergency issues not contained on the agenda may come before this Council for discussion, those issues may not be the subject of formal action during this meeting. Council action will be restricted to those issues specifically listed in this notice and any issues arising after publication of this notice that require emergency action under section 305(c) of the Magnuson-Stevens Act, provided the public has been notified of the Council's intent to take final action to address the emergency. The public also should be aware that the meeting will be recorded. Consistent with
16 U.S.C. 1852
, a copy of the recording is available upon request.

AGENCY:
Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC), Treasury.
ACTION:
Notice and request for comment.
SUMMARY:
The OCC, as part of its continuing effort to reduce paperwork and respondent burden, invites comment on a continuing information collection, as required by the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995 (PRA). In accordance with the requirements of the PRA, the OCC may not conduct or sponsor, and the respondent is not required to respond to, an information collection unless it displays a currently valid Office of Management and Budget (OMB) control number. The OCC is soliciting comment concerning the renewal of its information collection titled, “Mandatory Contractual Stay Requirements for Qualified Financial Contracts.”
DATES:
Comments must be received by January 4, 2027.
ADDRESSES:
Commenters are encouraged to submit comments by email, if possible. You may submit comments by any of the following methods:
Email:
prainfo@occ.treas.gov
.
Mail:
Chief Counsel's Office, Attention: Comment Processing, Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, Attention: 1557-0339, 400 7th Street SW, Suite 1E-216, Washington, DC 20219.
Hand Delivery/Courier:
400 7th Street SW, Suite 1E-216, Washington, DC 20219.
Fax:
(571) 293-4835.
Instructions:
You must include “OCC” as the agency name and “1557-0339” in your comment. In general, the OCC will publish comments on
www.reginfo.gov
without change, including any business or personal information provided, such as name and address information, email addresses, or phone numbers. Comments received, including attachments and other supporting materials, are part of the public record and subject to public disclosure. Do not include any information in your comment or supporting materials that you consider confidential or inappropriate for public disclosure.
(
printed page 69310)
Following the close of this notice's 60-day comment period, the OCC will publish a second notice with a 30-day comment period. You may review comments and other related materials that pertain to this information collection beginning on the date of publication of the second notice for this collection by the method set forth in the next bullet.
Viewing Comments Electronically:
Go to
www.reginfo.gov
.
Hover over the “Information Collection Review” tab and click on “Information Collection Review” from the drop-down menu. From the “Currently under Review” drop-down menu, select “Department of the Treasury” and then click “submit.” This information collection can be located by searching OMB control number “1557-0339” or “Mandatory Contractual Stay Requirements for Qualified Financial Contracts.” Upon finding the appropriate information collection, click on the related “ICR Reference Number.” On the next screen, select “View Supporting Statement and Other Documents” and then click on the link to any comment listed at the bottom of the screen.
For assistance in navigating
www.reginfo.gov
,
please contact the Regulatory Information Service Center at (202) 482-7340.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Shaquita Merritt, Clearance Officer, (202) 649-5490, Chief Counsel's Office, Office of the Comptroller of the Currency, 400 7th Street SW, Washington, DC 20219. If you are deaf, hard of hearing, or have a speech disability, please dial 7-1-1 to access telecommunications relay services.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Under the PRA (
44 U.S.C. 3501
et seq.
), Federal agencies must obtain approval from the OMB for each collection of information that they conduct or sponsor. “Collection of information” is defined in
44 U.S.C. 3502(3)
and
5 CFR 1320.3(c)
to include agency requests or requirements, imposed on ten or more persons, that members of the public submit reports, keep records, or provide information to a third party. Section 3506(c)(2)(A) of title 44 generally requires Federal agencies to provide a 60-day notice in the
Federal Register
concerning each proposed collection of information, including each proposed extension of an existing collection of information, before submitting the collection to OMB for approval. To comply with this requirement, the OCC is publishing notice of the renewal of this collection.
Title:
Mandatory Contractual Stay Requirements for Qualified Financial Contracts.
OMB Control No.:
1557-0339.
Type of Review:
Regular.
Frequency of Response:
On occasion.
Affected Public:
A national bank or Federal savings association (FSA) (or any subsidiary of either) that is a subsidiary of a global systemically important bank holding company that has been designated pursuant to
12 CFR 252.82
of the Federal Reserve Board's Regulation YY; a national bank or FSA (or any subsidiary of either) that is a subsidiary of a global systemically important foreign banking organization designated pursuant to
12 CFR 252.87
of the Federal Reserve Board's Regulation YY; a Federal branch or agency (or any U.S. subsidiary of a Federal branch or agency) of a global systemically important foreign banking organization designated pursuant to
12 CFR 252.87
of the Federal Reserve Board's Regulation YY; and any national bank or FSA that is not under a bank holding company and that has more than $700 billion in total assets as reported on its most recent Consolidated Reports of Condition and Income (Call Report).
Abstract:
Under
12 CFR part 47
, a covered bank is required to ensure that a covered qualified financial contract (QFC) (1) contains a contractual stay-and-transfer provision analogous to the statutory stay-and-transfer provision imposed under Title II of the Dodd-Frank Wall Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act (see
12 U.S.C. 5390(c)(9)-(10)
) and in the Federal Deposit Insurance Act (see
12 U.S.C. 1821(e)(8)-(10)
) and (2) limits the exercise of default rights based on the insolvency of an affiliate of the covered bank. A covered bank is defined in
12 CFR 47.3(b)
as:
A national bank or FSA that has more than $700 billion in total assets as reported on the national bank's or FSA's most recent Call Report;
A national bank or FSA that is a subsidiary of a global systemically important bank holding company that has been designated pursuant to § 252.82 of this title (Federal Reserve Board Regulation YY) (
12 CFR 252.82
);
A national bank or FSA that is a subsidiary of a global systemically important foreign banking organization that has been designated pursuant to § 252.87 of this title (Federal Reserve Board Regulation YY) (
12 CFR 252.87
);
A Federal branch or agency, as defined in subpart B of this chapter (governing Federal branches and agencies), of a global systemically important foreign banking organization that has been designated pursuant to § 252.87 of this title (Federal Reserve Board Regulation YY) (
12 CFR 252.87
); or
A subsidiary of a covered bank, except, as defined in
12 CFR 47.3(b)(3)
, subsidiaries held in satisfaction of debt previously contracted in good faith, a portfolio concern that is controlled by a small business investment company, and certain companies engaged in the business of making public welfare investments.
The requirements are intended to enhance the resilience and the safety and soundness of Federally chartered and licensed financial institutions by addressing concerns relating to the exercise of default rights of certain financial contracts that could interfere with the orderly resolution of certain systemically important financial firms.
Covered banks may comply either by amending the contractual provisions of their QFCs consistent with the requirements of §§ 47.4 and 47.5 within a specified period of time or by adhering to the International Swaps and Derivatives Association 2015 Universal Resolution Stay Protocol or U.S. Protocol (ISDA Protocols). Alternatively,
12 CFR 47.6(b)(1)
provides that a covered bank may request that the OCC approve as compliant with the requirements of §§ 47.4 and 47.5 provisions of one or more forms of covered QFCs, or amendments to one or more forms of covered QFCs, with enhanced creditor protection conditions.
In order for the OCC to evaluate a covered bank's request,
12 CFR 47.6(b)(3)
requires that the request include (1) an analysis of the proposal that addresses a range of factors laid out in § 47.6(d) that are intended to facilitate the OCC's consideration of whether the proposal would be consistent with the restrictions and the main objectives of the rule; (2) a written legal opinion verifying that the covered bank's proposed provisions or amendments would be valid and enforceable under applicable laws of the relevant jurisdictions, including, in the case of proposed amendments, the validity and enforceability of the proposal to amend the covered QFCs; and (3) any additional information relevant to the OCC's approval that the OCC requests. The OCC will then use the information collected to determine whether the covered bank's proposed alternative creditor protection conditions comply with the requirements of the rule and achieve its policy goals.
(
printed page 69311)
Estimated Burden
Estimated Number of Respondents:
51.
Estimated Burden per Respondent:
140 hours.
Estimated Total Annual Burden:
7,140 hours.
Comments submitted in response to this notice will be summarized and included in the request for OMB approval. All comments will become a matter of public record. Comments are invited on:
(a) Whether the collection of information is necessary for the proper performance of the functions of the OCC, including whether the information has practical utility;
(b) The accuracy of the OCC's estimate of the burden of the collection of information;
(c) Ways to enhance the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected;
(d) Ways to minimize the burden of the collection on respondents, including through the use of automated collection techniques or other forms of information technology; and
(e) Estimates of capital or start-up costs and costs of operation, maintenance, and purchase of services to provide information.

[Project No. 943-152, P-943-153, P-943-154]
Take notice that on October 16, 2026, Public Utility District No. 1 of Chelan County, Washington (Chelan PUD) filed with the Commission three applications for approval of contracts for the sale of power from its licensed Rock Island Hydroelectric Project No. 943 for periods beyond the expiration of its existing license for the project.
[
1
]
The project is located on the Columbia River in Chelan and Douglas Counties, Washington.
Section 22 of the Federal Power Act,
16 U.S.C. 815
, provides that contracts for the sale and delivery of power for periods extending beyond the termination date of a license may be entered into upon the joint approval of the Commission and the appropriate state public service commission or other similar authority in the state in which the sale or delivery of power is made.
Anyone may submit comments, a protest, or a motion to intervene in accordance with the requirements of Rules of Practice and Procedure,
18 CFR 385.210
, .211, .214, respectively. In determining the appropriate action to take, the Commission will consider all protests or other comments filed, but only those who file a motion to intervene in accordance with the Commission's Rules may become a party to the proceeding. Any comments, protests, or motions to intervene must be received on or before the specified comment date for the particular application.
The Commission's Rules of Practice and Procedure require all intervenors filing documents with the Commission to serve a copy of that document on each person on the official service list for the project. Further, if an intervenor files comments or documents with the Commission relating to the merits of an issue that may affect the responsibilities of a particular resource agency, they must also serve a copy of the document on that resource agency.
Any filing must (1) bear in all capital letters the title “COMMENTS”, “PROTEST”, or “MOTION TO INTERVENE” as applicable; (2) set forth in the heading the name of the applicant and the project number of the application to which the filing responds; and (3) otherwise comply with the requirements of
18 CFR 385.2001
through
385.2005
. All comments, motions to intervene, or protests must set forth their evidentiary basis. Any filing made by an intervenor must be accompanied by proof of service on all persons listed in the service list prepared by the Commission in this proceeding, in accordance with
18 CFR 385.2010
.
The applications may be viewed on the Commission's website at
http://www.ferc.gov/​docs-filing/​elibrary.asp
using the “eLibrary Search Form” link. Enter the docket number (P-943-152, P-943-153, and/or P-943-154) in the docket number field to access the document. For assistance, contact FERC Online Support at
FERCOnlineSupport@ferc.gov
or toll-free at 1-866-208-3676, or for TTY, (202) 502-8659.
All comments must be filed by November 30, 2026, 5:00 p.m. Eastern Time.
The Commission strongly encourages electronic filing. Please file motions to intervene and protests using the Commission's eFiling system at
https://ferconline.ferc.gov/​FERCOnline.aspx
.
Commenters can submit brief comments up to 10,000 characters, without prior registration, using the eComment system at
https://ferconline.ferc.gov/​QuickComment.aspx
.
For assistance, please contact FERC Online Support at
FERCOnlineSupport@ferc.gov
,
(866) 208-3676 (toll free), or (202) 502-8659 (TTY). In lieu of electronic filing, please send a paper copy via U.S. Postal Service to: Debbie Anne A. Reese, Secretary, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, 888 First Street NE, Room 1A, Washington, DC 20426. Submissions sent via any other carrier must be addressed to: Debbie Anne A. Reese, Secretary, Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, 12225 Wilkins Avenue, Rockville, Maryland 20852. The first page of any filing should include docket number P-943-152, P-943-153, and/or P-943-154.
For public inquiries and assistance with making filings such as interventions, comments, or requests for rehearing, contact the Office of Public Participation at (202) 502-6595 or
OPP@ferc.gov
.
For further information, contact Chris Chaney at (202) 502-6778 or
christopher.chaney@ferc.gov
.
(Authority:
18 CFR 2.1
)
Dated: October 29, 2026.

SUMMARY:
In this document, the Media Bureau of the Federal Communications Commission (Commission) adopts an Order that removes a section of the Commission's Rules and references to that section to conform the

DATES:

Joseph.Price@fcc.gov
,

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
This is a summary of the document of the Media Bureau's Order, in MB Docket No. 98-204, GN Docket No. 25-133, DA 26-1058, adopted and released on October 1, 2026. The full text of this document is available for public inspection online at
https://docs.fcc.gov/​public/​attachments/​DA-26-1058A1.pdf
and via the search function on the Commission's Electronic Document Management System (EDOCS) web page at
http://www.fcc.gov/​ecfs
.
Alternative formats are available for people with disabilities (Braille, large print, electronic files, audio format, etc.) and reasonable accommodations (accessible format documents, sign language interpreters, CART, etc.) may be requested by sending an email to
fcc504@fcc.gov
or call the Consumer & Governmental Affairs Bureau at 202-418-0530 (voice), (202) 418-0432.
Synopsis
The Order of the Media Bureau of the Federal Communications Commission (Commission) conforms parts 73 and 74 of the Commission's rules to the decision of the Fifth Circuit Court of Appeals (Fifth Circuit) in
National Religious Broadcasters
v.
FCC,
138 F.4th 282 (5th Cir. 2025), nullifying § 73.3612. In the
Delete, Delete, Delete
proceeding, the Commission stated the goal of reviewing its rules “to identify and eliminate those that are unnecessary in light of current circumstances.”
Delete, Delete, Delete,
GN Docket No. 25-133, Public Notice, 40 FCC Rcd 1601, 1601 (OMR 2025). Consistent with that goal, the Media Bureau finds § 73.3612 of the Commission's rules “no longer ha[s] any operative effect,” and therefore should not remain in the Code of Federal Regulations (CFR).
Section 73.3612 of the Commission's rules, requiring broadcasters to annually submit information regarding their employees' race, ethnicity, and gender within specified job categories, was originally adopted in 1969 and has been suspended since 2001. In 2024, the Commission reinstated § 73.3612.
Review of the Commission's Broadcast & Cable Equal Employment Opportunity Rules & Policies,
MB Docket No. 98-204, Fourth Report and Order and Order on Reconsideration, 39 FCC Rcd 1791, 1798-00, paras. 14-16 (2024). Parties appealed to the Fifth Circuit, challenging the reporting obligation, while § 73.3612 remained deferred. The Fifth Circuit subsequently found the “[t]he FCC lacks statutory authority to require broadcasters to submit employment data under Form 395-B,”
National Religious Broadcasters,
138 F.4th at 296, and, as a result of the court vacating the Commission's 2024 order, the text of § 73.3612 that currently appears in the CFR, and references to § 73.3612 in the CFR, have no legal effect and are obsolete. Accordingly, the Media Bureau of the Commission deletes § 73.3612 and references to § 73.3612 from parts 73 and 74 of the Commission's rules, finding that doing so has no effect on the scope and nature of the currently enforceable Commission requirements and effectuates the Fifth Circuit's holding in
National Religious Broadcasters.
Pursuant to the good cause exception under
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B)
, because we are simply conforming the text of the Commission's rules in the CFR to reflect the court's decision in
National Religious Broadcasters,
and we are not taking any independent action or exercising any discretion, we find that notice and the opportunity for public comment are unnecessary for this action. For the same reason, pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 553(d)
, this action will be effective immediately upon publication in the
Federal Register
.
The changes to parts 73 and 74 of the Commission's rules to conform to the Fifth Circuit decision in
National Religious Broadcasters
are reflected in Appendix A.
Accordingly,
it is ordered
that parts 73 and 74 of the Commission's rules, Title 47, are amended as set forth in Appendix A, effective upon publication in the
Federal Register
.
This action is taken pursuant to the authority contained in sections 4(i), 4(j), and 155(c) of the Communications Act of 1934, as amended,
47 U.S.C. 154(i)
,
154(j)
,
155(c)
, and sections 0.61 and 0.283(e) of the Commission's rules,
47 CFR 0.61
,
0.283(e)
.
The Bureau has determined, and the Administrator of the Office of Information and Regulatory Affairs, Office of Management and Budget, concurs that this rule is non-major under the Congressional Review Act,
5 U.S.C. 804(2)
. The Commission will send a copy of this Order to Congress and the Government Accountability Office pursuant to
5 U.S.C. 801(a)(1)(A)
.

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
The EPA finalized the Lime Manufacturing NESHAP technology review on July 16, 2024.
[
1
]
Following publication of this final rule, the EPA discovered an error in the regulatory text and is correcting the error in this action.
Specifically, the EPA is revising the Lime Manufacturing NESHAP July 16, 2024, final rule (2024 final rule) to correct 40 Code of Federal Regulations (CFR) part 63 section 7114. In the 2024 final rule amendatory text,
40 CFR 63.7114
was revised to include two new paragraphs describing the requirements for the emissions averaging compliance option. These additions were added to the section as paragraphs (b) and (c). Paragraph (c)(2) instructs lime manufacturing plants that chose to comply with emissions averaging for HCl or mercury to develop and submit to the applicable regulatory authority for review and approval, an implementation plan for emission averaging no later than 180 days before the date the facility intends to demonstrate compliance. The EPA is revising the 180-day plan submittal requirement to 60 days, as the Agency intended. In the 2024 final rule preamble, under section
E. What other changes have been made to the NESHAP?,
the EPA explains that the deadline for submitting the emissions averaging plan before the compliance demonstration was adjusted from 180 days, as proposed, to 60 days. Following publication of the 2024 final rule, the EPA discovered the regulatory text was not updated to reflect this change.
The correction in this action makes the regulatory text consistent with what the preamble to the 2024 final rule describes. The EPA's authority for the rulemaking procedures followed in this action is provided by the Administrative Procedure Act (APA),
5 U.S.C. 553
. In general, an agency issuing a rule must provide prior notice and an opportunity for public comment, but APA section 553(b)(B) includes an exemption from notice-and-comment requirements “when the agency for good cause finds (and incorporates the finding and a brief statement of reasons therefor in the rule issued) that notice and public procedure thereon are impracticable, unnecessary, or contrary to the public interest.” The EPA has determined that there is good cause for making this rule final without prior proposal and opportunity for comment because the changes to the rule are minor, noncontroversial in nature, and correct an inadvertent typographical error. The change aligns regulatory text with the EPA's expressed intent in the 2024 final rule preamble and does not substantively change the requirements of the 2024 final rule except to the extent necessary to align the regulatory text with the EPA's intent, which the preamble expressly states. Thus, the corrected regulatory text in this action has already had notice and opportunity for public comment, rendering further notice and opportunity for public comment unnecessary. The EPA finds that this constitutes good cause under
5 U.S.C. 553(b)(B)
.
For a complete discussion of all the statutes, executive orders and administrative requirements applicable to this action, see the final rule published in the Rules and Regulations section of the

SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Information Collection Request Title:
Faculty Loan Repayment Program OMB No. 0906-0082—Revision.
Abstract:
HRSA administers the Faculty Loan Repayment Program (FLRP). FLRP provides health professionals from disadvantaged backgrounds, defined as a geographic and/or economic vulnerability, the opportunity to enter into a contract with HHS to receive repayment of qualifying educational loans in exchange for a minimum of 2 years of service as a full-time or part-time faculty member at an eligible health professions school. The applicant completes and submits an electronic application that identifies for the Secretary of HHS that the applicant comes from an economically or geographically vulnerable background, has a contract with an eligible health professions school to serve as a full-time or part-time faculty member for a minimum of 2 years, and has qualifying outstanding educational loans. In addition, for each undergraduate and/or graduate loan for which repayment is sought, the applicant is required to submit loan documentation verifying the establishment of the educational loan(s) and lender account statements, promissory notes including the original date, and current balance of the outstanding educational loan(s).
This revised ICR contains two new forms. The first is the Employer's Agreement to Loan Repayment Match/Request for a Waiver of the Loan Repayment Match form, which is needed to ensure applicant eligibility and school compliance with the statute. The second is the Semi-annual In-Service Verification form, which is sent to current participants and the institution twice each year to confirm their employment status. The addition of these forms and an increased number of respondents/applicants to the FLRP will increase the estimated burden hours.
This proposed ICR also contains updated terminology with respect to Disadvantaged Background and accompanying definitions by updating the following:
Changing form title to “Certification Regarding Vulnerable Background,”
Replacing “disadvantaged” with “vulnerable” throughout the form, and
Replacing “environmentally disadvantaged” with “geographically vulnerable.”
These changes are needed to align the form with the Administration's priority of reinforcing programs that direct resources to areas of greatest need to improve health outcomes. The FLRP statute defines eligible individuals as coming from “disadvantaged backgrounds” (
42 U.S.C. 293b(a)
) but does not define the term. HRSA's use of “vulnerable background” operationalizes the statutory term by identifying individuals whose geographic or economic circumstances inhibited their ability to obtain the knowledge, skills, and abilities required to enroll in and graduate from an eligible health professions school. This approach remains consistent with the statute's intent while incorporating more current terminology. These updates were made throughout the form to improve consistency and help ensure that applicants and reviewers understand the criteria using current terminology.
FLRP will define “vulnerable background” as “coming from a geographically vulnerable background or an economically vulnerable background that has inhibited the individual from obtaining the knowledge, skills, and abilities required to enroll in and graduate from an eligible health professions school.”
Examples of indicators that an individual comes from a geographically vulnerable background include, but are not limited to:
(
printed page 69262)
Individuals who graduated from a high school with low average SAT/ACT scores or below-average state test results.
Individuals from a school district where 50 percent or less of graduates go to college.
Individuals raised in households where language barriers affected education access.
Individuals from a high school where at least 30 percent of enrolled students are eligible for free or reduced-price lunch.
Individuals who are the first generation in their family to attend college.
An individual from an economically vulnerable background is defined as someone who:
Comes from a low-income family. Low-income family is defined as a family that has an annual income below the 200 percent of the Department's poverty guidelines;
Is eligible for a Pell Grant; and/or
Comes from a family that receives public assistance (
e.g.,
Temporary Assistance to Needy Families, Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, Medicaid, public housing).
The Secretary of HHS defines a `low-income family' for programs included in Titles III, VII, and VIII of the Public Health Service Act as having an annual income that does not exceed 200 percent of the Department's poverty guidelines, which are based on the U.S. Census Bureau's low-income threshold. This threshold is simplified to facilitate the determination of financial eligibility for some federal programs and further adjusted by the Secretary of HHS based on the Consumer Price Index. Family is defined a group of two or more individuals related by birth, marriage, or adoption who live together, or an individual who is not living with any relatives.

SUMMARY:
The FAA proposes to adopt a new airworthiness directive (AD) for certain Airbus Helicopters Model AS350B2, AS350B3, and EC130B4 helicopters. This proposed AD was prompted by a report of an occurrence of partial blocking of a pilot pedal. This proposed AD would require modifying and reidentifying an affected fuse cover and would prohibit installing an affected fuse cover on any helicopter. The FAA is proposing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.

Background
EASA, which is the Technical Agent for the Member States of the European Union, has issued EASA AD 2026-0052R2, dated September 24, 2026 (EASA AD 2026-0052R2) (also referred to as the MCAI), to correct an unsafe condition on certain Airbus Helicopters Model AS 350 B2, AS 350 B3, and EC 130 B4 helicopters. The MCAI states that an occurrence of partial blocking of the pilot pedal was reported. The MCAI also states further investigation indicated that this event was caused by an interference between the left pedal of the pedal block and the partially detached fuse cover of the circuit breaker panel. This condition, if not corrected, could result in reduced yaw control of the helicopter.
You may examine the MCAI in the AD docket at
regulations.gov
under Docket No. FAA-2026-13795.
Material Incorporated by Reference Under
1 CFR Part 51
The FAA reviewed EASA AD 2026-0052R2, which specifies procedures for modifying and reidentifying a fuse cover with part number (P/N) 350A76-2395-20, P/N 350A76-2395-21, or P/N 350A76-2395-23, installed on a certain part-numbered control unit, except those which have been modified and reidentified. EASA AD 2026-0052R2 also prohibits installing an affected fuse cover on any affected helicopter.
This material is reasonably available because the interested parties have access to it through their normal course of business or by the means identified in
ADDRESSES
.

These products have been approved by the civil aviation authority (CAA) of another country and are approved for operation in the United States. Pursuant to the FAA's bilateral agreement with this State of Design Authority, that authority has notified the FAA of the unsafe condition described in the MCAI referenced above. The FAA is issuing this NPRM after determining that the unsafe condition described previously is likely to exist or develop on other products of the same type design.

Authority for This Rulemaking
Title 49 of the United States Code specifies the FAA's authority to issue rules on aviation safety. Subtitle I, section 106, describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII: Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the Agency's authority.
The FAA is issuing this rulemaking under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart III, Section 44701: General requirements. I. Executive Summary
A. Purpose and Scope of the Regulatory Action
PHMSA has been regulating the safety of LNG facilities for more than five decades. When PHMSA issued the first Federal safety standards in 1970, the U.S. LNG industry comprised mostly relatively small “peak-shaving” facilities used to liquefy and store natural gas for delivery to local markets during times of peak demand. The handful of large-scale LNG facilities at that time were primarily built to import natural gas for domestic consumption. The U.S. LNG industry did not have a significant role as an exporter of natural gas.
Market conditions have changed dramatically since the 1970s. U.S. natural gas production has increased significantly, particularly in the past two decades as technological advancements in the oil and gas industry have led to the development of energy resources from the Nation's shale plays. Domestic natural gas demand has continued to grow, and an increasing number of U.S.-based facilities are exporting LNG to foreign markets. These changes have created a need for the construction of new LNG facilities and for the expansion of existing LNG facilities.
Modern operational and maintenance practices within the LNG industry are considerably more sophisticated and robust, reflecting many thousands of hours of experience since the 1970s. New technologies have emerged, such as “membrane” tanks (which employ a thin cryogenic steel inner liner with a load-bearing, concrete outer tank—an approach offering improved storage capacity, reduced material costs, and faster construction schedules than earlier LNG storage tank designs) and pipe-in-pipe (PIP) transfer systems (which provide enhanced containment of releases from cryogenic piping).
PHMSA's oversight of the LNG industry has not kept pace with these dramatic changes. PHMSA's LNG regulations are largely based on the 2001 edition of an industry standard, NFPA 59A,
Standard for the Production, Storage, and Handling of Liquefied Natural Gas (LNG),
and have not been updated since 2006. NFPA 59A-2001 is now seven editions out of date, and multiple stakeholders have called on PHMSA to update its regulations to account for the latest practices in the siting, design, construction, operation, and maintenance of LNG facilities. For example, in the Protecting our Infrastructure of Pipelines and Enhancing Safety Act of 2016 (PIPES Act of 2016), Congress directed PHMSA to develop regulations for permanent, small-scale LNG facilities, an issue specifically addressed in the more recent editions of NFPA 59A.
[
1
]
In the Protecting our Infrastructure of Pipelines and Enhancing Safety Act of 2020 (PIPES Act of 2020), Congress directed PHMSA to develop alternative, risk-based operations and maintenance requirements for large-scale LNG facilities, an approach consistent with modern regulatory frameworks that apply in other industries.
[
2
]
The Government Accountability Office (GAO) has also advised PHMSA to update its regulations to align better with current editions of consensus industry standards.
[
3
]
To address these concerns, PHMSA proposes a comprehensive revision to its safety standards for LNG facilities. The proposed amendments would enhance public safety by incorporating the latest consensus industry standards for the siting, design, construction, operation, and maintenance of LNG facilities. These changes will promote the use of new technologies, reduce unnecessary barriers to investment, and provide regulatory certainty for
(
printed page 69315)
interested stakeholders. PHMSA's proposals will also address outstanding Congressional mandates and GAO recommendations and advance the President's commitments to unleashing American energy, sustaining U.S. defense operations, and ensuring the energy security of the U.S. and its allies.
B. Summary of the Major Regulatory Provisions
Below is a high-level summary of the most substantial changes proposed in this document. This NPRM discusses each change in more detail in the “Section-by-Section Discussion of the Proposed Changes.”
1. Calibrating Reporting Requirements to Public Safety Risks
PHMSA proposes to amend the reporting requirements for safety-related conditions and incidents. First, PHMSA proposes to clarify that operators of LNG facilities must report safety-related conditions and incidents during initial startup. This clarification would help ensure that operators are reporting incidents and safety-related conditions that occur at the earliest phase in the operational lifetime of an LNG facility, which is critical in determining its long-term integrity. PHMSA also proposes to broaden the definition of incidents and safety-related conditions to encompass hazardous fluids beyond LNG alone; this proposed change will improve risk mitigation and incident response by focusing on the various materials involved in gas processing activities at LNG facilities. Second, PHMSA proposes to revise the incident and annual report forms to eliminate content with little or no safety value, and to update the operator identification number (OPID) and annual report forms to accommodate the new requirements for permanent, small-scale LNG facilities in subpart D.
2. Incorporation by Reference Updated Editions of Leading Industry Standards
PHMSA proposes to incorporate by reference the 2026 edition of NFPA 59A.
[
4
]
PHMSA currently incorporates the 2001 edition of NFPA 59A for most purposes. Incorporating the 2026 edition is consistent with PHMSA's longstanding practice of integrating NFPA 59A as a key component of its regulations for LNG facilities. As part of that process, PHMSA proposes to redesignate or to remove certain duplicative or unnecessary regulatory requirements and to modify or to supplement certain provisions in NFPA 59A-2026 (
e.g.,
design wind resistance of certain LNG facilities; design spill assumptions in hazard modeling) to accommodate significant public safety risks or to facilitate implementation.
Incorporating NFPA 59A-2026 would enhance the requirements for the siting, design, installation, construction, operations, and maintenance of LNG facilities and align PHMSA's regulations with the latest safety-enhancing practices and technologies. It would also reduce certain compliance costs by allowing LNG operators to use those practices and technologies without obtaining special permits or waivers and address outstanding Congressional mandates and GAO recommendations.
3. Improved Alignment Between Facility Siting Requirements and Safety Risks
PHMSA proposes to incorporate by reference the traditional, prescriptive siting requirements in chapter 5 of NFPA 59A-2026. Incorporating chapter 5 would expand the universe of hazards operators must evaluate to comply with the part 193, subpart B siting requirements, ensuring that those analyses are consistent with current knowledge of the public safety risks posed by releases of hazardous fluids from LNG facilities.
PHMSA also proposes to incorporate the new risk-based siting requirements in chapter 19 (
Performance-Based LNG Plant Siting Using Quantitative Risk Analysis (QRA)
) of NFPA 59A-2026. PHMSA expects that the QRA-based approach will improve facility safety by allowing a more sophisticated understanding of public safety risks, enhancing the allocation of resources, and incentivizing deployment of innovative operational practices and technology. PHMSA expects that improved flexibility regarding LNG facility siting and internal layout under the QRA-based approach could enable investment in additional capacity at existing locations.
4. Introduction of Targeted Requirements for Permanent, Small-Scale LNG Facilities
PHMSA proposes to establish requirements for permanent, small-scale LNG facilities by incorporating chapter 17 of NFPA 59A-2026 by reference into a new subpart D. Permanent, small-scale LNG facilities entail lower risks to public safety and the environment than larger LNG facilities, primarily due to their distinguishable liquefaction processes, lower liquefaction capacity, and smaller LNG storage volumes, and should be regulated accordingly. Incorporating the chapter 17 requirements would also address the rulemaking mandate in section 27(b) of the PIPES Act of 2016 for permanent, small-scale LNG facilities.
5. Integration of an Alternative, Risk-based Operations and Maintenance Framework
Consistent with section 110 of the PIPES Act of 2020, PHMSA proposes to adopt an alternative, risk-based operations and maintenance (O&M) program for FERC-jurisdictional LNG facilities in a new subpart F. The risk-based O&M alternative would be a structured program with procedures developed and implemented to identify, to evaluate, and to mitigate or to eliminate hazards and the resulting risks. Operators employing this approach would have flexibility to tailor a risk-based approach to the specific risks from their facilities. Operators electing to use the risk-based O&M alternative would be required to submit an implementation plan specifying a timeline for integration of program elements.
C. Costs and Benefits
PHMSA estimates the annualized cost savings from the proposed rule to be approximately $98 million (discounted at three percent). PHMSA notes that some of the new compliance costs and many of the cost savings of the proposed rule could not be quantified based on the available data.
PHMSA anticipates significant unquantified safety benefits would result from adopting the safety-enhancing elements of NFPA 59A-2026, as supplemented and qualified by other proposed part 193 amendments. Because LNG facilities are complex systems whose failure generally involves multiple “but for” causes, PHMSA was not able to quantify a reduction in incident risk pursuant to the proposed rule. Other unquantified benefits include increased flexibility for LNG facility siting under the QRA-based approach in NFPA 59A-2026 chapter 19, increased regulatory flexibility for permanent, small-scale LNG facilities subject to the requirements in NFPA 59A-2026 chapter 17, and the use of new technologies, such as membrane tanks, single-walled ASME (American Society of Mechanical Engineers) containers, and PIP systems, which PHMSA was not able to quantify due to uncertainty around potential uptake of the proposed flexibilities.
The preliminary regulatory impact analysis (PRIA) provided in the docket for this rulemaking includes additional information about the costs, benefits,

printed page 69316)
and other impacts of the proposed rule. The PRIA's quantification of costs and benefits reflects assumptions and estimates based on the information and data available. PHMSA requests information and data from the public regarding the PRIA's evaluation of expected costs and benefits of its proposed requirements. PHMSA has preliminarily determined that, notwithstanding the uncertainties and data limitations discussed in the PRIA, the proposals in the NPRM would be justified by their corresponding compliance costs savings, enhanced regulatory flexibility, or improved public safety benefits.
II. Background
A. LNG as an Energy Source, Industry Growth, and Regulatory Safety
1. LNG as an Energy Source
Natural gas is vital to the energy and economic security of the United States and its allies abroad, serving as an economic driver and essential fuel source for residential, commercial, and industrial purposes. Total annual U.S. natural gas consumption has increased from 5.0 Tcf in 1949 to 33.5 Tcf in 2025.
[
5
]
Global natural gas consumption similarly is expected to grow from 152.9 Tcf to 194.3 Tcf by 2050 due to increasing demand in emerging markets and developing economies.
[
6
]
Domestic U.S. and international demand for natural gas has made it an important driver of the U.S. economy; a smaller U.S. natural gas sector in 2018 contributed over 3.4 million jobs and $408 billion to U.S. Gross Domestic Product (GDP).
[
7
]
Increased reliance on natural gas from a variety of applications is contributing to this growing demand. First, natural gas is a critical source of electric power generation capacity and grid stability. In addition to providing dispatchable electricity, natural gas electric power generation also supplies grid attributes (
e.g.,
inertia) increasingly vital to grid stability as more intermittent renewable energy generation capacity joins the grid and baseload coal and nuclear plants retire. Second, natural gas is essential for many industrial feedstock and process heat applications, as well as commercial and residential heating and cooking purposes. Third, natural gas is an increasingly vital fuel source in the transportation sector, powering maritime vessels (
i.e.,
marine bunkering), fueling truck fleets, and providing an alternative gas supply during pipeline testing activities.
But many regions—both within the United States and the wider world—do not have reliable access to natural gas. Some regions are far-removed from natural gas supply reservoirs; others have limited pipeline infrastructure enabling transportation of natural gas in gaseous form or are vulnerable to supply interruptions on natural gas pipelines. Reliable natural gas supply in such circumstances may turn on access to LNG—natural gas that has been cooled to low temperatures (minus 260 °F or minus 162 °C) and converted to a liquid state. This conversion process, known as liquefaction, reduces the volume of natural gas to approximately 1/600th of its volume in a gaseous state. The reduction in volume makes LNG efficient for transportation and storage purposes in areas with limited natural gas resources or limited pipeline supply of natural gas.
Prior to liquefaction, the natural gas must be treated (pre-treatment) to remove impurities and extract heavy hydrocarbons (extraction). The pre-treatment, hydrocarbon extraction, and liquefaction processes may involve a number of hazardous fluids—including materials that are flammable (
e.g.,
methane, ethane, ethylene, propane, butane, pentane, other heavy hydrocarbons including aromatic hydrocarbons, hydrogen sulfide, and anhydrous ammonia); toxic (
e.g.,
aromatic hydrocarbons, hydrogen sulfide, and anhydrous ammonia); and corrosive (
e.g.,
anhydrous ammonia, amine solution, and aromatic hydrocarbons). Such hazardous materials can be present in either gaseous or liquid form at different stages of these processes. Larger LNG facilities, such as import or export terminals, will typically employ more complex liquefaction processes (and different, and larger quantities of, hazardous fluids) than smaller LNG facilities, such as peak shavers and mobile and temporary facilities. After liquefaction, LNG is stored and transported in specialized tanks that are insulated and refrigerated to maintain low temperatures. When needed for use, LNG undergoes a regasification process in which it is warmed and converted back into its gaseous state. The vaporized natural gas can then be injected into a pipeline system for distribution or used as fuel for natural gas-operated equipment.
The flexibility arising from the transportation and storage of LNG has made it a vital element in natural gas supply infrastructures around the world. Within the United States, LNG peak shaving facilities provide local customers with access to natural gas during times of peak demand. There is also increasing interest in developing small-scale, mobile, or temporary LNG facilities to support novel applications (
e.g.,
ensuring continuity of power to data centers and for industrial applications). And U.S. LNG export facilities are a critical energy resource for a variety of countries—including strategic U.S. allies in Asia and Europe—which either have limited native energy resources, desires to diversify their energy portfolios, or plans to transition away from coal for electric power and process heat generation. Recent supply disruptions of LNG exports from international LNG suppliers like Qatar have also underscored the unique value of U.S. LNG exports to the energy security of America's trading partners.
2. Growth and Increasing Domestic and International Significance of the U.S. LNG Industry
The U.S. LNG industry has undergone significant changes in the two decades since PHMSA last amended its part 193 regulations. The design and configuration of the 117 regulated LNG facilities in service at that time reflected the more limited role of natural gas within the domestic U.S. economy and consisted mostly of the following:
Peak-shaving plants designed to store surplus natural gas for use during high demand periods, such as summer and winter. Peak-shaving plants ensure reliability by liquefying and storing natural gas when demand is low and re-gasifying and distributing natural gas when demand is high. Natural gas shortages in the 1970s drove a wave of construction of peak-shaving plants. Operators began slowly retiring those plants in subsequent decades. The number of peak-shaving plants decreased from 75 in 2006 to 67 in 2018.
Satellite plants serving peak-shaving purposes but lacking the processing equipment required to convert natural gas to LNG. Specially equipped trucks (or tanks transported on rail flatcars) deliver LNG to satellite plants, where the LNG is stored and later re-gasified and injected into natural gas distribution systems to meet
(
printed page 69317)
demand. In 2006, there were 23 satellite plants.
Mobile and temporary LNG plants designed to be easily movable rather than permanent structures. Mobile LNG plants, such as skid-mounted or trailer-mounted units, can be relocated as needed. Temporary LNG plants are used for short-term applications, providing supply during planned construction and maintenance activities or to meet unanticipated demand. Mobile and temporary LNG plants are compact and often located near end users to minimize transportation costs and enhance accessibility. In 2006, there were nine mobile and temporary facilities.
Large-scale terminals for importing LNG for domestic use, exporting LNG to foreign markets, or both. In 2006, the United States was a net importer of natural gas; there were four import terminals and one export terminal representing an aggregate 4.877 Bcf/d vaporization capacity. These terminals played a relatively small role in the U.S. and global energy economy in 2006.
The shale gas revolution has fundamentally reshaped domestic and international energy markets over the past two decades. Newly abundant natural gas supplies have resulted in a rapid expansion of natural gas power generation capacity and industrial and commercial applications within the United States—a trend that is expected to accelerate due to onshoring of industrial capacity and skyrocketing demand for continuous electric generation capacity supporting super intelligence and data centers.
[
8
]
The number of part 193-regulated U.S. LNG facilities has increased in response to these recent market developments. As of 2025, there are 69 peak shaving plants, many of which are larger, and more complex, than the smaller plants typical in 2006. The number of other PHMSA-jurisdictional LNG plants has increased as well: in 2004, there were 22 satellite plants, 8 mobile or temporary facilities, and 4 import terminals (representing 4.877 Bcf/d import capacity); in 2025 there were 32 satellite plants, 43 mobile or temporary facilities, and 9 import terminals (representing 14.934 Bcf/d import capacity). Abundant natural gas supplies have also resulted in proliferation of so-called “small-scale” applications of LNG catering to niche markets, including off-grid power generation, localized peak-shaving, industrial equipment usage (such as oil and gas drilling equipment), and transportation fuels for vehicles, rail, or maritime use.
[
9
]
But the most significant change since 2006 has been the emergence of enormous U.S. natural gas export capacity. The United States now boasts eight operational, PHMSA-jurisdictional export terminals providing ca. 17.0 Bcf/d of capacity. Sixteen additional projects (providing an additional ca. 31.28 Bcf/d capacity) either are in construction or are expected to begin construction in the near future.
[
10
]
And the United States—a net importer of natural gas in 2006—exported approximately 15.1 Bcf/d of LNG in 2024, making it the world's largest LNG exporter, responsible for roughly 21 percent of worldwide LNG supply.
LNG exports have become critical to U.S. economic prosperity and national security. A 2026 study predicts that through 2040 U.S. LNG exports will contribute an aggregate of around $1.4 trillion to U.S. GDP, more than $2.9 trillion in total revenues for U.S. businesses, $206 billion in Federal and State tax revenues, and more than $630 billion in labor income. The industry will support an average of over a half-million U.S. jobs annually.
[
11
]
U.S. LNG exports also reduce trade deficits with economic competitors and have become a focal point for U.S. policymakers in recent tariff negotiations with U.S. trading partners.
[
12
]
U.S. LNG exports are a vital form of support for key U.S. allies as well. Europe and Asia were the top destinations for U.S. LNG exports in 2025.
[
13
]
Japan alone imported 222.9 Bcf of U.S. LNG in 2025, roughly 4.0 percent of the U.S. LNG exports for 2025. The Netherlands imported 645.8 Bcf of U.S. LNG in 2025, the most of any country and roughly 11.7 percent of U.S. LNG exports that year.
[
14
]
Exports to Europe increased following Russia's invasion of Ukraine; in 2022, Europe received 69 percent of all LNG exports from the United States, up from 34 percent in 2021. From January through November 2025, Europe received 68 percent of U.S.-origin volumes.

3. The Regulatory Framework and Industry Efforts To Ensure LNG Facility Safety
Multiple Federal agencies play a role in ensuring the safety of onshore LNG facilities.

16

These agencies exercise their respective authorities through a variety of administrative tools—including implementing regulations, guidance, orders, and enforcement actions—that can govern different phases of the lifecycle (including authorization, construction, and operations) of LNG facilities. The States also have a role in administering the Federal safety framework for intrastate LNG facilities. Industry, too, has pursued continuous safety improvement, developing voluntary (but widely adopted) consensus and industry codes, standards, recommended practices, guidelines reflecting safety-enhancing best practices, and technological advances that have outpaced the development of Federal safety regulatory regimes. These mutually reinforcing approaches have yielded a strong historical safety record for all PHMSA-jurisdictional LNG facilities.

b. Industry Efforts Promoting LNG Facility Safety
The LNG industry plays an active role in ensuring the safety of PHMSA-jurisdictional LNG facilities, particularly through the development of voluntary consensus industry standards and recommended practices. The leading industry standard for LNG facilities is NFPA 59A. First published in 1967, PHMSA has incorporated NFPA 59A by reference into the Federal safety standards for LNG facilities since 1972.
[
44
]
The most recent edition of NFPA 59A, published in 2026, includes mandatory standards for the siting, design, construction, operation, and maintenance of LNG facilities. This edition incorporates a comprehensive list of other consensus industry standards addressing particular topics as well as several informational annexes providing guidance to facilitate compliance with its mandatory provisions.
[
45
]
A technical committee (Technical Committee) is responsible for drafting each edition of NFPA 59A to ensure its provisions reflect the latest safety-enhancing advances in operator practices and technologies. The Technical Committee consists of 35 principal experts and 21 alternates from State and Federal government and the LNG industry. Collectively, the Technical Committee has extensive expertise on all aspects of LNG safety. PHMSA and FERC are among the government participants on the Technical Committee, with representatives of each of those agencies serving as voting members.
The process employed by the Technical Committee in updating NFPA 59A has been accredited by the American National Standards Institute (ANSI). Development of each edition of NFPA 59A lasts between three to five years and involves a four-step process: (1) public input; (2) public comment; (3) NFPA Technical Committee meeting; and (4) standards council action. Public input from industry stakeholders and members of the general public is accepted for consideration in the Technical Committee's development of the initial draft of an updated edition. Once the initial draft is developed, the Technical Committee posts that initial draft (accompanied by reports summarizing and responding to input from the public and Technical Committee members) on a publicly available website and solicits comments. After analyzing any comments received, the Technical Committee prepares the second draft (and potentially subsequent drafts)
(
printed page 69321)
pursuant to a similar process and posts its responses to the comments received on the previous draft. After the Technical Committee approves the revised draft, the NFPA Standards Council approves issuance of the updated standard.
c. The LNG Industry's Strong Safety Record Since 2006
The U.S. LNG industry has a remarkably strong safety record. Since 2010, there has been more than a 50 percent increase in the number of all PHMSA-jurisdictional LNG facilities—121 facilities in 2010 compared to the 181 facilities in 2024. That increase has not led to more incidents. Incident data across all PHMSA-jurisdictional LNG facilities shows that there have been three or fewer significant incidents reported in each of the past 15 years.
[
46
]
In 11 out of those 15 years, one or fewer significant incidents were reported. Zero significant incidents were reported in six of those years, and only two reportable injuries occurred during that entire 15-year period—one at a peak shaving facility in 2014 and one at a mobile and temporary facility in 2023. And there was only a single fatality (at a mobile/temporary facility—not the more complex LNG export or peak shaving facilities).
The same strong safety record holds if the 15-year data is examined for each type of LNG facility. For LNG export facilities, there were no significant incidents reported in 10 out of the 15 years even as the number of those facilities has more than doubled between 2010 and 2024. Peak shaving facilities reported only three significant incidents, and mobile and temporary LNG facilities had only one significant incident—even as the number of each of those facilities increased since 2010. And non-marine baseload and satellite facilities had no significant incidents during the 15-year period even as the number of those facilities increased more than 100 percent.
4. Broad Demand for Updated PHMSA Regulations on LNG Facility Safety
Despite the significant changes that have occurred throughout the LNG industry, PHMSA has not updated its part 193 regulations since 2006. Instead, PHMSA has leaned more heavily on guidance in the form of its LNG FAQs implementing its part 193 regulations to accommodate innovations in facility design, function, construction and operational practices, and technology. But PHMSA's LNG FAQs—which have been updated nine times since their introduction in 2014—are not legally binding and do not provide interested stakeholders with the regulatory certainty needed to make informed decisions. PHMSA's delay in updating its part 193 regulations has in turn encouraged FERC to exercise its statutory authority to impose more legally binding, safety-related conditions in authorizing new LNG projects. Although this case-by-case approach is done with PHMSA and USCG as cooperating agencies and includes a fairly consistent set of conditions, PHMSA's or USCG's recommendations are subject to FERC's consideration, which can inject further uncertainty into the regulatory framework. As discussed in more detail below, a broad consensus has been reached about the need to update part 193 regulations to address these and other concerns.
