E. Section 191.23—Reporting Safety-Related Conditions
PHMSA proposes to revise the safety-related condition reporting requirements for LNG facilities to enhance safety monitoring and oversight. These changes would expand the scope of reporting to include releases of all hazardous fluids at LNG facilities and clarify that safety-related conditions during initial start-up (but not during earlier commissioning activities) must be reported.
First, PHMSA proposes to revise the list of safety-related conditions in § 191.23(a) to include the release of hazardous fluids involved in the processing of LNG. As discussed earlier, PHMSA proposes in § 191.3 to expand the definition of an “incident” to include releases of all hazardous fluids at an LNG facility. That change would require operators to notify PHMSA of incidents that involved releases of hazardous fluids. Similarly, PHMSA proposes to revise the notification requirements at § 191.23 to specify that releases of hazardous fluids at an LNG facility are reportable safety-related conditions. Including all hazardous fluids would ensure that PHMSA has a complete picture of safety-related conditions and would help identify potential risks and hazards associated with the release of substances used in processing activities—not just LNG—at an LNG facility.
Second, PHMSA proposes in § 191.23 to add a new paragraph (c) to clarify that each operator of an LNG facility must report any safety-related condition that occurs during initial startup as equipment and components begin commercial operation. Currently, § 191.23 requires LNG operators to notify PHMSA of safety-related conditions that occur while an LNG facility is “in service.” PHMSA has interpreted “in service” for these purposes to mean any time a hazardous fluid is introduced into an LNG facility, including during both commissioning and subsequent initial startup. PHMSA understands that historical reading is appropriate as to the latter but not the former.
Safety-related conditions present risks that are relevant throughout the life of

C. Subpart B—LNG Facility Siting
PHMSA's siting requirements for LNG facilities date to a rulemaking proceeding initiated in the 1970s and completed in 1980. As with the other regulations adopted in that proceeding, PHMSA incorporated multiple levels of conservatism into the siting requirements to address uncertainties and limitations in the data available at that time. Although PHMSA has updated certain aspects of those requirements over time, including by approving more modern versions of the models used to determine the amount of property that must be owned or controlled to site an LNG facility at a particular location, the underlying conservatism embodied in the 1980 regulations has remained largely unchanged. That degree of conservatism is no longer justified given the significant advancements in LNG safety that have occurred in the past two decades, many of which are reflected in the enhanced safety requirements throughout recent editions of NFPA 59A.
As discussed in more detail below, PHMSA is proposing substantial revisions to its siting requirements to address these concerns. First, PHMSA proposes adopting an updated version of the traditional, prescriptive approach for siting LNG facilities. The prescriptive approach would be consistent with the provisions in NFPA 59A-2026 chapter 5 and would serve as the default set of siting requirements. Second, PHMSA proposes adopting a more sophisticated quantitative risk assessment (QRA)-based approach for siting LNG facilities. The QRA-based approach would be consistent with the provisions in NFPA 59A-2026 chapter 19 and would only apply on an elective basis.
PHMSA believes that adopting these changes would eliminate much of the unnecessary conservatism embodied in the current regulations, generating significant cost savings without compromising safety. Additional information about the development of
(
printed page 69347)
PHMSA's siting regulations, and the proposed prescriptive and QRA-based siting approaches, is provided in the following sections.
C.1. Role of Siting in PHMSA's Safety Framework
By way of background, the siting requirements in subpart B date to a rulemaking proceeding initiated by one of PHMSA's predecessor agencies, the Materials Transportation Board (MTB), in the late 1970s. MTB undertook that effort to address concerns with the then-current version of the Federal safety standards for LNG facilities, which relied almost entirely on the provisions in a historical edition of NFPA.
[
96
]
MTB subsequently divided that rulemaking effort into two different proceedings, one of which focused on establishing O&M requirements for LNG facilities,
[
97
]
and the other of which focused on establishing design, construction, installation, testing, and siting requirements for LNG facilities.
[
98
]
Of particular importance for this proceeding, MTB took a very conservative approach in both proceedings, issuing final rules in 1980 that included layers of mutually reinforcing requirements, many of which incorporated cautious assumptions or relied on near-worst-case scenarios selected to provide robust protective safety margins.
[
99
]
MTB recognized that this approach imposed significant costs on operators, but concluded that those costs were justified by the limited historical release data for LNG facilities and the potential consequences of an incident.
The original part 193 siting regulations were a product of that philosophy. Highlighting the lack of meaningful safety standards in effect at the time, MTB focused on addressing the risks associated with two hazards: (1) thermal radiation,
i.e.,
the amount of heat that would be produced if an LNG spill ignited and (2) vapor-gas dispersion,
i.e.,
the dimensions of the vapor-gas cloud that would form as a result of an LNG spill, which could ignite or act as an asphyxiant.
[
100
]
MTB proposed an inherently conservative approach employed in regulating other high-consequence industrial facilities to address these risks. MTB required owners or operators to exercise control over an “exclusion zone,”
i.e.,
a buffer area around an LNG facility that could not be accessed by the public.
[
101
]
To provide broad safety margins, MTB required operators to use conservative assumptions (
e.g.,
emissive heat flux, flame length, flame tilt angle, and radiant heat exposure levels; neglect of active mitigation measures; assumption of 100 percent fatality or harm within exclusion zones) in calculating the extent of the exclusion zone for thermal radiation. The calculation needed to be made either by using a simple, default mathematical model that would yield “conservatively safe exclusion zone[s]” or by using an alternative, MTB-approved model that incorporated “additional and more valid information when it becomes available.”
[
102
]
MTB employed a similar approach in setting the boundaries of the exclusion zone for flammable vapor-gas dispersion, requiring the use of near-worst case assumptions (
e.g.,
a uniform concentration of methane half its actual lower flammable limit (LFL); default worst-case wind and atmospheric stability and design spill parameters) in response to an ignition scenario that MTB admitted was far less likely than the localized fire risk addressed in its thermal radiation hazard analysis.
[
103
]
This approach addressed probability of release characteristics and operating conditions by selecting assumptions MTB judged appropriately conservative in light of occurrence frequency and potential consequence magnitude.
Although subject to minor adjustments over time, the underlying approach of layering conservativism upon conservatism is still embodied in the current siting regulations. Subsequent rulemakings have adopted newer, and more accurate, models for calculating exclusion zones—even as they rejected stakeholder calls to update some of the conservative parameters that had been employed in addressing historical uncertainties.
[
104
]
PHMSA has continued to rely on legacy editions of NFPA 59A that incorporate additional layers of conservatism within the modeling of hazard distances (which subpart B regulations then translate into exclusion zones). Specifically, subpart B has since 2004 referenced NFPA 59A-2001 chapter 2's prescriptive siting requirements, which employ many of the conservative assumptions for modeling thermal radiation (section 2.2.3.2) and flammable vapor-gas (sections 2.2.3.3 and 2.2.3.4) hazards that PHMSA's predecessors had previously adopted in regulation.
[
105
]
In other places where NFPA 59A-2001 departed from historical, conservative modeling assumptions, PHMSA and its predecessors either retained those assumptions in subpart B text or supplemented them in FAQs.
[
106
]
These extra layers of conservatism affect the design and layout of LNG facilities, either by constraining the configuration or spacing of components and systems within a site or requiring the installation of additional onsite mitigation measures (
e.g.,
vapor shields) to accommodate the exclusion zone requirements.
Finally, PHMSA and its predecessors have supplemented the subpart B exclusion zone framework with additional siting requirements. For
(
printed page 69348)
example, RSPA's incorporation by reference in 2004 of the siting requirements within chapter 2 of NFPA 59A-2001 introduced prescriptive requirements covering everything from soil and geotechnical site investigation (section 2.1.4) to process equipment spacing (section 2.2.6). PHMSA has also read broad language at section 2.1.1(d) of NFPA 59A-2001 to require operators to consider “[o]ther [siting-related] factors,” including releases of hazardous fluids other than LNG, in conducting their exclusion zone analyses.
[
107
]
These changes, when combined with the inherent conservatism used in developing the exclusion zone requirements, have resulted in a siting regime for LNG facilities that no longer appropriately reflects the risks to public safety, particularly given the significant advancements in industry standards and practices that have occurred in the past four decades.
C.2. Prescriptive Siting Requirements (NFPA 59A-2026, Chapter 5)
This rulemaking proposes to modernize PHMSA's default, prescriptive siting requirements in subpart B. These requirements are currently governed by a patchwork of industry standards, part 193 regulatory provisions, and non-binding guidance—all of which magnify the inherent conservatism already provided through the other requirements (design, installation, testing, construction, operations, and maintenance) in part 193. Although the LNG industry has an excellent safety record as discussed in section II.A.3.c above, PHMSA does not agree that the conservative approach traditionally used in the siting requirements is necessary to maintain that level of safety. Rather, PHMSA believes that a more modern approach consistent with the enhanced safety provisions in NFPA 59A-2026 can be used to determine whether an LNG facility can be safely sited at a particular location.
PHMSA therefore proposes to incorporate by reference into subpart B the prescriptive siting requirements in chapter 5 of NFPA 59A-2026. Those requirements would serve as the default siting provisions in lieu of the current reference to chapter 2 of NFPA 59A-2001. PHMSA also proposes to supplement the provisions in NFPA 59A-2026 chapter 5 with a handful of additional regulatory requirements in subpart B. Adopting these changes would align the siting requirements with the latest hazard modeling techniques and current standards and practices in the LNG industry. In addition, PHMSA proposes to codify or to eliminate current non-binding guidance on LNG facility siting to improve regulatory certainty and to reduce unnecessary compliance burdens. PHMSA expects the proposed changes to the default, prescriptive siting requirements in subpart B will reduce public safety risks, particularly when combined with the other safety-enhancing proposals discussed elsewhere in this NPRM.
a. Sections 193.101 and 193.103(a)—Improved Hazard Modeling Under NFPA 59A-2026
PHMSA proposes to incorporate by reference into new §§ 193.101 and 193.103 certain enhanced hazard assessment and modeling requirements from chapter 5 of NFPA-2026. Specifically, PHMSA proposes to incorporate sections 5.2.1, 5.2.2, and 5.3.2 of NFPA 59A-2026 into these regulations, subject to certain exceptions and supplemental provisions as discussed below. PHMSA's discussion of those proposals is included in section IV.D of this NPRM.
The hazard modeling requirements in subpart B are currently based on the provisions in chapter 2 of NFPA 59A-2001 and certain additional regulatory requirements. NFPA 59A-2001 at section 2.1.1(d)—and, by extension, PHMSA's subpart B regulations at § 193.2051—requires operators to evaluate all “factors . . . that have a bearing on the safety of plant personnel and the surrounding public” when siting a new LNG facility or making significant expansions or other alterations to an existing LNG facility. PHMSA guidance at LNG FAQ H1 characterizes that regulatory language as requiring evaluation of releases from systems containing any hazardous fluid.
In addition, § 193.2051 requires operators to consider the effects of failure of certain equipment (
e.g.,
storage tank penetrations, piping ruptures) resulting in the release of LNG in conducting a siting analysis. The specific LNG releases that must be considered, otherwise known as “design spills,” generally reflect industry understanding of (in some cases) worst-case, plausible failures based on historical data. Sections 193.2057 and 193.2059 require operators to use certain models to predict the extent of the thermal radiation and flammable vapor-gas dispersion that would result from such a failure. The models, authorized by regulation or approved by PHMSA after an evaluation, calculate “hazard distances” bounding a “hazard footprint” at certain prescribed thresholds or “endpoints.”

NFPA 59A-2001 (at sections 2.2.3.2 and 2.2.3.3) assigns escalating safety requirements based on the magnitude of safety consequence associated with different endpoints. Operators must establish (or otherwise maintain) legal control of all activities within hazard footprints bounded by endpoints correlating to the most consequential risks: fatality and irreversible harm. The exclusion zone requirements in subpart B incorporate these concepts from NFPA 59A-2001.
The hazard modeling requirements in chapter 5 of NFPA 59A-2026 are more advanced than the comparable provisions in NFPA 59A-2001, improve subpart B's hazard analyses with the risk profiles of modern facilities (many of which can contain large quantities of hazardous fluids other than LNG), and provide a more robust evaluation of hazard phenomena. For example, rather than providing that operators merely “consider” unspecified siting-related factors potentially affecting safety as provided by NFPA 59A-2001, NFPA 59A-2026 section 5.2.1 specifies illustrative factors (process hazards, security threats, adjacent facility hazards, weather and geological conditions, and safety measures incorporated in facility design and operational practices) for operators to consider in conducting site evaluations. In addition, section 5.3.2.13 of NFPA 59A-2026 provides more detailed requirements for qualitative consideration of the potential for cascading damage than the analogous provisions in section 2.2.3.6 of NFPA 59A-2001.

Section 193.103(b)—Design Spill Criteria
PHMSA proposes to codify in § 193.103(b) the design spill criteria in LNG FAQ DS2 in lieu of the analogous criteria in Table 5.3.2.3 of NFPA 59A-2026. PHMSA's experience is that the undefined term “single accidental leakage source” (SALS) at Table 2.2.3.5 of NFPA 59A-2001 (for spills from process and transfer systems) has been a source of confusion. PHMSA, FERC, and NFPA have developed a series of clarifications characterizing (in some cases) worst-case, plausible spills from different types of transfer and process systems, including the design spill criteria in current LNG FAQs DS2(A) (hole size on process & transfer systems), DS2(B) (full-bore ruptures of single-ply construction expansion bellows), DS2(C) (hole size for pipe-in-pipe systems), and DS2(D) (hole size for truck transfer hoses). Each of these assumptions has been employed in subpart B siting analyses for multiple LNG facilities in the last decade.
First, LNG FAQ DS2(A) provides that a design spill should assume full-bore (or guillotine break) ruptures on transfer and process piping with a diameter less than six inches (

This line-drawing is based on identifying the largest plausible failures on such piping, since historical failure data demonstrates that full-bore ruptures are plausible failure modes on smaller piping, but not on large piping—failures of two inches or smaller hole size represent most of all failure data on piping of six inches or larger. PHMSA acknowledges that NFPA 59A-2026 (at section 5.3.2.3, referencing Table 5.3.2.3) employs different assumptions requiring full-bore ruptures only for piping smaller than three inches in diameter. PHMSA discusses below two issues regarding the scope of subpart B hazard modeling analyses that merit additional clarification.
Exemption of Feed Gas and Send-Out Gas Lines From Subpart B Hazard Modeling
LNG facilities are typically connected to pipelines that either supply gas for liquefaction (called “feed gas” lines) or receive gas after regasification (called “send out” lines). These pipelines are collectively referred to as “supply lines” and have historically been considered subject to PHMSA's part 192 requirements rather than its part 193 regulations (and by extension, NFPA 59A). Although neither NFPA 59A-2001 nor current subpart B regulations address the boundary between these regulatory regimes, PHMSA's practice has been to give operators discretion in designating the precise boundary—the “spec break”—where each of the part 192 and 193 regulatory regimes would begin to apply. Operators in practice have typically chosen the first aboveground segment of a supply line within the LNG facility boundary as the “spec break” marking the boundary of part 193 regulations. This approach is consistent with the practical realities that most modeled hazards are pertinent to aboveground (rather than buried) piping and that operators are unlikely to have legal control of areas outside the property lines of their facilities as may be required if they were to draw exclusion zones as supply piping crossed into their facility.
Consistent with that historical practice, NFPA 59A-2026 at section 5.3.2.1 (as well as section 1.1.2(6)) now explicitly excludes “feed gas and send out gas lines” from hazard modeling requirements—but remains silent regarding the meaning of those terms. PHMSA proposes to continue its current policy of deferring to operators in determining the precise boundary between part 193-regulated piping (which would be subject to subpart B hazard modeling requirements) and part 192-regulated as supply lines (which would not be subject to subpart B hazard modeling requirements). This approach ensures continuity with PHMSA's historical approach, which has proven effective in ensuring public safety. Because PHMSA is merely affirming its longstanding approach on this issue, PHMSA does not propose regulatory text memorializing that understanding.
d. Sections 193.5 and 193.105—Retention of Exclusion Zone Framework and Extension to Newly Modeled Hazards
PHMSA proposes in redesignated and revised §§ 193.5 and 193.105 to apply the subpart B “exclusion zone” framework to additional hazards. Consistent with the current definition of “exclusion zone” at § 193.2007, an operator or a governmental authority would be required by the redesignated § 193.5 to have legal control for the life of an LNG facility over activities within certain modeled hazards' footprints—not merely at initial siting as contemplated by the letter of NFPA 59A-2026. PHMSA also proposes to codify at § 193.105(b) longstanding and common-sense guidance providing certain exceptions to the § 193.5 requirement that an operator or a governmental authority maintain legal control over all activities within certain hazard footprints. Specifically, LNG FAQ H5 recognizes exceptions to the default legal control requirement—for exclusion zones that would otherwise extend past a property line onto a public road or a navigable waterway—as a concession to the practical reality that legal control may not be possible in some cases and may not meaningfully contribute to safety given that those areas are not typically locations of prolonged activity by individuals.
In addition, PHMSA proposes a new § 193.105 that would reference NFPA 59A-2026 provisions providing for exclusion zones based on the modeled thermal radiation and flammable vapor dispersion hazard footprints, similar to current regulations at §§ 193.2057 and 193.2059. C.3. Risk-Based Siting Alternative Using Quantitative Risk Analysis (NFPA 59A-2026, Chapter 19)
PHMSA proposes to retain a set of default, prescriptive siting requirements for all PHMSA-regulated LNG facilities at § 193.103. For operators willing to invest more resources, PHMSA also proposes at § 193.107 to adopt an alternative, QRA-based siting approach consistent with the provisions in NFPA 59A-2026 chapter 19.
As explained in more detail below, the QRA-based approach leverages decades of industry experience to provide a modern, comprehensive siting framework for LNG facilities. It also complements PHMSA's extensive experience administering risk-based regulatory frameworks for other pipeline facilities, including through gas transmission integrity management (part 192, subpart O), gas distribution integrity management (part 192, subpart P), and hazardous liquid pipeline integrity management (§ 195.452) programs. As discussed further in section IV.G, those risk-based regulatory regimes have resulted in improved safety outcomes since their adoption. And chapter 19 itself is the product of 15 years of effort to establish and refine a QRA-based alternative to historical, prescriptive siting requirements elsewhere within NFPA 59A, with the first attempt at a QRA-based siting alternative included within an optional Annex E to the 2009 edition of NFPA 59A.

C.4. Section 193.107—Proposed Chapter 19 QRA Alternative and Comparison to Chapter 5 Prescriptive Siting Requirements
PHMSA proposes at a new § 193.107 to incorporate by reference the QRA-based siting approach in NFPA 59A-2026 chapter 19. Operators may use the QRA-based siting approach as an alternative to the traditional, prescriptive siting approach in the current subpart B requirements and the proposed § 193.103 (incorporating NFPA 59A-2026 chapter 5). PHMSA expects the QRA-based approach will offer several advantages compared to the traditional siting approach.
First, the QRA-based approach will enhance operator risk assessment comprehensiveness and precision. Although chapters 5 and 19 both require operators to evaluate certain plausible releases in performing a siting analysis, chapter 19 goes further. The QRA-based approach requires operators to consider more release scenarios and integrates explicit quantification of release scenario and parameter probabilities. And rather than simply employing successive layers of conservatism, chapter 19 ensures safety through a more sophisticated approach: modeling for additional hazards and more fulsome integration of probability in quantifying risks of those hazards. Chapter 19's QRA-based approach can also enable advanced modeling techniques—including probit functions
[
125
]
—not contemplated in chapter 5's siting regime.
Second, chapter 19's QRA-based approach will allow policymakers to make more informed decisions about individual LNG projects. The layers of additional conservatism embedded in the traditional siting approach are not easily deconstructed and employ opaque policy judgements regarding risk acceptability that tend to obscure the real-world risks that might result from having an LNG facility at a particular location. The QRA-based siting approach is far more transparent; it quantifies potential harm to individuals and society in a manner explicitly accounting for probability. The QRA-based approach also compares quantified risk values for individual and societal harms against explicit, consensus-derived risk tolerance levels. The QRA-based approach more easily accommodates sensitivity analyses as well, which is helpful in identifying the trade-offs available among the various mitigation measures.

Third, the QRA-based approach will reinforce the various safety-enhancing

e.g.,

The QRA-based approach should help emergency responders in the surrounding community apply limited resources more effectively, focusing on drills and training for particularly high-consequence or high-probability risks. The QRA-based approach elevates the importance of operator mitigation measures by introducing explicit mechanisms for managing estimated individual and societal risks through the implementation of those measures. This enhanced approach can ensure operators direct finite personnel and capital resources toward the highest-risk components and processes.
Fourth, the QRA-based siting approach can enable greater flexibility for operators in selecting the site and internal layout of LNG facilities. As discussed at greater length in section 3.3.1 of the PRIA, the prescriptive approach in NFPA 59A-2026 chapter 5 can constrain the location of LNG facilities. The conservativism embedded in the prescriptive approach requires operators to acquire more land than is necessary from a risk perspective to construct or to expand an LNG facility, or to make adjustments in locating components and equipment within the boundaries of an LNG facility to avoid acquiring more land. Requirements at chapter 6 (plant layout) and elsewhere in NFPA 59A-2026 compound those constraints by prescribing minimum distances for placement of components that may be tied to facility boundaries or the location of other key equipment.

c. Mechanics of Chapter 19 QRA-Based Approach and Proposed PHMSA Enhancements
PHMSA discusses below the core elements of NFPA 59A-2026's chapter 19 QRA-based siting approach proposed for incorporation by reference into subpart B, as well as pertinent exceptions or additions that PHMSA is proposing to facilitate implementation and improve consistency with other part 193 requirements. PHMSA notes that operators may look to the explanatory guidance in Appendix A to NFPA 59A-2026 for assistance in implementation mechanics for the QRA-based alternative.
System Description & Release Scenario Identification
The first step in performing a siting analysis under chapters 5 and 19 is developing a system description and specifying the LNG and other hazardous material release scenarios to be modeled. Both approaches require operators to identify and evaluate siting-related, facility-specific information regarding layout, equipment, adjacent activities and hazards, and environmental conditions.
But the scope of release scenarios considered under the two approaches diverges thereafter. First, chapter 19 builds on the generic evaluation requirement at section 5.2.1 by requiring at section 19.5.1 that operators collect a “comprehensive” set of information regarding release scenarios for LNG and other hazardous materials. Chapter 19 also contemplates that the release scenarios considered explicitly account for quantified probabilities of a number of factors (including annual frequency of releases from different types of equipment; conditional probabilities
(
printed page 69355)
associated with environmental conditions and release parameters) affecting the consequence magnitude and frequency of releases.
Second, chapter 5 (at section 5.3.2) directs operators to establish, based on the information identified pursuant to section 5.2.1, a limited set of sufficiently plausible, (sometimes) worst-case release parameters (“design spills”) and release behavior (“source terms”) that must be evaluated by computer modeling. Release scenarios judged implausible need not be comprehensively analyzed. In contrast, section 19.5.1 requires operators to use a process hazard analysis to generate a more comprehensive, facility-specific list of possible hazard scenarios (of which “design spills” under chapter 5 could be a subset) and to evaluate various combinations of release conditions (
e.g.,
stream pressure and temperature, physical state, hole size, location, duration) for each scenario. This approach avoids a limitation of the prescriptive approach in chapter 5, which requires operators to evaluate each hazard in isolation and to distil artificially the risks associated with a complex system of an LNG facility and its surrounding environment into a limited set of release parameters yielding a single metric (the hazard endpoint distance). In contrast, the QRA-based approach leverages the latest understanding of (sometimes interrelated) failure modes and equipment failure rates in examining more potential release scenarios and quantifies the likelihood and consequences resulting from each release. The result is a comprehensive and nuanced view of the risks specific to each LNG facility.
PHMSA expects that a process hazard analysis performed pursuant to section 5.2.1(1) of NFPA 59A-2026, or in connection with the risk-based inspection and maintenance alternative framework (discussed in section IV.G), may satisfy the PHA requirement at section 19.5.1.2 if the analysis is reasonably “comprehensive” and otherwise complies with the requirements of sections 19.5.1 and 19.5.2.
Hazard Modeling
Chapters 5 and 19 both require operators to use computer models to calculate “hazard footprints” for LNG facilities. The hazard footprints depict the areas where individuals may be at risk of fatality or irreversible harm should certain hazard phenomena occur (
e.g.,
jet fires, pool fires, flammable gas/vapor dispersion, etc.). The computer models use threshold values denoting individual risk for hazard phenomena that are largely similar; exposure or concentration levels below these thresholds are not modeled under either approach.
[
132
]
Both approaches require operators to assess the contingency of “cascading damages” where primary release scenarios cause secondary releases. Both approaches contemplate that hazard modeling can account for operator mitigation measures.
But chapter 19 requires more comprehensive and sophisticated hazard modeling than chapter 5. Section 19.8 requires operators to consider additional phenomena (pressure vessel bursts, BLEVEs, and oxygen-displacing gas dispersion) not required under chapter 5 in modeling hazard footprints.
[
133
]
Chapter 19 incorporates quantified probability values for factors informing risk when calculating hazard endpoints. The probability values pertain not only to release frequency and parameters but may also incorporate probit functions. Chapter 5 uses a far less precise approach: conservative assumptions (
e.g.,
“design spills,” source terms, and high rates of harm from exposure within hazard thresholds) are used in hazard modeling in which consideration of probability is embedded but not explicitly quantified.
PHMSA acknowledges the resources supporting QRA-based hazard modeling under chapter 19 are not as mature as those available for hazard modeling under chapter 5. For example, PHMSA-approved MEPs and MVDs are not available for every hazard that must be modeled under chapter 19 (consistent with § 193.103(c) proposed above). PHMSA proposes at § 193.107(c) that operators use computer models for models that have been reviewed against PHMSA-approved MEPs and MVDs where available; for other hazards, operators should employ sound engineering judgment (and document their reasoning consistent with § 193.107(a)) in selecting and using appropriate modeling software and validation data. Operators would be required to validate hazard models against any MEPs and MVDs that PHMSA subsequently approves. Operators using the chapter 19 QRA-based alternative would be required to employ sound engineering judgment (and document their reasoning within materials submitted pursuant to § 193.107(a)) in selecting probit functions in modeling hazard endpoints; PHMSA will generally defer to an operator's choice of probit functions unless a compelling safety concern demands regulatory oversight intervention.
[
134

PHMSA also acknowledges that the mechanics of performing hazard modeling in chapter 19 are not as detailed as those in the longstanding approach in chapter 5. PHMSA therefore proposes supplemental provisions to facilitate implementation of chapter 19. For example, consistent with the exclusion of “feed and send-out lines” from the hazard modeling requirements at NFPA 59A-2026 section 5.2.1, PHMSA proposes language at § 193.107(d) providing the same exception for hazard modeling and risk analysis under the QRA-based alternative. Lastly, similar to the approach taken in its proposal at § 193.103, PHMSA proposes in § 193.107(a) that operators must document the effect that any active or passive mitigation measures have in assessing their hazard modeling and risk analysis.
Risk Characterization, Evaluation and Tolerance
The QRA-based approach in chapter 19 characterizes, evaluates, and determines tolerable risk levels in a way that is far more sophisticated than the prescriptive approach in chapter 5. For its part, chapter 5 focuses on risk of fatality or irreversible harm to individuals on a hazard-by-hazard basis without estimating societal risk or aggregated risk to an individual at different locations from all modeled hazard phenomena. And, as explained above, the estimates of individual risk in chapter 5 account for probability implicitly within conservative assumptions and do not integrate quantified probabilities in risk calculations. Further, chapter 5 evaluates risks within a framework marked by bright-line simplicity: exclusion zones bounded by one-size-fits-all hazard endpoints prescribed within tables in that chapter determine whether risks to individuals are intolerable (inside the exclusion zone)
(
printed page 69356)
or tolerable (outside the exclusion zone). Exclusion zones in turn define the outer boundaries of an LNG facility—and consequently the layout of buildings, equipment, and processes within its perimeter.
Chapter 19 uses a more nuanced and sophisticated approach. First, section 19.9.1 requires aggregation of each of the risks of fatality and irreversible harm to individuals across all modeled hazards. Operators calculate the estimated likelihood of fatality and irreversible harm from each hazard and then combine the risk from each to quantify the overall risk to an individual at each location within the LNG facility and surrounding area within the modeled hazard footprints (“location-specific individual risk,” or “IR”) in a manner which accounts for probabilities in a number of factors informing individual risk. Operators must present these IR values (which are expressed in terms of annual frequency) visually using topographic maps of constant individual risk (“isopleths”) throughout the LNG facility and surrounding area.
[
135
]
Chapter 19 then requires characterization of the aggregated, facility-wide societal risks of fatality and irreparable harm by accounting for the population within each modeled hazard. Section 19.9.2 requires operators to estimate the number of people within the hazard footprints using public demographic or census data. The resulting “number of affected persons” for each hazardous consequence is used to aggregate each of fatality and irreparable harm risks; the resulting “societal risks” appear as a graph of the likelihood of each of fatality and irreparable harm risks against the number of affected people for each hazard (“F-N curves”).
Second, chapter 19 at sections 19.10 and 19.11 sets explicit thresholds for intolerable, mitigation-required, and tolerable individual and societal risks against which aggregated IR and societal risks calculated pursuant to section 19.9 are compared (typically in graph form). IR and societal risks falling in the “zone” above the “intolerable” threshold are unacceptable under any circumstances. Intolerable IR risks must be addressed through land use and occupancy restrictions similar to exclusion zones provided in chapter 5 or mitigation to reduce risk to tolerable levels as documented in a follow-on QRA. Intolerable societal risks must be addressed through mitigation by way of re-design of the LNG facility or significant mitigation actions and the QRA must be performed again. Societal risks falling in the “zone” between intolerable and tolerable risks—termed the “as low as reasonably practicable (ALARP) region” in sections 19.10 and 19.11—must be mitigated to the point at which an additional mitigation measure would become unreasonably disproportionate to the incremental risk reduction expected. And IR and societal risks falling in the “zone” below the threshold for tolerable risk would be acceptable without land use restrictions or other forms of mitigation.

Risk Mitigation
The chapter 19 risk tolerance thresholds create an incentive for operators to develop innovative, and cost-effective, measures to reduce risks to acceptable levels to minimize land use restrictions. Altering the capacity or location of individual facility components and processes can alter the dimensions of isopleths mapping aggregated risks to individuals as well as the plotting of F-N curves depicting margins to intolerable societal risks. Alternatively, if commercial or other
(
printed page 69357)
considerations limit ability to adjust those variables, an operator can employ active and passive mitigation measures to compensate for the contribution to siting-based risks. For example, an operator may mitigate the risks from a hazard by introducing a vapor barrier to obstruct vapor dispersion or a thermal wall to reduce radiant heat exposure. An operator may also choose to decrease the expected duration of the release by introducing early detection and isolation equipment. Or an operator may adopt equipment and technologies with lower failure rates. Operators can use sensitivity analyses and Layer of Protection Analysis (LOPA) techniques to quantify the reduction in probability from adding a new layer of detection or protection against hazardous consequences.
[
140
]
Consistent with the approach proposed for addressing active mitigation measures under § 193.103(g), PHMSA will generally defer to an operator's documented (pursuant to § 193.107(a)) selection of active or passive mitigation measures and assessment of the effect of those measures on facility individual and societal risk profiles. PHMSA expects that the enhanced procedural and documentation requirements of the QRA-based alternative will provide adequate assurance of the safety value of specific mitigation measures. PHMSA will extend that deferential approach in assessing whether an operator has mitigated societal risk to levels “as low as reasonably practicable.” Because the precise trade-offs between risk reduction and practicability concerns (including costs) of any particular mitigation will turn on a number of facility-specific factors (
e.g.,
the characteristics of the hazard and facility design/technical features and parameters) that operators will be best-positioned to evaluate, PHMSA will refrain from imposing universal requirements or thresholds for such mitigation. PHMSA (as well as other State and Federal regulators, as appropriate) will retain regulatory oversight to ensure the adequacy of mitigation measures taken by operators in response to their chapter 19 siting analyses and take necessary actions to protect public safety.
Lastly, PHMSA notes that its proposal to incorporate by reference the chapter 19 QRA-based approach includes the risk criteria and land use restrictions for tolerable individual risks of fatality and irreversible harm at section 19.10.1 (referencing Tables 19.10.1(a) and (b)). However, consistent with PHMSA's proposal at § 193.105(b) to exempt public roads, rights of way, and navigable waters from the exclusion zone requirements of chapter 5, PHMSA similarly proposes language at § 193.107(e) excluding public roads, rights of way, and navigable waters from the land use restrictions and occupancy restrictions of chapter 19.

C.6. Section 193.101(b)—Delayed Compliance Date
PHMSA proposes to adopt a delayed compliance date at § 193.101(b). D. Subpart C—Design, Construction, and Installation
PHMSA proposes to consolidate the current subparts C (design), D (construction), and E (equipment) within a new subpart C, entitled “Design, Construction, and Installation.” The new subpart C will consist largely of incorporation by reference of pertinent chapters of NFPA 59A-2026.
As discussed in section IV.A above, subparts C, D, and E currently incorporate by reference “the requirements of NFPA 59A,” subject to a regulatory conflict preemption provision. The extent to which the “requirements of NFPA 59A” are incorporated by reference into these subparts is unclear. The preambles of the NPRM and final rules adopting the current regulatory language do not address this question, and the distinctions between each of “design,” “construction” and “equipment” requirements often blur in practice. Moreover, part 193's current sorting of requirements among its subparts can be challenging for stakeholders to follow (
e.g.,
location of wind force design requirements at § 193.2067 within subpart B “siting” requirements).
Nor does the organization of 2001 and 2006 editions of NFPA 59A reflect distinctions PHMSA has drawn between the subject matters addressed by different part 193 subparts.

(

D.2. Section 193.203—Plant Design—Wind Speed
PHMSA proposes language at a new § 193.203 supplementing the wind force requirements in NFPA 59A-2026 for certain FERC-jurisdictional facilities. Current PHMSA regulations locate design wind resistance requirements governing LNG facilities at § 193.2067.
[
152

That provision begins with a generic requirement at § 193.2067(a) that all LNG facilities be designed “to withstand . . . the direct effect of wind forces.” Paragraph (b) of that same provision supplements the generic wind forces requirement with facility-specific minimum requirements: low-capacity (70,000 gallons or less) shop-fabricated containers of LNG and other hazardous fluids must comply with the requirements of ASCE/SEI 7-2005, while all other LNG facilities must design for wind force resistance based on either a default sustained wind velocity of 150 mph
[
153
]
(with some flexibility to employ a lower value as approved by the PHMSA Administrator), or the “most critical combination” of wind velocity and duration over the equivalent of a 10,000-year mean recurrence interval (MRI).
Part 193's current design wind force resistance requirements reflect more than two decades of effort to strike an appropriate balance between compliance costs and adequate protection from the public safety risks. When proposing the design wind resistance requirements in 1979, MTB struggled to identify an appropriate balance between those values. Concerned with the high compliance costs for measures addressing uncertain public safety risks, MTB initially proposed more demanding requirements than those found in current regulations for a more limited universe of buildings and structures: only “critical components” would be subject to a generic, broadly worded design wind velocity requirement referencing a then-leading industry standard. And within
(
printed page 69361)
that limited universe, the most safety-consequential components (LNG storage tanks and dikes) would also be subject to a 250-mph default sustained wind velocity requirement, which MTB conceded may have been “too stringent.”
[
154

In the 1980 final rule, however, MTB landed on a different balance between the competing values of cost and safety risk. While expanding the application of design wind resistance requirements to the entirety of LNG facilities, MTB lowered the default sustained wind velocity requirement to 200 mph in response to cost concerns magnified by available wind speed data suggesting even that lower value was overly conservative.
[
155
]
Two decades later, RSPA lowered the default sustained wind velocity again, citing historical hurricane data noting the infrequency of winds above 150 mph in concluding that a 200 mph sustained wind velocity requirement was “excessive.”
[
156

This debate has continued in the years since. Operators have criticized PHMSA's design wind resistance requirements—particularly the default sustained wind velocity requirement at § 193.2067(b)(2)(i)—as needlessly expensive and overbroad, subjecting even structures (
e.g.,

Recent editions of NFPA 59A attempt to address this concern. The 2013 edition of NFPA 59A introduced within a new section 5.4 generally applicable design requirements covering all buildings, structures, and systems at LNG facilities. That new approach sorted buildings, structures, and systems within LNG facilities among different classifications by function—and, by extension, the potential public safety risks arising in the event of a structural failure from forces (including wind forces) on those buildings, structures, and systems. In assigning design requirements to each classification within LNG facilities, the 2013 edition of NFPA 59A leveraged design parameters (including design wind resistance) set forth in the 2010 edition of ASCE/SEI-7 for different categories of buildings and structures based on the risk to public safety from a failure of structural integrity. The specific design parameters addressing wind and other forces, moreover, reflect the considered, consensus judgment of regulators and industry subject matter experts throughout the LNG industry—as well as among the structural engineers contributing to ASCE/SEI-7-2022.

D.3. Section 193.205—Vaporizers: Isolation Valves
PHMSA proposes in a new § 193.205 to require vaporizer equipment to have both inlet and outlet isolation valves. These valves are positioned at the entry and exit points of equipment piping and play a crucial role in ensuring the safe operation, maintenance, and inspection of that equipment. For example, during maintenance or inspection, operators close these isolation valves to allow the piping to empty its contents and purge hazardous fluids, ensuring operator safety during equipment removal.
NFPA 59A-2001 at section 5.3.1 specifies that a manifolded vaporizer needs to have both inlet and discharge block valves at each vaporizer.
[
159
]
This requirement is essential because it ensures that inlet and outlet vaporizers can be isolated during maintenance while remaining vaporizers within the same manifold assembly continue to operate. However, the corresponding provisions of NFPA 59A-2026 (sections 9.3.3 and 9.4.1) do not explicitly state that an operator must install both an inlet and outlet discharge valves on each vaporizer. Given the safety value, PHMSA proposes to retain the historical NFPA 59A-2001 requirement at § 193.205, which would continue to mandate that each manifolded vaporizer be equipped with both inlet and outlet isolation valves.
D.4. Section 193.207—Impoundment Structural Requirements
PHMSA proposes to redesignate impoundment structural requirements at § 193.2155(a) in a new § 193.207 and to eliminate certain historical language that would be redundant with requirements in chapter 13 of NFPA 59A-2026. Under this proposal, PHMSA would maintain current § 193.2155 requirements that all impoundment systems must be designed and constructed to maintain their reliability and structural integrity while considering various factors. These factors include the effects of erosive impact of spilled LNG and potential impacts from the collapse of components or collisions by vehicles near LNG facilities.
D.5. Section 193.209—Water Removal From Impounding Areas
PHMSA proposes to redesignate the current impounding area water removal requirements in § 193.2173 within a new § 193.209, to revise current regulatory language to delete redundancies with NFPA 59A-2026 requirements (including those at section 13.13), and to retain other text supplementing NFPA 59A-2026 provisions where appropriate for safety.
Impoundment systems must be free of water to provide sufficient volume to contain LNG or other hazardous fluids from a potential spill. Water removal is also required because the vaporization rate of LNG increases if water is present in an impoundment, creating a larger vapor cloud and the potential for a rapid phase transition explosion. Given the importance of water removal, PHMSA proposes to retain in paragraph (a) existing performance-based language within § 193.2173(a) requiring the construction of impounding areas to ensure water is “completely” drained, rather than the less demanding and qualified (“as dry as practicable”) language in section 13.13.2 of NFPA 59A-2026. For the same reason, PHMSA also proposes retaining other language in § 193.2173(a) requiring operators to construct impoundment areas with proven, active water removal systems (including drainage pumps and piping), rather than relying exclusively on passive dewatering (
e.g.,
gravity drain) systems whose performance is hard to evaluate under real-world conditions and can be quickly degraded by clogging. Lastly, PHMSA proposes to revise the data source for determining rainfall amounts specified in § 193.2173(b) to reflect that the
Rainfall Frequency Atlas of the United States
published by the National Weather Service, which is now online and available through the Precipitation Frequency Data Server.

E. Subpart D—Permanent, Small-Scale LNG Facilities
Consistent with the mandate in the PIPES Act of 2016, PHMSA proposes to create a new subpart D prescribing calibrated, risk-based safety requirements for certain permanent (
i.e.,
stationary), small-scale LNG facilities appropriate. This new subpart will consist largely of the incorporation by reference of chapter 17 of NFPA 59A-2026 dedicated to those facilities.
When PHMSA last updated part 193 in 2001, a one-size-fits-all regulatory framework encompassing permanent, small-scale LNG facilities and larger facilities was appropriate. As discussed in section II.A. above, most LNG facilities at that time were peak shaving facilities with relatively small capacities and similar—and relatively simple—liquefaction and vaporization processes, often with fewer hazardous fluids and less extensive equipment. Many such facilities also operate intermittently or seasonally. But the LNG industry has evolved considerably in the past 25 years, and a consensus has emerged among interested stakeholders that the current part 193 requirements are no longer appropriate for most permanent, small-scale LNG facilities.

161
]

The 2019 edition of NFPA 59A introduced a new chapter 17 with targeted provisions for permanent (or, as referred to in NFPA 59A, “stationary”), small-scale facilities. Earlier editions of NFPA 59A (including NFPA 59A-2001 at chapter 10) had included specific requirements for LNG facilities with certain components (ASME containers) that had relatively small capacity—but did not address other smaller-capacity facilities, which created confusion as to whether those requirements supplemented or replaced requirements throughout the rest of NFPA 59A.
[
162
]
In developing the 2019 edition of NFPA 59A, NFPA formed a task group of industry representatives and Federal regulators (including personnel from PHMSA, FERC, and USCG) to address these concerns. The task group's work ultimately led to the addition of chapter 17 within NFPA 59A-2019. Section 17.1 establishes certain eligibility criteria (including individual LNG tanks and aggregate LNG plant-wide storage capacity; aggregate mass of hazardous fluids and toxic fluids within an LNG plant; pipe diameter; and maximum allowable working pressure) based on hazard consequence magnitude, an approach that had historically informed requirements throughout NFPA 59A.

F.3. Section 193.405—Communication Systems
PHMSA proposes to adopt a new § 193.405 with requirements for communication systems. Section 193.405 would incorporate certain standards in NFPA 59A-2026 for communications systems and retain requirements in the current regulation for communication systems at § 193.2519.
NFPA 59A-2026 in several places prescribes minimum communication system standards for transfer operations (section 15.9 and various places in chapter 18) and security functions (section 16.8.4). However, these standards only apply to certain operations and functions and do not require access to verbal communications from every workstation in an LNG plant as currently required by § 193.2519. NFPA 59A-2026 also prescribes certain standards for emergency communications systems, but these standards lack the requirement in § 193.2519(b) that such systems be independent of other communications systems.
Therefore, PHMSA proposes to retain within a new § 193.405 the more detailed communication requirements within current § 193.2519(a)-(b). Communication throughout an LNG plant is critical during normal and emergency operations alike; delays in initiating or receiving communication at the beginning of an incident can make the difference in timely avoidance and mitigation of significant public safety consequences. Retaining the current § 193.2519(a)-(b) requirements will help to ensure that reliable means of communications are available to personnel throughout an LNG plant in those critical moments.
F.4. Section 193.407—Maintenance Procedures
PHMSA proposes to adopt a new § 193.407 for maintenance procedures. Section 193.407 would supplement the standards in NFPA 59A-2026 for O&M procedures to ensure adequate safety-related condition reporting and adequate equipment isolation during maintenance activity. Section 18.10 of NFPA 59A-2026 contains detailed content standards for maintenance procedures. However, unlike the current regulations at § 193.2605(c), section 18.10 of NFPA 59A-2026 does not direct operator personnel to recognize and report safety-related conditions pursuant to § 191.23. PHMSA proposes to retain that longstanding requirement in a new § 193.407(a).
Similarly, although NFPA 59A-2026 acknowledges the safety value of robust system isolation practices to protect maintenance personnel in system design requirements and in non-binding guidance, the maintenance standards in section 18.10 do not articulate specific minimum requirements for mechanical and electrical isolation of systems during maintenance activity. PHMSA proposes to address that omission by adding a new requirement at § 193.407(c) that maintenance procedures provide for redundant methods of mechanical and electrical isolation. Mechanical isolation for hazardous fluid systems would require not only use of installed isolation valves, but also additional techniques (
e.g.,
removal of spool pieces or valves to “blank flange” piping; double block and bleed valving). Electrical isolation would be accomplished by “tag-out” procedures consisting of de-energizing and “locking out” electrical systems.
F.5. Section 193.409—Personnel Qualification and Training
Section 18.12 of NFPA 59A-2026 contains detailed standards for personnel qualification; training program design, content, and implementation; and recordkeeping of training activity. However, some of the standards in section 18.12 lack specificity necessary to support adequate implementation and oversight. PHMSA proposes a handful of additional requirements in a new § 193.409 to address these concerns.
First, PHMSA proposes to specify in paragraph (a) the minimum content (
e.g.,
name of personnel receiving training; the tasks for which they are being trained) of training records. The intent of this provision is to facilitate operator compliance with the training requirements and to ensure adequate regulatory oversight during investigations of contributing factors to incidents and safety-related conditions. Second, PHMSA proposes in paragraph (b) that all operator personnel must receive first-aid training to ensure that they can help other personnel in the event of an incident. Third, PHMSA proposes in paragraph (c) that all operator personnel involved in O&M activities—who are often best-positioned to identify safety-related conditions—receive training on recognition and reporting of the same as required by § 191.23. PHMSA also proposes that such training be held for immediate supervisors of such personnel (even if the immediate supervisors are only indirectly participating in the O&M activity) to help reinforce the training requirement for front-line O&M personnel. Fourth, PHMSA proposes in paragraph (d) to retain the requirement in the current version of § 193.2711 that operator training programs include protocols ensuring personnel do not have health conditions that would affect their performance of safety-critical responsibilities.

Among the LNG facility-focused provisions of the PIPES Act of 2020 was a mandate at section 110 to provide “large-scale [LNG] facilities” a “risk-based regulatory approach” as an alternative to the traditional, prescriptive O&M requirements in part 193. Section 110 further directed that PHMSA's regulatory framework contain certain required content. Paragraph (c) lists a series of elements reflecting a PHA-based approach to addressing public safety risks of an LNG facility. Paragraph (b) of section 110 further directs that the alternative, risk-based O&M regime adopted by PHMSA must “achieve a level of safety [at least] equivalent to the level of safety”
(

Multiple stakeholders have provided PHMSA with recommendations for implementing the section 110 requirements. 178

Consistent with the statutory mandate in section 110 of the PIPES Act of 2020, PHMSA proposes to adopt a new subpart F containing alternative, risk-based O&M requirements for FERC-authorized LNG facilities as a safety-equivalent alternative to most of the prescriptive requirements proposed for part 193, subpart E. The proposal—which complements safety-enhancing siting, design, installation, and construction requirements in existing part 193 or as proposed in this NPRM
[
179
]
—would leverage decades of industry experience employing facility-specific, PHA-based risk management approaches. The proposal would allow operators to focus their limited resources on managing risks from the most safety-consequential processes and equipment, rather than on complying with one-size-fits-all, prescriptive O&M requirements. The proposal would align PHMSA's regulations for LNG facilities with more mature and sophisticated regulatory regimes administered by EPA and OSHA for industrial facilities. PHMSA discusses its specific proposals below for implementing the section 110 mandate below and invites stakeholder comment.
G.1. Proven Safety Value of PHA-Based Approaches
Consistent with section 110 of the 2020 PIPES Act, PHMSA proposes to adopt a risk-based alternative to the traditional O&M requirements in part 193 for FERC-authorized LNG facilities. The core of the proposed framework is a PHA involving the identification and evaluation of hazards from potential releases of hazardous fluids employed in LNG facility processing activities, as well as the design and implementation of controls for managing the risks associated with those hazards.
PHA-based strategies first arose in the 1960s as a response to the limitations of traditional risk management approaches for increasingly complex industrial facilities. Traditional risk management approaches were generally reactive,
i.e.,
they focused on avoiding historical accidents, rather than on proactive identification and management of risks arising from the specific equipment and processes within a particular facility. That backward-looking orientation discouraged innovation and continual process improvement by diverting finite operator resources away from designing and employing robust mechanisms for incident prevention and toward compliance “safe harbors” to minimize regulatory liability. Historical risk management approaches (often implemented in checklist form) also tended to focus on isolated equipment or process-specific actions and personnel, rather than on employing a more holistic approach to identifying, evaluating, and mitigating the risks arising from interrelated processes equipment and systems. Regulatory frameworks informed by traditional risk management approaches tended toward top-down, highly prescriptive, one-size-fits-all requirements that proved to be either overly protective or inadequate—and rarely-fit-for-purpose.
Industry took the initial steps in developing a more sophisticated, holistic, alternative—process hazard analysis—in reference materials issued by dedicated consensus standard development organizations (
e.g.,
CCPS), and OSHA and EPA adopted PHA-based regulatory frameworks in subsequent proceedings.
[
180
]
OSHA established its PSM regulations to manage risks of releases from industrial facilities employing highly hazardous chemicals in 1991, and EPA established its RMP regulations directed toward minimizing offsite consequences of releases from certain point sources under the 1990 amendments to the Clean Air Act (Pub. L. 101-549) in 1996. Those PHA-based regulatory frameworks rested on the common-sense proposition that each operator—rather than a distant regulator—is often best-positioned to identify, evaluate, and design mitigation strategies for addressing facility-specific risks. OSHA and EPA gave affected operators greater freedom in the PSM and RMP regulations to design and to implement compliance programs than had been enjoyed under traditional regulatory frameworks.
PHA methodologies and regulatory frameworks have matured and been applied more broadly in subsequent years. Leading consensus industry standards, such as the CCPS's
Guidelines for Hazard Evaluation Procedures,
have been updated and expanded multiple times (from approximately 200 pages to over 500 pages in length).
[
181
]
The oil and gas industry has been active in this area, with leading trade associations issuing multiple recommended practices implementing PHA principles.
[
182
]
PHA methodologies have also been applied to LNG facilities. FERC requires LNG project applicants to submit the results of preliminary PHA within the front-end engineering information submitted during the pre-filing reviews, and to submit complete PHAs as it reviews final designs.
[
183
]
In addition, NFPA 59A has since 2019 required PHAs in connection with its traditional (section 5.2.1) and QRA-based (section 19.5.1.2) siting requirements. PHMSA also understands that many FERC-authorized LNG facilities conduct PHAs in response to commercial concerns (
e.g.,
as a material condition of financing or sales, or to obtain insurance coverage). PHMSA itself has commissioned studies evaluating how a PHA-based framework could be
(
printed page 69369)
integrated within its part 193 regulations.
[
184
]
Evidence indicates that PHA-based approaches have yielded significant safety benefits. For example, EPA data memorialized in a recent proposed rule revising its RMP regulations noted a long-term trend of decreasing releases from the nearly 12,400 RMP-jurisdictional facilities in the United States: a 45 percent drop in the annual number of reported accidents in each of 2014 (147 accidents) and 2023 (81 accidents). That positive safety trend also held for facilities most closely resembling LNG facilities, as the number of accidents for NAICS codes 324 (chemical facilities) and 325 (oil and gas facilities) decreased from 64 accidents in 2014 to only 37 accidents in 2023.
[
185
]
Similarly, accidents have been less severe, as EPA data between 2016-2020 and 2020-2023 evinces reduction in the severity of personal injuries and property damage.
Although less robust data is available for chemical facilities governed by OSHA's PSM regime, OSHA in 2016 noted that historical incident data from facilities subject to both RMP and PSM requirements demonstrated similar safety benefits: annual total incidents decreased by over 50 percent between 2000 (1,020) and 2010 (437); fatalities also decreased (from 14 to 10) in each of those years.
[
186
]
OSHA enforcement data evinces similar trends as industry has grown more familiar with the PSM framework, with potential violations having decreased over the lifetime of the PSM regime.
[
187
]
PHMSA expects that adopting a PHA-based approach in part 193 will produce similar safety benefits. FERC-authorized LNG facilities are similar (
e.g.,
in size, hazardous fluids employed, and the number and complexity of equipment and processes) to many of the facilities governed by the PSM and RMP regimes. In addition, PHMSA expects a PHA-based approach to accommodate the rapid pace of technological and process innovation occurring at LNG facilities better. Integration of a PHA-based approach within part 193 would also reinforce existing initiatives promoting continuous safety improvement within the LNG industry. As noted above, many FERC-certificated LNG terminals already employ PHA-informed approaches in response to regulatory obligations or commercial incentives. Congress included within the statutory charter for PHMSA's National Center for Excellence in LNG Safety an expectation that the Center would function as a vehicle for continual safety improvement and innovation within the industry. In alignment with this mandate, PHMSA's proposed subpart F would integrate a PHA-based approach on a targeted basis. As discussed below, subpart F would be an alternative only to subpart E O&M requirements; other layers of defense in depth requirements for siting, design, installation, and construction would remain applicable.
PHMSA has extensive experience administering other risk-based programs. PHMSA has adopted integrity management (IM) regulations for gas transmission lines (part 192, subpart O), hazardous liquid pipelines (§ 195.452), and gas distribution lines (part 192, subpart P). These IM-based regulatory programs employ many of the same elements (risk identification and evaluation; deployment of mitigation measures; continuous process improvement) that appear in PHA-based regimes. Like PHA-based approaches, PHMSA's IM regulations give operators flexibility in identifying and evaluating hazards and in selecting appropriate mitigation measures. That flexibility, as discussed in section II.A.3 above, is subject to rigorous PHMSA oversight and enforcement.
[
188
]
PHMSA's IM regulations have markedly improved pipeline safety. By way of example, a recent review of incident data on gas transmission lines since the 2003 introduction of PHMSA's part 192, subpart O IM requirements found significant reductions in per-mile frequency and severity of incidents on transmission lines subject to IM requirements.
[
189
]
For these reasons, PHMSA expects that the PHA-based alternative O&M requirements proposed for the new subpart F will improve public safety.

Required Content of Implementation Plans
PHMSA proposes at paragraph (c) the prescribed minimum content for operator implementation plans. As discussed earlier, the statutory text section 110 mandate specifies only limited required content for those plans—and the statute focused that content on providing merely an “overview” and implementation timelines for transitioning from a prescriptive O&M-based framework to a risk-based, subpart F-compliant program. This understanding of the statutory text reflects the practical reality that conducting PHAs and designing and implementing the program procedures, management controls, and training within a subpart F program necessarily will involve significant up-front work effort and time—indeed, implementation timelines were a topic of extensive negotiation with regulated entities in establishing EPA and OSHA's analogous risk-informed regulatory regimes.

Statutory Factors
The Pipeline Safety Laws specify certain mandatory considerations when adopting safety standards for gas pipeline facilities and LNG facilities. Section 60102(b) requires that safety standards for any gas pipeline facilities be “practicable” and “designed to meet the need for gas pipeline safety . . . and protecting the environment” based on consideration of its appropriateness for the type of transportation, reasonableness, and a risk assessment of the costs and benefits. Section 60103 supplies additional, LNG facility-specific considerations for requirements pertaining to each of siting (§ 60103(a)); design, installation, construction, inspection, and testing (§ 60103(b)); and operations and maintenance (§ 60103(d)). In addition, any proposed standard must, pursuant to
49 U.S.C. 60115(c)
, be reviewed by the GPAC for technical feasibility, reasonableness, cost-effectiveness, and practicability.
PHMSA has preliminarily determined that, notwithstanding the uncertainties and data limitations discussed in the PRIA, each of the proposals in the NPRM would be justified by either its corresponding compliance costs savings, enhanced regulatory flexibility, or improved public safety benefits. In reaching that preliminary determination, PHMSA has considered each of the pertinent statutory factors in proposing the requirements herein governing siting, design/installation/construction/inspection and testing, and operations and maintenance at LNG facilities. The core of the NPRM consists of incorporating by reference the (most recent) 2026 edition of NFPA 59A, an authoritative standard governing the safety of LNG facilities reflecting extensive technical deliberations among a broad consensus of Federal and State regulators and representatives across the spectrum of LNG industry stakeholders. Other NPRM proposals not derived from NFPA 59A either preserve current, longstanding part 193 requirements or enhance regulatory flexibility benefiting operators without adversely affecting safety. The origins of the NPRM's proposals consequently evince their appropriateness, technical feasibility, reasonableness, cost-effectiveness, and practicability as to the LNG facilities each such requirement would govern. And, as discussed at length in section IV above, PHMSA expects adoption of the proposals in the NPRM will improve public safety—and by extension, enhance protection of the environment.

I. National Technology Transfer and Advancement Act of 1995 (NTTAA)
The National Technology Transfer and Advancement Act of 1995 (
Pub. L. 104-113
) directs Federal agencies to use voluntary consensus standards and design specifications instead of government-developed voluntary technical standards when appropriate. Voluntary consensus standards are technical standards developed or adopted by domestic and international standards development organizations (SDOs). OMB Circular A-119,
Federal Participation in the Development and Use of Voluntary Consensus Standards and in Conformity Assessment Activities,
sets the policy for Federal use and development of voluntary consensus standards.
The legal effect of incorporation by reference (IBR) is that the material is treated as if it was published in full in the
Federal Register
and the CFR. Therefore, like any other rule issued in the
Federal Register
, the IBR standard has the force and effect of law. However, if an SDO publishes a new edition of a standard, the specific edition of the standard that was incorporated by reference remains as the standard carrying the force of law. Further, if a provision of a standard incorporated by reference conflicts with a regulation, the regulation takes precedence, unless expressly provided otherwise in a regulation. Congress authorized incorporation by reference to reduce the volume of material published in the
Federal Register
and the CFR (
see
5 U.S.C. 552(a)
and
1 CFR part 51
) and granted authority to the Director of the Federal Register to determine whether a proposed IBR serves the public interest. Unless expressly provided otherwise in a regulation, if a provision of a standard incorporated by reference conflicts with a regulation, the regulation takes precedence.
New or updated pipeline standards often consider new technologies, materials, management practices, and other innovations that improve the safety and operations of pipelines and pipeline facilities. Because the Pipeline Safety Regulations involve a great deal of technical subject matter, PHMSA has incorporated by reference over 80 standards and specifications into the regulations. PHMSA regularly reviews newer editions of currently referenced consensus standards and issues regulations to incorporate by reference updated standards that are consistent with the intent of the Pipeline Safety Regulations. This ensures that the Pipeline Safety Regulations incorporate the latest safety innovations. The lists of publications that PHMSA has incorporated by reference are found in §§ 192.7, 193.2013, and 195.3. The proposed revisions that this NPRM would make to the list of publications referenced in part 193 are found in § 193.9.
PHMSA employees participate in 25 domestic U.S. SDOs, including the NFPA, that address the design, construction, maintenance, inspection, operation, and repair of pipeline facilities. These subject matter experts represent the agency and participate in discussions and technical debates, register opinions, and vote in accordance with the procedures of the standards body at each stage of the standards development process (unless prohibited from doing so by law). PHMSA participates in this process to ensure the agency's safety and environmental priorities are considered and to avoid the need to develop separate, government-unique standards. PHMSA's participation does not, however, imply that the agency agrees with or endorses all decisions reached by such organizations. PHMSA has the responsibility to ensure the safe operation of pipeline systems and adopts only those portions of consensus standards that adequately protect public safety and the environment.

ASTM International (ASTM, formerly the American Society for Testing and Materials) often updates its more widely used standards every year. Sometimes multiple editions are published in a given year.

The proposed regulations § 193.503 establish an alternative, risk-based O&M framework for FERC-certificated LNG facilities. Operators must establish and implement written procedures to maintain the on-going integrity of process equipment. The operator shall document each inspection and test that has been performed on process equipment. The documentation shall identify the date of the inspection or test, the name of the person who performed the inspection or test, the serial number or other identifier of the equipment on which the inspection or test was performed, a description of the inspection or test performed, and the results of the inspection or test. Each operator shall issue a hot work permit for hot work operations conducted on or near a covered process. The permit shall document that the fire prevention and protection requirements in this part have been implemented prior to beginning the hot work operations; it shall indicate the date(s) authorized for hot work, and identify the object on which hot work is to be performed. The permit shall be kept on file until completion of the hot work operations. Operators would also need to establish and to implement written procedures to manage changes (except for “in-kind” replacements) to process chemicals, technology, equipment, and procedures, and changes to facilities that affect a covered process. And operators will need to certify that they have evaluated compliance with the provisions of this section at least every three years to verify that the procedures and practices under their risk-based O&M programs are adequate and are being followed. A report of the audit findings shall be developed, and operators shall retain the two (2) most recent compliance audit reports.

Abstract:
49 CFR part 193
requires operators of liquefied natural gas (LNG) facilities to maintain records, as needed, pertaining to facility design, operations, maintenance, and personnel training. The purpose of this mandatory information collection request is to ensure compliance with the recordkeeping requirements prescribed in the Pipeline Safety Regulations. LNG operators must make and maintain records as described and have those records available for compliance inspection by PHMSA staff upon request. Examples of such records include the results of personnel training activities; records of materials used for components, buildings, foundations, and LNG support systems; maps; and various facility maintenance activities. Most of the required records are to be kept for as long as the facility is in service. Personnel records must be maintained for one year after personnel are no longer assigned duties at the LNG plant. This information collection revision covers the new recordkeeping requirements contained in the Pipeline Safety: Amendments to Liquefied Natural Gas Facilities NPRM. PHMSA estimates that the operators will spend approximately 40 hours, annually, complying with the various recordkeeping requirements. The burden estimate below has been updated accordingly.

K. Severability
This NPRM represents a reasoned determination by PHMSA, based on its technical expertise and review of the administrative record, that the anticipated safety and avoided (compliance and opportunity) cost saving benefits of each of the amendments proposed herein preliminarily justify any associated compliance and other costs. As discussed throughout the NPRM, PHMSA's part 193 regulations governing LNG facilities consist of mutually-reinforcing elements of a conservative, defense-in-depth strategy to reducing public safety risks associated with siting, design, construction, installation, and operation of LNG facilities; NFPA 59A-2026 provisions which the NPRM proposes to incorporate by reference as the core of its part 193 regulations were selected by a consensus decision of a diverse group of technical experts from industry and State and Federal regulators consistent with that approach. Although the PRIA notes that the difficulty in identifying with precision the incremental safety contributions from particular proposed regulatory amendments in this NPRM (and by extension, provisions of NFPA 59A-2026), PHMSA generally understands that most of its proposed amendments could be severed from the rest of the proposals herein without adversely affecting the balance of cost and benefits justifying other proposed amendments—whether considered individually or in aggregate. This preliminary assessment holds in particular for those elements of the NPRM that function as alternatives to other, default requirements (
e.g.,
the QRA-based siting alternative at § 193.107; the risk-based operations and maintenance alternative at subpart F), as well as the application of various proposals throughout to any particular category of PHMSA-jurisdictional LNG facility (
e.g.,
application of subpart B siting requirements to peak shavers as well as FERC-jurisdictional LNG terminals).
PHMSA solicits stakeholder comment on which of the NPRM's proposals are severable from other elements of the rulemaking, or as applied to any particular category of PHMSA-jurisdictional LNG facility.
