§ 193.1
Scope of part.
(a) This part prescribes safety standards for LNG facilities used in the transportation of gas by pipeline that is subject to the pipeline safety laws (
49 U.S.C. 60101
et seq.
) and part 192 of this subchapter.
(b) This part does not apply to:
(1) LNG facilities used by ultimate consumers of LNG or natural gas.
(2) LNG facilities used in the course of natural gas treatment or hydrocarbon extraction that do not store LNG.
(3) In the case of a marine transfer area for LNG as defined in
33 CFR 127.005
, any matter other than siting.
(4) Any LNG facility located in navigable waters (as defined in section 3(8) of the Federal Power Act (
16 U.S.C. 796(8)
).
§ 193.3
Applicability.
(a) The requirements in this part governing siting, design, installation, or construction (including material incorporated by reference) do not apply retroactively to existing LNG facilities or to proposed LNG facilities that an appropriate authority approved before the requirements went into effect.
(b) If an LNG facility covered by paragraph (a) of this section is replaced, relocated, or significantly altered on or after [EFFECTIVE DATE OF THE FINAL RULE], then the LNG facility must comply with the applicable requirements of this part governing siting, design, installation, and construction, except that:
(1) The siting requirements apply only to LNG storage tanks that are significantly altered by increasing the storage capacity or relocated; and
(2) To the extent the operator determines compliance with design, installation, and construction requirements make any replaced, relocated, or altered LNG facility incompatible with other LNG facilities, or would otherwise be impracticable, the replaced, relocated, or significantly altered LNG facility may be designed, installed, or constructed in accordance with the original specifications for the LNG facility.

Definitions.
The definitions in chapter 3 of NFPA 59A (incorporated by reference,
see
§ 193.9) are incorporated by reference for use in this part except as substituted, modified, or supplemented in this section:
Administrator
means the Administrator, Pipeline and Hazardous Materials Safety Administration or a delegate.
Component
means any part, or system of parts functioning as a unit, whose integrity or reliability is necessary to maintain safety in controlling, processing, or containing a hazardous fluid, including, but not limited to, piping, pressure vessels, processing equipment, containers, control devices, impounding systems, lighting, security devices, fire control equipment, and communication equipment.
Design pressure
means the pressure used in the design of components for the purpose of determining the minimum permissible thickness or physical characteristics of its various parts. When applicable, the static head must be included in the design pressure to determine the thickness of any specific part.
Design spill
means a potential spill or release from LNG and hazardous fluid containers, piping, and equipment at liquefaction, storage, transfer, or other process areas in an LNG facility.
Determine
means to make a decision based on an appropriate investigation using scientific methods and sound engineering judgment, including documentation that demonstrates the basis of the decision.
Emergency
means a deviation from normal operation, a structural failure, or severe environmental conditions that would probably cause harm to people or property.
Exclusion zone
means an area within or surrounding an LNG facility in which an operator or government agency legally controls all activities in accordance with subpart B of this part for as long as the facility is in operation.
Gas
except when designated as inert, means natural gas, other flammable gas, or gas which is toxic or corrosive.
Hazardous fluid
means a hazardous liquid or gas that is flammable, toxic, or corrosive.
Hazardous liquid
means LNG or a liquid that is flammable, corrosive, or toxic.
Impounding system
includes an impounding area and dikes and floors for conducting the flow of spilled hazardous liquids to an impounding area.
Liquefied natural gas
or
LNG
means natural gas or synthetic gas having methane (CH
4
) as its major constituent that has been changed to a liquid.
LNG facility
means a pipeline facility that is used for liquefying natural gas or synthetic gas or transferring, storing, vaporizing liquefied natural gas, including on-site power generation facilities.
Maximum allowable working pressure (MAWP)
means the maximum gauge pressure permissible at the top of the equipment, containers, or pressure vessels while operating at design temperature.
Normal operation
means functioning within allowable ranges of pressure, temperature, flow, and other operating criteria consistent with the requirements of this part.
Operator
means a person who owns or operates a pipeline facility.
Person
means any individual, firm, joint venture, partnership, corporation, association, State, municipality, cooperative association, or joint stock association, including any trustee, receiver, assignee, or personal representative thereof.
Pipeline facility
means new and existing piping, rights of way, and any equipment, facility, or building used in the transportation of gas or in the treatment of gas during the course of transportation, including an LNG facility.
Piping
means line pipe, tubing, hoses, fittings, valves, pumps, connections, safety devices, or related components for containing the flow of hazardous fluids.
Transfer piping
means a system of permanent or temporary piping, or both, used for transferring hazardous fluids between any of the following: liquefaction process facilities, storage tanks, vaporizers, compressors, cargo transfer systems, and facilities other than pipeline facilities.
Transfer system
includes transfer piping and cargo transfer systems.
Vaporization
means the addition of thermal energy that changes a liquid to a vapor or gaseous state.

§ 193.13
Mobile and temporary LNG facilities.
(a) Operators of mobile and temporary LNG facilities used for peak-shaving, service maintenance during gas pipeline systems repair, alteration, or other short-term applications that are in compliance with chapter 14 of NFPA 59A (incorporated by reference,
see
§ 193.9) need not comply with the requirements of this part other than those in this subpart.
(b) Operators of mobile and temporary LNG facilities must provide to PHMSA or the applicable State agency a location description of each facility at least two weeks in advance of the installation, including the details of location, leakage containment or control, firefighting equipment, and methods employed to restrict public access, except that in the case of emergency where such notice is not possible, as much advance notice as possible must be provided.

§ 193.15
Investigations of failures.
(a) Operators must investigate and determine the cause of any event involving a failure of the integrity or function of systems containing hazardous fluids occurring during commissioning, initial start-up, or operation, as well as any explosion, fire, or hazardous fluid release that results in:
(1) Death or injury requiring hospitalization; or
(2) Estimated property damage of $122,000 or more, including loss to the operator and others, or both, but excluding the cost of gas lost. For adjustments for inflation observed in calendar year 2021 onwards, changes to the reporting threshold will be posted on PHMSA's website. These changes will be determined in accordance with the procedures in appendix A to part 191 of this subchapter.
(b) If the Administrator or relevant State agency under the pipeline safety laws (
49 U.S.C. 60101
et seq.
) investigates a failure, the operator involved shall make available all relevant information and provide reasonable assistance in conducting the investigation. Unless necessary to restore or maintain service, or for safety, no component involved in the incident may be moved from its location or otherwise altered until the investigation is complete or the investigating agency otherwise authorizes. Where components must be moved for operational or safety reasons, they must not be removed from the LNG facility and must be maintained intact to the extent practicable until the investigation is complete, or the investigating agency otherwise authorizes.
(c) Operators must maintain investigation records for a minimum of 5 years from conclusion of the investigation.
Subpart B—Siting
§ 193.101
Scope.
(a) This subpart prescribes requirements for LNG facility siting.
(b) Except as specified in § 193.3 or as provided otherwise by this subpart, each LNG facility that is designed, constructed, replaced, relocated, or significantly altered on or after [5 YEARS AFTER DATE OF PUBLICATION OF THE FINAL RULE], must comply with the requirements of this subpart and sections 5.2.1 and 5.3.1 of NFPA 59A (incorporated by reference,
see
§ 193.9). In the event of a conflict between NFPA 59A and the provisions of this subpart, the provisions of this subpart shall prevail.
§ 193.103
Hazard analysis.
Each operator shall perform an evaluation of hazards and calculation of the extent of hazards for each container, piping, and other equipment containing LNG or other hazardous fluids in accordance with this section and section 5.3.2 of NFPA 59A (incorporated by reference, see § 193.9) and:
(a) Each operator shall submit a siting package consisting of the following material documentation:
(1) Project description, background, purpose and details describing the proposed LNG facility;
(2) Hazard reports, including any attachments and referenced reports;
(3) Facility location map(s), topography map(s), and site aerial photography;
(4) Engineering drawings including an overall plot plan showing the LNG facility's property boundary and unit plot plans for each process area or system showing the location and elevation of major equipment;
(5) Piping and instrument drawings;
(6) Process Flow Diagrams;
(7) Heat and Material Balance Sheets;
(8) Piping Inventory Table;
(9) Pump and compressor curves for pumps and compressors used for hazardous fluid service;
(10) Sketch on plot plan showing expected locations and elevations of major potential single accidental leakage sources;
(11) Dimensions, capacities, and thermal properties for any impoundments associated with the project;
(12) Design details for mitigation measures (including vapor barriers and pipe-in-pipe systems) and assessment of the effect of such measures on evaluation of and calculation of the extent of hazards; and
(13) The summary report of all input and output parameters for hazard modeling.
(b) The design spill criteria for “Piping and Other Equipment” shall include, in lieu of design spill criteria in Table 5.3.2.3 of NFPA 59A, the following:
(1) For piping within process systems or transfer areas involving hazardous fluids greater than or equal to six inches in diameter, a hole two inches in diameter applied at any location along the piping segment;
(2) For piping within process systems or transfer areas involving hazardous fluids less than six inches in diameter, a hole size equivalent to a full-bore rupture applied at any location along the piping segment;
(3) For pipe-in-pipe systems serving as secondary containment, an unobstructed release from a hole one inch in diameter applied at the operating conditions of the inner pipe;
(4) For single-ply construction expansion bellows, a hole size equivalent to a full-bore rupture of the expansion joint applied at any location along the piping segment applied at the expansion joint; and
(5) For transfer hoses, a hole size equivalent to a full-bore rupture of the transfer hose applied at any location along the transfer hose.
(c) Evaluation and calculation of the extent of hazards shall employ source terms and hazard models reviewed against PHMSA-approved Model Evaluation Protocols and Model Validation Databases maintained on PHMSA's website:
https://www.phmsa.dot.gov
.
(d) Evaluation and calculation of the extent of flammable and toxic vapor-gas dispersion hazards shall employ an elevation parameter of 0.5 meters.
(e) Calculation of the extent of flammable vapor-gas and toxic vapor dispersion hazards shall continue until the greater of the time for the dispersion
(
printed page 69384)
hazards to reach their maximum extent and the design spill duration pursuant to section 5.3.2.4 of NFPA 59A.
(f) Calculation of the extent of hazards shall employ any uncertainty factor generated under PHMSA-approved model evaluation protocols pursuant to paragraph (c) of this section.
(g) Evaluation and calculation of the extent of hazards shall consider any supporting documentation for active mitigation measures identified in the siting package.
§ 193.105
Exclusion zones.
Each operator (or applicant, as applicable) evaluating and calculating the extent of hazards pursuant to § 193.103 must establish exclusion zones, occupancy restrictions, and develop any public notification protocols in consultation with applicable State and local emergency management and response organizations with respect to each LNG and hazardous fluid container, piping, and other equipment in accordance with this section and section 5.3.2 of NFPA 59A (incorporated by reference,
see
§ 193.9) provided that:
(a) Operators shall, for a design spill resulting in a toxic cloud with concentration levels corresponding to AEGL-2 and AEGL-3 levels and an exposure duration of one hour or less, establish exclusion zones and occupancy restrictions for toxic vapor dispersion hazards pursuant to Table 5.3.2.9 of NFPA 59A; for other areas with toxic vapor concentration levels and exposure durations at or above AEGL-1, development of any public notification procedures in consultation with applicable State and local emergency management and response organizations will be required in accordance with the facility's emergency response plan; and
(b) An operator need not demonstrate legal control of activities in, or be subject to occupancy restrictions with respect to, any public road, any public right-of-way, and navigable waters.
§ 193.107
Quantitative risk assessment.
As an alternative to the requirements of §§ 193.103 and 193.105, an operator may perform an evaluation of hazards, including calculation of risks to individuals and society with respect to each of fatality and irreversible harm from those hazards, for each container, piping, and other equipment containing LNG or other hazardous fluids in accordance with this section and chapter 19 of NFPA 59A (incorporated by reference, see § 193.9), provided that:
(a) Each operator shall submit material documentation required by NFPA 59A section 19.2.1;
(b) NFPA 59A section 19.1.3 shall not apply;
(c) Evaluation of hazards and risks shall employ hazard models reviewed against PHMSA-approved Model Evaluation Protocols and Model Validation Databases maintained on PHMSA's website:
https://www.phmsa.dot.gov
;
(d) Operators need not evaluate hazards from releases on feed gas or send-out gas lines;
(e) The land use restrictions and risk mitigation requirements of NFPA 59A sections 19.10 and 19.11 shall not apply to public roads, public rights-of-way, and navigable waters; and
(f) Each operator shall comply with risk tolerability criteria (including land use restrictions) in NFPA 59A section 19.10 and risk mitigation requirements in NFPA 59A section 19.11.

§ 193.207
Impoundment structural requirements.
Each impoundment, in addition to pertinent requirements in NFPA 59A (incorporated by reference,
see
§ 193.9), must be designed and constructed to prevent impairment of the reliability and structural integrity of the system after considering:
(a) The imposed loading from the impingement of the trajectory of an LNG jet discharged at any predictable angle.

Subpart F—Risk-Based Operations and Maintenance
§ 193.501
Scope.
LNG facilities subject to the jurisdiction of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission may establish a risk-based program pursuant to the requirements of this subpart as an alternative to operations and maintenance requirements of subpart E of this part other than those pertaining to the following:
(a) Physical security; and
(b) Emergency procedures governing coordination of emergency awareness and response actions by facility personnel and the public in sections 18.4.4, 18.4.5, 18.4.7, and 18.4.8 of NFPA 59A (incorporated by reference, see § 193.9).
§ 193.503
Program content requirements.
An operator electing this subpart must develop and follow a written program pursuant to the Center for Chemical Process Safety's Guidelines for Hazard Evaluation Procedures (incorporated by reference,
see
§ 193.9) and containing the elements described in paragraphs (a) through (k) of this section:
(a)
Employee participation.
Operators shall provide for participation by their personnel and their representatives as required by this paragraph (a):
(1) Operators shall consult with their personnel and their representatives on the conduct and development of process hazards analyses and on the development of the other elements of process safety management in this section.
(2) Operators shall provide to their personnel and their representatives access to process hazard analyses and to all other information required to be developed by this section.
(b)
Process safety information.
Operators shall compile written process safety information before conducting any process hazard analysis required by the section, including information pertaining to:
(1) Hazards of the hazardous fluids used or produced (
e.g.,
toxicity information; permissible exposure limits; physical data; reactivity data; corrosivity data; thermal and chemical stability data; and hazardous effects of inadvertent, reasonably foreseeable mixing);
(2) Technology of the process (
e.g.,
block flow diagrams; process chemistry; inventory limits; and evaluation of consequences from deviations); and
(3) Equipment in the process (
e.g.,
materials of construction; piping and instrumentation drawings; electrical classification; safety systems and their bases; ventilation system design; design codes and standards; material energy balances) along with documentation that equipment either:
(i) Complies with recognized and generally accepted good practices; or
(ii) In the case of existing equipment, was designed and constructed in accordance with codes, standards, or practices that are no longer in general use, but which the operator has determined and documented is designed, maintained, inspected, tested, and operating in a safe manner.
(c)
Process hazard analysis.
(1) The operator shall perform an initial process hazard analysis (PHA) on processes covered by this section. The PHA shall be appropriate to the complexity of the process and shall identify, evaluate, and control the hazards involved in the event of an accidental release of hazardous fluids that could result in an incident. PHAs conducted in connection with FERC review of a certificate application for an LNG facility that meet the requirements of this paragraph (c) are acceptable as initial PHAs.
(2) Operators shall use one or more of the following PHA methods: What-If; checklist; HAZOP, FMEA; Fault Tree Analysis; or an appropriate equivalent.
(3) The PHA shall address the following: hazards of the processes employed; facility siting; identification of pertinent previous incidents; human factors; applicable design and administrative controls, along with the potential consequences of failure of those controls; and a qualitative evaluation of possible safety and health effects of failure of controls.
(4) The process hazard analysis shall be performed by a team with expertise in engineering and process operations, and the team shall include at least one employee who has experience and knowledge specific to the process being evaluated. Also, one member of the team must be knowledgeable in the specific process hazard analysis methodology being used.
(5) The operator shall establish a system to address the team's findings and recommendations promptly; assure that the recommendations are resolved in a timely manner and that the resolution is documented; document what actions are to be taken; complete actions as soon as possible; develop a written schedule of when these actions are to be completed; communicate the actions to operating, maintenance and other employees whose work assignments are in the process and who may be affected by the recommendations or actions.
(6) At least every 5 years after the completion of the initial process hazard analysis, the process hazard analysis shall be updated and revalidated by a team meeting the requirements in paragraph (c)(4) of this section, to assure that the process hazard analysis is consistent with the current process.
(7) Operators shall retain process hazards analyses and updates or revalidations for each process covered by this section, as well as the documented resolution of recommendations described in paragraph (c)(5) of this section for the life of the process.
(d)
Operating procedures.
(1) The operator shall develop and implement written operating procedures that provide clear instructions for safely conducting activities involved in each covered process consistent with the
(
printed page 69387)
process safety information and shall address at least the following elements:
(i) Steps for each operating phase including initial startup; normal operations; abnormal operations; emergency shutdown including the conditions under which emergency shutdown is required, and the assignment of shutdown responsibility to qualified personnel to ensure that emergency shutdown is executed in a safe and timely manner; emergency operations; cooldown; normal shutdown; and, startup following a planned shutdown, or after an emergency shutdown.
(ii) Operating limits, including consequences of deviation, and steps required to correct or avoid deviation.
(iii) Safety and health considerations including properties of, and hazards presented by, the hazardous fluids used in the process; precautions necessary to prevent exposure, including engineering controls, administrative controls, and personal protective equipment; control measures to be taken if physical contact or airborne exposure occurs; quality control for raw materials and control of hazardous fluid inventory levels; and any special or unique hazards.
(iv) Safety systems and their functions.
(2) Operating procedures shall be readily accessible to personnel who work in or maintain a process.
(3) The operating procedures shall be reviewed as often as necessary to assure that they reflect current operating practice, including changes that result from changes in process chemicals, technology, and equipment, and changes to facilities. The operator shall certify annually that these operating procedures are current and accurate.
(4) The operator shall develop and implement safe work practices to provide for the control of hazards during operations such as lockout/tagout; confined space entry; opening process equipment or piping; and control over entrance into a facility by maintenance, contractor, laboratory, or other support personnel. These safe work practices shall apply to operator and contractor personnel.
(e)
Training—
(1)
Initial training.
Operator personnel presently involved in operating a process, and personnel before being involved in operating a newly assigned process, shall be trained in an overview of the process and in the operating procedures as specified in paragraph (d) of this section. The training shall include emphasis on the specific safety and health hazards, emergency operations including shutdown, and safe work practices applicable to the employee's job tasks. In lieu of initial training for those personnel already involved in operating a process as of [EFFECTIVE DATE OF THE FINAL RULE], an operator may certify in writing that each of its personnel has the required knowledge, skills, and abilities to carry out safely the duties and responsibilities as specified in the operating procedures.
(2)
Refresher training.
Refresher training shall be provided at least every three years, and more often if necessary, to personnel involved in operating a process to assure that each understands and adheres to the current operating procedures of the process. The operator, in consultation with the personnel involved in operating the process, shall determine the appropriate frequency of refresher training.
(3)
Training documentation.
The operator shall ascertain that each of its personnel involved in operating a process has received and understood the training required by this paragraph (e). The operator shall prepare a record which contains the identity of each of its personnel, the date of training, and the means used to verify that the personnel understood the training.
(f)
Contractors—
(1)
Application.
This paragraph (f) applies to operations or maintenance activity performed by contractors on or adjacent to a covered process. It does not apply to contractors' provision of incidental services which do not influence process safety, such as janitorial, food and drink, laundry, delivery or other supply services.
(2)
Operator responsibilities.
(i) The operator, when selecting a contractor, shall obtain and evaluate information regarding the contractor's safety performance and programs.
(ii) The operator shall inform contract operators of the known potential fire, explosion, or toxic release hazards related to the contractor's work and the process.
(iii) The operator shall explain to contractor the applicable provisions of the emergency procedures required under subpart E of this part.
(iv) The operator shall develop and implement safe work practices consistent with this section, to control the entrance, presence and exit of contractors and contractor personnel in covered process areas.
(v) The operator shall ensure contractor personnel are trained in the work practices necessary to perform their jobs safely.
(vi) The operator shall ensure contractor personnel are instructed in the known potential fire, explosion, or toxic release hazards related to his/her job and the process, and the applicable provisions of the emergency action plan.
(vii) The operator shall ensure the contractor has documented that each of its personnel has received and understood the training required by this paragraph (f), and has prepared a record which contains the identity of its personnel, the date of training, and the means used to verify that each of its personnel understood the training.
(viii) The operator shall assure that all contractor personnel follow the safety rules of the facility including the safe work practices required under this section.
(ix) The operator shall ensure that the contractor advises it of any unique hazards presented by the contractor personnel's work, or of any hazards found by the contractor personnel's work.
(g)
Pre-startup safety review.
(1) The operator shall perform a pre-startup safety review for new facilities and for modified facilities when the modification requires a change in the process safety information.
(2) The pre-startup safety review shall confirm that prior to the introduction of hazardous fluids to a process:
(i) Construction and equipment is in accordance with design specifications;
(ii) Safety, operating, maintenance, and emergency procedures are in place and are adequate;
(iii) For new facilities, a process hazard analysis has been performed and recommendations have been resolved or implemented before startup; and modified facilities meet the management of change requirements contained in paragraph (k) of this section.
(iv) Training of personnel involved in operating a process has been completed.
(h)
Mechanical integrity—
(1)
Application.
Paragraphs (h)(2) through (5) of this section apply to the following process equipment:
(i) Pressure vessels and storage tanks;
(ii) Piping systems (including piping components such as valves);
(iii) Relief and vent systems and devices;
(iv) Emergency shutdown systems;
(v) Controls (including monitoring devices and sensors, alarms, and interlocks); and
(vi) Pumps.
(2)
Written procedures.
The operator shall establish and implement written procedures to maintain the on-going integrity of process equipment.
(3)
Training for process maintenance activities.
The operator shall train each employee involved in maintaining the on-going integrity of process equipment in an overview of that process and its hazards and in the procedures applicable to the personnel's job tasks to
(
printed page 69388)
assure that personnel can perform the job tasks in a safe manner.
(4)
Inspection and testing.
(i) Inspections and tests shall be performed on process equipment.
(ii) Inspection and testing procedures shall follow recognized and generally accepted good engineering practices.
(iii) The frequency of inspections and tests of process equipment shall be consistent with applicable manufacturers' recommendations and good engineering practices, and more frequently if determined to be necessary by prior operating experience.
(iv) The operator shall document each inspection and test that has been performed on process equipment. The documentation shall identify the date of the inspection or test, the name of the person who performed the inspection or test, the serial number or other identifier of the equipment on which the inspection or test was performed, a description of the inspection or test performed, and the results of the inspection or test.
(5)
Equipment deficiencies.
The operator shall correct deficiencies in equipment that are outside acceptable limits (defined by the process safety information in paragraph (b) of this section) before further use or in a safe and timely manner when necessary means are taken to assure safe operation.
(i)
Hot work permit.
(1) The operator shall issue a hot work permit for hot work operations conducted on or near a covered process.
(2) The permit shall document that the fire prevention and protection requirements in this part have been implemented prior to beginning the hot work operations; it shall indicate the date(s) authorized for hot work; and identify the object on which hot work is to be performed. The permit shall be kept on file until completion of the hot work operations.
(j)
Management of change.
(1) The operator shall establish and implement written procedures to manage changes (except for “in-kind” replacements) to process chemicals, technology, equipment, and procedures; and, changes to facilities that affect a covered process.
(2) The procedures shall assure that the following considerations are addressed prior to any change:
(i) The technical basis for the proposed change;
(ii) Impact of change on safety and health;
(iii) Modifications to operating procedures;
(iv) Necessary time period for the change; and,
(v) Authorization requirements for the proposed change.
(3) Operator personnel involved in operating a process and maintenance and contractor personnel whose job tasks will be affected by a change in the process shall be informed of, and trained in, the change prior to start-up of the process or affected part of the process.
(4) If a change covered by this paragraph (j) results in a change in the process safety information required by paragraph (b) of this section, such information shall be updated accordingly.
(5) If a change covered by this paragraph (j) results in a change in the operating procedures or practices required by paragraph (d) of this section, such procedures or practices shall be updated accordingly.
(k)
Compliance audits.
(1) Operators shall certify that they have evaluated compliance with the provisions of this section at least every three years to verify that the procedures and practices developed under this section are adequate and are being followed.
(2) The compliance audit shall be conducted by at least one person knowledgeable in the process.
(3) A report of the findings of the audit shall be developed.
(4) The operator shall promptly determine and document an appropriate response to each of the findings of the compliance audit, and document that deficiencies have been corrected
(5) Operators shall retain the two (2) most recent compliance audit reports.
§ 193.505
Implementation plans.
(a) Operators electing this subpart shall submit for PHMSA review and approval pursuant to implementation plans under § 190.9 of this subchapter, copying the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, the Department of Homeland Security, and each cognizant Coast Guard Captain of the Port (COTP). PHMSA shall review, and either deny or approve, each plan within 30 calendar days from receipt; plans not approved within 30 days shall be deemed denied.
(b) Implementation plans shall set forth, on a process-by-process, system-by-system, or an organization-by-organization basis, intermediate and final milestones specifying work streams and dates for an operator's transition to compliant operations and maintenance programs under this subpart.

Nuclear Regulatory Commission
[NRC-2026-4687]
AGENCY:
Nuclear Regulatory Commission.
ACTION:
License amendment request; notice of opportunity to comment, request a hearing, and petition for leave to intervene; order imposing procedures.
SUMMARY:
The U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) received, and is considering approval of one amendment request. The license amendment request is for Calvert Cliffs Nuclear Power Plant, Units 1 and 2. For the license amendment request, the NRC proposes to determine that it involves no significant hazards consideration (NSHC). Because the amendment request contains sensitive unclassified non-safeguards information (SUNSI), the NRC is issuing an order imposing procedures to obtain access to SUNSI for contention preparation by persons who file a hearing request or petition for leave to intervene.
DATES:
Comments must be filed by December 3, 2026. A request for a hearing or petitions for leave to intervene must be filed by January 4, 2027. Any potential party as defined in section 2.4 of title 10 of the
Code of Federal Regulations
(10 CFR) who believes access to Sensitive Unclassified Non-Safeguards Information and Safeguards Information (SUNSI) is necessary to respond to this notice must request document access by November 13, 2026.
ADDRESSES:
You may submit comments by any of the following methods; however, the NRC encourages electronic comment submission through the Federal rulemaking website.
Federal rulemaking website:
Go to
https://www.regulations.gov
and search for Docket ID NRC-2026-4687. Address questions about Docket IDs in
Regulations.gov
to Bridget Curran; telephone: 301-415-1003; email:
Bridget.Curran@nrc.gov
.
For technical questions, contact the individual(s) listed in the
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT
section of this document.
Mail comments to:
Office of Nuclear Material Safety and Safeguards, Mail Stop: TWFN-5-A85, U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission, Washington, DC 20555-0001, ATTN: Guidance and Publications Branch.
For additional direction on obtaining information and submitting comments, see “Obtaining Information and Submitting Comments” in the
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION
section of this document.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Susan Lent, Office of Nuclear Reactor Regulation, U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission, Washington, DC 20555-0001; telephone: 301-415-1365; email:
Susan.Lent@nrc.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Obtaining Information and Submitting Comments
A. Obtaining Information
Please refer to Docket ID NRC-2026-4687, facility name, unit number(s), docket number(s), application date, and subject when contacting the NRC about the availability of information for this action. You may obtain publicly available information related to this action by any of the following methods:
Federal Rulemaking Website:
Go to
https://www.regulations.gov
and search for Docket ID NRC-2026-4687.
NRC's Agencywide Documents Access and Management System (ADAMS):
You may obtain publicly available documents online in the ADAMS Public Documents collection at
https://www.nrc.gov/​reading-rm/​adams.html
.
To begin the search, select “Begin ADAMS Public Search.” For problems with ADAMS, please contact the NRC's Public Document Room (PDR) reference staff at 1-800-397-4209, at 301-415-4737, or by email to
PDR.Resource@nrc.gov
.
The ADAMS accession number for each document referenced (if it is available in ADAMS) is provided the first time that it is mentioned in this document.
NRC's PDR:
The PDR, where you may examine and order copies of publicly available documents, is open by appointment. To make an appointment to visit the PDR, please send an email to
PDR.Resource@nrc.gov
or call 1-800-397-4209 or 301-415-4737, between 8 a.m. and 4 p.m. eastern time (ET), Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays.
B. Submitting Comments
The NRC encourages electronic comment submission through the Federal rulemaking website (
https://www.regulations.gov
). Please include Docket ID NRC-2026-4687, facility name, unit number(s), docket number(s), application date, and subject, in your comment submission.
The NRC cautions you not to include identifying or contact information that you do not want to be publicly disclosed in your comment submission. The NRC will post all comment submissions at
https://www.regulations.gov
as well as enter the comment submissions into ADAMS. The NRC does not routinely edit comment submissions to remove identifying or contact information.
If you are requesting or aggregating comments from other persons for submission to the NRC, then you should inform those persons not to include identifying or contact information that they do not want to be publicly disclosed in their comment submission. Your request should state that the NRC does not routinely edit comment submissions to remove such information before making the comment submissions available to the public or entering the comment into ADAMS.
II. Background
Pursuant to section 189a.(1)-(2) of the Atomic Energy Act of 1954, as amended (the Act), the NRC is publishing this notice. The Act requires the Commission to publish notice of any amendments issued or proposed to be issued and grants the Commission the authority to issue and make immediately effective any amendment to an operating license or combined license, as applicable, upon a determination by the Commission that such amendment involves NSHC, notwithstanding the pendency before the Commission of a request for a hearing from any person.
This notice includes a notice of amendments containing SUNSI.
III. Notice of Consideration of Issuance of Amendments to Facility Operating Licenses, Proposed No Significant Hazards Consideration Determination, and Opportunity for a Hearing
The Commission has made a proposed determination that the following amendment request involves NSHC. Under the Commission's
(
printed page 69278)
regulations in
10 CFR 50.92
, this means that operation of the facility in accordance with the proposed amendments would not (1) involve a significant increase in the probability or consequences of an accident previously evaluated, or (2) create the possibility of a new or different kind of accident from any accident previously evaluated, or (3) involve a significant reduction in a margin of safety. The basis for this proposed determination for the amendment request is shown as follows.
The Commission is seeking public comments on this proposed determination. Any comments received within 30 days after the date of publication of this notice will be considered in making any final determination.
Normally, the Commission will not issue the amendments until the expiration of 60 days after the date of publication of this notice. The Commission may issue the license amendments before expiration of the 60-day period provided that its final determination is that the amendments involve NSHC. In addition, the Commission may issue the amendments prior to the expiration of the 30-day comment period if circumstances change during the 30-day comment period such that failure to act in a timely way would result, for example, in derating or shutdown of the facility. If the Commission takes action on the amendments prior to the expiration of either the comment period or the notice period, it will publish a notice of issuance in the
Federal Register
. If the Commission makes a final NSHC determination for the amendments, any hearing on the amendments will take place after issuance. The Commission expects that the need to take this action will occur very infrequently.
A. Opportunity To Request a Hearing and Petition for Leave To Intervene
Within 60 days after the date of publication of this notice, any person (petitioner) whose interest may be affected by any of these actions may file a request for a hearing and petition for leave to intervene (petition) with respect to that action. Petitions shall be filed in accordance with the Commission's “Agency Rules of Practice and Procedure” in
10 CFR part 2
. Interested persons should consult
10 CFR 2.309
. If a petition is filed, the Commission or a presiding officer will rule on the petition and, if appropriate, a notice of a hearing will be issued.
Petitions must be filed no later than 60 days from the date of publication of this notice in accordance with the filing instructions in the “Electronic Submissions (E-Filing)” section of this document. Petitions and motions for leave to file new or amended contentions that are filed after the deadline will not be entertained absent a determination by the presiding officer that the filing demonstrates good cause by satisfying the three factors in
10 CFR 2.309(c)(1)(i)
through
(iii)
.
If a hearing is requested, and the Commission has not made a final determination on the issue of no significant hazards consideration, the Commission will make a final determination on the issue of NSHC, which will serve to establish when the hearing is held. If the final determination is that the license amendment request involves NSHC, the Commission may issue the amendments and make it immediately effective, notwithstanding the request for a hearing. Any hearing would take place after issuance of the amendments. If the final determination is that the license amendment request involves a significant hazards consideration, then any hearing held would take place before the issuance of the amendment unless the Commission finds an imminent danger to the health or safety of the public, in which case it will issue an appropriate order or rule under
10 CFR part 2
.
A State, local governmental body, Federally recognized Indian Tribe, or designated agency thereof, may submit a petition to the Commission to participate as a party under
10 CFR 2.309(h)
no later than 60 days from the date of publication of this notice. Alternatively, a State, local governmental body, Federally recognized Indian Tribe, or designated agency thereof, may participate as a non-party under
10 CFR 2.315(c)
.
For information about filing a petition and about participation by a person not a party under
10 CFR 2.315
, see ADAMS Accession No. ML20340A053 (
https://adamswebsearch2.nrc.gov/​webSearch2/​main.jsp?​AccessionNumber=​ML20340A053
) and the NRC's public website (
https://www.nrc.gov/​about-nrc/​regulatory/​adjudicatory/​hearing.html#participate
).
B. Electronic Submissions (E-Filing)
All documents filed in NRC adjudicatory proceedings, including documents filed by an interested State, local governmental body, Federally recognized Indian Tribe, or designated agency thereof that requests to participate under
10 CFR 2.315(c)
, must be filed in accordance with
10 CFR 2.302
. The E-Filing process requires participants to submit and serve all adjudicatory documents over the internet, or in some cases, to mail copies on electronic storage media, unless an exemption permitting an alternative filing method, as further discussed, is granted. Detailed guidance on electronic submissions is located in the “Guidance for Electronic Submissions to the NRC” (ADAMS Accession No. ML13031A056), and on the NRC's public website (
https://www.nrc.gov/​site-help/​e-submittals.html
).
To comply with the procedural requirements of E-Filing, at least 10 days prior to the filing deadline, the participant should contact the Office of the Secretary by email at
Hearing.Docket@nrc.gov
,
or by telephone at 301-415-1677, to: (1) request a digital identification (ID) certificate, which allows the participant (or their counsel or representative) to digitally sign submissions and access the E-Filing system for any proceeding in which it is participating; and (2) advise the Secretary that the participant will be submitting a petition or other adjudicatory document (even in instances in which the participant, or its counsel or representative, already holds an NRC-issued digital ID certificate). Based upon this information, the Secretary will establish an electronic docket for the proceeding if the Secretary has not already established an electronic docket.
Information about applying for a digital ID certificate is available on the NRC's public website (
https://www.nrc.gov/​site-help/​e-submittals/​getting-started.html
). After a digital ID certificate is obtained and a docket is created, the participant must submit adjudicatory documents in the Portable Document Format. Guidance on submissions is available on the NRC's public website (
https://www.nrc.gov/​site-help/​electronic-sub-ref-mat.html
). A filing is considered complete at the time the document is submitted through the NRC's E-Filing system. To be timely, an electronic filing must be submitted to the E-Filing system no later than 11:59 p.m. ET on the due date. Upon receipt of a transmission, the E-Filing system time-stamps the document and sends the submitter an email confirming receipt of the document. The E-Filing system also distributes an email that provides access to the document to the NRC's Office of the General Counsel and any others who have advised the Office of the Secretary that they wish to participate in the proceeding, so that the filer need not serve the document on those participants separately. Therefore, applicants and other participants (or their counsel or representative) must apply for and receive a digital ID certificate before adjudicatory
(
printed page 69279)
documents are filed in order to obtain access to the documents via the E-Filing system.
A person filing electronically using the NRC's adjudicatory E-Filing system may seek assistance by contacting the NRC's Electronic Filing Help Desk through the “Contact Us” link located on the NRC's public website (
https://www.nrc.gov/​site-help/​e-submittals.html
), by email to
MSHD.Resource@nrc.gov
,
or by a toll-free call at 1-866-672-7640. The NRC Electronic Filing Help Desk is available between 9 a.m. and 6 p.m., ET, Monday through Friday, except Federal holidays.
Participants who believe that they have good cause for not submitting documents electronically must file an exemption request, in accordance with
10 CFR 2.302(g)
, with their initial paper filing stating why there is good cause for not filing electronically and requesting authorization to continue to submit documents in paper format. Such filings must be submitted in accordance with
10 CFR 2.302(b)-(d)
. Participants filing adjudicatory documents in this manner are responsible for serving their documents on all other participants. Participants granted an exemption under
10 CFR 2.302(g)(2)
must still meet the electronic formatting requirement in
10 CFR 2.302(g)(1)
, unless the participant also seeks and is granted an exemption from
10 CFR 2.302(g)(1)
.
Documents submitted in adjudicatory proceedings will appear in the NRC's electronic hearing docket, which is publicly available on the NRC's public website (
https://ehd.nrc.gov
), unless otherwise excluded pursuant to an order of the presiding officer. If you do not have an NRC-issued digital ID certificate as previously described, click “cancel” when the link requests certificates and you will be automatically directed to the NRC's electronic hearing docket where you will be able to access any publicly available documents in a particular hearing docket. Participants are requested not to include personal privacy information such as social security numbers, home addresses, or personal phone numbers in their filings, unless an NRC regulation or other law requires submission of such information. With respect to copyrighted works, except for limited excerpts that serve the purpose of the adjudicatory filings and would constitute a Fair Use application, participants should not include copyrighted materials in their submission.

Order Imposing Procedures for Access to Sensitive Unclassified Non-Safeguards Information for Contention Preparation; Constellation Energy Generation, LLC; Calvert Cliffs Nuclear Power Plant, LLC; Calvert Cliffs Nuclear Power Plant, Units 1 and 2; Calvert County, MD
A. This Order contains instructions regarding how potential parties to this proceeding may request access to documents containing Sensitive Unclassified Non-Safeguards Information (SUNSI).
B. Within 10 days after publication of this notice of hearing or opportunity for hearing, any potential party who believes access to SUNSI is necessary to respond to this notice may request access to SUNSI. A “potential party” is any person who intends to participate as a party by demonstrating standing and filing an admissible contention under
10 CFR 2.309
. Requests for access to SUNSI submitted later than 10 days after publication of this notice will not be considered absent a showing of good cause for the late filing, addressing why the request could not have been filed earlier.
C. The requestor shall submit a letter requesting permission to access SUNSI to the Office of the Secretary, U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission, Washington, DC 20555-0001, Attention: Rulemakings and Adjudications Staff, and provide a copy to the Deputy General Counsel for Licensing, Hearings, and Enforcement, Office of the General Counsel, U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission, Washington, DC 20555-0001. The expedited delivery or courier mail address for both offices is: U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Commission, 11555 Rockville Pike, Rockville, Maryland 20852. The email addresses for the Office of the Secretary and the Office of the General Counsel are
Hearing.Docket@nrc.gov
and
RidsOgcMailCenter.Resource@nrc.gov
,
respectively.
[
1
]
The request must include the following information:
(
printed page 69280)
(1) A description of the licensing action with a citation to this
Federal Register
notice;
(2) The name and address of the potential party and a description of the potential party's particularized interest that could be harmed by the action identified in C.(1); and
(3) The identity of the individual or entity requesting access to SUNSI and the requestor's basis for the need for the information in order to meaningfully participate in this adjudicatory proceeding. In particular, the request must explain why publicly available versions of the information requested would not be sufficient to provide the basis and specificity for a proffered contention.
D. Based on an evaluation of the information submitted under paragraph C, the NRC staff will determine within 10 days of receipt of the request whether:
(1) There is a reasonable basis to believe the petitioner is likely to establish standing to participate in this NRC proceeding; and
(2) The requestor has established a legitimate need for access to SUNSI.
E. If the NRC staff determines that the requestor satisfies both D.(1) and D.(2), the NRC staff will notify the requestor in writing that access to SUNSI has been granted. The written notification will contain instructions on how the requestor may obtain copies of the requested documents, and any other conditions that may apply to access to those documents. These conditions may include, but are not limited to, the signing of a Non-Disclosure Agreement or Affidavit, or Protective Order
[
2
]
setting forth terms and conditions to prevent the unauthorized or inadvertent disclosure of SUNSI by each individual who will be granted access to SUNSI.
F.
Filing of Contentions.
Any contentions in these proceedings that are based upon the information received as a result of the request made for SUNSI must be filed by the requestor no later than 25 days after receipt of (or access to) that information. However, if more than 25 days remain between the petitioner's receipt of (or access to) the information and the deadline for filing all other contentions (as established in the notice of hearing or opportunity for hearing), the petitioner may file its SUNSI contentions by that later deadline.
G.
Review of Denials of Access.
(1) If the request for access to SUNSI is denied by the NRC staff after a determination on standing and requisite need, the NRC staff shall immediately notify the requestor in writing, briefly stating the reason or reasons for the denial.
(2) The requestor may challenge the NRC staff's adverse determination by filing a challenge within five days of receipt of that determination with: (a) the presiding officer designated in this proceeding; (b) if no presiding officer has been appointed, the Chief Administrative Judge, or if this individual is unavailable, another administrative judge, or an Administrative Law Judge with jurisdiction pursuant to
10 CFR 2.318(a)
; or
(c)
if another officer has been designated to rule on information access issues, with that officer.
(3) Further appeals of decisions under this paragraph must be made pursuant to
10 CFR 2.311
.
H.
Review of Grants of Access.
A party other than the requestor may challenge an NRC staff determination granting access to SUNSI whose release would harm that party's interest independent of the proceeding. Such a challenge must be filed within 5 days of the notification by the NRC staff of its grant of access and must be filed with: (a) the presiding officer designated in this proceeding; (b) if no presiding officer has been appointed, the Chief Administrative Judge, or if this individual is unavailable, another administrative judge, or an Administrative Law Judge with jurisdiction pursuant to
10 CFR 2.318(a)
; or
(c)
if another officer has been designated to rule on information access issues, with that officer.
If challenges to the NRC staff determinations are filed, these procedures give way to the normal process for litigating disputes concerning access to information. The availability of interlocutory review by the Commission of orders ruling on such NRC staff determinations (whether granting or denying access) is governed by
10 CFR 2.311
.
[
3
]
I. The Commission expects that the NRC staff and presiding officers (and any other reviewing officers) will consider and resolve requests for access to SUNSI, and motions for protective orders, in a timely fashion in order to minimize any unnecessary delays in identifying those petitioners who have standing and who have propounded contentions meeting the specificity and basis requirements in
10 CFR part 2
. The attachment to this Order summarizes the general target schedule for processing and resolving requests under these procedures.
It is so ordered.

Under Administrative and Technical Support for the Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA) New Chemical Program (NCP) solicitation number 47QRAA20D002D, task order number 68HERW27F0013, Avanti Corporation will perform technical and administrative tasks to support activities for the TSCA New Chemicals Program, including and not limited to: Tracking regulatory decisions, coordinating communications, preparing correspondences, drafting TSCA Section 5(e) and 5(f) Orders, sanitizing documents containing TSCA CBI, preparing information to be uploaded into ChemView, performing analyses, and other related tasks to support the program. In accordance with the requirements of
40 CFR 2.306(f)
, EPA has determined that the disclosure of CBI submitted to EPA under all sections of TSCA is necessary for Avanti Corporation to satisfactorily carry out the work required by the contract. Accordingly, Avanti Corporation personnel will be given access to information, including information submitted to EPA under all sections of TSCA, some of which may be claimed or determined to be CBI.

TSCA CBI Protection Manual.
Access to TSCA data, including CBI, will continue until October 31, 2029. If the contract is extended, this access will also continue for the duration of the extended contract without further notice. In accordance with the requirements of
40 CFR 2.306(f)
, the contract prohibits disclosure of information to a third party without prior written approval from the Agency.
Avanti Corporation personnel will sign nondisclosure agreements and will be briefed on appropriate security procedures before they are permitted access to TSCA CBI. Records of information provided to Avanti Corporation will be maintained by EPA project officers for this contract. All information supplied to Avanti Corporation by EPA for use in connection with this contract will be returned to EPA when Avanti Corporation has completed its work.

AGENCY:

ACTION:
Notice of approval to implement Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program demonstration project.
SUMMARY:
On September 15, 2026, the Food and Nutrition Administration (FNA) posted
Federal Register
Number 2026-18880, which invited public comment on the State of Virginia's Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) demonstration project authorized under section 17(b) of the Food and Nutrition Act of 2008. The comment period closed October 15, 2026. FNA has considered all comments received and is announcing its decision to proceed with approval of Virginia's request to implement its SNAP demonstration project.
DATES:
The project is effective November 1, 2026.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
Shiela Corley, Acting FNA Administrator, at
SM.FN.RPMDHQ-WEB@usda.gov
with subject line of “VA SNAP Demonstration Project”.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Section 17(b) of the Food and Nutrition Act of 2008,
7 U.S.C. 2026(b)
, authorizes FNA to approve demonstration projects to test changes to the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP) that may increase programmatic efficiency and improve the delivery of SNAP benefits to raise levels of nutrition among eligible households. This demonstration project is implemented by the State, and FNA will carefully review the results of the project based on the State's evaluation data. All relevant documents, including the State's demonstration project request(s) and FNA approval(s), can be found in the supporting document section. Additionally, to support implementation and ensure transparency, FNA created a central web page on May 21, 2025, to post State agencies' project requests and approvals and provide exact implementation timelines. That web page is accessible at the following address:
https://www.fna.usda.gov/​snap/​waivers/​foodrestriction
.
Discussion of Demonstration Project
State of Virginia Demonstration Project Request
The State of Virginia requested to conduct a demonstration project to amend the SNAP definition of food for purchase to exclude “sweetened beverages.” The State formally requested to conduct this project on November 4, 2025. On February 3, 2026, the State requested to modify the initial project request to amend the implementation date to October 1, 2026. Subsequently, in consultation with FNA, the State revised its planned implementation date to November 1, 2026. The State's project request and the subsequent modification request can be found in the supporting document section and on the FNA website at the following address:
https://www.fna.usda.gov/​snap/​waivers/​foodrestriction/​virginia
.
USDA Approval of Initial Demonstration Project Request
FNA approved the State's initial demonstration project request on December 10, 2025. The approval can be found in the supporting document section and at the following address:
https://www.fna.usda.gov/​snap/​waivers/​foodrestriction/​virginia
.
Discussion of Public Comments
FNA received 30 comments on Virginia's demonstration project request. Most commenters opposed the project, citing concerns about potential health and nutrition impacts, limits on participant choice, added burden on SNAP households, retailer and consumer confusion, and the project's evaluation measures. Supporters stated that the project advances SNAP's nutrition objectives, could improve public health outcomes, and would promote responsible use of taxpayer-funded benefits.
FNA carefully considered all comments and determined that none of the comments received were significant. FNA has decided to allow Virginia's revised project request to proceed without modification, effective November 1, 2026. SNAP's statutory purpose is to improve nutrition among low-income households, and FNA believes the project is consistent with that purpose and represents an appropriate policy intervention to address diet-related disease and obesity. FNA has supported the State in its efforts to prepare retailers and provide notice to SNAP households. FNA also notes that SNAP benefits are supplemental and do not restrict participants from purchasing excluded items with non-SNAP funds. FNA has determined that approval is authorized under section 17(b) of the Food and Nutrition Act of 2008 and that Virginia is prepared to implement the project successfully.
Shiela Corley,
Acting Administrator, Food and Nutrition Administration, USDA.

Title:
Individual Retirement Account Compliance Resolution System.
OMB Control Number:
1545-NEW.
Form Number:
15443, 15745, 15745-A, 15745-B, 15745-C.
Regulation Project Number:
Revenue Procedure 2026-33.
Abstract:
This revenue procedure establishes the IRA Compliance Resolution System (ICRS), a new correction program for individual retirement accounts and annuities (IRAs). The program permits IRA custodians and IRA owners to correct certain eligible inadvertent failures that occur due to custodian errors or inadvertent errors by a service provider. ICRS also transitions requests for waivers of the 60-day rollover requirement from private letter ruling requests under Rev. Proc. 2026-4 to requests for waivers under ICRS.
Form 15443 is used by an IRA custodian or owner to apply for the Individual Retirement Account/Annuity (IRA) Voluntary Correction Program (IVCP) or to request a pre-submission conference to discuss a potential IVCP submission.
Form 15745 is used by IVCP applicants to describe the eligible inadvertent failures the applicant wishes to correct under IVCP and the proposed methods of correction. If applicable, applicants that are IRA custodians also describe proposed procedures to locate lost IRA owners or beneficiaries and proposed revisions to administrative procedures.
Form 15745-A is used by IVCP applicants to identify required minimum distribution failures, to describe proposed methods of correction, and request relief related to those failures. If applicable, applicants that are IRA custodians also describe changes to administrative procedures.
Form 15745-B is used by IVCP applicants to identify nonspouse beneficiary distribution or rollover failures and IRA establishment failures and to describe proposed methods of correction and request relief related to those failures. If applicable, applicants that are IRA custodians also describe changes to administrative procedures.
Form 15745-C is used by IVCP applicants to identify 60-day rollover failures and to describe proposed methods of correction and request relief related to those failures.

ACTION:
Notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM).
SUMMARY:
The FAA proposes to supersede Airworthiness Directive (AD) 2024-25-09, which applies to certain The Boeing Company Model 757 airplanes. AD 2024-25-09 requires installing new relays and changing certain wire bundles leading to the power transfer unit (PTU) control valve. Since the FAA issued AD 2024-25-09, the FAA determined that the requirements bulletin mandated by AD 2024-25-09 contains errors. In some cases, those errors prevent the actions
(
printed page 69228)
required by AD 2024-25-09 from being fully accomplished. In other cases, the errors would allow actions that could introduce new hazards affecting the operation and thus the availability of the PTU. This proposed AD would require, depending on the airplane configuration, installing new relays and new connectors, changing certain wire bundles, doing an operational test, and applicable on-condition actions. The FAA is proposing this AD to address the unsafe condition on these products.

Comments Invited
The FAA invites you to send any written relevant data, views, or arguments about this proposal. Send your comments using a method listed under the

Confidential Business Information
CBI is commercial or financial information that is both customarily and actually treated as private by its owner. Under the Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) (
5 U.S.C. 552
), CBI is exempt from public disclosure. If your comments responsive to this NPRM contain commercial or financial information that is customarily treated as private, that you actually treat as private, and that is relevant or responsive to this NPRM, it is important that you clearly designate the submitted comments as CBI. Please mark each page of your submission containing CBI as “PROPIN.” The FAA will treat such marked submissions as confidential under the FOIA, and they will not be placed in the public docket of this NPRM. Submissions containing CBI should be sent to Katherine Venegas, Aviation Safety Engineer, FAA, 2200 South 216th St., Des Moines, WA 98198; phone: 562-627-5353; email:
katherine.venegas@faa.gov
.
Any commentary that the FAA receives that is not specifically designated as CBI will be placed in the public docket for this rulemaking.
Background
The FAA issued AD 2024-25-09, Amendment 39-22911 (
90 FR 1850
, January 10, 2025) (AD 2024-25-09), for certain The Boeing Company Model 757 airplanes. AD 2024-25-09 was prompted by reports of several occurrences of a PTU control valve that failed to open when commanded. AD 2024-25-09 requires installing new relays and changing certain wire bundles leading to the PTU control valve. The agency issued AD 2024-25-09 to address failure of the PTU control valve, which, in conjunction with a loss of the left engine or engine-driven pump during takeoff, may result in a failure of the landing gear to retract in a timely manner. This condition, if not addressed, could result in additional drag, a reduced climb gradient, and an inability to clear obstacles on takeoff. This condition can result in loss of continued safe flight and landing.
Actions Since AD 2024-25-09 Was Issued
An operator reported errors in the instructions of Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 757-29A0071 RB, dated November 16, 2023, that prevented its accomplishment on airplanes identified as Group 3 airplanes in that requirements bulletin. Since the FAA issued AD 2024-25-09, Boeing has identified additional errors affecting all of the groups in that requirements bulletin, including errors that would allow actions that could introduce new hazards.
The FAA assessed the new hazards. Although the agency quantitatively assessed the new hazards to be of relatively low risk, the FAA determined that they could affect the operation and thus the availability of the PTU. The PTU is required to operate as a safety system backup. The new hazards that the errors could introduce are therefore a safety concern. The original unsafe condition also remains, because the corrective action AD 2024-25-09 requires cannot be accomplished as intended on certain airplanes.
On April 6, 2026, the FAA issued Special Airworthiness Information Bulletin 2026-09 as an interim action to advise owners and operators of the errors and to recommend actions before AD 2024-25-09 is superseded by this proposed AD. Boeing has since issued Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 757-29A0071 RB, Revision 1, dated May 28, 2026, to correct the errors.
The FAA also issued FAA letter 523-26-00077, dated April 29, 2026, to identify the applicable set of deviations approved as an alternative method of compliance (AMOC) to AD 2024-25-09. Accomplishing Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 757-29A0071 RB, dated November 16, 2023, in combination with the applicable AMOC specified in the FAA letter achieves a configuration consistent with Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 757-29A0071 RB, Revision 1, dated May 28, 2026.
(
printed page 69229)
FAA's Determination
The FAA is issuing this NPRM after determining that the unsafe condition described previously is likely to exist or develop on other products of the same type design.
Material Incorporated by Reference Under
1 CFR Part 51
The FAA reviewed Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 757-29A0071 RB, Revision 1, dated May 28, 2026. This material specifies procedures for, depending on the airplane configuration, installing new relays and a new connector in the P33 panel, installing new connectors and changing certain wire bundles (
e.g.,
changing bundles leading to the PTU control valve, changing bundles between certain panels, changing bundles between certain panels and certain disconnect brackets, and other wire bundle changes that include installing a new wire bundle clamp and lacing tape on wire bundle W4236, changing the position of a wire bundle W4236 ground wire, installing white lacing tape on wire bundle W2514), and doing general visual inspections for correct wire bundle W2514 routing and for a missing seal ring at the right body fairing feedthru seal. This material also specifies applicable on-condition actions. On-condition actions include correcting the routing of wire bundle W2514 through the clamp aft of disconnect bracket AD0880, installing a seal ring at the right body fairing feedthru seal, and doing applicable corrective actions to address failed operational tests and repeating the operational test until the test passes.
This material is reasonably available because the interested parties have access to it through their normal course of business or by the means identified in the
ADDRESSES
section.

This proposed AD would require accomplishing the actions specified in the material already described, except for any differences identified as exceptions in the regulatory text of this proposed AD.

Authority for This Rulemaking
Title 49 of the United States Code specifies the FAA's authority to issue rules on aviation safety. Subtitle I, section 106, describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII: Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the Agency's authority.
The FAA is issuing this rulemaking under the authority described in Subtitle VII, Part A, Subpart III, Section 44701: General requirements. Under that section, Congress charges the FAA with promoting safe flight of civil aircraft in air commerce by prescribing regulations for practices, methods, and procedures the Administrator finds necessary for safety in air commerce. This regulation is within the scope of that authority because it addresses an unsafe condition that is likely to exist or develop on products identified in this rulemaking action.

Boeing Alert Requirements Bulletin 757-29A0071 RB, dated November 16, 2023, was incorporated by reference in AD 2024-25-09.
(2) The applicable set of deviations approved as an AMOC to AD 2024-25-09 and identified in the enclosure to FAA letter 523-26-00077, dated April 29, 2026, which is not incorporated by reference in this AD.

Authority for This Rulemaking
Title 49 of the United States Code specifies the FAA's authority to issue rules on aviation safety. Subtitle I, section 106, describes the authority of the FAA Administrator. Subtitle VII: Aviation Programs, describes in more detail the scope of the Agency's authority.

AGENCY:
Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS), Department of Health and Human Services (HHS).
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
This final rule revises the Conditions for Coverage for Organ Procurement Organizations (OPOs) to clarify outstanding procedural questions and provide additional operational flexibility for OPOs to achieve high performance resulting in the successful procurement, distribution, and transplantation of more life-saving organs. This rule revises definitions, revises the designation requirements for OPOs, clarifies when an OPO's service area is open for competition, and updates the process for appeals. We are committed to holding all OPOs accountable for their performance and this final rule does not revise the focus on improving the volume of donors and transplants assessed in the outcome measures or the tier structure used for re-certification and de-certification of OPOs.
DATES:
These regulations are effective on January 4, 2027.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
The Clinical Standards Group, (410) 786-6633,
HealthandSafetyInquiries@cms.hhs.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
I. Executive Summary and Severability
A. Executive Summary
1. Purpose
At any given time, at least 100,000 people are on the waiting list for a lifesaving transplant and every 8 minutes, another person is added to the transplant waiting list.
[
1
]
Many individuals on the organ transplant waiting list will wait several years for a suitable donor, while others will die before an organ becomes available. A variety of factors affect wait times for an organ transplant, including how well a waitlisted individual matches with available donors, how sick the person is, and the availability of organs in the region. Despite continued growth in organ donation, procurement, and transplantation, the need for transplantable organs continues to grow. The success of organ procurement organizations (OPOs) in performing their essential functions (obtaining consent for donation, working with the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network (OPTN) to match organs with recipients, procuring viable organs, and delivering those organs in transplantable condition to their recipients) is a rate limiting factor on the success of the entire organ transplant system. Therefore, optimal performance of OPOs is critical to ensure that the maximum possible number of transplantable human organs are available to the yearly average of more than 100,000 seriously ill people on waiting lists for a lifesaving organ transplant.
In 2019, President Trump issued
Executive Order 13879
“Advancing American Kidney Health,” directing the Secretary to enhance the procurement and utilization of organs available through deceased donation and to establish more transparent, reliable, and enforceable metrics for evaluating an OPO's performance. In response, CMS published the final rule, “Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Organ Procurement Organization Conditions for Coverage: Revisions to the Outcome Measure Requirements for Organ Procurement Organizations” in 2020 (
85 FR 77898
, referred to hereafter as the December 2020 OPO final rule), which, among other changes, revised the previous outcome measures to drive performance improvement and increase the number of transplantable organs. OPOs are evaluated on their performance on both the donor and transplantation measures. Since publishing the December 2020 OPO final rule, CMS has received many inquiries from OPOs and others seeking clarification on operational and administrative elements. These inquiries increased in frequency and volume as the system moved closer to the end of the 2022-2026 re-certification cycle. Therefore, CMS published a proposed rule, “Medicare and Medicaid Programs; Organ Procurement Organization Conditions for Coverage: Revisions to the Outcome Measure Requirements for Organ Procurement Organizations” on January 30, 2026 (
91 FR 4190
, hereinafter referred to as the January 2026 OPO proposed rule).
The proposed rule contained operational and administrative provisions which would govern the competition process, provide programmatic clarity, and address interested party requests for additional guidance. Additionally, the proposed rule contained provisions aimed at driving further quality and improvement in OPO operations, reflecting our continued commitment to enhancing the organ procurement and transplant system, and better serving prospective organ donors, their families, and patients on the transplant waitlist.
B. Severability
To the extent a court may enjoin any part of the rule, the Department intends that other provisions or parts of provisions should remain in effect. Any provision of this rule held to be invalid or unenforceable by its terms, or as applied to any person or circumstance, shall be construed so as to continue to give maximum effect to the provisions as permitted by law, unless such holding shall be one of utter invalidity or unenforceability, in which event the provision shall be severable from this rule and shall not affect the remainder thereof or the application of the provision to persons not similarly situated or to dissimilar circumstances.
C. Summary of Costs and Benefits
This final rule is important due to its functional relationship to the December 2020 OPO final rule. Its purpose is to clarify and refine operational and administrative requirements related to OPO designation, re-certification, competition, appeals, information management, and Quality Assessment and Performance Improvement (QAPI), while maintaining the accountability framework established in the December 2020 OPO final rule.
We estimate that this final rule will cost approximately $16.5 million in the first year and $7.9 million annually thereafter. These costs are incremental to the broader framework established in the December 2020 OPO final rule and reflect targeted operational and administrative refinements rather than fundamental system restructuring. We also estimate that this final rule will result in approximately $598,000 in annual benefits due to reduced implementation inquiry and compliance-interpretation burden, as well as an additional one-time benefit associated with clarified requirements and implementation efficiencies.
(
printed page 69391)
II. Organ Procurement Organizations (OPOs)
A. Background
OPOs are vital partners in the procurement, distribution, and transplantation of human organs in a safe and effective manner for all potential transplant recipients. The role of OPOs is critical to ensuring that the maximum possible number of transplantable human organs are available to individuals with organ failure who are on a waiting list for an organ transplant. Section 371(b) of the Public Health Service (PHS) Act sets out certain requirements for OPO certification. There are currently 54 OPOs that are responsible for identifying patients who may become prospective donors and recovering organs from deceased donors in the United States (U.S.). These 54 OPOs currently serve 55 Donation Service Areas (DSAs), because each OPO serves at least one DSA and one OPO currently serves more than one DSA. The Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) views OPO performance as a critical element of the organ transplantation system in the U.S. We established conditions for coverage (CfCs) for OPOs at
42 CFR part 486, subpart G
, and
OPOs
must meet these requirements for their organ procurement costs to be eligible for payment under the Medicare and Medicaid programs. The CfCs include reliable, data-based outcome measures related to donor and transplant volume that are used to assess OPO performance for Medicare certification and re-certification purposes and a three-tier structure that incentivizes high OPO performance on these outcome measures.
