In general, we are committed to using objective data to assess OPO performance and continuously incentivize OPO performance improvement.
In 2025, there were a total of 49,065 organ transplants, compared to 48,150 and 46,634 transplants in years 2024 and 2023, respectively.
[
2
]
Although the volume of transplants has increased over time, there continues to be an ongoing shortage of transplantable organs. At any given time, at least 100,000 people are on the waiting list for a lifesaving organ transplant.
[
3
]
Many people face tremendous quality of life burdens, illness progression, or death while on the waiting list. An OPO that is efficient in procuring organs and delivering them to recipients will help more people on the waiting list receive lifesaving organ transplants and reduce the waiting time, which could ultimately save more lives and improve health outcomes.
B. Regulatory History
The December 2020 OPO final rule (
85 FR 77898
) revised the OPO CfCs with the policy goal of increasing organ donation and transplantation to better serve patients on the organ transplant waiting list. The December 2020 OPO final rule revised the outcome measures that are used to assess OPO compliance for purposes of certification, shifting from heavily risk-adjusted metrics that were not capable of demonstrating changes in OPO performance to metrics that measure OPO volume and drive OPO performance in areas most important to patients on the transplant waiting list. It also revised the assessment criteria to move from a bifurcated pass/fail system to a three-tier system with dynamic performance thresholds and incentives for achieving the highest level of performance. Finally, the December 2020 OPO final rule utilizes increasing competition to drive performance improvement. An OPO's performance in its DSA(s) is ranked in comparison to the performance of all other OPOs in their assigned DSAs relative to a numerical threshold, using competition for higher ranking as a tier 1 as an incentive for performance improvement. We believe that the absence of meaningful competition contributed to the very slow pace of system improvement prior to CMS initiating its OPO regulatory reform efforts in 2019, culminating with publication of the December 2020 OPO final rule.
On February 2, 2021, we published a notice in the
Federal Register
(
86 FR 7814
) temporarily delaying the effective date of the December 2020 OPO final rule by 60 days and providing an additional 30-day public comment period, during which we received over 150 timely public comments. The comments received included both support for immediate implementation of the December 2020 OPO final rule and requests for additional time before implementation. We considered the additional public comments and the rule subsequently became effective on March 30, 2021.
On December 3, 2021, we published a “Request for Information (RFI); Health and Safety Requirements for Transplant Programs, Organ Procurement Organizations, and End-Stage Renal Disease (ESRD) Facilities” (
86 FR 68594
) (“December 2021 RFI”), which solicited comments that would help to inform potential changes that would create system-wide improvements, including improvements in organ donation, organ transplantation, quality of care in dialysis facilities, and access to dialysis services.
We received almost 400 timely comments in response to the December 2021 RFI. Commenters included transplant recipients, those awaiting transplants, donor families, and donor representatives. A range of health care providers, including donor hospitals, transplant programs, ESRD suppliers, hospital systems, OPOs, and tissue banks; researchers and academic institutions; professional organizations; trade groups such as technology and pharmaceutical companies as well as insurers; and advocacy and philanthropic organizations also provided comments. These comments informed the proposed rule and may be used in future rulemaking for system-wide changes to advance organ transplant system performance.
On January 30, 2026, we published the January 2026 OPO proposed rule (
91 FR 4190
). In the rule we proposed to: revise several definitions; remove the requirement that an OPO have been re-certified from 2002 through 2005 to be eligible for certification; revise the designation framework to account for scenarios where an OPO is designated to more than one DSA and clarify when DSAs are open for competition; clarify and categorize actions affecting OPO agreements, including non-renewal and de-certification; revise the appeal process; refine re-certification and competition policies, including evaluating each DSA separately for outcome measures and an OPO as a single entity for process performance; address OPO accountability on outcome measures when taking over another OPO's DSA; require appropriate staff licensure; expand information management requirements to include records for organs procured for research; and add new Quality Assessment and Performance Improvement (QAPI) requirements related to medically complex donors and organs.
C. Statutory and Regulatory Provisions
To be an OPO, an entity must meet the applicable requirements of both the Social Security Act (the Act) and the PHS Act. Section 1138(b) of the Act provides the statutory qualifications and requirements that an OPO must meet for its organ procurement costs to be paid under the Medicare program or the Medicaid program. Section 1138(b)(1)(A) of the Act specifies that
(
printed page 69392)
payment may be made for organ procurement costs only if the agency is a qualified OPO operating under a grant made under section 371(a) of the PHS Act or has been certified or re-certified by the Secretary of the Department of Health and Human Services (the Secretary) as meeting the standards to be a qualified OPO, as described in section 371(b) of the PHS Act, within a certain time period. Section 1138(b)(1)(C) of the Act provides that payment may be made for organ procurement costs only if the OPO meets the performance-related standards prescribed by the Secretary. Section 1138(b)(1)(F) of the Act requires that to receive payment under the Medicare or Medicaid programs for organ procurement costs, the entity must be designated by the Secretary. The requirements for such designation are set forth in § 486.304 and include being certified as a qualified OPO by CMS. Regulations at § 486.303 address the requirements to be certified as a qualified OPO.
Pursuant to section 371(b)(1)(D)(ii)(II) of the PHS Act, the Secretary is required to establish outcome and process performance measures for OPOs to meet based on empirical evidence, obtained through reasonable efforts, of organ donor potential and other related factors in each service area of the qualified OPO. Section 1138(b)(1)(D) of the Act requires an OPO to be a member of, and abide by the rules and requirements of, the OPTN. OPOs must also comply with the regulations governing the operation of the OPTN (
42 CFR part 121
). The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS) has explained that only those OPTN policies approved by the Secretary as enforceable will be considered “rules and requirements” of the OPTN for purposes of section 1138 of the Act.
[
4
]
The OPTN is a membership organization that oversees the U.S. organ transplant system, links all professionals in the U.S. organ procurement and transplantation system, and maintains a national registry for matching donated organs with recipients in need of transplantation. OPOs are required under OPTN regulations (§ 121.11(b)(2)) and § 486.328 of the OPO CfCs to report information specified by the Secretary to the OPTN, including the data used to calculate the outcome measures for OPOs.
In addition, OPOs are required to comply with existing Federal civil rights laws, including Title VI of the Civil Rights Act of 1964 (Title VI),
42 U.S.C. 2000d
, section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973,
29 U.S.C. 794
, section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act,
42 U.S.C. 18116
, and the Age Discrimination Act of 1975,
42 U.S.C. 6101
et seq.
[
5
]
Title VI protects individuals from discrimination on the basis of race, color, and national origin. Section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act protects individuals from discrimination on the basis of race, color, national origin, age, disability, or sex. Among other things, these laws require OPOs to ensure nondiscrimination on the bases protected in the operation of their programs. Also, section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act and section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act protect qualified individuals with a disability, including prospective organ recipients with a disability and prospective organ donors with a disability, from discrimination in the administration of covered organ transplant programs. Under these laws, OPOs must ensure that qualified individuals with disabilities are afforded opportunities to participate in or benefit from the organ donation programs that are equal to opportunities afforded to others. Furthermore, OPOs and transplant teams risk violating these Federal civil rights laws through discriminatory actions during the organ donation process. Such violations may include providing a prospective donor with a disability with a benefit or service that is not as effective as the benefits or services provided to those prospective donors without a disability, based solely on that disability.
Qualified individuals with disabilities are also entitled to reasonable modifications needed to participate in and benefit from a program, as well as appropriate auxiliary aids and services needed for effective communication. These rights extend in some circumstances to companions of a prospective organ donor or recipient. For example, covered health care providers and organ donation programs are required to provide auxiliary aids and services (including sign language interpreters) when necessary for effective communication between a relative involved in a prospective donor or recipient's care and a health care provider or procurement program.
Section 1102 of the Act gives the Secretary the authority to make and publish such rules and regulations as may be necessary for the efficient administration of the functions with which the Secretary is charged under the Act. Moreover, section 1871 of the Act gives the Secretary broad authority to establish regulations that are necessary to carry out the administration of the Medicare program.
We established CfCs for OPOs at
42 CFR part 486, subpart G
. These regulations set forth the certification and re-certification processes, outcome requirements, and process performance measures for OPOs. The outcome measures, found under § 486.318, are used to assess OPO outcome performance for re-certification and competition purposes (see § 486.316(a) and (d)).
III. Summary of the Proposed Provisions and Responses to Public Comments
In response to the January 2026 OPO proposed rule, we received 129 timely pieces of correspondence. Commenters included individual OPOs, transplant hospitals, national associations and coalitions, academic researchers, advocacy organizations, health care professionals and corporations, donor families, and numerous individuals from the general public.
In this final rule, we provide a summary of each proposed provision, a summary of the public comments received and our responses to them, and an explanation for any changes in the policies that we are finalizing. We note that this final rule is written in order by topic as they appear in the regulations.
A. General Comments
Comment:
Most commenters supported CMS' overarching goals of strengthening safety, accountability, and public trust in the organ donation and transplantation system. A commenter stated that the recent increase in organ procurement demonstrates the effectiveness of increased accountability under the 2020 framework. However, some commenters expressed concerns about whether the proposed rule would drive meaningful improvement and recommended that CMS provide greater clarity regarding certain proposals.
Response:
We believe the proposals we are finalizing will enforce accountability in organ procurement and support broader goals of improving patient safety and transparency in the organ procurement and transplantation system. We have reviewed the proposals and, where appropriate, have revised or clarified provisions in this final rule to better reflect the intent of the underlying policy and to support effective implementation. These revisions are discussed in detail in the
(
printed page 69393)
relevant sections later in this section of the preamble.
Comment:
Many commenters expressed concern that the proposed rule does not adequately address their longstanding concerns with the 2020 Final Rule, particularly with respect to the outcome measures. Specifically, commenters stated that the outcome metrics: (1) do not reliably or accurately assess the comparative performance of OPOs, noting that the donation and transplantation measures are calculated using the same denominator; (2) are biased against large OPOs; (3) fail to account for demographic and geographic differences across service areas; (4) evaluate OPOs based on factors outside their control; and (5) are calculated using data that does not accurately estimate donor potential and contains errors. Commenters also expressed concern that significant fluctuations in the data confirm that a 12-month measurement period is insufficient as a basis for CMS' outcome metric calculations. Commenters recommended that CMS replace the tiering system with an Observed-to-Expected (O/E) model; replace the use of cause, age, and location consistent with organ donation (CALC) methodology and death certificate data with hospital referral data, include risk adjusted outcome measures; and use multi-year measurement periods.
Response:
The comments regarding the type of outcome measures that CMS uses, risk adjustment, data sources, and the number of data years used for assessing compliance with the CfCs, all set forth in the December 2020 OPO final rule, are outside the scope of this final rule, which is intended to clarify and refine CMS policies and processes for implementing the accountability framework established in the December 2020 OPO final rule. While we proposed a regulatory refinement that will affect the outcome measures as it relates to the inclusion of pancreata used for islet cell research in those calculations, we did not propose any changes to the type of outcome measures that CMS uses, risk adjustment of those measures, data sources, or the number of data years used for assessing compliance with the CfCs. We stand by the underlying outcome measure framework set forth in the December 2020 OPO final rule.
Comment:
Commenters stated that the current tiered system creates perverse incentives for OPOs to prioritize increasing donation and transplant rates over patient-centered care and ethical decision-making.
Response:
Procuring organs from donors in a safe, ethical, and transparent manner supports performance on the CMS outcome measures. Research has shown that approaching potential donor families with sensitivity and compassion, providing adequate explanations of brain death, and allowing potential donor families sufficient time to make decisions all support higher donation rates.
[
6
]
By extension, we believe that OPOs that do not engage in patient-centered care and violate the CfCs (for example, pressuring next of kin for consent for organ donation) ultimately harm their own performance and that of the entire transplant system as these practices contribute to public mistrust in the system. CMS policies holding OPOs accountable for their outcomes, thereby increasing the number of lifesaving organs available for transplantation, are not responsible for poor OPO decision making. Additionally, under the process measures, an OPO is responsible for ensuring proper training and supervision of its staff (§ 486.326(c)) and otherwise maintaining compliance with process performance requirements at §§ 486.320 through 486.360 and should never jeopardize the health and safety of potential donors in the interest of bolstering its performance.
Comment:
Several commenters stated that CMS would de-certify and replace an unreasonable number of OPOs, potentially disrupting the organ donation and transplantation system. They emphasized that stability is critical to maintaining relationships with donor families and hospital partners and to ensuring that organs are not lost due to operational disruption. They recommended that CMS prioritize sustainable performance improvement strategies such as technical assistance and corrective action plans and establish alternative pathways for remediation and performance improvement as a means of avoiding de-certification and minimizing disruption to the system. Commenters stated these options would enable a cure for any non-compliance, be less burdensome than an appeal, and provide a collaborative resolution-focused approach that would better serve patients.
Response:
We disagree with the commenters' premise that prioritizing system stability and retaining current OPOs in their low performing DSAs is preferable to replacing these low performers with OPOs that have demonstrated better performance. The outcome measures and tier system are designed such that all OPOs have an equal opportunity to succeed. OPO performance in a DSA is measured against the median observed performance level of the previous year, meaning that each OPO begins each assessment period with a blank slate and need only achieve the performance level of the previous year's median. All OPOs are capable of meeting the previous year's median performance level in their DSAs and it is our intent to drive improved performance across all OPOs to the extent that the minimum performance standard is met in every DSA, and, ultimately, to save more lives.
We appreciate commenters' recommendations to establish alternative remediation pathways prior to de-certification. These pathways already exist and are required by regulation. Section 486.348(d) requires OPOs to identify and address performance deficiencies that might lead to regulatory action (that is, de-certification). The performance of each OPO is assessed annually, and this information is provided to each OPO. OPOs are required to evaluate their outcome measure performance through their Quality Assessment and Performance Improvement (QAPI) programs and implement corrective actions when performance falls statistically significantly below the top 25th percentile during an assessment period. As such, lower performing OPOs are already expected to develop plans to correct their actions in ways that improve performance and ultimately meet the minimum CMS performance standards. In addition, for the 2022-2026 certification cycle, CMS provided direct technical assistance to OPOs through the OPO Special Innovation Project (SIP), conducted by CMS-funded Quality Improvement Organizations (QIOs) from December 2023 through March 2025, and facilitated OPO collaboration through the ESRD Treatment Choices Learning Collaborative.
OPOs may remedy non-compliance with the process performance measures at §§ 486.320 through § 486.360 by submitting an acceptable plan of correction to CMS (see § 488.28) and implementing corrective actions to achieve and sustain compliance. However, there is no opportunity to remedy past failure to meet the minimum standards for compliance with the outcome measures at § 486.318 because those standards are based on OPO performance in the final assessment period of the re-certification cycle. Actions taken after the final
(
printed page 69394)
assessment period cannot cure the OPO's failure to meet the outcome measure standards as set forth at § 486.318. As discussed previously in this final rule, OPOs have an opportunity to address performance deficiencies in advance of the final assessment period as set forth in § 486.348(d).
We did not propose to modify the outcome measure performance standards to allow for alternative pathways to compliance, and any suggestions to that effect are outside the scope of this rule. Furthermore, as we explained in the December 2020 OPO final rule, allowing a poorly performing OPO to continue serving the DSA through a systems improvement agreement or similar mechanism would not benefit the patients in that DSA who would be better served by a higher performing OPO (
85 FR 77912
). OPOs that do not meet the outcome measures in a DSA in the final assessment period will either be de-certified under the requirements of § 486.312(a)(2) or (3) or have designation removed from the DSA if it has more than one DSA as specified at § 486.316(a)(3).
While we agree with commenters that system stability is a factor for consideration, we also note that such stability led to stagnation in performance. We do not agree with the premise that replacing a low performing OPO with a higher-performing OPO that is willing and able to provide those services will result in long term system disruptions that decrease donation and transplantation or otherwise disrupt the overall accelerated progress that the system has made in light of increased oversight. Retaining an OPO in a DSA where it has failed to meet CMS regulatory standards would not best serve the people in that DSA or the system at large. We are committed to ensuring that any transition between OPOs is conducted in a manner that minimizes disruption to organ procurement activities.
We also note that Health Resources and Services Administration (HRSA) and the OPTN continue to provide resources and technical support to assist OPOs in improving performance and strengthening organ procurement and transplantation practices.
Comment:
Commenters raised concerns regarding the timing of the proposed rule in relation to the 2022 through 2026 re-certification cycle. Many commenters requested that CMS refrain from issuing de-certification notices or conducting competitions and instead develop a revised re-certification process that more accurately and fairly measures OPO performance or delay implementation to allow time to assess the impact of new requirements on OPO performance. Some commenters stated that any finalized policies should not be applied to the 2022 through 2026 re-certification cycle, noting that OPOs cannot retroactively adjust past performance to comply with new standards. Several commenters requested clarity in when changes to the definitions would become effective. Some commenters expressed concerns that CMS would apply the changes retroactively.
Response:
The January 2026 OPO proposed rule, and this subsequent final rule, seek to address operational questions that CMS has received from interested parties and provide additional detail on how the policies adopted in the December 2020 OPO final rule will be effectuated. CMS will not retroactively apply these provisions to any OPO, but will apply them prospectively, as of the effective date of this final rule, in effectuating the enforcement framework adopted in the December 2020 OPO final rule. While we proposed and are finalizing a change to the definition of “organ”, which has implications for how the transplantation rate outcome measure will be calculated and reported to OPOs, this change will only apply as a regulatory requirement to outcome measure data reporting after the effective date of this final rule, beginning with the 2027 assessment period (as defined in § 486.302). In addition, we note that in assessing OPO performance in 2027, we will take steps to ensure OPO performance is appropriately and accurately compared to 2026 performance based on the updated definition of “organ.” Data from the 2027 assessment period will be used to calculate performance described in the 2029 OPO Public Performance Report. OPO performance in 2027 will be measured against the median and top 25 percent thresholds set by OPO performance in 2026. To ensure that 2027 performance is appropriately measured against 2026 performance, for purposes of the 2029 OPO Public Performance Reports we will recalculate the median and top 25 percent thresholds for 2026 applying the revised definition of “organ” that excludes pancreata used for islet cell research and not transplanted from the transplantation rate. This recalculation will model what the transplantation rate outcome measure performance would have been in 2026, had the revised definition been effective at that time. This will ensure a comparison of like data sets, establish an accurate and consistent performance threshold for the 2027 performance data to be measured against, and ensure that OPOs are not evaluated against 2026 performance data that include a broader range of procured organs in the transplantation rate. Therefore, the 2029 OPO Public Performance Report, based upon the 2027 assessment period performance data evaluated against recalculated 2026 performance thresholds for the transplantation rate, will provide OPOs with accurate information about their performance. We will continue applying the revised definition to future outcome measure calculations.
We note that the data reported by OPOs and the coding guidance that they use to perform this data reporting will not change when the revised definition of “organ” is applied to the organ transplantation rate. Existing data coding practices, as required by the OPTN (consistent with § 486.328) already support CMS' ability to calculate performance on the organ transplantation rate outcome measure with and without pancreata used for islet cell research. What will change is how CMS selects the organ disposition codes that OPOs and transplant programs already enter into the data reporting system and applies those codes to the organ transplantation rate calculation.
Likewise, OPOs will not be required to comply with changes to the CfCs finalized in this rule, such as changes to address situations in which a single OPO is simultaneously designated to more than one DSA, until the effective date of this final rule. As some commenters noted, OPO performance for the 2022 through 2026 re-certification cycle is already complete. Given that the policies finalized in this rule will not impact OPO performance for the 2022 through 2026 re-certification cycle, there is no need to delay enforcement decisions for that cycle to assess any impact of this rule on OPO performance.
Comment:
Several commenters stated that the proposed rule placed disproportionate emphasis on OPO performance without adequately accounting for the roles of other interested parties in the donation and transplant system. They stated that greater shared accountability is needed across OPOs, donor hospitals, and transplant centers, including improved transparency around transplant center acceptance practices and better alignment of performance expectations across the system.
Response:
We agree that organ transplantation is a system that includes many actors, each performing their essential functions to the best of their
(
printed page 69395)
ability. Coordination and collaboration among OPOs, donor hospitals, and transplant centers are important to supporting timely organ recovery, placement, and transplantation. We will consider these comments for potential future rulemaking for other related members of the organ donation and transplantation ecosystem.
Comment:
Several commenters suggested that CMS issue guidance prior to implementation. They encouraged CMS to continue interested parties' engagement and collaborate with HRSA and OPTN to ensure alignment and avoid duplicative or conflicting regulatory requirements.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' suggestions, and we intend to continue working closely with HRSA and the OPTN to avoid duplicative or conflicting regulatory requirements. We will provide guidance through sub-regulatory channels, including updates to the State Operations Manual (SOM), to support compliance with these requirements.
Comment:
CMS received several comments pertaining to issues that are outside the scope of the proposed rule. Those comments concerned transplant program outcome measures/harmonizing outcome measures, inclusion of new risk-adjusted outcome measures, harmonization of Federal requirements with State anatomical gift laws, donor registry enrollment and informed consent, the intersection between donation after circulatory death (DCD) processes and first-person authorization (FPA), public education regarding clinical processes associated with organ donation, including DCD, revising the definition of organ to include lifesaving tissue, clearer authorization communication requirements, the use of a DNA-authenticated blockchain system to secure the organ transplant process, a requirement to make all patient records available to a potential donor's next of kin, and donor care units/organ recovery centers.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their feedback. However, these issues are outside the scope of the final rule.
B. Definitions (§ 486.302)
We proposed to revise our current regulations defining the terms “adverse event,” “donor,” “medically complex donors,” “medically complex organs”, “organ,” and “unsound medical practices” at § 486.302 to provide greater clarity.
1. General Comments
Comment:
Commenters urged CMS to test any new definitions more thoroughly to assess downstream effects on measures and re-certification decisions.
Response:
We have carefully considered the impact of these definition changes on the meaning and application of the regulations where these terms are used, as well as public comments we received on these proposed changes. The changes are prospective in nature and OPOs are expected to comply with them upon the effective date of this final rule. We do not expect significant downstream effects on measures and re-certification decisions as a result of any definition changes finalized in this rule. For example, we conducted an internal analysis based on preliminary data used for the 2026 OPO report to assess the projected impact of revising the definition of “organ” to exclude pancreata used for islet cell research from the organ transplantation rate and noted minimal effects on OPO tier status. We expect similarly minimal effects on OPO tier status when this change takes effect. In addition, the change to the definition of organ is appropriate to meet our regulatory goals of incentivizing organ transplants while complying with the requirements of the Pancreatic Islet Cell Transplantation Act of 2004 (PICTA 2004).
Comment:
Some commenters recommended that any definitions should be aligned or harmonized with OPTN and HRSA definitions to promote consistency in interpretation and implementation of requirements. A few commenters noted that OPTN and HRSA are working on revising various requirements that could affect proposed changes to definitions.
Response:
CMS and HRSA continually work to align policies as appropriate to the statutory authorities that govern our actions and the regulatory approaches that we employ. We note that “alignment” does not always require exact duplication, as there are instances when a compatible, nuanced approach is better suited to addressing an issue than a broad, standardized approach. Currently, the OPTN does not have a comprehensive, standardized definition for “adverse events.” However, the OPTN does require that a narrow set of high-severity patient safety events (“HRSA-reportable” or “Wakefield” events) be reported to HRSA and to the OPTN Patient Safety Reporting Portal. Those events include: (1) wrong organ transplants or near misses, (2) transplants into the wrong recipient or near misses, and (3) suspected or confirmed donor-derived HIV transmission.
[
7
]
Our current definition of “adverse event” is broad enough to encompass the OPTN and HRSA requirements for reportable events. Additionally, alignment of requirements is one factor that CMS considered related to the proposed definitions for medically complex organ and medically complex donor. Please see section III.B.4. of this final rule for additional discussion.
2. Adverse Event
Section 486.302 currently defines “adverse event” as “an untoward, undesirable, and usually unanticipated event that causes death or serious injury or the risk thereof. As applied to OPOs, adverse events include, but are not limited to, transmission of disease from a donor to a beneficiary, avoidable loss of a medically suitable potential donor for whom consent for donation has been obtained, or delivery to a transplant center of the wrong organ or an organ whose blood type does not match the blood type of the intended beneficiary.” We proposed to relocate the illustrative examples of adverse events from the definition of “adverse event” to the QAPI requirements at § 486.348(c). We also proposed revising the list to clarify that the list of examples does not constitute an exhaustive list of adverse events. We solicited public comment on the proposed changes to the definition of adverse events. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Commenters stated that the proposed definition of “adverse events” was overly broad, ambiguous, and susceptible to inconsistent interpretation by both OPOs and surveyors. They expressed concern that legitimate disagreements between the OPO and a surveyor on whether an incident was an adverse event could result in inappropriate and inconsistent deficiency determinations and other inconsistent enforcement actions, which would limit the QAPI requirements' usefulness as a quality improvement tool.
Response:
While we proposed to move a revised, non-exhaustive list of examples of adverse events from the definitions section to the QAPI section at § 486.348(c)(3), we note that the
(
printed page 69396)
remaining definition at § 486.302, defining an “adverse event” as “an untoward, undesirable, and usually unanticipated event that causes death or serious injury or the risk thereof,” is the same one that was adopted in the 2006 final rule (
71 FR 30982
,
31046
). CMS and OPOs have been applying this definition for the last 20 years. We are not aware of any evidence that inconsistent interpretation by OPOs or surveyors or legitimate disagreements between the OPO and a surveyor on whether an incident was an adverse event has resulted in inappropriate or inconsistent deficiency determinations or other inconsistent enforcement actions. We encourage OPOs to seek guidance from CMS related to whether an incident is an adverse event if they are ever unsure about a particular incident. In addition, CMS provides sub-regulatory guidance, particularly surveyor guidelines in Appendix Y of the State Operations Manual.
Comment:
Several commenters requested objective criteria to ensure clarity and uniformity. They recommend limiting the definition of “adverse events” to clinical or operational failures that pose risks to patient safety. Others recommend restricting the scope of reportable “adverse events” to violations of the OPO's internal policies, OPTN policies and bylaws, and Federal regulations.
Response:
While we agree with the commenters that clinical or operational failures that pose risks to patient safety and violations of the OPO's internal policies, OPTN policies and bylaws, and Federal regulations may all constitute “adverse events”, we disagree that the regulatory definition of the term should be restricted to them. We believe that a restrictive definition would likely leave out possible incidents that should be identified as “adverse events” and require compliance with § 486.348(c)(1) and (2). We believe the definition of the term “adverse events” set forth in § 486.302, coupled with the revised, non-exhaustive list of examples we proposed to move to the QAPI requirements at § 486.348 (c)(3) provides sufficient guidance on whether an incident constitutes an adverse event.
Comment:
Most commenters supported our proposed revision to move the list of examples of incidents that would be considered “adverse events” from the definition in § 486.302 to the QAPI section at § 486.348 of the regulations. Some commenters agreed that this shift from defining the term with examples to using them in the context of QAPI emphasized that the list was not exhaustive. However, some commenters disagreed with relocating the list of examples, and a commenter suggested that removing the list of examples would result in more confusion.
Response:
We agree that retaining and revising the examples and moving them to the QAPI section of the regulations clarifies that the list of examples is not exhaustive. We reiterate that the list of examples is not being removed from the CfCs. It is being moved to the QAPI requirements related to adverse events (§ 486.348(c)(3)), which should reduce confusion.
Comment:
Several commenters sought clarification about whether “risk thereof” includes near-misses or latent safety conditions.
Response:
The definition of “adverse events” would include actions or omissions that could have resulted in death or serious injury but were somehow stopped before that could happen (that is, a “near miss”). We would also note that OPTN Patient Safety Portal reportable events
[
8
]
also include events that could have resulted, but did not, in death or serious injury. Regarding latent safety conditions, we believe that depends upon whether the latent safety conditions resulted in an incident sufficient to constitute an adverse event. We believe these instances would be very fact-specific scenarios and would encourage an OPO to speak with or consult with CMS for further guidance.
Final Rule Action:
After consideration of the public comments, we are finalizing the “adverse event” definition as proposed.
3. Donor and Organ
Section 486.302 currently defines “donor” as “a deceased individual from whom at least one vascularized organ (heart, liver, lung, kidney, pancreas, or intestine) is transplanted. An individual also would be considered a donor if only the pancreas is procured and is used for research or islet cell transplantation.” We proposed to revise the definition of the term “donor” to clarify that an individual from whom only the pancreas is procured and used for islet cell transplantation or for islet cell research is included in the definition of “donor” for purposes of the donation rate outcome measure. This clarification would ensure consistency and continued compliance with the statutory requirement
[
9
]
that pancreata used for islet cell transplantation or research be counted for purposes of certification and re-certification. We solicited public comment on the proposed changes to the definition of “donor”.
Additionally, section 486.302 currently defines “organ” as “. . . a human kidney, liver, heart, lung, pancreas, or intestine (or multivisceral organs when transplanted at the same time as an intestine). The pancreas counts as an organ even if it is used for research or islet cell transplantation.” The inclusion of pancreata used for islet cell bench research within the definition of “organ”—and by extension the “organ transplantation rate”—is inconsistent with CMS' goals to increase the number of actual transplants, as it creates a perverse performance incentive that allows OPOs to count research activity as equivalent to a transplant, potentially masking poor performance in facilitating actual organ placements for patients on transplant waitlists. Therefore, we proposed to remove pancreata used for research from the definition of “organ”, meaning that such pancreata are removed from the organ transplantation rate outcome measure. Research activity would no longer count as a transplant for purposes of certification and re-certification. We solicited public comment on the proposed changes to the definitions of “donor” and “organ”. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
The majority of commenters were supportive of the proposed changes to the definitions of “donor” and “organ”. However, some commenters indicated that the proposed changes did not go far enough and recommended additional changes. Many commenters stated that pancreata procured for islet cell research should be removed entirely from the outcome measures while others proposed alternative ways to count pancreata. Several commenters stated that CMS should create a separate outcome measure specifically for pancreata. A commenter recommended creating a process performance measure for pancreatic islet cell procurement.
Response:
We appreciate the support for revisions to the definitions of “donor” and “organ”. PICTA 2004, which amended the PHS Act to add section 371(c), requires pancreata procured and used for islet cell transplantation or research to be counted for certification and re-
(
printed page 69397)
certification purposes. Therefore, we cannot remove pancreata from the numerical outcome measures entirely or assess compliance through an observed process performance measure. At this time, establishing a separate outcome measure is contrary to CMS policy goals, as it would overly incentivize pursuit of donors for islet cell research, likely to the detriment of pursuit of donors for transplantable organs. The organ quality standards and procurement process for research organs differ from those of organs for transplant, focusing less on optimal organ transplant viability that may require precise organ retrieval timing and techniques and costly perfusion equipment for delivery to the transplant program. Establishing a standard that may be easier for OPOs to meet could incentivize OPOs to shift procurement resources away from transplantable organs, and that shift would not be consistent with patient needs and our policy goals. As such, we believe the proposed changes to the definitions are the most appropriate approach to accomplish our policy goals. This would enable counting donors when pancreata were procured for islet cell transplantation or islet cell research, but pancreatic islet cells would only count as a transplant when actually transplanted into a recipient, including transplantation that is conducted under research protocols.
Comment:
Several commenters recommended narrowing the scope of research that would qualify for inclusion of pancreata in the outcome measures. A commenter recommended that CMS only include “pancreata recovered for research focused on pancreatic islet cell transplantation and conducted under FDA approved clinical research.” Another commenter stated that OPOs may not have access to requested research protocols or other documentation necessary to evidence that the pancreata were actually used for bona fide islet cell research.
Response:
We thank commenters for these recommendations. Our proposed revisions to the definition of “donor” were intended to emphasize that pancreata must be procured and used for islet cell research or islet cell transplantation, consistent with PICTA 2004, to be counted in the outcome measures. We previously clarified this point in a memorandum issued on January 18, 2024. With respect to the commenter's suggestion to restrict pancreatic islet cell research to only include “FDA approved clinical research,” PICTA 2004 requires pancreata procured by an OPO and used for islet cell transplantation or research to be counted for certification or re-certification decisions. That statutory requirement is not limited to clinical research that FDA has allowed to proceed. We also note that we have previously worked with HRSA to revise and clarify coding for pancreata submitted for research (See QSO-24-19-OPO). If an OPO is unable to obtain records demonstrating the pancreata were used for research for islet cell transplantation, it should not code the disposition as “accepted for islet cell research” to be included in the CMS outcome metrics.
Comment:
Several commenters stated they supported the changes and the exclusion of pancreata islet cells used for research from the transplant rate when the islet cells are not transplanted. A commenter indicated that the proposal strikes a balance between the statutory requirements and concerns about accurate measurement of transplantation rates, suggesting it will facilitate more consistent reporting.
Response:
We thank commenters for acknowledging the importance of this change. In our proposed rule, we stated the inclusion of pancreatic islet cell bench research in the definition of “organ” has proven to be inconsistent with the goals of the 2020 rulemaking to increase the number of transplants. Our proposed change to the definitions of “donor” and “organ” are refinements to remove pancreatic islet cell bench research from the transplant rate while appropriately retaining it in measurement of the donation rate. These changes better incentivize both pancreata islet cell research and transplantation via the donation rate and pancreatic islet cell transplantation via the transplant rate while more precisely measuring performance and complying with the PICTA 2004.
Comment:
Several commenters indicated that research on pancreatic islet cells when not transplanted, sometimes called “bench research”, does not involve living persons so approval by an institution review board (IRB) is generally not required. In these instances, the OPO would not have a record of approval from an IRB.
Response:
We acknowledge this consideration and how it may impact records for organ disposition when those organs are sent for research. The requirements at § 486.330(b)(2) as finalized in this rule only require an OPO to maintain information documenting approval of an IRB or other formal authorizing body “as appropriate.” Where no such approval is required, the OPO is not required to maintain approval documentation. The OPO would, however, continue to be required to maintain records showing the disposition of the organ as set forth in § 486.330(b)(2), including the research institution, principal investigator, and study contacts. Regardless of the information that is available, if an OPO is coding and reporting pancreata procurement and disposition in a manner that would count in the outcome measures, it must be able to provide CMS and the OPTN with sufficient records to support and justify the coded disposition for pancreatic islet cell research.
Comment:
Several commenters state that the changes risk creating inconsistent treatment of pancreata across the two outcome measures that may introduce gaming.
Response:
The changes to the definition of “donor” and “organ” increase specificity of reporting and better align the incentives of the measures (more donors and more transplants) to mitigate any potential gaming. These changes fairly count donors of organs that are used for transplantation or islet cell research and transplants that directly benefit patients on the waitlist while complying with the PICTA 2004.
Comment:
A commenter questioned the rationale for excluding pancreata used for bona fide islet cell research from the transplant rate. The commenter stated that this exclusion could inadvertently discourage OPOs from supporting research that advances transplantation science.
Response:
Pancreata will continue to be counted in the donation rate when procured for islet cell research regardless of whether the final disposition is bench research or transplantation. Pancreatic islet cells will continue to be counted in the transplant rate when actually transplanted. This change continues to incentivize transplant science and transplantation of pancreatic islet cells.
Comment:
A commenter recommended that CMS allow supplemental QAPI tracking for pancreata recovered for islet cell research to enhance the integrity of tracking this information.
Response:
We appreciate this comment. While we have not proposed a corresponding QAPI requirement for tracking pancreata procured for islet cell research at this time, nothing prevents OPOs from utilizing their QAPI program for this purpose. We will continue to monitor procurement practices in this area and may consider a corresponding QAPI requirement in future rulemaking.
Final Rule Action:
We are finalizing as proposed the definition of “donor”, at § 486.302, as a deceased individual
(
printed page 69398)
from whom at least one vascularized organ (heart, liver, lung, kidney, pancreas, or intestine) is transplanted. An individual will also be considered a donor if only the pancreas is procured and is used for islet cell transplantation or for islet cell research. Additionally, we are finalizing as proposed the definition of “organ” as a human kidney, liver, heart, lung, pancreas, or intestine (or multivisceral organs when transplanted at the same time as an intestine). The pancreas counts as an organ even if it is used for islet cell transplantation.
4. Medically Complex Donors and Medically Complex Organs
We proposed to add a definition for “medically complex donor” and “medically complex organ”. We proposed to define the term “medically complex donor” as a donor whose medical history requires special or additional considerations to identify the best recipient for the organs. These donors would include all DCD donors and donors with elevated KDPI scores of 50 or more. We also proposed to define the term “medically complex organ” as an organ procured from a “medically complex donor”. These definitions are linked to a proposed new QAPI requirement that would require OPOs to facilitate appropriate placement and utilization of these organs, to increase the pool of organs available for transplantation. We solicited public comments on the proposed definitions of “medically complex donors” and “medically complex organs”. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Comments on the definition for “medically complex donor” were mixed. Some commenters strongly supported DCD and HIV+ patients being included in the definitions. While some supported a KPDI of 50 or greater, others suggested a score of 85 or greater. Other commenters wanted to include additional comorbidities, such as hypertension or diabetes. Several commenters stated that the proposed definition already applied to most of their deceased donors and raised burden concerns. Other commenters expressed concern that the proposed thresholds, such as KDPI scores, could disadvantage underserved communities. Some commenters recommended using other criteria, such as the criteria previously used for expanded criteria donors (ECDs). Some commenters mentioned considering clinical indications, in addition to medical history.
Response:
We would like to thank all the commenters for their valuable input into this definition. After considering the public comments we received, we have determined that there is a lack of consensus among relevant interested parties as to what constitutes a “medically complex donor.” Comments on this topic varied significantly, making it extremely difficult to describe a narrowed or specific population of donors. Some commenters recommended utilizing the previous construct of “expanded criteria donor.” However, this is no longer utilized by the OPTN nor is it reported by the SRTR. Commenters raised valid concerns regarding burden if the definitions were overly broad which could hamper their QAPI activities from those donors that they believe to be most challenging for placement of organs. In addition, evolving practice patterns, such as the increase in DCD donation, and increased use of technology, such as advanced perfusion technology, are advancing the recovery and placement of organs that were previously considered difficult to place for transplantation. Hence, after consideration of public comments, we are not finalizing these definitions at this time. We will monitor for new constructs that may emerge in the future that would support this proposal, including a consensus on consistent, nationally accepted standards for what constitutes a medically complex donor. Therefore, we will continue to monitor this issue and consider revisiting a proposal regarding medical complexity in the future.
Comment:
Some commenters stated that the usefulness of this requirement for OPOs will be limited without corresponding requirements for donor hospitals and transplant programs. For example, some commenters thought that transplant programs should be held accountable for not accepting medically complex organs.
Response:
As explained previously in this final rule, we will not be finalizing these definitions. However, we may consider proposing requirements regarding medical complexity in the future. If we do, the commenters' recommendations about corresponding requirements for donor hospitals and transplant programs and accountability will be considered. at that time.
Final Rule Action:
After consideration of the public comments we received, we are not finalizing the following definitions: “Medically complex donor” and “Medically complex organ”. Additionally, we are not finalizing the corresponding QAPI requirement as discussed in section III.L. of this final rule.
5. Unsound Medical Practices
In the 2006 final rule, CMS finalized § 486.312(b), which states CMS may terminate an OPO's agreement immediately in cases of urgent need, such as the discovery of unsound medical practices. In addition, we finalized a definition for “urgent need” in § 486.302. Urgent need occurs when an OPO's noncompliance with one or more conditions for coverage has caused, or is likely to cause, serious injury, harm, impairment, or death to a potential or actual organ donor or an organ recipient. While we referenced “unsound medical practices” as grounds for immediate termination, the OPO CfCs do not currently include a definition for “unsound medical practices”.
We proposed to define “unsound medical practices” as “failures by OPOs that create an imminent threat to patient health and safety or pose a risk to patients or the public. These practices include, but are not limited to, failures in governance; patient or potential donor evaluation and management; and procurement, allocation, and transport practices and procedures.” This definition was proposed to ensure that unsound medical practices would be addressed appropriately, and that OPOs would continue to provide high quality care to patients, potential donors and potential transplant recipients. We solicited public comment on the proposed definition of “unsound medical practices”. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Many commenters expressed support for CMS' goal of clarifying the definition of “unsound medical practices” and establishing strong regulatory consequences for conduct that poses an imminent threat to patient safety. Commenters generally agreed that egregious breaches of medical or ethical standards warrant serious enforcement action and that OPOs engaging in reckless or dangerous practices should be held accountable. However, many commenters expressed concerns that the proposed definition of “unsound medical practices” is overly broad and vague. They stated that the definition, as proposed, could permit CMS to penalize OPOs even when they are in compliance with existing regulations and may grant CMS excessive discretion, potentially leading to inconsistent or arbitrary enforcement.
Response:
We appreciate the opportunity to clarify our intent in proposing this definition. The proposed definition of “unsound medical practices” was intended to provide a
(
printed page 69399)
clear, enforceable basis for urgent de-certification to protect patients and maintain public trust in the donation and transplantation system. We chose not to be overly prescriptive and specify the exact practices or instances that constitute unsound medical practice, as a narrow definition would risk creating regulatory gaps that could allow unsafe practices to go unaddressed. Rather, we focused on the outcomes of those specific practices and instances and their impacts on health and safety so that we could evaluate each case individually. We disagree that this outcome-oriented approach would lead to arbitrary or inconsistent enforcement. Making individualized determinations that are based on health and safety impacts does not equate to arbitrary enforcement. When we receive complaints or identify potential issues, trained surveyors investigate allegations of unsafe practices that arise, and all determinations are based on the evidence gathered during those investigations. CMS surveyors receive extensive training in assessing facilities for non-compliance, determining the seriousness of outcomes that pose imminent threats to patient health, and deciding when rapid action is needed to ensure safety to eliminate a risk to patients or the public. Additionally, any determination of unsound medical practices would be made carefully after consideration by CMS, given the seriousness of this determination and enforcement actions that would ensue.
Comment:
Several commenters expressed concerns that the proposed definition could be interpreted to permit de-certification based on a single, isolated incident. They recommended that CMS clarify that findings of unsound medical practices would be based on objective evidence of repeated or sustained failures and that immediate de-certification would be reserved for the most egregious cases involving clear, severe violations that pose an imminent threat to patient safety or public trust.
Response:
A single event may constitute “unsound medical practices” and the finding of “unsound medical practices” is not limited to patterns of repeated unsafe practices. If a single event creates an imminent threat to patient health and safety or poses a risk to patients or the public, then it can constitute “unsound medical practices” and CMS can act immediately to protect patients. This gives CMS a clear, enforceable basis for urgent de-certification to protect patients and maintain public trust in the system. The question is not whether the situation is isolated or recurring, but whether it meets the threshold established by the definition. We will evaluate each situation based on the totality of the evidence and the specific circumstances involved before making a determination.
Comment:
Many commenters requested that CMS more clearly distinguish between “adverse events” and “unsound medical practices,” noting that the two concepts carry different regulatory consequences. They also requested clarification on how QAPI findings would be used in enforcement decisions and suggested that less severe or correctable deficiencies be addressed through standard compliance mechanisms such as plans of correction and enhanced oversight, consistent with CMS' approach to immediate jeopardy with other provider types.
Response:
We agree that “adverse events” and “unsound medical practices” are distinct concepts that carry different regulatory consequences. Adverse events, while serious, generally can be addressed through an OPO's internal QAPI program if they do not rise to the degree of severity and impact on patient or public health and safety to be considered unsound medical practices. Section 486.348(c) requires that OPOs establish written policies to address, at a minimum, the process to identify, report, analyze, and prevent adverse events that occur during the organ donation process. It also requires that OPOs conduct a thorough analysis of any identified adverse event and use that analysis to drive process improvement by effecting changes in their policies and practices to prevent repeat incidents. “Unsound medical practices” are failures by the OPO in which the OPO knows, or should have known, that its inaction, actions, or outcomes has caused, or is likely to cause, serious injury, harm, impairment, or death to a potential or actual donor or an organ recipient, creating an imminent threat to patient health and safety or public safety. The critical distinction between an “adverse event” that can be addressed through a QAPI program under § 486.348(c) and “unsound medical practices” that may support de-certification for urgent need lies not in whether an incident is isolated or repeated, but rather in the degree of severity and impact on patient or public health and safety and the need for immediate action. If an adverse event is of such severity and impact to health and safety that it rises to the level of an unsound medical practice, standard compliance mechanisms such as QAPI are insufficient to address the concern. Therefore, CMS would apply its regulatory standards for unsound medical practices within the context of de-certification due to urgent need and proceed accordingly. Less severe deficiencies would be addressed through standard compliance mechanisms—such as acceptable plans of correction and additional oversight. We believe the definitions of adverse events and unsound medical practices strike the appropriate balance between providing CMS with the enforcement flexibility necessary to protect patient and public safety and ensuring that enforcement actions are based on objective, evidence-based findings.
Comment:
Several commenters objected to the inclusion of “failures in governance” within the definition, stating that governance issues are administrative rather than clinical in nature and do not directly threaten patient health and safety.
Response:
We disagree that “failures in governance” are solely administrative in nature or that they cannot directly threaten patient health and safety. Governance establishes the oversight and accountability framework necessary to ensure that clinical practices are performed safely and in accordance with applicable requirements. For example, a circumstance in which an OPO's governing board directs staff to undertake actions that are inconsistent with standards of practice, OPO policies, CMS rules and requirements, and/or local, State, or Federal laws that knowingly create an imminent threat to patient health/safety or pose a risk to patients or the public, would reflect a failure in governance. Specifically, it would reflect a failure of the governing board to enforce established policies and procedures, placing patients at immediate risk of serious harm. Therefore, we are finalizing a definition of unsound medical practices that includes failures in governance.
Comment:
A commenter recommended that CMS expand the definition to include OPO staff conduct toward patients' families, such as overly assertive behavior in the consent process and failure to collaborate with hospital staff in establishing referral criteria and donation protocols.
Response:
Approaching donor families with compassion, sensitivity, and respect during the donation process and allowing for adequate time to make a decision are incredibly important practices and have been shown to improve donation consent rates.
[
10
]
(
printed page 69400)
Families should never feel rushed, coerced, or disregarded when making decisions about organ donation. Overly assertive or pressuring behavior not only undermines public trust in the donation system but may also constitute a violation of existing requirements under § 486.342, which mandates that OPOs encourage discretion and sensitivity with respect to the circumstances, views, and beliefs of potential donor families. Complaints against an OPO may be submitted through various channels, including CMS,
[
11
]
State survey agencies, HRSA,
[
12
]
the OPO, or the hospital. Similarly, CMS emphasizes the importance of strong collaboration between OPOs and hospital staff throughout the donation and procurement process. These collaborative responsibilities are reflected in existing requirements under § 486.322(a), which requires OPOs and donor hospitals to establish written agreements defining certain responsibilities and protocols—including definitions of “timely referral” and “imminent death.” Additional guidance is available in the SOM, Appendix Y—Organ Procurement Organizations. While we are not expanding the definition of “unsound medical practices” to include these areas at this time, the existing regulatory framework provides clear expectations for OPO conduct toward patients' families, such as overly assertive behavior in the consent process and failure to collaborate with hospital staff in establishing referral criteria and donation protocols.
Comment:
Several commenters objected to the term “unsound medical practices” itself, stating that OPOs do not practice medicine or provide care to living patients and instead function in a coordination and procurement role. They suggested alternative terms such as “unsound donation practices” or “unsound procurement practices,” to better reflect OPO responsibilities and reduce potential confusion among interested parties and the public.
Response:
The term “unsound medical practices” is not intended to refer to clinical activities outside the scope of an OPO's activities; rather, it is intended to encompass the full range of OPO activities during the donation and procurement process, including transport of a viable organ intended for a living person. We do not believe that either “unsound procurement practices” or “unsound donation practices” adequately captures that full range. For instance, “unsound procurement practices” would be too narrow because the proposed definition includes “procurement . . . practices and procedures” as a subset of unsound medical practices. Similarly, “unsound donation practices” may be overly limiting and would not necessarily encompass additional activities included in the definition, such as transport practices and procedures. The term “unsound medical practices” best reflects the full range of OPO activities the definition is intended to cover and avoids the ambiguity that either alternative term would introduce.
Comment:
Many commenters expressed concerns that examples of “unsound medical practices” provided in the proposed rule are unclear, overly broad, and, in some cases, inconsistent with the role of OPOs. Commenters stated that the example, “failure to ensure the potential donor is declared dead according to applicable State law and hospital policies,” inaccurately suggests that OPOs are responsible for, or influence, the clinical determination of death. They recommended that CMS revise the example to clarify that the OPO's role is limited to verifying that death has been declared in accordance with applicable requirements.
Several commenters also raised concerns that the phrase “necessary and customary tests” lacks specificity and is not clearly defined. They recommended that CMS provide additional detail regarding what constitutes such testing and align any requirements with existing OPTN policies governing donor evaluation. Commenters further emphasized that OPOs should only be held accountable for testing activities within their direct control. Some commenters expressed concern that unclear or expanded testing requirements could create operational burdens, delay the donation process, and potentially increase organ non-use.
Additionally, commenters stated that the example “pursuing patients with inappropriately high neurologic function” lacks clinical specificity and is not defined in current CMS or OPTN policy. They cautioned that this language could lead to inconsistent interpretation and discourage appropriate donor evaluation, including for patients with severe neurologic injury, donation after circulatory death candidates, or individuals with conditions such as ALS or spinal cord injury, thereby potentially reducing donation opportunities.
A commenter suggested expanding the examples of unsound medical practices to include failures by OPOs to utilize perfusion technologies when procuring and transplanting organs. Overall, several commenters urged CMS to revise the examples to more clearly reflect OPO responsibilities and include objective clinical criteria where applicable.
Response:
We appreciate commenters' requests for additional clarification regarding the scope and intent of the examples discussed in the proposed rule. The examples referenced in the proposed rule are illustrative only and are not intended to be interpreted as part of the regulatory definition of “unsound medical practices.”
Regarding the example referencing “failure to ensure the potential donor is declared dead according to applicable State law and hospital policies,” we note that the decision to withdraw life support and the subsequent declaration of death, if death occurs, are solely the responsibility of the patient's attending physician or a hospital physician designee in accordance with hospital policy and applicable State law.
[
13
]
OPOs may not be involved in the decision to withdraw life support, the timing of withdrawal, or the declaration of death in any way. However, OPOs are required to verify that the pronouncement of death for potential donors adheres to applicable local, State, and Federal laws (§ 486.344(b)(1)), including in cases involving DCD. Following the declaration of death and prior to initiating the organ recovery process, the OPO should confirm that death has been pronounced and obtain documentation of the pronouncement of death.
Regarding the example referencing “necessary and customary tests,” we do not intend to establish a new requirement or expand existing testing expectations. Under OPTN Policy 2.9, OPOs are required to ensure that infectious disease testing is performed for all potential deceased donors. This includes standardized screening for communicable diseases, as well as additional testing as clinically indicated by donor risk assessment. OPOs are also responsible for ensuring that specimens are collected within appropriate timeframes, that testing is performed in Clinical Laboratory Improvement Amendment (CLIA) certified laboratories, and that all required and relevant results are accurately documented and communicated to transplant centers in a timely manner.
(
printed page 69401)
These testing requirements align with § 486.346 by promoting safe organ recovery and minimizing the risk of disease transmission through transplantation.
Finally, regarding the example referencing “pursuing patients with inappropriately high neurologic function,” this example is not intended to establish clinical eligibility criteria, define neurologic thresholds, substitute for clinical judgment, or discourage OPOs from pursuing particular categories of potential donors. Rather, it is intended to emphasize the importance of adhering to established clinical and regulatory safeguards, including requirements related to the determination of death and appropriate donor evaluation, to protect patient safety. OPOs are expected to immediately cease the procurement process if signs of life are observed at any point before or during organ recovery. A prior declaration of death by the attending hospital physician does not authorize an OPO to continue the donation process if signs of life are subsequently detected. Failure to adhere to these safeguards could constitute conduct that poses an imminent threat to patient health and safety.
[
14
]
Comment:
Several commenters urged CMS to align implementation guidance with OPTN and HRSA standards and to consider issuing additional surveyor guidance to promote national consistency.
Response:
We intend to develop and issue implementation and surveyor guidelines to provide additional clarity regarding the application of the definition of “unsound medical practices,” including how surveyors will identify, document, and evaluate any conduct that may constitute unsound medical practices.
Final Rule Action:
After consideration of the public comments we received, we are finalizing as proposed. We define unsound medical practices as failures by OPOs that create an imminent threat to patient health and safety or pose a risk to patients or the public. These practices include, but are not limited to, failures in governance; patient or potential donor evaluation and management; and procurement, allocation, and transport practices and procedures.
C. Requirements for Certification (§ 486.303)
CMS has historically interpreted the OPO Certification Act of 2000 (the Certification Act), which added section 371(b)(1)(D) of the PHS Act, to mean the Secretary lacks the authority to certify new OPOs. Upon recent reassessment, however, we determined that the statute was not intended to strip the Secretary of his authority to certify new OPOs. Therefore, we proposed to remove § 486.303(e), which conditions OPO certification on an entity having been re-certified as an OPO from January 1, 2002, through December 31, 2005. This eliminates a regulatory barrier that prevents the Secretary from implementing a process for certifying new OPOs. We also believe that removing this requirement would address concerns about market consolidation by creating a more diverse and robust market that enhances competition among OPOs.
We also solicited public comments on a process to certify new OPOs. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Several commenters stated that CMS lacks statutory authority to certify new OPOs and that CMS' reinterpretation of the PHS Act expands its authority beyond what Congress authorized. Commenters stated that Congress unambiguously used the past tense in requiring OPOs to “ha[ve] been certified or re-certified by the Secretary within the previous 4-year period,”
42 U.S.C. 273(b)(1)(D)
, and that entities not yet in existence as of January 1, 2000, cannot satisfy that requirement.
Additionally, commenters noted that Congress required the Secretary to “use multiple outcome measures as part of the certification process,” (
42 U.S.C. 273(b)(1)(D)(ii)(III)
). Commenters stated that outcomes are, by definition, retrospective and therefore Congress must have intended that CMS could certify only OPOs already in existence.
Commenters also stated CMS cannot create new performance measures to justify certifying new entities or lawfully permit newly certified OPOs to compete with established, statutorily qualified organizations, and noted that the statute does not authorize CMS to favor new entrants. They recommended that any policy changes to allow the certification of new OPOs should be pursued through legislative action rather than regulatory interpretation.
Response:
We appreciate these comments and disagree that CMS lacks the authority to certify new OPOs. The Certification Act amended the PHS Act to add subparagraph (D) to section 371(b)(1), which defines a qualified OPO as an organization that “has met the other requirements of this section and has been certified or re-certified by the Secretary within the previous 4-year period as meeting the performance standards to be a qualified organ procurement organization through a process” defined in regulations.
While we have previously interpreted the Certification Act to strip CMS of its prior authority to certify new OPOs, we no longer believe that interpretation to be the best reading of the statute. Upon further review, we no longer believe that the Certification Act is best read to require all qualified OPOs to have been previously certified as of January 1, 2000. Instead, the statute is better read to mean that whenever the agency initially certifies a new OPO or recertifies an existing OPO as meeting the Secretary's performance standards within a 4-year period, OPOs must demonstrate at the end of that period that they continue to meet those standards. We note also that
Executive Order 14219
directs Federal agencies to review existing regulations for potential candidates for rescission, prioritizing those that can no longer be justified under several recent decisions of the U.S. Supreme Court, including
Loper Bright Enterprises
v.
Raimondo,
603 U.S. 369 (2024). In
Loper Bright,
the Court explained that statutes have a “single, best meaning” that agencies must follow. Because we believe this is the best reading of the statute, it is consistent with the rationale of
Loper Bright
to adopt it.
Section 371(b)(1)(D)(ii) of the PHS Act specifically provides that a qualified OPO is an OPO that, among other things, “has been certified or re-certified . . . within the previous 4-year period” through “a process” that is “defined through regulations . . . promulgated by the Secretary.” There is no language in that provision requiring an OPO to demonstrate that it was certified as of January 1, 2000, as part of those standards. This language is past tense in that it refers to an OPO that “has been” certified or re-recertified within the previous 4-year period. But the statutory language does not indicate that the “previous 4-year period” refers only to the 4-year period prior to enactment of the statute, as commenters suggest. A new OPO could meet this standard upon initial certification. In addition, the statute requires the Secretary to “use multiple outcome measures as part of the certification process” (emphasis added). The fact that the statute contemplates a certification process that uses outcome measures, rather than restricting the application of outcome
(
printed page 69402)
measures to re-certification, further indicates that the Secretary is not limited to recertifying existing OPOs and that Congress considered it possible to use outcome measures in the certification process. Thus, nothing in the text of the statute supports reading it to strip the Secretary of his authority to certify either an entirely new OPO or one that was previously de-certified.
Comment:
A few commenters supported CMS' goal of ensuring that all communities are served by high-performing OPOs and acknowledged that permitting new entities may improve accountability and performance across the system, but only if the new entities can demonstrate sufficient readiness and capability. Many commenters expressed concern that certifying organizations without an established performance history could disrupt continuity of care and negatively affect both donors and transplant recipients. These commenters emphasized that any certification of new entities should be contingent on demonstrated operational readiness and capability, rather than projected performance.
Commenters offered a range of recommendations on the certification of new OPOs. Many commenters suggested that new entities must be nonprofit organizations, while one OPO recommended that CMS allow any entity to become an OPO regardless of nonprofit status. Another commenter recommended that any new entity be required to meet all existing CfCs under
42 CFR part 486, subpart G
, prior to certification, without exception or phased implementation. A commenter suggested that, in the absence of historical outcome data, CMS should permit new entities to demonstrate readiness through alternative evidence—such as leadership experience, operational readiness, and systems capability—while still requiring compliance with applicable CfCs and process performance requirements. Two commenters proposed alternative certification pathways—one through an expedited process for applicants demonstrating clinical infrastructure, transplant center partnerships, and sufficient financial reserves, and another through accreditation by national accrediting organizations. Commenters also requested additional clarity on how new OPOs would be monitored, measured, and benchmarked, including whether they would be evaluated differently from incumbent OPOs. Commenters also sought clarification on whether OPOs de-certified in one cycle could be re-certified in a subsequent cycle and, if so, under what conditions.
