Commenters also offered a range of recommendations on the designation of a DSA to a new OPO. A few commenters stated that, at a minimum, new OPOs should be subject to the same competition selection criteria as existing OPOs when applying for an open DSA. Another commenter recommended that CMS develop a standardized DSA Readiness Assessment to ensure that a new OPO is capable of performing immediately upon designation. This commenter suggested that at a minimum, this assessment should include: established clinical and operational capacity with qualified staffing and 24/7 readiness; demonstrated ability to effectively engage with donor families and communities; data-driven and third-party validated analysis of donor potential; and evidence of financial stability to sustain operations. A commenter stated that new OPOs should not receive any advantage in the selection process, as they lack experience and historical performance data and cannot be presumed to outperform existing OPOs. Another commenter suggested that CMS limit the certification of new entities to scenarios in which an OPO has been de-certified and no existing OPO seeks to compete for the open DSA.
Response:
We agree that each DSA should be served by a qualified OPO capable of performing organ procurement services. Given the complexity and significance of establishing a certification process for new OPOs, we did not propose a specific initial certification framework in the January 2026 OPO proposed rule. We intend to address certification of new OPOs and the process by which a newly certified OPO might be designated to a DSA in future rulemaking and will take the recommendations received into consideration at that time.
Final Rule Action:
After consideration of the public comments we received, we are finalizing as proposed removing § 486.303(e). We will address the process to certify new OPOs, as well as the process by which a newly certified OPO might be designated to a DSA, in future rulemaking.
D. Designation of One OPO for Each Service Area (§ 486.308)
Currently, § 486.308(a) states that, “CMS designates only one OPO per service area. A service area is open for competition when the OPO for the service area is de-certified and all administrative appeals under § 486.314 are exhausted.” We proposed to revise requirements at § 486.308 to further address changes made in the December 2020 OPO final rule related to when a DSA is open for competition. Additionally, current requirements indicate that “[a]n OPO is normally designated for a 4-year agreement cycle. The period may be shorter, for example, if an OPO has voluntarily terminated its agreement with CMS and CMS selects a successor OPO for the balance of the 4-year agreement cycle. Additionally, the period may be shorter due to involuntary termination of an OPO due to non-compliance with the process performance measures (§§ 486.320 through 486.360). In rare situations, a designation period may be longer, for example, a designation may be extended if additional time is needed to select a successor OPO to replace an OPO that has been de-certified.” We proposed to clarify how an OPO is assigned a DSA and how we determine the OPO designation period. Specifically, we proposed to (1) clarify the normal designation period and when CMS may adjust the length of the period; (2) clarify designation periods for newly acquired DSAs; (3) specify the circumstances that trigger a DSA to become available for competition; and (4) establish criteria for successor selection when insufficient time exists for a full competition process.
We proposed to clarify all circumstances when a designation period may be adjusted. We proposed at § 486.308(a)(1) that CMS may adjust the length of a designation period when: (i) there is a voluntary termination of an OPO's agreement with CMS; (ii) there is an involuntary termination of an OPO's agreement with CMS; (iii) additional time is needed to complete an appeal, conduct a competition, select a successor OPO, or transition the DSA to a successor OPO; or (iv) there is an extension of the agreement cycle for extraordinary circumstances as specified at § 486.316(f).
We proposed at § 486.308(a)(2) that CMS would conduct a competition for all vacated DSAs. We also proposed at § 486.308(a)(3) that the designation period for any newly acquired DSA, whether following a competition or as the result of being assigned a DSA, will be the remaining portion of the agreement for the acquiring OPO's existing re-certification cycle. We proposed at § 486.308(a)(4) that if an OPO does not fulfill the terms of its agreement, whether voluntarily or involuntarily, and there is insufficient time to conduct a competition to select a successor OPO for its DSA, CMS may designate another OPO without first
(
printed page 69403)
conducting a competition. We stated that we would exercise this option only if there were concern for continuity of organ donation in the DSA in situations such as a termination for urgent need, a cessation of business, or because the incumbent OPO was unable to sustain services to provide an orderly transition to a successor OPO. In selecting an OPO under these circumstances, CMS would consider the following factors: contiguity to the DSA; performance on outcome measures at § 486.318; history of compliance with the process performance measures at §§ 486.320 through 486.360; and willingness of the OPO to perform the responsibilities.
Currently, § 486.308(a) states that a service area is open for competition when the OPO for the DSA is de-certified and all administrative appeals at § 486.314 are exhausted. We proposed to amend this language to conform with requirements for competition at § 486.316 and outcome measures at § 486.318 to implement the tiered system for competition from the December 2020 final rule and clarify competition requirements if an OPO were to voluntarily terminate its agreement. Additionally, with the exception of de-certification for urgent need, revisions to this section clarify that de-certification would not occur until after any applicable appeal is completed, competition for the open DSA is completed, and the DSA is transitioned to the successor OPO.
Specifically, we proposed to address all circumstances under which a DSA is open for competition. A DSA is open for competition when:
An OPO's DSA is assigned tier 3 status in the final assessment period and all administrative appeals are exhausted;
An OPO's DSA is assigned to tier 2 for outcome measures in the final assessment period;
An OPO is not in compliance with the process performance measures at §§ 486.320 through 486.360, all administrative appeals are exhausted, and the OPO is pending de-certification; or
An OPO requests to voluntarily terminate its agreement to participate, except where the voluntary termination is associated with a change in control, ownership, or service area resulting from a merger with another OPO.
We solicited public comment on these proposed changes at § 486.308. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
A commenter recommended that CMS revise the OPO certification period to end on December 31 of the last year of the re-certification cycle and start the next cycle on January 1. The commenter stated that this would provide the public and the OPO community more time to verify the outcome measures, appeals, and competition. The commenter stated that the outcome measures from the final assessment period should be available for at least 6 months prior to the expiration of the OPO contracts. The commenter stated that these changes would effectively minimize potential disruptions in the area if the incumbent OPO is not redesignated to the DSA.
Response:
The dates of the re-certification cycle and the OPO agreement period are not within the scope of this rule, as we did not propose any changes to them. We note that once OPO annual public aggregated performance reports are published, OPOs are provided a preview period to verify their data and outcomes and raise any concerns to CMS prior to the public report being posted. Re-certification cycles end on July 31 every four years. However, the current OPO agreements end 6 months later on January 31, 2027. Additionally, we may extend agreements beyond this timeframe under § 486.314(n) (revised and moved from § 486.314(j)), if necessary to complete appeals and any necessary competitions and facilitate an orderly transition of the DSA. An extension of an agreement under § 486.314(j), or § 486.314(n) as finalized in this rule, serves the limited purpose of allowing for these processes, where necessary, and does not extend the agreement cycle.
Comment:
A commenter stated that the designation of a DSA to an OPO in the middle of the OPO's current agreement period should not shorten the designation period for the OPO. The commenter recommended that an OPO be permitted to complete the remainder of the agreement period for the newly designated DSA and should be re-certified at the end of that agreement period for at least another 4-year agreement term regardless of manner or circumstance of the designation of the new DSA.
Response:
We appreciate the opportunity to clarify the designation periods described at § 486.308(a)(3), as finalized in this rule, and existing requirements at § 486.310(b)(2) and our rationale for the requirements for when OPOs would be held accountable on the outcome measures at § 486.318(c)(3) and (4), as finalized in this rule. If an OPO is designated to a DSA mid-cycle, meaning after August 1 of the first year of the re-certification cycle, we will designate the OPO to the new DSA for the remainder of that re-certification cycle regardless of the reason for the designation. The OPO's re-certification and designation to the new DSA for the subsequent re-certification cycle would be based on the nature of the circumstances that resulted in the designation and availability of outcome measures from the final assessment period. If the initial designation was the result of a competition or resulted from CMS assigning the DSA to the OPO, we would re-certify the OPO at the end of the re-certification cycle, provided it is in compliance with the process performance measures, and redesignate the OPO to the DSA to provide additional time for it to operate in the DSA before holding it accountable on the outcome measures in the subsequent re-certification cycle as specified at § 486.318(c)(4). This policy is due to the greater challenge of assuming responsibility for a DSA in potentially contentious or unanticipated circumstances. If the designation was the result of a change of control or ownership or service area under § 486.310, which generally occur under planned, cooperative circumstances, we would hold the OPO accountable on the outcome measures after 12 months of data are available as specified at § 486.318(c)(3). Re-certification and redesignation to the DSA would depend on the timing of the change that resulted in being designated to a new DSA and the availability of outcome measures for that DSA under new leadership. A change of control or ownership or service area results from extensive pre-planning, cooperation, and sharing of information, all of which are likely to advantage the OPO in meeting the CMS outcome measure standards. Given these built in features that support more timely compliance with the outcome measure standards, it is our policy that if outcome measure data are available for the new DSA at the time of re-certification, CMS would hold the OPO accountable on the outcome measures for that DSA. The OPO's re-certification and redesignation would depend on the OPO's performance and tier standing in the final assessment period, provided the OPO met all other process performance requirements. We believe this approach balances performance expectations and timeframes with the circumstances and challenges posed by the nature of the change. Therefore, we are not adopting the commenter's recommendations.
Comment:
Several commenters stated that an OPO that is involuntarily assigned a DSA will expend significant administrative and clinical resources in the newly assigned DSA to the possible
(

detriment of the OPO's original DSA. These commenters stated that the OPO should not be disadvantaged by the involuntary assignment and accommodation should be made to that OPO for both of its DSAs if performance decreases.
Response:
We thank the commenters for sharing these concerns. The instances when CMS would assign a DSA to an OPO include when there is insufficient time to conduct a competition as specified at § 486.308(a)(4), as finalized in this rule, and if there are no competitors in a competition as specified at § 486.316(e). While we appreciate the additional responsibility that the OPO would be taking on, we will continue to require OPOs to meet the minimum performance standards on the outcome measures. However, in response to the concerns raised by commenters regarding the potential for assignment to temporarily lower an OPO's performance in its existing DSAs, and to avoid disadvantaging OPOs that are assigned a new DSA without a competition, we are adding a provision to § 486.316(a)(2) to provide that when CMS assigns an OPO to a new DSA under § 486.308(a)(4) or § 486.316(e), that OPO's new and existing DSAs will not be opened for competition at the end of that re-certification cycle if the OPO's performance in those DSAs qualifies for tier 2 in the final assessment period. But an OPO must satisfactorily meet the outcome measures in its original DSAs by achieving tier 1 or tier 2 performance in the final assessment period to retain those DSAs. This provision would partially address concerns by commenters regarding the impact of unplanned expansion to an OPO's other DSAs. However, we cannot permit an OPO to retain its other DSAs if performance in those DSAs decreases to tier 3. Therefore, if an OPO's performance in its original DSA decreases to the extent that the DSA is assigned to tier 3, we would issue an initial notice of de-certification or a notice of removal of designation to a tier 3 DSA without de-certification in accordance with the process set forth at § 486.314(a). If the assignment occurs on a date later than January 1 of the first year of the agreement cycle, the OPO will be held accountable for its performance in the newly assigned DSA as set forth at § 486.318(c)(4).
Comment:
Several commenters expressed concern with proposed designation requirements at § 486.308(a)(4), in the circumstance when CMS would designate an OPO to a DSA where there is insufficient time to conduct a competition. Commenters stated that the DSA should not be opened for competition and the OPO should retain designation until a full re-certification cycle is completed. Commenters stated that the OPO should retain the DSA if its performance is acceptable at that time. Commenters highlighted the significant undertaking of accepting a DSA in this circumstance and stated that they should be given the opportunity to retain the DSA if its performance supports this.
Response:
We agree with the commenters on this issue. While our standard approach is to provide competition for open DSAs, the commenters raise valid concerns regarding the commitment of administrative and clinical resources necessary to stabilize a DSA under these circumstances. We are modifying proposed § 486.308(a)(2) and (4) to indicate that we would not open a DSA for competition following assignment of the DSA to an OPO under the circumstances described in § 486.308(a)(4). The OPO would retain designation to the DSA for the remainder of the designation period rather than opening for competition at the earliest possible time. In response to the concerns raised by commenters, we are modifying proposed § 486.308(a)(3) to include assignment of a DSA where there is insufficient time to conduct a competition as another scenario in which the OPO will be designated for the remaining portion of the current re-certification cycle. We are also modifying the language of proposed § 486.318(c)(4) to make clear that that an OPO that is assigned a new DSA under either § 486.308(a)(4) or § 486.316(e) will be assessed on the outcome measures in the new DSA for re-certification purposes based on the final assessment period of the next full re-certification cycle. However, to facilitate assessment of the OPO's performance in the newly assigned DSA, we will retain the language of proposed § 486.309(b), which excludes assignment of a DSA due to insufficient time to conduct a competition from the scenarios in which an OPO may choose to consolidate DSAs. Finally, we are adding regulatory references for competition (§ 486.316(d)) and assignment of a DSA by CMS (§ 486.308(a)(4)).
Comment:
Several commenters recommended that CMS better define the circumstances at § 486.308(a)(4) under which it would designate an OPO to a DSA without conducting a competition. Commenters stated that CMS should prioritize continuity of donation operations and provide realistic timelines, recognizing that transitions involve complex operational, legal, and governance factors in addition to clinical operations. Another commenter stated that CMS should clearly explain how the objective factors identified to guide designation decisions are weighed when competition is not feasible.
Response:
We thank commenters for sharing these concerns and recommendations. While it may be difficult to predict every circumstance when we would assign a DSA to an OPO without conducting a competition as specified at § 486.308(a)(4), we anticipate this would be an extremely rare occurrence that would be utilized to ensure continuity of organ donation activities. De-certification due to urgent need, as set forth at § 486.312(a)(4), or an OPO ceasing operations or voluntarily terminating its agreement with CMS without adequate notice to conduct a competition could all necessitate CMS assignment of a DSA to preserve organ donation activities. Although we did not receive any comments specifying alternative factors to consider when assigning a DSA in this situation, a commenter requested information about how we would weigh various factors under consideration. These factors include contiguity to the DSA, performance on outcome measures at § 486.318, history of compliance with the process performance measures at §§ 486.320 through 486.360, and willingness of the OPO to perform the responsibilities for the remainder of the designation period. Additionally, we are finalizing a modification to the proposed language at § 486.308(a)(4) to indicate that we would assign the DSA to a single OPO, rather than “one or more”. Given that CMS will only select a successor OPO under § 486.308(a)(4) when there is insufficient time to conduct a competition, we expect that there would also be insufficient time in that scenario to take additional action to divide the DSA among multiple successor OPOs. Accordingly, we are finalizing a modification to the proposed language of § 486.308(a)(4) to reflect that CMS would only select a single successor OPO for designation to the DSA when that provision applies.

We are modifying paragraph (a)(3) to add regulatory references “§ 486.316(d)” and “§ 486.308(a)(4)” to the paragraph to identify all instances when CMS may

Additionally, we are modifying the first sentence to indicate that we would select a single OPO when assigning a DSA in this situation. We are also modifying § 486.316(a)(2) to address concerns of commenters to ensure that an OPO is not disproportionately impacted in the event an OPO's performance decreases or fails to improve after being assigned a DSA by CMS.
E. Designation of an OPO to More Than One Service Area (§ 486.309)
Since the December 2020 OPO final rule was issued, some OPOs have requested guidance on how an OPO could manage more than one DSA. Section 1138(b)(2) of the Act provides that the Secretary may not designate more than one OPO for each service area and the current OPO CfCs only address one OPO being designated to only one DSA. Given that OPOs have expressed interest in this area and the statute does not explicitly restrict this situation, we proposed to replace obsolete requirements at § 486.309 related to the re-certification of OPOs during August 1, 2006, through July 31, 2010 with new requirements to address situations in which an OPO is responsible for more than one DSA.
Permitting an OPO to separately maintain multiple DSAs could maintain some level of market diversity to support future competition. OPOs have also expressed concern for assuming responsibility for DSAs where other OPOs have historically underperformed and merging those areas with their existing DSA. These OPOs have indicated they would prefer to manage DSAs separately to ensure they could improve performance without risk to their existing DSA if they were to combine DSAs and have outcome measures assessed for the combined areas. To give OPOs additional flexibility to maintain separate DSAs, we proposed that an OPO could be assigned to more than one DSA: (1) following a change in control, ownership, or service area; (2) as the result of a competition; or (3) as a result of CMS assignment when there is insufficient time to conduct a competition. In these instances, the OPO would need to determine how best to manage its organization for the respective areas. We proposed that if an OPO was made responsible for more than one DSA following a change in control, ownership, or service area, or a competition, the OPO could choose to consolidate the DSAs, maintain separate DSAs, or a combination thereof if more than two DSAs were involved. Additionally, we proposed that if CMS were to assign a DSA to an OPO following a voluntary or involuntary termination, the OPO would be required to maintain the newly assigned DSA separately to facilitate future competition. We also proposed that the DSA would be opened for competition at the end of the designation period, as designation of an OPO to a DSA in this situation would be a temporary measure intended to maintain organ procurement services and to provide time to facilitate an orderly transition of the DSA to a successor OPO following a competition.
We also proposed an approach for the application of both the outcome and process performance measures when an OPO is designated to multiple DSAs. We proposed that when an OPO consolidated multiple DSAs, regardless of contiguity, into a single DSA, we would assess the OPO's performance on the outcome measures as a single DSA. At the final assessment period, if the OPO could not satisfy the outcome measures for the merged DSA, the OPO would be de-certified (subject to the available appeal rights). An OPO with one DSA faces de-certification if it is non-compliant with any of the CfCs, including the process performance measures (§§ 486.320 through 486.360) or the outcome measures (§ 486.318), at the time of re-certification. However, our proposed approach would permit an OPO that obtained a new additional DSA to choose to maintain separate DSAs, rather than consolidating its new DSA with its existing DSA. While the OPO would still be required to meet the process performance measures in the conditions for coverage for all of its DSAs to avoid de-certification, we proposed that we would consider the OPO's performance on the outcome measures separately for each DSA when the OPO chooses to maintain separate DSAs. This would enable the OPO to meet the outcome measures in one DSA, even if the OPO did not satisfy the outcome measures in a separate DSA at the time of re-certification. Specifically, we proposed that when an OPO is designated to more than one DSA, CMS would remove designation to a tier 3 DSA in the event of non-compliance with the outcome measures for that DSA at the end of the re-certification cycle. We proposed that such removal of designation would not result in de-certification unless an OPO is no longer designated to any DSA due to tier 3 outcome measure performance across all of its DSAs (see corresponding requirements at § 486.316). We also proposed that an OPO may appeal the decision to remove its designation to a tier 3 DSA, and that the removed DSA would be opened for competition after any appeal for that DSA is exhausted and the decision is upheld.
We solicited public comment on the proposed changes in § 486.309. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Some commenters were supportive of the proposal allowing OPOs to choose to maintain separate DSAs. They were also generally supportive of allowing OPOs the flexibility to manage their DSAs in a manner that best suits their organizational and operational needs, noting that the factors considered in these decisions may vary based on the DSA and the OPO. A commenter supported CMS retaining final authority over multi-DSA arrangements with clear criteria, including operational capacity and accountability safeguards, while still allowing OPOs the flexibility to maintain separate DSAs, as appropriate.
Response:
We agree that OPOs designated to serve more than one DSA should have flexibility to establish their organizational and operational structure in a manner that best enables them to most effectively provide organ procurement services. There are many organizational and operational factors OPOs would need to consider in determining how to best design their operations. As a result, some OPOs may determine that consolidating DSAs into a single DSA is beneficial, while others may determine that maintaining separate DSAs is more appropriate.
Comment:
A commenter requested confirmation that an OPO is permitted to establish a distinct Standard Acquisition Charge (SAC) for each DSA, regardless of whether those DSAs are operated through separate legal entities or unincorporated divisions within a single legal entity. The commenter also sought clarification on CMS' expectations for allocating shared overhead, executive, and administrative expenses across multiple DSAs in distinct cost reports, specifically asking whether time studies conducted one week per month would be a sufficient methodology or if an alternative mechanism is recommended.
Response:
We thank the commenter for raising this concern. We will develop and issue guidance to address cost reporting questions for OPOs with multiple DSAs.
Final Rule Action:
After consideration of the public comments we received, we are finalizing changes to § 486.309 as proposed.

F. Non-Renewal of Agreement (§ 486.311) and De-Certification (§ 486.312)
To address the implementation of the tier system for re-certification of OPOs, we proposed to establish a new CfC at § 486.311 for non-renewal of an OPO agreement. Additionally, we proposed to revise § 486.312 to address enforcement actions that may result in de-certification of an OPO.
We proposed changes to address implementation of the tiered system for re-certification and competition from the December 2020 final rule and to clarify the difference between non-renewal of an agreement and de-certification. We also proposed to revise the public notice requirements for when there is a non-renewal or de-certification to clarify that CMS would be providing these notices.
We proposed that CMS would not renew an agreement with an OPO if the following conditions are met: the OPO's DSA is subject to a competition and the OPO is unsuccessful in the competition to retain its DSA. The OPO would not be afforded appeal rights for loss of a competition, consistent with our long-standing policy, as described in the 2006 final rule (see
71 FR 30998
). We proposed that CMS would provide notification to the OPO at least 90 days before the effective date of the non-renewal and that the notice would state the reasons for non-renewal and include the end date of the agreement. We also proposed that CMS would not renew an agreement in the case of a voluntary termination of an agreement by an OPO.
In our proposed approach, an OPO with only tier 2 DSAs that fails to retain any of its DSAs in competition would be re-certified without designation to a DSA. This would permit the OPO to compete in any additional open competitions during the following 4-year certification period. If the OPO is successful in a concurrent or subsequent competition, assigned a DSA by CMS, or selected for an open DSA when there is insufficient time to conduct a competition, it could then be designated to another DSA during this period. If the OPO does not obtain a new DSA through competition, assignment, or selection (including circumstances where there is insufficient time to conduct a competition) for an open DSA by the end of the next re-certification cycle following the non-renewal of the OPO's agreement, it would not meet outcome measure standards for that cycle. Consequently, the OPO would be de-certified at that time. The OPO would have appeal rights for de-certification. While an appeal would not be available for the assignment of a DSA to tier 2 or the result of a competition, all OPOs are provided with a preview of their outcome measure results and an opportunity to raise concerns with the data before performance reports are finalized.
The current requirement for voluntary termination of an agreement is located at § 486.312. We proposed to relocate the voluntary termination of agreement provision from § 486.312 to new § 486.311 and remove the requirement that we would de-certify the OPO. An OPO voluntarily withdrawing from its agreement or ceasing to furnish organ procurement services has taken an affirmative step to end its duties under the OPO agreement, but that action does not entitle the OPO to appeal a de-certification on substantive or procedural grounds. As such, the withdrawing OPO would not be afforded appeal rights. The OPO would no longer have an agreement and would no longer be designated to any DSAs, as of the effective date determined by CMS.
For non-renewal of an agreement after a competition, we proposed that we would provide notification to the OPO at least 90 calendar days before the effective date of the non-renewal, and the notice would state the reasons for non-renewal and include the end date of the agreement.
We also proposed a public notice requirement consistent with the current public notice requirements at § 486.312 to inform the public in the affected service areas. We would inform the public of the date on which a new OPO will be designated for that DSA. We also proposed to retain the policy which states that no payment under titles XVIII or XIX of the Act will be made with respect to organ procurement costs attributable to an OPO that no longer has an agreement with CMS.
We proposed to revise the requirements at § 486.312 to clarify the actions we may take to de-certify an OPO. Specifically, we proposed that we may de-certify an OPO if the OPO no longer meets the requirements for certification at § 486.303, including the conditions for coverage at §§ 486.320 through 486.360. We proposed that we may de-certify an OPO if the OPO is designated only to tier 3 DSAs in the final assessment period at the end of the re-certification cycle as specified at 486.318(b)(6) and 486.316(b)(iii)(3)(A). We also proposed that we would de-certify an OPO if it is no longer designated to any DSA and does not have data available from the final assessment period to demonstrate compliance with the outcome measures at the end of the re-certification cycle. This would address the potential outcome of a tier 2 OPO that was re-certified but did not have an agreement renewed because it did not win a competition and was not otherwise assigned a DSA by CMS.
We also proposed to relocate and revise the provision allowing for immediate de-certification in cases of urgent need, such as the discovery of unsound medical practices.
We proposed to revise and relocate the requirements regarding notice of de-certification to the OPO. We proposed that except in cases of urgent need, the initial notice of de-certification would be provided to the OPO at least 90 calendar days before the effective date of the de-certification. In cases of urgent need, the notice would be provided at least 3 calendar days prior to the effective date of the de-certification. The notice would state the reasons for de-certification, explain the available appeal rights, and include the effective date of the de-certification.
Finally, we proposed to revise and redesignate the requirements pertaining to public notice of de-certification. We proposed to replace the requirement that the OPO provide public notice in situations of involuntary termination and de-certification with a new process that CMS will provide public notice. We proposed that CMS would notify the public within the service area of both the date of de-certification and the date that a new OPO will be designated for the DSA. We solicited public comment on these proposed changes in §§ 486.311 and 486.312. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Several commenters were supportive of the proposed changes in clarifying the differences between non-renewal and de-certification in the competition framework. These commenters recommended advance notice and transition plans to allow for orderly transfer of operations to the successor OPO. A commenter recommended collaboration with HRSA in implementing changes to relevant information technology (IT) systems.
Response:
We thank commenters for their support and recommendations. We are establishing notification requirements for non-renewal at § 486.311(c) and (d) for both the OPO and the public respectively. Additionally, we are finalizing a requirement at § 486.316(g) for transition plans to facilitate an orderly transfer of a DSA between an incumbent and successor OPO. CMS and HRSA have coordinated the transition of DSAs for several mergers and a recent de-
(
printed page 69407)
certification. We continue to collaborate to refine this process and ensure continuity of IT systems during the transition.
Comment:
Many commenters recommended due process considerations for an OPO that received a notice of non-renewal due to competition loss and was therefore no longer designated to a DSA. Commenters stated that non-renewal of an OPO's agreement would effectively be the same as de-certification and the lack of due process protections was unfair and lacked transparency. A commenter stated that the absence of any mechanism to challenge the underlying competitive determination would be a serious procedural gap. Several commenters stated that CMS should ensure that procedural safeguards are commensurate with the operational and public health consequences of DSA removal and recommended that CMS establish a structured administrative review pathway for OPOs in this situation. Another commenter raised concerns for procedural equity, indicating that tier 3 OPOs were afforded a pathway to contest de-certification, while tier 2 OPOs that lost their DSA through a competitive process would not have such a pathway.
Response:
We thank commenters for sharing their concerns but disagree with their recommendations. The competition process is designed to enable CMS to choose the OPO that is most likely to increase organ donation in the service area and thereby serve the best interests of organ donation, potential organ donors and recipients in the service area. OPOs with tier 2 DSAs that are unsuccessful in competition and no longer designated to a DSA may compete in concurrent or subsequent competitions for other DSAs or be assigned a DSA by CMS throughout the term of the re-certification cycle. While there could be a gap in designation, impacted OPOs may have multiple opportunities to demonstrate that they are the best qualified OPO for a specific DSA.
Assignment of a DSA to tier 2 is not a determination that the OPO designated to that DSA is out of compliance with the outcome measure requirements. An OPO with a DSA that meets tier 2 performance standards has met the minimum performance standards for re-certification and will be re-certified, provided that it also meets the process performance measures at §§ 486.320 through 486.360. However, it will not automatically retain its designation to the tier 2 DSA for another full agreement cycle. Instead, an OPO with a tier 2 DSA would compete to retain its designation to the DSA for another agreement cycle.
To clarify this distinction between re-certification and the retention of designation to a DSA, we are revising § 486.311 to clarify that when an OPO is unsuccessful in the competition process, as set forth at § 486.316(a)(2), and the OPO is no longer designated to the DSA, CMS will not renew its agreement for designation to that DSA. This means that the OPO would enter into a new Form CMS 576A (Health Insurance Benefits Agreement) to reflect its re-certification for the next 4 year cycle, but the OPO would no longer be designated to a DSA as identified on its Form CMS 576 (Request for Designation as an OPO). This clarification reflects that OPOs that meet the tier 2 thresholds for the outcome measures and are compliant with the process performance measures will be re-certified and will maintain an agreement with CMS reflecting their status as a certified OPO, but must be successful in competition for an open DSA (their original DSA or a different one) in order to have an agreement for designation to a DSA for another full agreement cycle. We are also making a conforming change to § 486.316(b)(2)(ii) to clarify that an OPO with a tier 2 DSA will not have the agreement for designation to a DSA renewed if it is not successful in at least one competition.
When an OPO's DSA is assigned to tier 3 based on performance in the final assessment period, on the other hand, the OPO has failed to meet minimum outcome measure standards in that DSA, resulting in either de-certification or removal of designation to the tier 3 DSA. In light of this adverse determination, OPOs with tier 3 DSAs are granted an appeal. Furthermore, as we have previously explained, allowing appeals of competition results would be unwieldy and would create uncertainty, both for the OPO that prevailed in competition and within the DSA (
71 FR 30998
). As a result, we do not believe that appeal of competition results would best serve the interests of organ donation in the DSA. While some commenters cite operational and public health concerns for transitioning a DSA, we note the public health considerations for the nearly 100,000 people on the organ transplant waiting list, many of whom will die waiting for a lifesaving transplant. While OPOs with tier 2 DSAs meet minimum outcome measure requirements, they may not be the best OPO to serve a DSA if there is a more capable OPO that can demonstrate the ability to procure more lifesaving organs.
Comment:
Several commenters indicated that consistent turnover of DSA assignments risks undermining important community relationships and could negatively affect donation rates in affected communities. A commenter was concerned that DSA reassignments and associated changes will lead to major setbacks in the important work Tier 3 OPOs have done in reaching out to diverse communities, educating the community, and establishing trust. The commenter stated that the loss of personnel, programs, and expertise that these communities have come to know and trust could upset the progress that has been made and detrimentally impact organ donation rates in these communities.
Response:
We appreciate the concerns expressed by these commenters and recognize that many OPOs have invested in building deep community ties. We believe every community should be served by a high performing OPO that meets our performance standards. Additionally, we believe it is vital to continue improving donation rates in diverse communities and replacing underperforming OPOs with higher performers that have a demonstrated record of overcoming challenges in their DSA is one way to further this goal. We anticipate that successor OPOs will apply the lessons learned in their own DSAs to newly designated DSAs and build upon those successes to engage all population groups throughout its newly designated DSA, including those groups associated with historically low donation rates in the DSA. Additionally, as CMS develops future requirements for new entities seeking to become certified OPOs, we anticipate developing and proposing criteria to evaluate their plans to engage all population groups for organ donation.
Comment:
A commenter recommended CMS consider other factors to cure tier 3 performance in a DSA when the OPO would be de-certified or have its designation removed. The commenter recommended that CMS retain the OPO's designation to the tier 3 DSA in the following circumstances: (1) if there were no competitors for the DSA; (2) if the OPO had substantially improved performance in the DSA despite remaining in tier 3; (3) if the subsequent year's performance improved significantly; or (4) if performance during the assessment year was aberrant due to a natural disaster or other unusual circumstance. Another commenter recommended that CMS implement a process for an OPO to develop and submit a performance improvement or corrective action plan
(
printed page 69408)
that would include peer-assisted improvement initiatives with measurable goals and frequent reporting requirements.
Response:
We thank the commenter for sharing these recommendations. As previously explained, the outcome measure performance standards are set forth at § 486.318, and we did not propose to modify those performance standards to allow for alternative pathways to compliance. Under section 1138(b)(1) of the Act and section 371(b)(1)(D) of the PHS Act, an OPO must meet the Secretary's performance standards to be recertified and to remain eligible for payment of its organ procurement costs under Medicare or Medicaid. Accordingly, an OPO that does not meet minimum performance standards on the outcome measures(tier 3) in any of its DSAs in the final assessment period is not compliant with the Secretary's performance standards and will be de-certified under § 486.312(a)(2). An OPO that meets the minimum performance standards in at least one of its DSAs is eligible to be re-certified, but will have its designation removed from any DSA in which its outcome measure performance qualified as tier 3 as specified at § 486.316(a)(3). However, CMS regulations do allow for an extension of an OPO's agreement cycle in one limited scenario. Specifically, under § 486.316(f), an OPO can seek a 1-year extension of its agreement cycle if there are extraordinary circumstances beyond the control of the OPO that has affected the data of the final assessment period so that it does not accurately capture their performance. An OPO must request this extension within 90 days of the end of the occurrence of the extraordinary circumstance but no later than the last day of the final assessment period.
We note also that nothing in the current requirements prevent an OPO from engaging in a peer-assisted improvement initiative with another OPO and we encourage underperforming OPOs to consider this activity in advance of the final assessment period. However, this type of arrangement cannot be utilized to remedy non-compliance with the outcome measures based on tier 3 performance in the final assessment period.
Comment:
A commenter stated that they support maintaining CMS' authority to de-certify an OPO immediately in cases of urgent need, including unsound medical practices. The commenter stated that patient safety must remain the paramount concern, and CMS should not be constrained in addressing serious failures that pose imminent risk to donors or recipients. Another commenter stated that they advocate for low-performing OPOs to be de-certified and believes that every community deserves to be served by a high-performing OPO.
Response:
We thank the commenter for the support of this provision. We believe it is important to be able to respond swiftly in the event of urgent need, such as the discovery of unsound medical practices. We have undertaken further actions to strengthen this provision by adding a definition of “unsound medical practices” which could trigger an urgent need de-certification decision. See Section X of this final rule for more information on the definition of “unsound medical practices”.
Final Rule Action:
After considering public comments, we are finalizing § 486.311 with modifications to paragraphs (a)(1) and (b) clarify that the non-renewal of an agreement after loss of a competition is limited to the OPO's agreement for designation to a DSA, rather than a non-renewal of an agreement for certification. Additionally, we are finalizing § 486.312 as proposed with a minor wording change at § 486.312(b) to align with the corresponding requirement at § 486.314(a)(1). In the proposed rule, § 486.312(b) stated “Except in cases of urgent need, CMS gives written notice of the initial de-certification decision to an OPO at least 90 calendar days before the effective date of the de-certification.” The corrected language in this final rule aligns with the title of § 486.314(a)(1) and is revised as follows: “Except in cases of urgent need, CMS provides an initial notice of de-certification to an OPO in writing at least 90 calendar days before the effective date of the de-certification.”
G. Appeals (§ 486.314)
We proposed several changes to the appeals process. We proposed modifying the timeframes in the appeal process and converting all timeframes to calendar days. We proposed to codify a process for discretionary review by the CMS Administrator and clarify the appeal process for OPOs that are de-certified based on urgent need. Additionally, we proposed to allow an OPO to appeal the removal of a designation to a tier 3 DSA without de-certification for situations where an OPO has another DSA that is assigned to performance tier 1 or 2 in the final assessment period for re-certification. These changes would make sure that OPOs have timely appeal rights for any adverse determinations regarding an OPO's compliance with outcome measure standards in a particular DSA. For more details on the basis for our proposals related to the appeals process, see the January 2026 OPO proposed rule (
91 FR 4209
through
4212
).
We proposed to modify the time periods in this section for existing requirements from “business days” to “calendar days” to facilitate consistent implementation of the process. We also proposed to use “calendar days” for all proposed requirements to further facilitate consistent application.
Currently, the OPO has 15 business days from receipt of the notice to request reconsideration from CMS, and we proposed to change this to 20 calendar days. CMS currently has 10 business days from receipt of the reconsideration request to make a written reconsidered determination that would affirm, reverse, or modify the initial de-certification determination. We proposed to modify this to 15 calendar days to make a written reconsidered determination that would affirm or reverse the initial de-certification determination. We also proposed that CMS would have the right to extend this time based on a determination that additional time was necessary to thoroughly review and make a decision and the extension did not prejudice either party. Finally, we proposed to remove the option for the reconsideration official to “modify” the initial de-certification determination. If the de-certification decision was upheld, the OPO then would have 40 business days from receipt of CMS' reconsideration decision to request a hearing before a CMS hearing officer. The hearing officer would have to set a date for the hearing that was no more than 60 calendar days after receiving that request for a hearing and would have to render his or her decision within 20 business days of the hearing. We proposed reducing the number of days within which an OPO could request a hearing before a CMS hearing officer from 40 business days to 15 calendar days.
The hearing officer would be required to send the administrative record to both parties (for example, CMS and OPO) within 10 business days of receipt of the request for a hearing. Because the Office of Hearings now uses an electronic case management system in which both parties have access to each other's filings, the reconsideration official would not need to forward their administrative record to the hearing officer unless and until there had been a request for a hearing. We proposed that upon receipt of a request for a hearing, the hearing officer would
(
printed page 69409)
promptly request the administrative record from the reconsideration official. We also proposed that the hearing officer, within 15 calendar days of receipt of the request for a hearing, would send the administrative record to both parties, or make it available through their electronic filing system, rather than the current 10 business days.
We proposed establishing requirements related to the scope of review and burden of proof related to an appeal. We proposed that the scope of review would be limited to (1) de-certification of an OPO and (2) removal of designation to a tier 3 DSA. The appeal must be based on substantive or procedural grounds. We also proposed that the OPO would bear the burden of proof by a preponderance of the evidence to demonstrate that the adverse determination by CMS should be reversed.
Additionally, we proposed to change the time that the hearing officer would be allotted to render their decision to from 20 business days to 90 calendar days. We also proposed allowing the hearing officer to extend that time upon notifying both the OPO and CMS, if the extension did not unduly prejudice either of the parties and is necessary for the hearing officer to issue a legally sufficient decision. Consistent with CMS longstanding policy, the hearing officer could affirm or reverse the notice of de-certification. We proposed to add that the hearing officer could also affirm or reverse the removal of designation to a tier 3 DSA without de-certification. The hearing officer would then promptly forward the decision and the administrative record to the CMS Administrator.
We proposed to codify the process for discretionary review of the hearing officer's decision by the CMS Administrator. Specifically, we proposed that the CMS Administrator would have 30 calendar days from receipt of the hearing officer's decision to elect to review or decline to review the hearing officer's decision. If the CMS Administrator elected to review the hearing officer's decision within the 30-day period, the CMS Administrator would promptly notify the OPO and CMS of his or her decision to review and the parties' right to submit written arguments within 15 calendar days of the notification. If the Administrator did not elect to review the decision within 30 calendar days of its receipt, the hearing officer's decision would be final.
We proposed that within 45 calendar days of notification of the CMS Administrator electing to review the hearing officer's decision, the CMS Administrator would be required to render a final decision, in writing, to the parties. The CMS Administrator could affirm, reverse, or remand the hearing officer's decision to CMS. We believed that there might be circumstances in which the CMS Administrator would want CMS to conduct further review or have other instructions for CMS regarding the appeal. Hence, we proposed that the CMS Administrator could remand the appeal to CMS for any appropriate reason. Remanding the appeal means that the appeal would be sent back to CMS for re-evaluation and a new initial determination regarding de-certification or removal of designation for a DSA without de-certification. Also, if the appeal was remanded to CMS, the agency would comply with any instructions in the remand. We did not propose to establish remand authority for the hearing officer.
We also proposed that the CMS Administrator would have the right to extend the review time if he or she determined they needed more time to thoroughly review and make a decision, provided the extension did not prejudice either party. We proposed that the CMS Administrator's review would be limited to the hearing's administrative record developed by the hearing officer and written arguments submitted by the OPO or CMS.
We proposed that CMS' reconsideration decision on de-certification or designation removal would become final if the OPO did not request review by a hearing officer in the time allowed under these regulations, or after the CMS Administrator declined to review the hearing officer's decision, render a decision in writing to the parties, or did not render a final decision or a remand in writing to the parties within 45 calendar days of electing to review the hearing officer's decision (or by the extended deadline, if the Administrator extends the 45-day period).
As noted later in this section of the preamble, a decision would not take effect until (among other things) all administrative appeals were exhausted to avoid any undue prejudice to the OPO. Given the range of tasks that must be completed, we also proposed that CMS could offer to extend an OPO's agreement if additional time would be needed for completion of the appeals process, competition of the service area and, if necessary, transition of the service area to a successor OPO.
We proposed to clarify when the OPO's DSA would be opened for competition. Consistent with longstanding CMS policy, we proposed that an OPO would not be de-certified or lose its designation to a DSA until all administrative appeals were exhausted. If at the end of the appeals process the notice of de-certification or removal of designation has been confirmed, the decision would be final. At that time, the OPO's DSA would be opened for competition and a successor OPO would be chosen. CMS would then determine a transition period that was sufficient for the new OPO to take full responsibility for the DSA. After the transition period was determined by CMS, CMS would forward to the de-certified OPO a written communication indicating the effective date of de-certification. As of that effective date, Medicare and Medicaid payments would no longer be made for organ procurement costs attributable to the OPO. For an OPO that lost its designation to a tier 3 DSA without being de-certified, CMS would forward a written communication indicating the effective date of the decision. As of that effective date, Medicare and Medicaid payments would no longer be made for organ procurement costs attributable to the affected OPO for that particular DSA. We would not begin the competition process before the appeals process was exhausted.
We also proposed to address special considerations regarding appeals in cases of de-certification due to urgent need. The appeals process would be the same for an OPO de-certified due to urgent need regardless of the reason for the OPO's de-certification. However, if an OPO was de-certified due to urgent need, it could be de-certified immediately. In such circumstances, the affected OPO's service area would be reassigned to one or more other OPOs by the effective date specified in the notice of de-certification provided. Hence, if the de-certified OPO pursued an appeal, it would not be operating its DSA while proceeding through the appeals process.
We solicited public comments on these proposed changes to the appeals process. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
General Comments
Comment:
Most commenters generally supported the proposed change from using business days to calendar days.
Response:
We thank the commenters for their support. We are finalizing the proposed change from calendar days to business days.
Comment:
Some commenters were concerned about the status of OPOs during the appeals process. They wanted to know what happens to their agreements with CMS and their
(
printed page 69410)
payments for organ procurement activities during that time.
Response:
When an OPO is going through the appeals process after receiving an initial notice of de-certification for non-compliance with the CfCs or a notice of removal of designation to a tier 3 DSA without de-certification, the OPO is still certified and designated to its DSA(s). During this period, the OPO's agreement is still in effect, and the OPO will remain eligible for payment. If the de-certification decision or the removal of designation decision is upheld, this status continues until the effective date of the de-certification or removal of designation to the tier 3 DSA. However, as set forth in § 486.314(p), if an OPO is de-certified due to urgent need, the affected OPO's service area will be reassigned to one or more other OPOs as set forth at § 486.308(a)(4) by the effective date specified in the notice of de-certification provided under § 486.312(b). The OPO has 20 calendar days from receipt of that notice to file a request for reconsideration from CMS. The remainder of the appeals process proceeds as set forth in § 486.314. As the OPO's de-certification for urgent need is already in effect during the appeal timeframe, the OPO is not eligible for payment for organ procurement activities during the appeals process.
Comment:
Some commenters questioned our authority to create an appeals process for OPOs and were concerned with the proposed timeframes. They indicated that with Medicare claim appeals there is typically a much longer timeframes for the provider to act, such as 120 calendar days to request a redetermination, 180 calendar days to file for a reconsideration, and 60 calendar days to request review by an administrative law judge.
Response:
Section 371(b)(1)(D)(ii)(IV) of the PHS Act, added by the Certification Act,
[
15
]
requires the Secretary to issue regulations that provide for an OPO to appeal a de-certification to the Secretary on substantive and procedural grounds. Hence, an appeal process is explicitly required by statute and the Secretary delegated to CMS authority to implement this statutory requirement through the OPO CfCs. We are not persuaded by the commenters' argument regarding the extended timeframes allowed in the Medicare claims process, as that process applies to a matter entirely distinct from OPO certification. Every DSA can only have one OPO designated at a time, meaning that an OPO has a mandated monopoly on organ procurement services for an entire geographic area. An OPO that fails to meet the standards to be a qualified OPO should be removed as promptly as possible to reduce uncertainty in the OPO's DSA and support the entire organ donation and transplantation system. An OPO that receives an initial notice of de-certification (§ 486.314(a)(1), as finalized in this rule) continues to be designated for that DSA unless and until the OPO is de-certified. The DSA cannot be transitioned to a successor OPO until the appeals process has been exhausted. OPOs must be afforded the right to appeal a de-certification on substantive or procedural grounds; however, that appeals process must be conducted in a timely manner to reduce uncertainty in the DSA and protect the rights of the patients on the waiting list. We believe the proposed changes that we are finalizing in this rule not only provide the appropriate balance needed to provide OPOs an adequate opportunity to appeal a de-certification, but also ensure that the rights of the patients on the waiting list, including the right to have an OPO that is in compliance with the OPO CfCs and to avoid any unnecessary disruptions in the organ procurement and placement of organs, are preserved.
Comment:
Some commenters were concerned that the appeals requirements were very burdensome and weakened the due process protections to which OPOs are entitled. Several commenters criticized the proposed changes to the appeals process, especially the change for OPOs to request a hearing from 40 business days to 15 calendar days, as denying OPOs' right to a meaningful due process in the appeals process. Commenters stated that OPOs facing de-certification deserve a meaningful appeals process with sufficient opportunity to prepare and defend against the de-certification. They stated that these appeals are complex and often require extensive preparation, such as review of multi-year performance and outcome data, statistical methods, hospital-level documentation, and thorough legal analysis. Commenters stated that this could be exceptionally difficult for smaller OPOs with fewer resources. Commenters further stated that the appeals process requires meaningful procedural protection, including clear standards, fair timelines, and transparent opportunities for participation. A few commenters recommended that the CMS hearing officer have the authority to grant filing extensions. This would provide flexibility for OPOs that need more time to file a request for hearing and still preserve their appeal rights.
Response:
A request for the hearing is not a formal document in which an OPO is required to submit its arguments about why the OPO should not be de-certified. The request does not require all the information, data, or legal analysis needed for the hearing. It serves only as a notice that the OPO seeks a hearing before a CMS hearing officer. The OPO may continue preparing for the hearing, including reviewing relevant data and developing legal analyses, both before and after the request for hearing is filed. An OPO is free to file a request for hearing to preserve its appeal rights and later withdraw that request if, in the course of preparing for the hearing, it determines that it no longer wants to proceed with the appeal process. We believe that the proposed changes provide OPOs with clear, transparent standards for participation in the appeal process and a meaningful opportunity to appeal on substantive and procedural grounds, while still ensuring the appeals process moves forward in a timely manner to reduce uncertainty in the DSA and protect the interests of patients on the transplant waiting list.
Comment:
Some commenters stated that the proposed changes to the appeals process granting CMS officials additional time, if needed, to fulfill their responsibilities without allowing OPOs to request additional time for required steps in the appeal process created an asymmetrical process that was inequitable and illegal. Other commenters were concerned about fairness and requested protection against conflicts of interest and for the hearing to have a standardized, objective process for all hearing officers. Some commenters recommended allowing the CMS hearing officer to grant extensions to file a request for a hearing.
Response:
Section 371(b)(1)(D)(ii)(IV) of the PHS Act provides that an OPO is entitled to appeal a de-certification on substantive and procedural grounds. An OPO subject to de-certification for non-compliance with the CfCs will continue operating in its DSA pending resolution of any appeal unless the de-certification was based on urgent need. Accordingly, the appeals process must be efficient and timely to reduce any disruption to the organ procurement activities in the DSA and ensure that OPOs that fail to comply with minimum standards are removed as promptly as possible. We believe the requirements for appeals
(
printed page 69411)
that are being finalized in this rule provide OPOs with adequate notice and a meaningful opportunity to pursue their appeal. Permitting CMS officials the opportunity to extend timelines supports this by assuring that CMS officials have enough time to adequately consider the OPO's arguments, particularly since CMS officials are likely to be responsible for multiple appeals simultaneously. In addition, the hearing officer may extend the timeframe for issuing its decision beyond 90 calendar days only if the hearing officer determines that 90 calendar days is insufficient for the hearing officer to develop the administrative record and render a legally sufficient decision and that extending the timeframe for issuing its decision would not unduly prejudice either the OPO or the government. The hearing officer must also provide notice of the extension to the OPO and the government.
With respect to the commenters' concerns about fairness and conflicts of interest, we want to assure the commenters and the public that CMS hearing officers are highly qualified and hear numerous cases involving CMS and other parties across a range of programs and providers and suppliers. In addition, the powers and responsibilities of the hearing officer are clearly set out in § 486.314.
We do not believe it is necessary to grant the CMS hearing officer authority to grant an extension to file a request for a hearing. The appealing OPO should have sufficient time to file the request. As previously explained, the request for a hearing serves only as a notice that the OPO seeks a hearing before a CMS hearing officer. It does not require all the information, data, or legal analysis needed for the hearing. The OPO may continue preparing for the hearing, including reviewing relevant data and developing legal analyses, both before and after the request for a hearing is filed.
Comment:
Some commenters supported codifying a process for the CMS Administrator's review. However, several commenters did not support the discretionary nature of the review and stated that, due to the severe consequence of de-certification as the loss of eligibility for designation and reimbursement under Medicare or Medicaid, the CMS Administrator should be required to review every hearing officer decision.
Response:
We agree with commenters that de-certification warrants a meaningful opportunity to appeal on substantive and procedural grounds, as required by statute. We proposed that under § 486.314(k)(3), each hearing officer's decision and the accompanying administrative record would be promptly forwarded to the CMS Administrator for his or her discretionary review. Thus, the CMS Administrator will have access to each hearing officer decision when deciding whether to exercise discretionary review. We continue to believe that it is appropriate to permit the CMS Administrator to exercise his or her judgement in determining whether to review the hearing officer decision. It is also important to note that prior to the CMS Administrator's discretionary review, the appealing OPO would have gone through reconsideration by a CMS official and a hearing before a CMS hearing officer. Thus, the appealing OPO has already had a meaningful review of its initial notice of de-certification or notice of removal of designation to a tier 3 DSA without de-certification.
Comment:
Some commenters stated that the OPOs should be allowed to submit new evidence during the appeals process, especially during the CMS Administrator's review. They pointed out that data used for the outcome measures could be up to two years old. As such, the OPO's performance could have substantially improved before it receives the initial notice of de-certification.
Response:
We acknowledge that there is a delay in obtaining the outcome measure denominator data due to the nature of the data source, and that the performance reflected in the calculated outcome measures reflect data collected two years prior. However, as stated previously, OPOs have a 4-year re-certification cycle. The data that will be used for the outcome measures are not collected until the third year of the re-certification cycle, meaning that OPOs had time prior to the final assessment period to improve their performance. CMS provides annual performance data reports to every OPO and requires those OPOs that have DSAs in tier 2 and tier 3 to conduct performance improvement projects that will contribute to improved performance on the CMS outcome measures. OPOs have sufficient time, regulatory structure, and incentives to improve their performance, including getting assistance from OPTN, HRSA, CMS, or consultants, before the data that will be used for re-certification begins to be collected. Hence, we believe OPOs have sufficient time to ensure compliance with the OPO CfCs.
Final Rule Action:
After consideration of the public comments we received, we are finalizing changes to § 486.314 as proposed. However, we are modifying § 486.314(p) to reflect a revision to § 486.308(a)(4) which has been revised to indicate that CMS would only select a single successor OPO for designation to the DSA when there is insufficient time to conduct a competition.
H. Re-Certification and Competition (§ 486.316)
The current requirements at § 486.316 address OPO re-certification and competition. These requirements do not currently address one OPO being designated to more than one DSA and the impact this may have on the re-certification and competition processes. We proposed to make conforming changes to this section to clarify the requirements related to OPO designation, re-certification, and competition to also include situations when an OPO is designated to more than one DSA.
We proposed to address the impact of the OPO outcome measures on OPO designation at the time of re-certification. We proposed to determine OPO designation to the DSA based on its performance on the outcome measures and tier assignment in each DSA at the final assessment period of the agreement cycle. Depending on its performance on the outcome measures, an OPO's performance in each DSA would be assigned to tier 1, tier 2, or tier 3.
We proposed that an OPO with a DSA that is assigned to tier 1 would retain designation to the DSA for another agreement period. We also proposed that an OPO with a DSA that is assigned to tier 1 would be re-certified, provided that CMS also determined that the OPO is compliant with the requirements for certification at § 486.303, including the process performance measures at §§ 486.320 through 486.360 during the most recent survey. Furthermore, we proposed that an OPO that was compliant with the requirements of §§ 486.320 through 486.360 and that has a tier 1 DSA would be eligible to compete for any open DSAs.
We proposed that an OPO with a DSA that was assigned to tier 2 would have to successfully compete and be awarded a DSA through a competition to retain designation to a DSA for another agreement period. We also proposed that an OPO with tier 2 DSAs would also need to be found compliant with the requirements for certification at § 486.303, including the conditions for coverage at §§ 486.320 through 486.360 during the most recent survey to be eligible for re-certification. We proposed that an OPO that was compliant with the conditions for coverage at §§ 486.320 through 486.360 and had a
(
printed page 69412)
DSA assigned to tier 2 would be eligible to compete for any open DSAs. We also proposed that if the OPO was not successful in at least one competition, it would receive a notice of non-renewal. As finalized in this rule, § 486.311(a) clarifies that this notice of non-renewal is limited to the OPO's designation to the DSA and would not impact the OPO's agreement with CMS reflecting its status as a certified OPO (Form CMS 576A, Health Insurance Benefits Agreement). Because the OPO was re-certified, we proposed that it would remain eligible to compete in future competitions, be assigned a DSA, or be selected for an open DSA during the next re-certification cycle.
We proposed that an OPO with a DSA that was assigned to tier 3 would have the designation to the tier 3 DSA removed at the end of the agreement period. Additionally, we proposed that an OPO with all of its DSAs assigned to tier 3 would not be eligible to compete in competitions for any open DSAs. We proposed that an OPO that was designated to a DSA that was assigned to tier 3 in the final assessment period would receive one of two notices. The OPO would receive an initial notice of de-certification, as specified at § 486.314(a)(1), for an OPO that has no other designated DSA that is assigned to tier 1 or tier 2, or no other designated DSA that is pending evaluation of its outcome measures at the end of the re-certification cycle. The OPO would receive a notice of removal of designation to a tier 3 DSA without de-certification, as specified at § 486.314(a)(2), for an OPO that has another designated DSA assigned as tier 1 or tier 2, or another designated DSA that is pending evaluation of its outcome measures at the end of the re-certification cycle. We proposed that an OPO would have the right to appeal a de-certification or removal of designation to the DSA assigned as tier 3. If an OPO did not appeal the determination, or the OPO appeals and the determination is upheld after the appeal process is completed, the OPO's tier 3 DSA is opened for competition from other OPOs that qualify to compete for open service areas.
We also proposed updates to the re-certification and competition requirements. We proposed that an OPO would have to maintain compliance with the process performance measures at all times. We proposed that non-compliance with the requirements at §§ 486.320 through 486.360 in any DSA at any time during the re-certification cycle would result in the OPO receiving an initial de-certification determination and that the OPO would have the right to appeal the de-certification due to non-compliance with the requirements at §§ 486.320 through 486.360. If the OPO did not appeal the determination, or the OPO appeals and the determination was upheld after the appeal process was completed, the OPO's service areas would be opened to competition from other OPOs that were qualified to compete for open service areas.
We retained the existing policy that DSAs assigned as tier 2 or tier 3 in the final assessment period would be opened for competition, but proposed updated language to reflect that the tier assignment based on the outcome measures at § 486.318 would be specific to the DSA and not assigned globally to the OPO since OPOs may have more than one DSA. A tier 2 or tier 3 service area would be opened for competition from other OPOs that qualify to compete for open service areas. Competition for DSAs assigned to tier 3 would not begin until after any applicable appeal under § 486.314 had been exhausted.
We retained the existing criteria to compete for an open DSA, but proposed updated language to reflect that tier assignment for the outcome measures at § 486.318 would be specific to the DSA and not assigned globally to the OPO. To compete for an open DSA, an OPO would have to be designated to at least one DSA that meets the performance requirements for the outcome measures for tier 1 or tier 2, as specified at proposed § 486.318(b)(4) or (5), respectively. The OPO would also have to meet the requirements for certification at § 486.303 and would have to meet the process performance measures at §§ 486.320 through 486.360 during the most recent routine survey. Additionally, the OPO would have to compete for the entire open DSA. We proposed to revise these criteria to address competition eligibility for any OPO subject to non-renewal of their agreement for failure to be designated to a DSA after competition. We proposed that an OPO in this situation would be eligible to compete in additional competitions after its agreement expired and could enter into a new agreement with CMS, provided it had not been de-certified and met the criteria to compete at that time it entered the competition process that resulted in non-renewal. As explained in this final rule, we are clarifying that in this situation the OPO would enter into a new agreement with CMS reflecting its status as a certified OPO for the next re-certification cycle (Form CMS 576A, Health Insurance Benefits Agreement) but the OPO would no longer be designated to a DSA as identified on the Form CMS 576, Request for Designation as an OPO. This would enable the OPO to participate in subsequent competitions and enter into a new designation agreement with CMS if it was successful in a competition. If the OPO did not obtain a new DSA before the end of the next re-certification cycle, it would not be able to demonstrate compliance with the outcome measures for that re-certification cycle and would de-certified at that time.
Finally, we proposed a new requirement to facilitate DSA transitions. We proposed to codify the requirement for OPOs to cooperate during transitions following a competition to facilitate a smooth transition and continuity of organ donation activities in the DSA. We proposed that an incumbent OPO must cooperate with a successor OPO that is newly designated to facilitate an orderly transition of the DSA and submit a transition plan, as specified by CMS, that provides details on how all aspects of the OPO operation will be transmitted, including timeframes, to a new OPO. We proposed that the successor OPO must submit a transition plan and periodic reports, as specified by CMS, related to progress on its transition activities until the process is completed. We also proposed that the successor OPO would be required to provide a final notice to CMS no later than 30 calendar days after completion of the transition and prior to the end of the incumbent OPO's agreement.
We solicited public comment on these proposed changes to § 486.316. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Several commenters supported the proposal to assess an OPO with multiple DSAs separately on the outcome measures. A commenter stated that evaluating each DSA separately on outcome measures ensures that OPOs serving multiple areas are held accountable for performance in each geographic region. Another commenter stated the specific proposals related to re-certification and competition for OPOs serving more than one DSA are logical and consistent with policies already finalized. Another commenter suggested that labeling the performance of the DSA rather than the OPO as a whole may decrease disincentives for high-performing OPOs to consider competing to provide service in a DSA with an outgoing underperforming (tier 3) OPO. Commenters stated that not only is this approach fair to an OPO on its face, but it may also advance the goal of ensuring continued provision of procurement
(
printed page 69413)
services to communities with an outgoing underperforming (tier 3) OPO.
Response:
We thank commenters for these responses. Our intention for this proposal at § 486.316(a) was to support the provisions at § 486.309 that would enable an OPO to be designated to more than one DSA as well as mitigate the geographical consolidation of DSAs. We believe that evaluating DSAs separately on outcome measure performance, when an OPO decides to operate them separately, is a reasonable and equitable approach. This also supports OPOs in deciding how to best operate when expanding beyond their initial DSA.
Comment:
A commenter requested clarification on how CMS would evaluate outcome measures when an OPO is designated to multiple DSAs and elects to merge or maintain separate DSAs. The commenter stated that each DSA is evaluated independently, resulting in the unit of accountability effectively shifting from the organization as a whole to the DSA level.
Response:
We thank the commenter for seeking additional clarification on the evaluation framework.
