The framework of evaluating outcome measure performance at the DSA level enables CMS to evaluate an OPO both at the DSA level, carefully monitoring variations and enabling OPOs to conduct targeted performance improvement activities where they are most needed, while also retaining an overall evaluation and accountability structure that assesses compliance with the process measures at the organization level.
At § 486.316(b)(1), we address compliance with the process performance measures at §§ 486.320 through 486.360 and indicate that we will evaluate OPOs as a single entity across all DSAs. The process performance requirements are the broad operational requirements that are common across all DSAs and we expect compliance with these requirements at all times. Therefore, non-compliance with a process performance measure in one DSA would potentially impact an OPO's certification, affecting all DSAs if the OPO were to be de-certified. The OPO would have the opportunity to submit a corrective action plan to remedy the non-compliance and avoid de-certification, provided the plan of correction is acceptable in resolving the deficiency that resulted in the non-compliance determination.
At the time of re-certification, we will evaluate each DSA managed by an OPO separately on the outcome measures from the final assessment period as specified at § 486.316(a) to determine impact on DSA designation and subsequently make a re-certification decision based on the provisions at § 486.316(b)(2). Under this framework, an OPO that is designated to at least one DSA that is assigned to tier 1 in the final assessment period will be re-certified for another re-certification cycle, provided it is compliant with the process performance measures during the most recent survey as specified at § 486.316(b)(2)(i). Additionally, an OPO that is designated to at least one DSA that is assigned to tier 2 but is not designated to any DSA assigned to tier 1 in the final assessment period will be re-certified, provided it is compliant with the process performance measures during the most recent survey. The OPO will be eligible to compete in competitions for any open DSA but will not have its agreement for designation to a DSA renewed if it is not successful in at least one competition as specified at § 486.311(a)(1) or assigned a DSA under the provision at § 486.308(a)(4) or § 486.316(e) as specified at § 486.316(b)(2)(ii). Finally, OPOs with tier 3 DSAs in the final assessment period will have designation to those DSAs removed as specified at § 486.316(a)(3). We will consider the status of any other DSA in which the OPO is designated to make a re-certification decision as described at § 486.316(b)(2)(iii). If the OPO has no other DSA designated as tier 1 or tier 2, or no other DSA that is pending future evaluation of the outcome measures, as specified at § 486.318(c)(3) or (4), it will receive an initial notice of de-certification as specified at § 486.314(a)(1). If the OPO has another designated DSA assigned as tier 1 or tier 2, or another designated DSA that is pending evaluation of its outcome measures as specified at § 486.318(c)(3) or (4), it will be re-certified and receive a notice of removal of designation to a tier 3 DSA as specified at § 486.314(a)(2). This re-certification framework enables removing a DSA where an OPO is not meeting the outcome measure standards while maintaining the OPO's designation to DSAs where it has not been determined to be out of compliance on outcome measure standards.
Comment:
A commenter urged CMS to provide details regarding the timeline for when the competition process will begin for open DSAs.
Response:
Competition for tier 3 DSAs will occur once any administrative appeals have been exhausted. CMS will announce specific timelines and details for any competitions in advance of these events.
Comment:
Several commenters recommended revisions to the criteria for selection. Other commenters recommended that CMS establish more objective criteria for selecting a successor OPO in a competition. Many of the commenters recommended giving weight to OPOs with a record of sustained performance improvement trajectories. Other commenters stated that incumbent tier 2 OPOs should be given priority when competing for their own DSA over other competitors.
Response:
We thank commenters for these recommendations. We did not propose changes to the content of the existing selection criteria; therefore, we are not finalizing any changes at this time. However, we will consider these comments for potential changes to the selection criteria in future rulemaking. In the proposed rule we sought to clarify how we would apply the criteria under the tiered system for re-certification. Since implementing the 2020 final rule, OPOs have provided feedback expressing concern that CMS would rigidly apply the tiered structure in a competition and select a marginally better tier 1 OPO over a relatively high performing incumbent tier 2 OPO. They indicated that any benefit of selecting a higher performing OPO in this situation would be offset by the disruption from transitioning the DSA to another OPO. We indicated in the proposed rule that the selection criteria would not be applied rigidly when considering performance on the outcome measures and that we would consider the degree in performance differences among competitors and consider small differences to be relatively insignificant. Additionally, we do not believe that it is necessary to consider and weigh incumbency in a DSA independently of other factors because the current criteria will be sensitive to this issue when the performance difference between competing OPOs is relatively small. Additionally, in the proposed rule we discussed the issue of sustained improvements and how that would be considered when an OPO describes how it overcame barriers in its DSA.
Comment:
Several commenters provided recommendations for considering contiguity in a competition. Some commenters recommended that CMS give greater weight to contiguity while others stated it is a less important factor.
Response:
We continue to believe that contiguity is important, but it may not be the deciding factor in every situation. While contiguity may make the expansion of services easier from a logistics standpoint, it should not outweigh other considerations relevant
(
printed page 69414)
to decisions about the OPO who is most likely to achieve performance improvement and best serve a DSA. We are not revising the criteria at this time.
Comment:
Several commenters requested greater specificity for expectations on what should be submitted to address the selection criteria. A commenter stated that CMS should provide a clear, objective definition of “success overcoming barriers,” specify what data and documentation CMS expects, and ensure the criteria are applied consistently and in a reviewable manner.
Response:
In the proposed rule, we stated that the competition application process would provide an OPO the opportunity to describe the barriers it has faced and document its performance gains over time. The regulation at § 486.316(d)(4) states that we will consider an OPO's success in identifying and overcoming barriers to donation within its own service area and the relevance of those barriers to barriers in the open area. The regulation further states that an OPO competing for an open service area must submit information and data that describe the barriers in its service area, how they affected organ donation, what steps the OPO took to overcome the barriers, and the results. This information is important for competing OPOs in demonstrating a record of performance gains and a trajectory of improvement that could enable us to make the determination that the OPO is likely to continue improving, has the potential to achieve tier 1 status in the DSA in the near term, and should be designated to the DSA.
We realize that an OPO may face different challenges over different time periods as it works to address performance in its DSA. We believe that it is important for OPOs to use a data driven approach to identify areas for improvement, monitor changes over time, and document actual performance improvement. Additionally, we expect clear identification of the barriers and evidence of a plan to address those barriers. Qualitative information can augment quantitative results in describing improvements. Data may include data reported to the OPTN, CMS outcome measures, and/or other data and information that is part of the OPO's QAPI program. Some OPOs have suggested that they have their own data teams that independently calculate and stratify CMS outcome measures to analyze performance. We encourage other OPOs and the SRTR to consider this approach as well. The SRTR could include this type of information in their OPO Specific Reports (OSRs).
[
16
]
Comment:
Several commenters shared concerns related to the proposal for DSA transitions, highlighting a range of issues that they believe may materialize. Commenters stated that there would need to be close coordination and cooperation among the incumbent OPO, successor OPO, and CMS since the competition and transition periods would occur over a relatively short timeframe. Several commenters stated that the incumbent OPO may have difficulty maintaining staff and services throughout the duration of the transition. Other commenters highlighted non-profit status requirements and State requirements such as licensure that would need to be met. A commenter mentioned that the successor OPO needed sufficient time to establish agreements with donor hospitals. Another commenter questioned how the transition would occur with two OPOs operating simultaneously during the transition.
Response:
We acknowledge that the transition of a DSA to a successor OPO will be a significant undertaking, which is a reason we are codifying a requirement for OPOs to cooperate to facilitate a smooth transition and continuity of organ donation activities in the DSA. Additionally, we note the competition application procedures in the State Operations Manual Chapter 2 (CMS Pub 100-07) include many planning and transition elements to be included in the applicant's transition plan to support a stable transition of a DSA should the competitor be successful in a competition and eventually designated to the DSA. CMS worked closely with the OPOs involved in the recent transition of the Southern Florida DSA that was previously designated to the Life Alliance Organ Recovery Agency to monitor the process, assist in addressing any challenges, and ensure there was sufficient time to complete all requirements necessary to transition the designation to the successor OPO. Since only one OPO can be designated to a DSA, it is critical that all requirements be completed to transition the designation at the appropriate time. Therefore, the process must ensure that only one OPO is designated to a DSA at any given time with designation for the incumbent ending at the same time designation to the successor OPO begins. This activity also requires close coordination between CMS and HRSA to ensure a seamless transition in the information technology system that transmits information to support organ allocation activities.
Comment:
A commenter stated that CMS does not have the authority to force a de-certified or replaced OPO to bear the costs of transitioning to a new OPO, specifically, the transfer of proprietary information without providing adequate compensation to the incumbent OPO for these activities. The commenter interpreted the proposed rule as suggesting that OPOs would be forced to transfer “procedural manuals and other materials used in conducting OPO operations,” that could include proprietary operational data, internal quality improvement analyses, workflow optimizations, and institutional knowledge developed by the incumbent OPO over an extended period of time.
Response:
We thank the commenter for sharing this concern but disagree with their interpretation of the proposal. The requirement that was proposed at § 486.316(g) addresses transition of a DSA and requires that an incumbent OPO submit a transition plan that would provide details on how all aspects of the OPO operation will be transmitted, including timeframes, to a new OPO. This is separate from the existing information management requirement at § 486.330(d), most recently updated in our 2006 final rule, that OPOs must maintain data in a format that can readily be transferred to a successor OPO. Records and data subject to this requirement include donor and transplant beneficiary records and procedural manuals and other materials used in conducting OPO operations, but only to the extent necessary to ensure uninterrupted service by a successor OPO. An OPO should discuss any concerns it has regarding information sharing with CMS during a transition.
We expect the incoming OPO to have its own operations plan, including documentation and activities such as operational policies and procedures, QAPI data collection, and training programs, to serve the DSA in a way that improves performance, such that the type of information that the commenter characterizes as potentially proprietary would not be necessary to ensure uninterrupted service. Additionally, section 2812.4 of the SOM describes competition application materials to be submitted by an OPO competing for the DSA, including a transition plan that would address many of the operational aspects needed to transition the DSA. However, DSA-
(
printed page 69415)
specific information maintained by the incumbent and necessary to ensure uninterrupted service, such as donor and recipient data, must be maintained in a format that can readily be transferred to a successor OPO and provided to CMS in the event of a transfer, consistent with the longstanding requirement set forth in § 486.330(d). Given that an OPO is required under § 486.330(d) to maintain this information in a format that can readily be transferred to a successor OPO, we would not expect the OPO to incur significant costs related to the transfer of such information.
Final Rule Action:
We are finalizing the proposed changes to § 486.316 with a modification at § 486.316(a)(2) to address the impact of outcome measures to OPO designation when an OPO is assigned a new DSA by CMS. We are clarifying that when DSAs are assigned by CMS under the provisions at § 486.308(a)(4) or § 486.316(e) as discussed in section III.D., we will not open any tier 2 DSA managed by that OPO for competition until a full 4-year re-certification cycle is completed for the newly assigned DSA. We are also clarifying the language at § 486.316(b)(1) regarding the notice to the OPO. It is being revised from “initial de-certification determination” to an “initial notice of de-certification” as specified at § 486.314(a)(1). Additionally, we are revising § 486.316(c)(2) to clarify that a competition loss would result in non-renewal of the agreement for designation to a DSA.
I. Outcome Measures (§ 486.318)
We proposed to remove obsolete outcome measure provisions that expired on July 31, 2022. The requirements for the previous outcome measures that were superseded by the December 2020 final rule are located at § 486.318(a) through (c). These requirements are no longer in effect and have been superseded by new requirements at § 486.318(d) through (f). We proposed to remove the obsolete requirements at paragraphs (a) through (c) and to redesignate paragraphs (d) through (f) as paragraphs (a) through (c). We proposed a conforming change at the proposed redesignated paragraph (a)(1) (currently paragraph (d)(1)) by removing the reference to paragraph (d)(2) and replacing it with paragraph (a)(2). We proposed a conforming change at the proposed redesignated paragraph (b)(5) (currently paragraph (e)(5)) by removing the reference to paragraph (e)(4) and replacing it with paragraph (b)(4). We proposed a conforming change at the proposed redesignated paragraph (b)(7) (currently paragraph (e)(7)) by removing the reference to paragraphs (e)(4), (5), and (6) and replacing it with paragraphs (b)(4), (5), and (6).
We also proposed revisions to address OPOs managing multiple service areas, such as replacing “OPO” with “DSA” when referencing the outcome measures as applied to each DSA. We proposed tailored timelines for assuring OPO accountability in cases of adding new DSAs due to a change of control, ownership, or service area (CHOW), an expansion following a competition, or an expansion due to CMS assignment. Specifically, we proposed that if an OPO expands through the CHOW process after January 1 of the first year of the agreement cycle, the OPO would be held accountable for its QAPI responsibilities related to outcome measure performance in the new DSA once 12 calendar months of data are available. The timing of the CHOW in the re-certification cycle will impact whether the OPO is assessed for its performance on the outcome measures during the final assessment period for the current re-certification cycle or the subsequent re-certification cycle. For OPOs that acquire a new DSA through competition or CMS assignment after January 1 of the first year of the agreement cycle, we proposed that outcome measure accountability would apply: (1) for QAPI purposes, once 12 calendar months of data are available; and (2) for re-certification purposes, in the final assessment period of the following re-certification cycle. We proposed these changes based on the nature of the transaction and availability of data and information to support the change. For instance, a voluntary merger would provide a new OPO with the sharing of critical insights into the existing operations; access to proprietary data sets and internal analyses; enable pre-formed relationships and contacts; leverage established financial, personnel, and physical resources; and include other intangible elements that smooth a transition. This greatly impacts an OPO's preplanning activities and readiness to assume responsibility for a new DSA. An OPO that has won a competition or has been assigned an open DSA when no OPO competes for it must begin with significantly limited information and resources. OPOs in these situations could have large information gaps coupled with potentially significant expansion demands. Therefore, we believe that an OPO that assumes responsibility for a new DSA after a competition or has been assigned a DSA by CMS should have an additional amount of time to demonstrate improvement before being held accountable on its performance for re-recertification purposes.
We solicited public comment on these proposed changes to § 486.318. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Several commenters recommended that timeframe for accountability on the outcome measures for a new DSA acquired through a change of control or ownership or service areas, competition, or assignment by CMS should be the same. A commenter stated the proposal makes an arbitrary distinction between merger and competition. A commenter stated that the proposal puts OPOs that participate in mergers at a disadvantage due to the shorter timeframe for assessment on the outcome measures and risks related to a successor OPO taking over a DSA. Other commenters stated that impactful changes may take longer than 12 months with one commenter stating that operational integration in healthcare mergers typically unfold over a multi-year horizon due to the complexities involved. These commenters indicated that the timeframe for organizational stability as well as performance improvement is years. A commenter stated that last-minute changes will be more challenging even with good faith efforts and will take longer time frames.
Response:
We understand the concerns of commenters and our proposed approach that we will be finalizing balances providing an appropriate level of time for improvement with the statutory requirements for performance accountability. We do believe there is a difference in challenges faced between a change of control or ownership or service area (§ 486.310), being awarded a DSA in a competition (§ 486.316(d)), or being assigned a DSA by CMS (§ 486.308(a)(4) or § 486.316(e)) and that we have provided the appropriate amount of time under each circumstance. We note that a change of control or ownership or service area that happens prior to the start of the final assessment period would be accountable for the outcome measures in the same re-certification period. Any changes after the start of the final assessment period would not have outcomes data available at the time of re-certification so the OPO would not be assessed for compliance on the outcome measures in the new DSA for re-certification purposes until the final assessment period of the next re-certification cycle. We believe the prior
(
printed page 69416)
planning that is afforded to OPOs in a change of control or ownership or service area warrants accountability on the outcome measures at that time when that data is available at the time of re-certification. Therefore, we will be finalizing this provision as proposed.
Comment:
Several commenters were supportive of the changes related to accountability for the outcome measures when an OPO is designated to a new DSA. A commenter stated the different scenarios described in the proposed rule appropriately account for transition periods and the time needed for a new OPO to implement its operational approach in an acquired DSA. A commenter stated that they support revising the requirement for when CMS will hold an OPO accountable on the outcome measures when it takes over another OPO's DSA. Another commenter stated the timeframe for an OPO assuming responsibility of a DSA after a competition is appropriate.
Response:
We thank commenters for support of this approach for tailoring accountability to the nature of the transaction, the availability of outcomes data, and the challenges anticipated with the different reasons for designation of a new DSA.
Comment:
Several commenters requested clarity on how this provision would be implemented. A commenter stated CMS should specify which data period applies before performance accountability takes effect and how performance will be measured during transitional phases. Another commenter stated that CMS should clarify how it will measure performance for OPOs that assume responsibility for new DSAs following de-certification or reassignment, particularly given that the current outcome measures rely on data with a 1-to 2-year data lag.
Response:
We appreciate the opportunity to provide clarity on this provision. We will provide the 2026 through 2030 re-certification period as an example. In the event of a change of control or ownership or service area (§ 486.310) that occurs prior to the start of the final assessment period in 2028, meaning prior to January 1, 2028, the OPO would be held accountable on the outcome measures in the new area at the time of re-certification in 2030. If the change was approved after the start of the final assessment period, outcome data would not be available so the OPO would be held accountable on the outcome measures for re-certification purposes for the first time in the new area in 2034 with outcome measures from 2032 (see § 486.318(c)(3)). Alternatively, an OPO that is designated to a DSA by assignment (§ 486.308(a)(4) or § 486.316(e)) or as the result of a competition (§ 486.316(d)) at any point during the 2026 through 2030 re-certification period, would be held accountable on the outcome measures in the new DSA for re-certification purposes for the first time in the new area with outcome measures from the final assessment period (2032) of next re-certification cycle (2030 through 2034). In each instance, the OPO would be surveyed at the time of re-certification in 2030 and must be in compliance with all process measures passing the survey at that time to be recertified. Additionally, an OPO that is designated to a DSA by assignment (§ 486.308(a)(4) or § 486.316(e)) would not have its original or new DSA opened for competition at the end of the re-certification cycle (for example, 2030) if the OPO's performance in those DSAs qualifies for tier 2 in the final assessment period.
Final Rule Action:
We are finalizing the changes to § 486.318 as proposed.
J. Human Resources (§ 486.326)
We proposed to revise the medical director requirement to specify that an OPO's medical director would be required to be a physician licensed in at least one of the States or territories within one of the OPO's service areas or as required by State or territory law or by the jurisdiction in which the OPO is located. This proposed change was intended to accommodate the proposal that an OPO may be designated to more than one DSA while still having a single medical director. We also proposed revising personnel qualifications for other OPO staff that engage in clinical practice, whether they are in explicitly clinical positions or other positions in which clinical decision making or actions are expected. We proposed to require that personnel performing clinical duties be legally authorized (licensed, certified, or registered) in accordance with applicable Federal, State and local laws. Furthermore, we proposed that these staff would be required to act only within the scope of the individual's State license, certification, or registration. Finally, we proposed that the individual's licensure, certification, or registration be required to be kept current at all times. While OPOs are already required by § 486.326 to ensure that all individuals who provide services and/or supervise services, including services furnished under contract or arrangement, are qualified to provide or supervise those services, we proposed these changes due to the expertise required to fulfill the broad responsibilities and functions of OPOs. These responsibilities span a range of activities from educating donor hospitals to conducting internal QAPI activities to implementing donor management protocols. We proposed licensure requirements to establish minimum qualifications to assure quality and to facilitate more organ transplants.
We solicited public comment on these proposed changes in § 486.326. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
CMS received a small number of comments related to the changes to the medical director requirement. Commenters requested more flexibility so that OPOs could have more than one medical director or be able to fulfill this role through flexible staffing models with multiple staff filling this position at various times.
Response:
For purposes of clear and direct accountability, we require a single individual to fulfill the role of medical director and be responsible for the overall medical direction of the OPO's operations. Currently, the medical director must be licensed as a physician in at least one of the States or territories within the OPO's service area or as required by State or territory law or by the jurisdiction in which the OPO is located. Many OPOs currently have multi-state DSAs and have been operating under this requirement since it was implemented in the 2006 final rule (
71 FR 30982
). We continue to believe that a single person should be accountable for overall medical direction of an OPO's activities. Our proposed change to this provision is limited to a conforming change to reflect that an OPO may be designated to more than one DSA. Therefore, we are finalizing this requirement as proposed.
Comment:
Many commenters raised concerns about the practical implications of requiring personnel performing clinical duties to be legally authorized (licensed, certified or registered) in accordance with applicable Federal, State and local laws, and to act only within the scope of the individual's State license, or State certification, or registration. Commenters indicated that the organ procurement and transplantation workforce operates in a unique, specialized, and complex clinical environment and that much of the work performed by OPO staff does not require medical licensure because it is not medical treatment. Commenters stated that licensure frameworks are focused on treatment of living patients and that State and local laws and regulations do not contemplate licensure of professionals engaged in deceased donor management and organ recovery.
(
printed page 69417)
Commenters highlighted that State licensure laws, including nurse and physician practice acts, are written to govern the care of living patients and do not define or contemplate the management of a legally deceased individual and drew the distinction that supporting clinical teams in donor management is operationally distinct from direct patient care. Additionally, commenters stated that there are many clinical roles in the OPO industry for which there is not a role-specific licensure, certification, or registration. Some commenters noted that nurses and paramedics, disciplines for which State licensure exists, often coordinate donations or transplants and that these non-clinical coordination tasks do not require the same licenses as working with living patients. A commenter stated that strict reliance on State licensure standards would ignore the specialized, multidisciplinary scope of practice inherent to organ procurement and another stated that if CMS were to implement this proposal, rigid application of State-specific licensure for every staff role would be problematic because no State-specific licensure requirement exists for every OPO staff role. Some commenters noted that organ recovery procedures are often completed by surgeons that received training in other countries and are not currently board-certified in the United States and by non-physician practitioners that are not typically licensed to perform surgical procedures on living patients. Commenters stated the proposal could create significant operational and compliance challenges for OPOs that would negatively impact the OPO workforce and donation activities. The commenters stated that requiring licensure of these procurement staff would be incredibly challenging, if not impossible, and suggested that such a requirement would negatively impact OPO ability to maintain the current level of donor cases by strictly relying only on fellows or transplant surgeons in an OPO's service area. Commenters stated the proposal could create significant operational and compliance challenges for OPOs that would negatively impact the OPO workforce and donation activities. In place of licensure requirements, some commenters focused on OPO onboarding and training processes and stated that CMS requirements for OPO staff should focus on training and demonstration of specific skills.
Response:
We thank commenters for articulating the unique concerns and needs of the OPO workforce. While it was not our intent to require licensure for individuals that only perform non-clinical work, such as coordination logistics and obtaining consent for donation, we understand that the roles may be mixed and blurred within OPO operations such that operationalizing our original intent may create staffing difficulties that ultimately undermine organ donation and transplantation, contrary to our policy goals. We are committed to establishing CfC requirements to assure the safety of patients who may become donors and organ recipients. We continue to believe that there is an opportunity to better ensure such safety through the establishment of more robust personnel qualifications and training standards. We will work with HRSA, the OPTN, and our OPO partners to explore ways to drive improvements in OPO staffing that support safe organ procurement and more lifesaving transplants. Upon consideration of the public comments received, we are not finalizing the proposed requirement at § 486.326(e) for licensure at this time and will consider the information shared in any future rulemaking in this area.
Comment:
While a commenter stated that the educational infrastructure to support a national credentialling requirement does not exist because there's only a single specialized transplantation and donation sciences training program serving the entire country, several other commenters stated that CMS should recognize national credentialing through the American Board for Transplant Certification (ABTC) as nationally recognized standards for training and competency. The commenters stated certifications for transplant procurement coordinators and transplant preservationists represent nationally recognized training and competency standards for personnel involved in organ donation coordination and recovery operations. The comment noted that there are currently 1,175 Certified Procurement Transplant Coordinators working directly in OPO environments across 48 OPOs. Another commenter stated that it is developing specific standards related to organ recovery for clinical personnel who procure organs and is advocating for a certification program for organ recovery staff.
Response:
We thank commenters for this information. We note the certifications referenced by commenters assist in addressing the multidisciplinary roles fulfilled by OPO staff. While we are not finalizing the proposed licensure requirements at § 486.326(e) at this time, we encourage OPOs to apply existing standards for training and competency, as well as existing certification programs, to their hiring standards to support improvements in safety and performance.
Final Rule Action:
After considering public comments, we are finalizing the medical director requirement at § 486.326(d) as proposed. However, we are not finalizing the proposed licensure requirement at § 486.326(e) at this time. We may consider comments from the licensure proposal in future rulemaking.
K. Information Management (§ 486.330)
To assure the accuracy of data reported to the OPTN and the integrity of the CMS donation rate outcome measure that uses data reported by OPOs regarding pancreata procured for islet cell research, we proposed to establish a new documentation requirement specific to organs procured by OPOs for research, including pancreata procured for islet cell research. We proposed that OPOs would maintain records regarding the disposition of organs recovered and sent for
bona fide
research studies, including information identifying approval by an institutional review board (IRB) or other formal authorizing body, as appropriate, research institution, principal investigator, and contact information. This recordkeeping would foster OPO accountability in the responsible disposition of any organ sent for research, including pancreata that are used for islet cell research, and be consistent with existing OPO practices for maintaining records regarding the disposition of transplanted organs. CMS would use the survey process to review OPO organ disposition records and may conduct validation efforts to confirm their accuracy. We solicited public comment on these proposed changes to § 486.330. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Several comments requested CMS to define “qualified researcher” and “bona fide research”. Another commenter recommended that CMS clarify that OPOs can base documentation on the principal investigator's home institution Institutional Review Board review and indicate that a separately arranged review is not necessary.
Response:
We appreciate the commenters' requests for additional clarity related to these terms and the associated documentation requirements. In the 2020 final rule, we clarified that in counting pancreatic islet cell research for inclusion in the outcome measures, only bona fide research conducted by a
(
printed page 69418)
qualified researcher would be included (
85 FR 77937
). In memorandum QSO-24-19-OPO,
[
17
]
published August 29, 2024, addressing the reporting of data related to pancreata procured for research, we noted that research approved by the National Institutes of Health would be one example of bona fide research conducted by a qualified researcher. We have not specifically defined “qualified researcher” or “bona fide research.” We are relying on OPOs to provide organs for research to qualified researchers for bona fide research based on accepted industry standards and practices. This may involve placement directly to a researcher, institution, or to an intermediary that facilitates placement of the organs. Records related to organ disposition must provide sufficient information to validate disposition of the organ as it is coded in the OPTN data set. The records to be maintained include, but are not limited to, information documenting approval from an IRB or other formal authorizing body, as appropriate, research institution, principal investigator, and study contacts for the research. These records may be utilized if validation of the information is required at a later time.
Comment:
A commenter recommended additional clarification on the types of documentation or information that could be used for record keeping purposes. The commenters recommended items such as researcher credentials, statements of research purpose with a description of how the organ would be used, material transfer agreements, and attestation forms. The researcher also suggested that CMS require OPO governing boards to periodically review research programs documentation against regulatory requirements and formally approve participation in research activities, specifically referring to pancreas research activities.
Response:
We appreciate this comment and recommendations. We believe the current record keeping requirements are written broadly enough to capture the information recommended by the commenter; however, we encourage OPOs to record all available and necessary information to validate final disposition of organs sent for research. We also realize that in some instances there may be limited information provided to the OPO. L. Quality Assessment and Performance Improvement (QAPI) (§ 486.348)
We proposed revisions to the existing QAPI standards to revise and clarify the requirements for tracking adverse events and establish new requirements for monitoring medically complex organ performance.
We proposed to relocate the adverse event examples included in the current definition of “adverse event” to the QAPI requirements and expand the list from three to six categories, including: transmission of infectious or communicable diseases or malignancies; avoidable loss of medically suitable potential donors; deviations from standards of practice in evaluation and management; delivery of a wrong organ or blood type mismatch; organs lost or delayed in transit; and organs arriving in unsuitable condition. For greater specificity and to avoid confusion, we proposed to replace “the wrong organ” with “an organ that was not for the intended organ recipient”. We also proposed to remove the two references to “beneficiary” that currently appear in the examples in the “adverse event” definition. All OPOs must comply with the OPO CfCs, which apply to all patients regardless of payor source. Hence, the term “beneficiary” in the OPO CfCs is not appropriate. We proposed to remove the two references to “beneficiary” and instead use “organ recipient”.
To further the goal of improving procurement and transplantation of medically complex organs, we proposed to require each OPO, as part of its QAPI program, to: (1) assess its policies and procedures regarding medically complex donors and organs to ensure that opportunities for recovery and placement are being optimized; (2) assess its performance by tracking, at least annually, the number of medically complex donors from whom consent was obtained, organs recovered, and medically complex organs transplanted; and (3) implement improvement actions when opportunities are identified.

M. Proposed Conforming Changes to § 486.322 Relationships With Hospitals, Critical Access Hospitals, and Tissue Banks; § 486.324 Administration and Governing Body; and § 486.360 Emergency Preparedness
The previous OPO CfCs were developed based on the assumption that each OPO would only be responsible for a single DSA at any time. While section 1138(b)(2) of the Act requires that only one OPO may be designated to a DSA, it does not prohibit one OPO from being designated to multiple DSAs at one time. OPOs have expressed interest in a single OPO being designated to multiple DSAs. We proposed conforming changes to address provisions in the CfCs related to the number of DSAs an OPO may be responsible for. Specifically, we proposed to require OPOs to have written agreements with 95 percent of Medicare and Medicaid participating hospitals and CAHs with both a ventilator and an operating room in each of their designated DSA. We proposed replacing “area” with “area(s)” in several provisions. Additionally, we proposed that data used for OPO re-certification must include data for all deaths in all hospitals and CAHs across all DSA(s), unless a waiver has been granted. Finally, we proposed to revise the emergency preparedness requirements for OPOs. We proposed that OPOs are required to have an emergency communication plan with the names and contact information for transplant and donor hospitals in each of the OPO's DSA(s), and to replace “DSA” with “DSA(s)”. We did not receive comments opposing these conforming changes.

IV. Comment Solicitation and Discussion on Emerging Issues
A. Conflicts of Interest
We solicited public comment on how OPOs address conflicts of interest, the adequacy of current regulatory requirements, and potential modifications to the OPO CfCs to assure consistent development and implementation of conflicts of interest policies that protect health and safety and the integrity of the organ donation system. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comments:
Several commenters expressed support for strong, transparent conflict of interest (COI) policies for OPOs, emphasizing their importance in maintaining public trust in the organ donation and transplantation system. While some commenters stated that current CMS requirements were sufficient, many welcomed clearer Federal guidance to ensure consistency across all OPOs. Other commenters raised concerns regarding the creation of additional requirements, noting that OPOs already operate under established nonprofit governance standards, including IRS requirements and existing conflict-of-interest policies. These commenters stated that new requirements could be duplicative and impose unnecessary administrative burden and recommended that any new requirements be evidence-based and aligned with broader healthcare governance practices.
A few commenters disagreed with the suggestion that tissue recovery activities conflict with OPO and organ donation operations. They stated that organ donation and tissue donation are not competing activities and that many OPOs maintain separate organ and tissue service lines with distinct budgets, staffing structures, and operational processes, which function as internal safeguards against potential conflicts of interest.
Some commenters recommended that CMS require OPOs to have formal, written COI policies that mandate disclosure of secondary employment and require routine disclosure and documentation of conflicts and their resolutions. These commenters also encouraged CMS to collaborate with HRSA and the OPTN to avoid duplicative or overlapping regulatory requirements.
Response:
We thank commenters for their feedback. We note that the comments we received may be taken into consideration for potential future rulemaking.
B. Allocation Out of Sequence (AOOS)
We provided an overview of Federal organ allocation requirements to address recent concerns related to an increase in organ AOOS, which reflects a deviation from allocation policy and may only occur if necessary to prevent organ wastage due to discard. We clarified expectations for regulatory and policy compliance necessary for maintaining public trust. The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Several commenters agreed that inappropriate organ allocation out of sequence practices undermines fairness, accountability, and public trust in the transplant system. However, several commenters emphasized that AOOS reflects broader systemic challenges within the organ allocation system rather than solely OPO conduct. These commenters stated that outdated allocation technology, prolonged sequential allocation processes, and variability in transplant center organ acceptance practices all contribute significantly to AOOS and organ non-use. A commenter stated that the current allocation system cannot dynamically adjust as donor information changes and does not include transplant center acceptance behavior into allocation decisions.
While commenters acknowledged that there may be reasons for non-sequential placement, including clinical urgency, logistical constraints, or organ viability concerns, commenters stated that insufficient documentation or explanation of such deviations creates the perception that allocation decisions may occur outside established policy. They recommended stronger oversight and auditing of AOOS decisions, clear documentation requirements for deviations from standard allocation order, and increased transparency regarding expedited placement practices to preserve public confidence in the transplant system.
Several commenters raised concerns that AOOS may unintentionally disadvantage certain patient populations, including pediatric candidates, minority communities, medically complex recipients, and underserved populations. A commenter stated that multi-organ allocation and AOOS practices may divert suitable organs away from pediatric candidates or delay pediatric access to transplantation. Other commenters expressed concern that existing allocation and performance frameworks do not adequately account for disparities affecting minority populations or patients requiring medically complex transplants. Commenters recommended that CMS monitor allocation practices for unintended equity impacts, evaluate pediatric utilization separately, consider health equity impacts in oversight activities, and ensure that medically
(
printed page 69421)
complex organs are not disproportionately rejected or diverted in ways that worsen existing disparities in access to transplantation.
Some commenters stated that transplant center acceptance practices significantly contribute to AOOS and organ non-use. These commenters noted that transplant centers vary substantially in their willingness to accept medically complex organs and stated that current transplant program oversight and outcomes requirements create disincentives for transplant centers to accept higher-risk organs. They suggested that CMS work with transplant system interested parties to develop policies that (1) increase transparency regarding transplant center organ acceptance patterns, including accepting multiple offers for the same candidate and data on declines after acceptance; (2) encourage adoption of best practices for organ utilization; and (3) reduce unnecessary organ declines.
Several commenters emphasized the importance of coordination among CMS, HRSA, and the OPTN regarding AOOS and expedited placement policies. Commenters expressed concern that differing definitions and regulatory expectations related to medically complex organs, expedited placement, and AOOS may create confusion for OPOs and transplant centers. A few commenters suggested that CMS align its terminology and oversight expectations with OPTN policies related to expedited placement and allocation out of sequence practices.
Response:
We thank commenters for sharing this information and recommendations. We believe the existing CMS regulatory requirements under §§ 486.324(b)(6) and 486.344 support an OPO's responsibilities for allocating organs in accordance with the rules and requirements of the OPTN. Section 486.324(b)(6) of the OPO CfCs enables the OPO advisory board to recommend policies for a system to allocate organs among transplant patients that is consistent with the rules and requirements of the OPTN. In addition, § 486.344 requires that each OPO have a system to allocate donated organs among transplant patients that is consistent with the rules and requirements of the OPTN, and that each OPO maintain written documentation from the OPTN showing the intended organ beneficiary's ranking in relation to other suitable candidates if the intended beneficiary has been identified prior to recovery of an organ for transplantation. Consistent with these requirements, HHS regulations governing the operation of the OPTN also require that organ offers are made to transplant patients—rather than to transplant centers—in a manner that is consistent with OPTN policies.

OPOs that become aware of potential noncompliance with OPTN policy—including by themselves—are obligated to report such instances to the OPTN. To support OPO and transplant program compliance, the OPTN has developed an Allocation Out of Sequence resource page

C. Automated Electronic Referrals
We solicited public comment on how to leverage technology to support automated electronic referrals and ensure appropriate privacy and security protections for the information.
The following is a summary of the comments we received and our responses.
Comment:
Commenters were generally supportive of requiring automated electronic referrals from donor hospitals to OPOs. Commenters noted that an automated referral process would streamline hospital workflows, reduce reliance on manual phone-based referrals, lower the risk of missed or delayed referrals, and provide OPOs with more accurate and timely clinical information. A commenter noted, however, that automated referrals should supplement rather than replace direct communication between hospital staff and OPO personnel, as clinical discussions and coordination between providers and OPO staff remain essential throughout the donation process. A few commenters expressed concerns about privacy and data security protections for both potential and actual organ donors and recommended that OPOs be required to comply with the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA).
Several commenters also recommended leveraging platform-independent standards, such as Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR®), to integrate automated referral systems across diverse software environments. FHIR is a widely used health information technology standard that enables different healthcare systems and software platforms to securely share and exchange patient data in a consistent format. By adopting FHIR-based standards, automated referral systems can be integrated across a wide range of software environments, reducing dependence on any single vendor and supporting ongoing innovation. Commenters noted that most electronic health record (EHR) systems currently include functionality to initiate actions based on defined clinical triggers. However, these triggers must typically be configured individually by each hospital, as no universal standard currently exists. Commenters encouraged the standardization of these clinical triggers and their consistent implementation across all healthcare organizations, noting that establishing a national standard would significantly streamline the deployment and scalability of automated referral systems.
Commenters also raised concerns about the operational and financial challenges associated with implementation, particularly for rural and under-resourced hospitals with limited information technology (IT) infrastructure, fragmented EHR systems, staffing limitations, or insufficient technical resources. Commenters recommended that CMS establish cost-sharing or incentive frameworks such as pilot grants or partnerships with health IT vendors to help offset implementation and maintenance costs.

V. Collection of Information Requirements
Under the Paperwork Reduction Act of 1995, agencies are required to obtain approval from the Office of Management and Budget (OMB) before conducting or sponsoring a collection of information. A “collection of information” includes agency requests or requirements that members of the public submit reports, keep records, or provide information to a third party. This final rule contains information collection requirements associated with the information management requirements at § 486.330.
In the proposed rule, we provided a 60-day notice and solicited public comment on these information collection requirements, including the need for the information collection, the accuracy of our burden estimates, the quality, utility, and clarity of the information to be collected, and ways to minimize the information collection burden on affected entities. We considered the public comments received in developing this final rule. Commenters generally requested additional clarity regarding the meaning of “bona fide” research and “qualified researcher” under the information management requirements, and noted that much deceased donor research is bench research that may not require approval by an institutional review board. Commenters also raised concerns that expanded QAPI requirements could increase documentation burden, particularly with respect to medically complex donors and organs.
After consideration of public comments, we are finalizing the information management requirements at § 486.330 as proposed. In response to public comments raising concerns about the lack of a standardized and nationally recognized definition of medical complexity, we are not finalizing the proposed definitions of “medically complex donor” and “medically complex organ” at § 486.302, and we are not finalizing the QAPI requirement proposed at § 486.348(e). Accordingly, this final rule does not include the information collection burden associated with QAPI activities for medically complex donors and organs (IC-2) that was included in the proposed rule.
In analyzing the burden for these information collection requirements, we rely on wage and salary information. Unless otherwise indicated, we obtained salary information from the May 2025 National Occupational Employment and Wage Estimates, United States, from the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). Based on this information, we calculated estimated adjusted hourly rates based on the national mean salary for each position increased by 100 percent to account for overhead costs and fringe benefits. The raw wage and salary data from BLS do not include health, retirement, and other fringe benefits, or the rent, utilities, information technology, administrative, and other overhead costs supporting each employee. HHS department-wide guidance on preparation of regulatory and paperwork burden estimates states that doubling salary costs is a good approximation for these overhead and fringe benefit costs.
Table 1 presents the BLS occupation code and title, the associated OPO staff position in this final rule, the estimated average hourly wage, and the adjusted hourly wage, with a 100 percent markup for fringe benefits and overhead. In addition, throughout this analysis, any amount ending with 0.50 or more is rounded up to the next nearest dollar amount, and any amount ending with 0.49 or less is rounded down to the next nearest dollar amount.
A. ICRs Regarding Information Management (§ 486.330)
This final rule establishes new information management requirements for OPOs at § 486.330. These requirements establish documentation requirements specific to organs procured by OPOs and sent for research, including pancreata procured and sent for islet cell research. To meet this requirement, OPOs must maintain records regarding the disposition of organs sent for research studies, including information identifying approval by an institutional review board (IRB) or other formal authorizing body, as appropriate, the research institution, the principal investigator, and study contact information.
Estimating the number of organs procured by OPOs per research study is complex because estimates vary depending on the study's design, objectives, and resources, as well as the type of organ utilized. To estimate the burden for pancreata procured and sent for islet cell research, hereinafter referred to as IC-1(a), we use program data from the research institute City of
(
printed page 69423)
Hope. According to their research data, 15 OPOs participate in their research, with each OPO submitting on average 110 pancreata per year. We use this data to estimate that, on average there are a total of 1,650 pancreata submitted for islet cell research per year (110 pancreata × 15 OPOs).
Furthermore, according to CMS correspondence with a participating OPO, this OPO submitted a total of 783 pancreata to three different studies from 2021 through 2024, with an annual average of 196 pancreata submitted to 3 principal investigators. To comply with this requirement, this OPO would need to document 196 pancreata with the associated research study information. We assume an OPO's organ procurement coordinator, at an adjusted hourly wage of $98 per hour, will be responsible for this activity and will take 5 minutes, or 0.083 hours, to map each pancreas with its corresponding research study information.
The total annual burden for the 15 participating OPOs is estimated at 244 hours per year (0.083 hours × 196 responses × 15 OPOs). The total annual cost is $23,912 (244 hours × $98 per hour). This is approximately 16 hours per participating OPO (244 hours ÷ 15 participating OPOs), at a cost of $1,568 per participating OPO (16 hours × $98). When distributed across all 54 OPOs for purposes of presenting an average burden across the industry, the annualized burden for IC-1(a) is approximately 5 hours per OPO (244 hours ÷ 54 OPOs), at a cost of approximately $443 per OPO ($23,912 ÷ 54 OPOs).
Estimating the burden for other organs that are procured and used for research, such as kidneys, hearts, lungs, livers, intestines, and pancreata used for research other than islet cell research, hereinafter referred to as IC-1(b), is more difficult because we do not have reliable data on which to base these estimates. In the absence of data, we illustrate the upper bound of possible burden. We assume one organ is procured and used for one research study.
According to data maintained by the Organ Procurement and Transplantation Network (OPTN), as of June 4, 2025, there was an annual average of 5,631 organs submitted annually for research between 2022 and 2024. Additionally, recent research by the National Academies indicates that between 2013 and 2015, there was an annual average of 4,903 organs recovered and used for research programs. As we anticipate the number of pancreata used for islet cell research to return to historic levels, we assume the average number of all organs procured for research to be 5,267 per year, ((4,903 organs + 5,631 organs) ÷ 2).
Assuming an average of 5,267 organs per year, we anticipate that OPOs will submit a total of 5,267 responses per year. For IC-1(b), this results in annual burden of 437 hours (5,267 responses × 0.083). Distributed across 54 OPOs, this is approximately 8 hours per OPO (437 hours ÷ 54 OPOs). We assume the responses will be completed by an OPO's organ procurement coordinator, at an adjusted hourly wage of $98 per hour. This results in an annual burden cost of $42,826 (437 hours × $98), or approximately $793 per OPO ($42,826 ÷ 54 OPOs).
The annual burden for IC-1, including IC-1(a) and IC-1(b), is estimated at 681 burden hours (244 hours + 437 hours), at an estimated annual cost of $66,738 ($23,912 + $42,826). Distributed across all 54 OPOs, this is approximately 13 hours per OPO (681 hours ÷ 54 OPOs), at a cost of approximately $1,236 per OPO ($66,738 ÷ 54 OPOs).
The information collection request under OMB control number 0938-0688 will be revised and submitted to OMB for approval.

The annualized burden for all information collections finalized in this rule, including IC-1(a), IC-1(b) for all 54 OPOs would be approximately 681 burden hours at an estimated annual cost of $66,738. Comment:
Several commenters requested additional clarity regarding the meaning of “bona fide” research and “qualified researcher” under the information management requirements and noted that much deceased donor research is bench research that may not require approval by an institutional review board. Several commenters also expressed concern that expanded QAPI requirements, including requirements related to medically complex donors and organs, could increase documentation burden and divert resources from clinical operations.
Response:
We considered these comments in developing this final rule. We are finalizing the information management requirements at § 486.330 as proposed. The final rule requires an OPO to maintain records showing the disposition of each organ recovered and sent for research, including, but not limited to, information documenting approval from an IRB or other formal authorizing body, as appropriate. We recognize that IRB approval may not be
(
printed page 69424)
required for certain types of research, including some bench research involving deceased donor organs. As set forth in § 486.330(b)(2)(i), an OPO is only required to maintain information documenting approval from an IRB or other formal authorizing body “as appropriate.” Where approval from an IRB or other formal authorizing body is not required, the OPO is not required to maintain documentation of such approval. In those circumstances, the OPO is still required to maintain records showing the disposition of the organ as reported as described in § 486.330(b)(2), including the research institution, principal investigator, and study contacts. In response to comments raising concerns about the lack of a standardized definition of medical complexity for medically complex donors and organs, we are not finalizing the proposed definitions of “medically complex donor” and “medically complex organ,” and we are not finalizing the related QAPI requirement proposed at § 486.348(e).
VII. Regulatory Impact Analysis
A. Statement of Need
More than 100,000 people are currently waiting for an organ transplant and demand for organs continues to exceed supply.
[
32
]
OPOs play a critical role in ensuring that as many organs as possible reach patients who need them. In 2019, President Trump issued
Executive Order 13879
“Advancing American Kidney Health,” directing the Secretary to enhance the procurement and utilization of organs available through deceased donation and to establish more transparent, reliable, and enforceable metrics for evaluating an OPO's performance. In response, CMS published the December 2020 OPO final rule, which, among other changes, established new performance measures and a three-tier ranking system for OPOs. The December 2020 OPO final rule created a baseline implementation framework with annual costs of $126.7 million.
Since the December 2020 OPO final rule was published, CMS has received many questions from OPOs and other interested parties seeking clarification about how the new system works, particularly as the system approaches the end of the 2022-2026 re-certification cycle. This final rule clarifies procedures for competitions, designation to multiple DSAs, non-renewal and de-certification, appeals, outcome-measure accountability, information management, QAPI, and other operational details. The final rule also reflects changes made in response to public comments, including not finalizing the proposed definitions of “medically complex donor” and “medically complex organ” and the related QAPI requirement at § 486.348(e), modifying the designation framework for certain CMS-assigned DSAs, and not finalizing the proposed licensure requirement for personnel performing clinical duties.
We estimate that this final rule will cost approximately $16.4 million in the first year and $7.9 million annually thereafter. These costs are incremental to the broader framework established in the December 2020 OPO final rule and reflect targeted operational and administrative refinements rather than fundamental system restructuring. We also estimate that this final rule will result in approximately $583,000 in annual benefits due to reduced implementation inquiry and compliance-interpretation burden, as well as a one-time benefit of $500,000 due to increased operational flexibility for OPOs designated to multiple DSAs.

This final rule builds on the December 2020 OPO final rule, which established new OPO performance measures and re-certification processes for the 2022 through 2026 certification period and future re-certification cycles. The December 2020 OPO final rule created baseline implementation costs of $126.7 million annually, comprising: (1) CMS administrative costs of $1.0 million annually for oversight, technical assistance, appeals processing, and additional FTE to support system implementation; (2) OPO management transition costs of $2.9 million annually for incumbent OPOs transitioning to new performance standards and administrative and operational adjustments; and (3) OPO operational costs of $122.8 million annually associated with procurement of additional organs and enhanced performance activities under new outcome measures.
As outlined in Table 3, this final rule would cost an estimated $16.4 million in Year 1 and $7.9 million in recurring annual costs. Year 1 costs include approximately $15.11 million for OPOs and $1.37 million for CMS. Recurring annual costs include approximately $7.56 million for OPOs and $340,000 for CMS. These incremental costs reflect clarifications and refinements to operational and administrative requirements from the December 2020 OPO final rule rather than fundamental system restructuring. The final rule costs differ from the proposed rule estimates primarily because CMS is not finalizing the proposed licensure requirement for personnel performing clinical duties, is using updated tier-assignment data showing 35 DSAs expected to open for competition,

a. Overview

b. Data Sources and Key Assumptions
Our analysis relies on data from several sources and includes key assumptions about OPO operations and regulatory implementation. Labor costs are based on Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS) May 2025 National Occupational Employment and Wage Estimates, adjusted by a factor of 2.0 or 100 percent, for fringe benefits and overhead. Baseline costs are established by the December 2020 OPO final rule, which documented annual costs of $126.7 million. The weighted average hourly rate of $186 for OPO staff reflects a mix of executive directors, medical directors, quality managers, and administrative personnel.
[

]
The CMS GS-14 hourly rate of $145 reflects staff conducting oversight, policy development, and technical assistance activities, based on the 2025 General Schedule (GS) salary table for the Washington-Baltimore-Arlington locality pay area.
Recurring annual cost estimates in this RIA reflect the average annual cost of activities that recur each re-certification cycle, rather than a constant level of effort in every calendar year. For provisions tied to cycle-end events—including designation management, competition administration, and successor transitions under §§ 486.308 and 486.309—CMS expects activity to be concentrated in the year the re-certification cycle concludes and the following transition year, with comparatively limited activity in intervening years. The annualized figures presented reflect the total expected cost across the cycle, divided evenly for presentation purposes.
For this final rule, we use an assumption of 54 OPOs serving 55 DSAs. We also use updated performance data showing 14 tier 3 DSAs and 21 tier 2 DSAs, resulting in an estimated 35 DSAs opened for competition during the re-certification cycle. We estimate that approximately 35 to 40 OPOs would participate in competitions, with an average of 3 to 5 OPOs competing for each open DSA. Because an OPO may apply for more than one open DSA, the estimated number of applications exceeds the estimated number of participating OPOs. This results in approximately 140 total competition applications across the cycle, calculated as 35 DSAs × 4 OPOs per DSA.
We also estimate that no more than 14 OPOs will expand to serve multiple DSAs following implementation of the December 2020 OPO final rule's performance standards and the designation framework finalized in this rule. The estimate that no more than 14 OPOs will expand to serve multiple DSAs reflects the number of OPOs expected to assume responsibility for at least one additional DSA, not the total number of DSAs that may be opened for competition. This estimate assumes a one-to-one relationship between expanding OPOs and newly opened DSAs. For example, the illustrative benefit estimate discussed under § 486.316 assumes that 14 tier 3 DSAs will be awarded across 14 successor OPOs. We acknowledge, however, that there could be cases where an OPO wins the competition for more than one additional DSA.
In response to public comments, CMS is not finalizing the proposed licensure requirement for personnel performing clinical duties. Therefore, the final RIA removes the proposed OPO and CMS costs associated with licensure verification, tracking, recruitment, training, and related monitoring. CMS is finalizing only the medical director conforming change at § 486.326(d), which is not expected to impose meaningful incremental costs.

d. Incremental Benefits
This section presents the incremental benefits of this final rule organized by benefit category. For each category, we distinguish between quantified benefits that can be monetized with reasonable certainty and qualitative benefits that are real but difficult to quantify precisely. Benefit estimates are presented over the 5-year analysis period, 2027 through 2031, and are compared to the baseline established by the December 2020 final rule.
For quantified benefits, we provide a detailed calculation methodology showing data sources and assumptions, annual benefit estimates, and acknowledgment of uncertainty where appropriate. For qualitative benefits, we describe each benefit, explain why monetization is not feasible, and connect the benefit to the overarching regulatory objectives of improving organ procurement and transplantation outcomes.
The quantified benefits total approximately $598,000 in annual recurring benefits from reduced implementation inquiry and compliance-interpretation burden and $500,000 in one-time benefits due to increased operational flexibility for multi-DSA operations. These quantified benefits represent only a portion of the total value generated by this final rule. Significant qualitative benefits also exist that, while difficult to monetize, are important to the effective implementation of the December 2020 final rule's performance measurement, re-certification, designation, competition, and appeals framework and directly support the goal of increasing organ availability for the 100,000 plus individuals on transplant waiting lists.

(1) Quantified Benefits
This section presents the quantified incremental benefits of this final rule organized by benefit category. For each benefit, we provide baseline context identifying what was already captured in the December 2020 final rule versus what is genuinely incremental in this final rule, detailed calculation methodology showing data sources and assumptions, annual and 5-year benefit estimates, and acknowledgment of uncertainty where appropriate. The quantified benefits focus on measurable impacts that can be monetized with reasonable certainty based on available data and conservative assumptions.
(a) Reduced Implementation Inquiry and Compliance Interpretation Burden
The December 2020 final rule (
85 FR 77898
) established new performance measures and a three-tier system. As CMS, OPOs, and other interested parties have prepared to operationalize that framework, particularly as the end of the re-certification cycle approached, CMS has received inquiries regarding implementation of re-certification, designation, competition, appeals, and related operational processes. The benefit estimate below captures expected reductions in future time spent by CMS and OPOs on repetitive implementation inquiries and compliance-interpretation activities as a result of the clarifications finalized in this rule.
This final rule is expected to reduce repetitive implementation inquiries by clarifying procedures for competitions, multi-DSA operations, non-renewal versus de-certification distinctions, appeals processes, outcome-measure accountability, information management, and QAPI adverse event and outcome-measure requirements.
We expect the clarifications finalized in this rule to reduce CMS staff time spent responding to repetitive inquiries, OPO staff time spent reviewing and seeking guidance on implementation issues, and disputes during the re-certification and competition process.
We estimate that absent this final rule, each OPO would spend approximately 60 hours annually seeking clarification. With the clarifications finalized in this rule, we estimate this would decline to 20 hours annually, saving 40 hours per OPO. This time involves executive directors, legal staff, and compliance officers researching requirements, preparing requests, coordinating with CMS, and implementing guidance. At a weighted average hourly rate of $132, adjusted by 100 percent for fringe benefits and overhead consistent with the 2020 methodology, this yields an annual OPO benefit of $285,120, calculated as 40 hours × $132 × 54 OPOs, rounded to $285,000.
Similarly, absent this rule, CMS would receive approximately 162 substantive requests annually, calculated as 3 requests per OPO × 54 OPOs. With the clarifications finalized in this rule, we expect a reduction to 54 requests annually, calculated as 1 request per OPO × 54 OPOs, eliminating 108 requests. Each request requires approximately 20 hours of GS-14 staff time for research, coordination, drafting responses, and quality review. At a GS-14 hourly rate of $145 (OPM 2025 pay tables, adjusted for locality and benefits), this yields an annual benefit of $313,200, calculated as 108 requests × 20 hours × $145, rounded to $313,000. The total annual benefit from reduced implementation inquiry and compliance-interpretation burden is therefore approximately $598,000, calculated as $285,000 in OPO benefits + $313,000 in CMS benefits. Over the 5-year analysis period, the undiscounted benefit is approximately $2.99 million, using the unrounded annual estimate.

This estimate is conservative because it captures only direct time savings. It excludes indirect costs of associated with case-specific implementation questions, including delayed strategic planning, deferred operational decisions, potential disputes and appeals, and opportunity costs when staff time is diverted from core organ procurement activities. (b) Operational Flexibility for Multi-DSA Operations
The December 2020 final rule established a three-tier performance system and de-certification procedures but did not explicitly address how OPOs managing multiple DSAs would be evaluated when performance varies across service areas. Without clarification, the baseline framework could potentially result in de-certification of an OPO even when some of its DSAs perform well, requiring unnecessary transitions in well-performing territories and imposing avoidable costs on the system.
This final rule allows OPOs designated to serve more than one DSA to continue serving well-performing DSAs while losing designation only for an underperforming tier 3 DSA, provided the OPO remains designated to at least one other DSA that is not tier 3. The final provisions at §§ 486.309 and 486.316 establish that CMS may remove designation to a tier 3 DSA without de-certification when an OPO is designated to other DSAs that are not tier 3. This enables continuity of service in well-performing territories, preserves OPO staff relationships with hospitals and donor families, and avoids unnecessary operational transition costs in tier 1 and tier 2 DSAs.
Using preliminary analysis of 2026 OPO performance data, we estimate that approximately 14 DSAs may be classified as tier 3 and therefore opened for competition as part of the 2026 re-certification process, after any applicable appeals are exhausted. Tier 2 DSAs will also be opened for competition; however, because a tier 2 OPO may retain its DSA through competition, we do not assume additional DSA transitions resulting from tier 2 competitions for purposes of this illustrative benefit estimate. For purposes of this estimate, we assume that the 14-tier 3 DSAs will be awarded to 14 successor OPOs, with each successor OPO assuming responsibility for one additional DSA.
In the subsequent performance evaluation cycle ending in 2030, we assume that 5 of these 14 successor OPOs will have mixed performance across their DSAs, meaning each will have at least one DSA with tier 1 or tier 2 performance and one DSA with tier 3 performance. Under the final policy, CMS would remove designation only for the underperforming tier 3 DSA, rather than de-certifying the OPO, provided the OPO remains designated to at least one other DSA that is not tier 3. For purposes of this estimate, we assume that this policy avoids one unnecessary transition for each of the 5 mixed-performance OPOs. Using the baseline transition cost of $100,000 per DSA from the December 2020 final rule, avoiding 5 unnecessary transitions produces an estimated one-time benefit of $500,000, calculated as 5 avoided transitions × $100,000 per transition.
This estimate is conservative because it captures only avoided direct
