transition costs. It does not quantify additional benefits from maintaining hospital relationships, preserving staff knowledge, avoiding disruption in well-performing DSAs, or reducing CMS administrative burden associated with managing unnecessary transitions. The estimate also depends on the number of successor OPOs that are ultimately designated to multiple DSAs and the share of those OPOs with mixed-tier performance in the subsequent evaluation cycle.
(2) Qualitative Benefits Not Monetized
The following benefits are real and significant but cannot be readily monetized due to the difficulty of isolating causal effects, the diffuse nature of the benefits, or the lack of empirical data to support quantification. For each qualitative benefit, we describe the benefit, explain why monetization is not feasible, and connect the benefit to the regulatory objectives of improving OPO accountability, organ procurement, transplantation outcomes, and system stability.
(a) Improved System Efficiency and Continuity
This final rule reduces the risk of service disruptions by establishing clearer procedures for successor selection, multi-DSA transitions, non-renewal, de-certification, appeals, and transitions between incumbent and successor OPOs. The final rule clarifies when CMS may select a successor OPO when there is insufficient time to conduct a full competition, the criteria CMS will consider in successor selection, and how OPOs must cooperate during transitions.
In addition, this final rule includes targeted modifications in response to comments regarding CMS-assigned DSAs.
When CMS assigns an OPO to an additional DSA because no other OPO applies for competition or there is insufficient time to conduct a competition, CMS would not open the OPO's original DSA for competition solely because performance in the original DSA declines from tier 1 to tier 2 or fails to improve from tier 2 to tier 1, provided that the original DSA does not fall to tier 3. In practical effect, the OPO would not have to compete to retain its original DSA based solely on tier 2 performance following the CMS assignment. The final rule also allows an OPO assigned a DSA when there is insufficient time to conduct a competition to remain designated to that DSA for a full re-certification cycle. These final modifications may reduce disincentives for OPOs to accept CMS assignment and may support continuity of organ procurement services in DSAs that otherwise could experience disruption.
We cannot readily quantify this benefit because the number of future CMS assignments, changes in DSA tier assignments following CMS assignment, and transition scenarios is uncertain. The impact of any service disruption would vary based on DSA-specific circumstances, including hospital relationships, geography, staffing capacity, donor volume, and the operational readiness of the successor OPO. However, the benefit is important because maintaining continuity of organ procurement services during transitions supports the stability of the organ donation and transplantation system.
(b) Enhanced Competition Efficiency
The December 2020 final rule established a three-tier performance system and competition framework but did not provide procedural and technical details on multi-DSA competition scenarios, designation consequences, or transition requirements. This final rule enhances competition procedures, including separate DSA-level outcome-measure evaluation when an OPO is designated to multiple DSAs, OPO-level evaluation of process performance measures, competition eligibility for OPOs subject to non-renewal, and transition requirements between incumbent and successor OPOs.
Based on updated performance data, we estimate that 35 DSAs may open for competition during the re-certification cycle. Clear procedures are especially important given the scale of expected competition activity. The final rule helps OPOs understand when they may compete, how CMS will evaluate tier assignments across DSAs, how transition plans will be handled, and how CMS will apply the existing competition selection criteria. We cannot readily quantify this benefit because the dynamic effects of enhanced competition on OPO performance improvement are difficult to isolate and measure. The counterfactual—what performance would have been without clearer competition procedures—is speculative. The benefit also manifests over time as the competitive environment drives continuous improvement across the OPO system rather than generating a discrete, immediately measurable outcome.
This benefit is significant because the efficiency of the competition process directly affects the quality and continuity of organ procurement services in DSAs opened for competition. Clear procedures support transparent decision-making, reduce uncertainty for OPOs and CMS, and help ensure that competition decisions focus on maximizing organ procurement and transplantation outcomes.
(c) Improved Definitional Clarity
This final rule revises definitions at § 486.302 to support consistent interpretation across OPOs and CMS. These revisions include revising the adverse event framework, clarifying “donor” and “organ” for purposes of pancreata used in islet cell research, and defining “unsound medical practices.”
We cannot readily quantify this benefit because the value of regulatory clarity is diffuse and difficult to monetize. It manifests in reduced confusion, more consistent implementation, better strategic planning, and fewer disputes—benefits that are real but difficult to isolate and measure. The causal link between definitional clarity and specific operational improvements is indirect and influenced by multiple factors, including OPO organizational culture, staff training, leadership priorities, and transplant-center practices.
This benefit is significant because interested parties' inquiries and public comments demonstrate that definitional ambiguity creates operational challenges. Clear definitions help OPOs implement requirements consistently and support CMS survey and oversight activities.
C. Alternatives Considered
Throughout the preamble sections, we summarize the policies proposed in the January 2026 proposed rule, the public comments received, and the policies we are finalizing in this final rule. In developing this final rule, we considered alternative approaches that could have provided additional flexibility, imposed more prescriptive requirements, or retained the existing regulatory text without revision. We selected the policies finalized in this rule to provide clearer operational and administrative requirements, maintain OPO accountability, support continuity of organ procurement services, and avoid unnecessary burden or disruption.
With respect to the definitions of “medically complex donor” and “medically complex organ” and the related QAPI requirements, we considered finalizing the proposed definition with specific clinical criteria, including DCD donors and donors with elevated KDPI scores, as well as a modified, guideline-based definition. After considering public comments
(
printed page 69435)
raising concerns that no standardized, nationally recognized definition of a medically complex donor currently exists and that the associated QAPI requirement could increase documentation burden without a current consistent basis for identifying affected donors and organs, we are not finalizing the proposed definitions of “medically complex donor” or “medically complex organ,” and we are not finalizing the QAPI requirement proposed at § 486.348(e). CMS may consider this issue in future rulemaking if a consensus emerges to support a standardized definition of medically complex donor.
With respect to designation, re-certification, competition, and OPOs designated to more than one DSA, we considered alternative approaches that would have imposed more prescriptive requirements on how OPOs structure their operations when designated to multiple DSAs. These alternatives included requiring OPOs to maintain separate DSAs in all circumstances or adopting additional approval requirements before an OPO could determine whether to maintain separate DSAs or consolidate DSAs where permitted under the regulation. We also considered alternative approaches for CMS-assigned DSAs and the impact of assignment on an OPO's existing DSAs. After considering public comments, we are finalizing an approach that provides OPOs flexibility to structure operations in a manner appropriate for their DSAs while maintaining CMS oversight and accountability through the certification, designation, re-certification, competition, survey, and enforcement framework. We are also finalizing targeted modifications for CMS-assigned DSAs to reduce disincentives for OPOs to accept assignment while preserving accountability for tier 3 performance.
With respect to non-renewal, de-certification, appeals, and competition procedures, we considered retaining the existing regulatory text without further clarification. We also considered alternative approaches to the timing and structure of the appeals process and the transition process for DSAs opened for competition. We are finalizing revisions to clarify the distinction between non-renewal, de-certification, and removal of designation to a tier 3 DSA without de-certification; update appeal procedures; and establish transition requirements. We believe these final policies provide greater transparency and predictability for OPOs and CMS while supporting timely resolution of enforcement and designation decisions and continuity of organ procurement services.
With respect to human resources, we considered finalizing the proposed licensure, certification, or registration requirement for personnel performing clinical duties. Commenters raised concerns that the proposed requirement could create operational challenges because OPO staff roles are specialized, may not align neatly with State licensure frameworks, and may include activities that are distinct from direct patient care. After considering public comments, we are not finalizing the proposed licensure, certification, or registration requirement at this time. We are finalizing only the medical director conforming change for multi-DSA operations and may consider broader personnel qualification issues in future rulemaking.
With respect to information management, we considered whether to impose additional reporting or documentation requirements related to organs recovered and sent for research, including pancreata used for islet cell research. We are finalizing the recordkeeping requirement at § 486.330(b) as proposed because it supports CMS' ability to validate the disposition of organs sent for research while allowing OPOs flexibility in the types of records that may be maintained, provided they maintain documentation from an IRB or other formal authorizing body, as appropriate, the research institution, the principal investigator, and study contacts. We are not finalizing additional reporting requirements in this rule.
Overall, we believe the alternatives finalized in this rule appropriately balance accountability, operational flexibility, administrative clarity, and continuity of organ procurement services. The final policies clarify and refine the regulatory framework established by the December 2020 OPO final rule without imposing unnecessary requirements beyond those needed to support implementation, oversight, and continued improvement in the organ donation and transplantation system.
D. Regulatory Review Cost Estimation
Due to the uncertainty involved with accurately quantifying the number of entities that will review this proposed rule, we assume that all 54 OPOs will review this rule. While other individuals and providers may also review the rule, we estimate that doubling the number of OPOs (108 reviewers) provides a reasonable approximation of the total number of reviewers. We acknowledge that this assumption may understate or overstate the actual review costs.
For purposes of this estimate, we assume each reviewer reads approximately 100 percent of the rule and the average reading speed is 250 words per minute. This rule contains approximately 60,000 words, which equates to 4 hours reviewing the rule. Using a weighted average hourly rate of $132 for OPO executive directors and legal staff, adjusted by 100 percent for fringe benefits and overhead consistent with the 2020 final rule methodology, we estimate total review costs of $57,024, calculated as 108 reviewers × 4 hours × $132, rounded to $57,000.

et seq.

For purposes of the RFA, we treat all OPOs as small entities. Under the RFA, a “small entity” includes a “small organization,” which includes a not-for-profit enterprise which is independently owned and operated and is not dominant in its field. ). Thus, they are not dominant in their field and qualify as small entities.

Section 1102(b) of the Social Security Act requires us to prepare a regulatory impact analysis if a rule may have a significant impact on the operations of a substantial number of small rural hospitals. This analysis must conform to the provisions of section 603 of the RFA. For purposes of section 1102(b) of the Act, we define a small rural hospital as a hospital that is located outside of a Metropolitan Statistical Area for Medicare payment regulations and has fewer than 100 beds. We are not preparing an analysis for section 1102(b) of the Act because we have determined, and the Secretary has certified, that this final rule will not have a significant impact on the operations of a substantial number of small rural hospitals. G. Unfunded Mandates Reform Act (UMRA)
Section 202 of the Unfunded Mandates Reform Act of 1995 (UMRA) requires that agencies assess anticipated costs and benefits before issuing any rule whose mandates require spending in any 1 year of $100 million in 1995 dollars, updated annually for inflation. In 2026, that threshold is approximately $193 million.
This final rule imposes estimated costs of approximately $16.4 million in Year 1 and $7.91 million in recurring annual costs, which is well below the UMRA threshold. Recurring annual costs beyond Year 1 comprise $7.56 million for OPOs and $349,000 for CMS. The final rule does not mandate any spending requirements for State, local, or tribal governments. While the rule imposes costs on OPOs, which are private sector entities, these costs are substantially below the UMRA threshold.
These costs represent clarifications and refinements to the operational and administrative requirements established in the December 2020 OPO final rule, rather than fundamental system restructuring. The costs are primarily administrative and operational in nature and include training, documentation updates, enhanced coordination activities, competition-related costs, transition planning, multi-DSA operational costs, and compliance with clarified requirements.
As noted in the December 2020 OPO final rule, reimbursement by both public and private payers would cover reasonably estimated costs associated with organ procurement activities. OPOs are reimbursed for their organ acquisition costs through Medicare, Medicaid, and private insurance payments. The estimated costs are well below the UMRA threshold. Therefore, the requirements of UMRA do not apply to this final rule.
H. Federalism
Executive Order 13132
establishes certain requirements that an agency must meet when it promulgates a proposed rule (and subsequent final rule) that imposes substantial direct requirement costs on State and local governments, preempts State law, or otherwise has Federalism implications.
This final rule is directed at OPOs, which are private nonprofit organizations certified by CMS to coordinate organ procurement activities within designated service areas. The proposed rule does not impose substantial direct requirement costs on State and local governments, preempt State law, or have Federalism implications. The proposed clarifications and refinements to the OPO conditions for coverage affect only OPOs and CMS administrative processes. State and local governments are not directly regulated by these provisions. While some State and local government entities may interact with OPOs in their capacity as healthcare providers or in other roles, the proposed rule does not impose requirements or costs on governmental entities in their governmental capacity. The estimated costs of this final rule, approximately $16.4 million in Year 1 and $7.9 million in recurring annual costs, fall entirely on OPOs and the Federal Government. Year 1 costs include approximately $15.11 million for OPOs and $1.37 million for CMS. Recurring annual costs include approximately $7.56 million for OPOs and $349,000 for CMS. No costs are imposed on State, local, or tribal governments. Since this final rule does not impose substantial direct requirement costs on State or local governments, does not preempt State law, and does not have Federalism implications, the requirements of
Executive Order 13132
are not applicable to this final rule.

CMS may extend the effective date of the de-certification as needed to allow for completion of the appeal process under § 486.314, competition of the service area and, if necessary, transition of the service area to a successor OPO. In cases of urgent need, CMS gives written notice of de-certification to an OPO at least 3 calendar days prior to the effective date of the de-certification. The initial notice of de-certification states the reasons for de-certification, explains the available appeal rights, and includes the effective date of the de-certification.
(c)
Public notice.
In cases of urgent need, CMS will provide prompt public notice in the service area of the date of de-certification and the date that a new OPO will be designated for the DSA. With respect to cases described in paragraph (a)(1) or (2) of this section, CMS will provide such public notice after the available appeal rights are exhausted.
(d)
Cessation of payment.
No payment under titles XVIII or XIX of the Act will be made with respect to organ procurement costs attributable to an OPO on or after the effective date of de-certification.

§ 486.314
Appeals.
OPOs may appeal a de-certification as described at § 486.312(a) or the removal of designation to a tier 3 DSA without de-certification as described at § 486.316(b)(2)(iii)(B).
(a)
Notice of initial determination.
If an OPO is either de-certified or has its designation to a tier 3 DSA removed without de-certification, CMS will send the OPO either a notice of initial de-certification or a notice of removal of designation for a DSA without de-certification.
(1)
Initial notice of de-certification.
An OPO will receive an initial notice of de-certification if it is determined to be non-compliant with the process performance measures at § 486.312(a)(1) or non-compliant with the outcome measures as specified at § 486.312(a)(2) or § 486.312(a)(3).
(2)
Notice of removal of designation to a tier 3 DSA without de-certification.
An OPO will receive a notice of removal of designation to a tier 3 DSA without de-certification if it is determined to be non-compliant with the outcome measures in that DSA but the OPO has other designated DSAs assigned as tier 1 or tier 2, or another designated DSA that is pending evaluation of its outcome measures as specified at § 486.318(c)(3) or (4) at the end of the re-certification cycle.
(b)
Reconsideration
—(1)
Filing request.
If the OPO is dissatisfied with the de-certification determination or the removal of a tier 3 DSA without de-certification, it has 20 calendar days from receipt of the notice of de-certification or removal of designation for a tier 3 DSA without de-certification to file a reconsideration request with CMS. The request for reconsideration must state the issues or findings of fact with which the OPO disagrees and the reasons for the disagreement.
(2)
Failure to request reconsideration.
An OPO must file a reconsideration request before it is entitled to seek a hearing before a hearing officer. If an OPO does not request reconsideration or its request is not made timely, the OPO has no right to further administrative review.
(3)
Reconsideration determination.
CMS makes a written reconsidered determination within 15 calendar days of receipt of the request for reconsideration affirming or reversing the initial determination and the findings on which it was based. CMS reserves the right to extend the 15-calendar day limitation if:
(i) CMS determines more time is needed to thoroughly review and make a reconsideration decision; and
(ii) The extension of time does not prejudice either of the parties.
(4)
Preparing the administrative record.
CMS augments the administrative record to include any additional materials submitted by the OPO and a copy of the reconsideration decision and sends the supplemented administrative record to the CMS hearing officer.
(c)
Request for hearing.
An OPO dissatisfied with the CMS reconsideration decision can file a request for a hearing before a CMS hearing officer within 15 calendar days after receipt of the notice of the reconsideration determination. If an OPO does not request a hearing or its request is not timely received, the OPO has no right to further administrative review and the reconsideration determination becomes the final agency decision.
(d)
Administrative record.
Upon receipt of a request for a hearing, the hearing officer will promptly request the administrative record from the reconsideration official. The hearing officer will send the administrative record to both parties, or make it available through their electronic filing system, within 15 calendar days of receipt of the request for a hearing.

(i)
Scope of review.
An OPO may appeal a de-certification as described at § 486.312(a) and the removal of designation to a tier 3 DSA on substantive or procedural grounds.
(j)
Burden of proof.
The OPO bears the burden of proof by a preponderance of the evidence to demonstrate the notice of de-certification or removal of designation to a tier 3 DSA should be reversed.
(k)
Hearing officer's decision.
(1) The hearing officer renders a decision on the appeal of the notice of de-certification or removal of designation to a tier 3 DSA within 90 calendar days of the hearing. The hearing officer may extend the timeframe for issuing its decision beyond 90 calendar days if the hearing officer determines that 90 calendar days is insufficient for the hearing officer to develop the administrative record and render a legally sufficient decision and that extending the timeframe for issuing its decision would not unduly prejudice either the OPO or the government. If, consistent with the preceding sentence, the hearing officer extends the timeframe for issuing its decision beyond 90 calendar days, the hearing officer shall provide notice of the extension to the OPO and the government.
(2) The hearing officer can affirm or reverse the notice of de-certification or removal of designation to a tier 3 DSA without de-certification.
(3) The hearing officer's decision and the administrative record will be promptly forwarded to the CMS Administrator for his or her discretionary review.
(l)
CMS Administrator discretionary review.
(1) After receiving the hearing officer's decision for review, the CMS Administrator may elect to review the hearing officer's decision or to decline to review the hearing officer's decision. If the CMS Administrator does not elect to review that decision within 30 calendar days of receipt of the hearing officer's decision and the administrative record, the hearing officer's decision is final.
(2) If the CMS Administrator elects to review the hearing officer's decision, the CMS Administrator promptly notifies CMS and the OPO in writing of that election and that each party has the
(
printed page 69441)
right to submit arguments on the administrative record from the hearing officer within 15 calendar days of the date of the notification.
(3) The CMS Administrator determines whether the hearing officer's determination should be upheld, reversed, or remanded according to paragraph (m) of this section.
(4) The CMS Administrator's administrative record is composed of:
(i) All documents submitted to the hearing officer or developed during the hearing, including the hearing officer's decision;
(ii) Written arguments from the OPO or CMS explaining why either or both parties believe the hearing officer's determination was correct or incorrect; and
(iii) The CMS Administrator's written decision explaining the reasons for their decision.
(5) The CMS Administrator may render a final decision in writing to the parties within 45 calendar days of notifying the parties that the Administrator has elected to review the hearing officer's decision.
(6) The decision of the hearing officer is final if the CMS Administrator does not render a final decision in writing to the parties within 45 calendar days of electing to review the hearing's administrative record or by a date specified under paragraph (l)(7) of this section.
(7) The CMS Administrator may extend the 45-calendar-day limitation if the:
(i) CMS Administrator determines he or she requires more time to thoroughly review and make a decision regarding the appeal; and
(ii) Extension does not prejudice either of the parties.
(m)
Remand.
(1) The CMS Administrator may remand the appeal to CMS for any appropriate reason, except for:
(i) In cases where the appeal was previously remanded to CMS, evaluation of evidence that was known or reasonably should have been known at the time the appeal was originally remanded.
(ii) Change in a party's representation, regardless of when made.
(iii) Presentation of an alternative legal basis concerning an issue in dispute.
(2) If the appeal is remanded to CMS, the original de-certification or removal of designation for a DSA without de-certification decision is vacated. The agency will comply with any instructions in the remand and will make a new determination.
(n)
Extension of agreement.
If there is insufficient time prior to expiration of an agreement with CMS to allow for completion of the appeals process, competition of the service area and, if necessary, transition of the service area to a successor OPO, CMS may choose to offer to extend the OPO's agreement with CMS.
(o)
Effects of de-certification.
Medicare and Medicaid payments may not be made for organ procurement services the OPO furnishes on or after the effective date of de-certification. If an OPO's designation to a tier 3 DSA is removed without de-certification, Medicare and Medicaid payments may not be made for organ procurement services the OPO furnishes in the affected DSA on or after the effective date of the removal of designation for the tier 3 DSA without de-certification. Once the appeals process is exhausted and the notice of de-certification or removal of designation for a tier 3 DSA without de-certification has not been reversed by the CMS Administrator, CMS will then open the OPO's affected service area for competition as set forth in § 486.316(c).
(p)
De-certification due to urgent need.
If an OPO is de-certified due to urgent need, the affected OPO's service area will be reassigned to another OPO as set forth at § 486.308(a)(4) by the effective date specified in the notice of de-certification provided under § 486.312(b). The OPO has 20 calendar days from receipt of that notice to file a request for reconsideration from CMS. The remainder of the appeals process proceeds as set forth in this section.

§ 486.316
Re-certification and competition processes.
(a)
Impact of outcome measures to OPO designation.
Each OPO DSA will be assigned to either Tier 1, Tier 2, or Tier 3, based upon performance on the outcome measures set forth in § 486.318 for the final assessment period of the agreement cycle. The tier assignment of each DSA will determine OPO designation to the DSA.
(1)
Tier 1.
An OPO designated to a DSA that is assigned to tier 1, as specified at § 486.318(b)(4), will retain designation to the DSA for another agreement period. An OPO with tier 1 DSAs is eligible to compete in competitions for any open DSAs if it has been shown by the most recent survey to be in compliance with the requirements for certification at § 486.303, including the conditions for coverage at §§ 486.320 through 486.360.
(2)
Tier 2.
An OPO designated to a DSA that is assigned to tier 2, as specified at § 486.318(b)(5), must successfully compete and be awarded a DSA to retain designation to a DSA for another agreement period. An OPO with tier 2 DSAs is eligible to compete in competitions for any open DSAs if it has been shown by the most recent survey to be in compliance with the requirements for certification at § 486.303, including the conditions for coverage at §§ 486.320 through 486.360. OPOs with DSAs assigned by CMS under the provisions at § 486.308(a)(4) or paragraph (e) of this section will not have any existing or newly assigned DSA opened for competition based on assignment to tier 2 until a full re-certification cycle is completed for the newly assigned DSA.
(3)
Tier 3.
An OPO designated to a DSA that is assigned to tier 3, as specified at § 486.318(b)(6), will have the designation removed at the end of the agreement period. An OPO with all of its DSAs assigned to tier 3 is not eligible to compete in competitions for any open DSAs.
(b)
OPO re-certification and competition
—(1) Compliance with process performance measures. An OPO must maintain compliance with the process performance measures at all times. An OPO with non-compliance in the process performance measures set forth at §§ 486.320 through 486.360 in any DSA will receive an initial notice of de-certification and has the right to appeal that determination as established in § 486.314. If an OPO does not appeal the determination, or the OPO appeals and the determination is upheld after the appeal process is completed, the OPO's service areas are opened for competition from other OPOs that qualify to compete for open service areas as set forth in paragraph (c) of this section.
(2)
Compliance with the outcome measures.
CMS will consider an OPO's DSA tier assignments in the final assessment period for re-certification.
(i) An OPO designated to at least one DSA that is assigned to tier 1 in the final assessment period will be re-certified for another re-certification cycle, as long as it is compliant with conditions for coverage at §§ 486.320 through 486.360 during the most recent survey.
(ii) An OPO that is designated to at least one DSA that is assigned to tier 2 but is not designated to any DSA assigned to tier 1 in the final assessment period will be re-certified if it is compliant with conditions for coverage at §§ 486.320 through 486.360 during the most recent survey. The OPO will be eligible to compete in competitions for any open DSA but will not have the agreement for designation to a DSA
(
printed page 69442)
renewed if it is not successful in at least one competition, in accordance with § 486.311(a)(1). If the OPO is not successful in at least one competition, it will receive a notice of non-renewal as specified in § 486.311(b).
(iii) An OPO that is designated to a DSA(s) assigned to tier 3 in the final assessment period will receive one of the following notices:
(A) A notice of its initial de-certification for an OPO that has no other designated DSA that is assigned to tier 1 or tier 2, or another designated DSA that is pending evaluation of its outcome measures as specified at § 486.318(c)(3) or (4) at the end of the re-certification cycle.
(B) A notice of removal of designation to the DSA assigned as tier 3 for an OPO that has another designated DSA assigned as tier 1 or tier 2, or another designated DSA that is pending evaluation of its outcome measures as specified at § 486.318(c)(3) or (4) at the end of the re-certification cycle.
(iv) The OPO has the right to appeal de-certification or removal of designation to a tier 3 DSA as established in § 486.314. If an OPO does not appeal the determination, or the OPO appeals and the determination is upheld after the appeal process is completed, the OPO's tier 3 DSAs are opened for competition from other OPOs that qualify to compete for open service areas as set forth in paragraph (c) of this section.
(3)
Competition.
DSAs assigned as tier 2 or tier 3 in the final assessment period will be opened for competition. A DSA assigned to tier 3 will be opened for competition after any appeal under § 486.314 has been exhausted. The DSA is opened for competition from other OPOs that qualify to compete for open service areas as set forth in paragraph (c) of this section.
(c)
Criteria to compete.
(1) To compete for an open DSA, an OPO would have to be designated to at least one DSA that meets the performance requirements of the outcome measures for Tier 1 or Tier 2, as specified at § 486.318(b)(4) or (5), the requirements for certification at § 486.303, and the conditions for coverage at §§ 486.320 through 486.360 at the most recent routine survey. The OPO must compete for the entire DSA.
(2) An OPO that was subject to non-renewal of its agreement for designation to a DSA for failure to retain its DSA after competition is still eligible to compete in future competitions and enter into a new agreement with CMS, provided it has not been de-certified and met the criteria to compete at the time it entered competition that resulted in non-renewal.
(d)
Criteria for selection.
CMS will select an OPO for designation to an open DSA based on the following criteria:
(1) Performance on the outcome measures at § 486.318.
(2) Relative success in meeting the process performance measures and other conditions at §§ 486.320 through 486.360.
(3) Contiguity to the open service area.
(4) Success in identifying and overcoming barriers to donation within its own service area and the relevance of those barriers to barriers in the open area. An OPO competing for an open service area must submit information and data that describe the barriers in its service area, how they affected organ donation, what steps the OPO took to overcome them, and the results.

DSA transition.

§ 486.318
Condition: Outcome measures.
(a) Each OPO's DSA is evaluated by measuring the donation rate and the organ transplantation rate in the DSA.
(1) For all DSAs, except as set forth in paragraph (a)(2) of this section:
(i) The donation rate is calculated as the number of donors in the DSA as a percentage of the donor potential.
(ii) The organ transplantation rate is calculated as the number of organs transplanted from donors in the DSA as a percentage of the donor potential. The organ transplantation rate is adjusted for the average age of the donor potential.
(iii) The numerator for the donation rate is the number of donors in the DSA. The numerator for the organ transplantation rate is the number of organs transplanted from donors in the DSA. The numbers of donors and organs transplanted are based on the data submitted to the OPTN as required in §§ 486.328 and 121.11 of this title. For calculating each measure, the data used is from the same time period as the data for the donor potential.
(iv) The denominator for the outcome measures is the donor potential and is based on inpatient deaths within the DSA from patients 75 or younger with a primary cause of death that is consistent with organ donation. The data is obtained from the most recent 12-months data from State death certificates.
(2) For the Hawaii DSA:
(i) The donation rate is calculated as the number of donors in the DSA as a percentage of the donor potential.
(ii) The kidney transplantation rate is calculated as the number of kidneys transplanted from kidney donors in the DSA as a percentage of the donor potential.
(iii) The numerator for the donation rate is the number of donors in the DSA. The numerator for the kidney transplantation rate is the number of kidneys transplanted from kidney donors in the DSA. The numbers of donors and kidneys transplanted are based on the data submitted to the OPTN as required in §§ 486.328 and 121.11 of this title. For calculating each measure, the data used is from the same time period as the data for the donor potential.
(iv) The denominator for the outcome measures is the donor potential and is based on inpatient deaths within the DSA from patients 75 or younger with a primary cause of death that is consistent with organ donation. The data is obtained from the most recent 12-months data from State death certificates.
(b) Success on the outcome measures will be assessed based on the following parameters and requirements:
(1) For each assessment period, threshold rates will be established based on donation rates during the 12-month period immediately prior to the period being evaluated:
(i) The lowest rate among the top 25 percent in DSA's, and
(ii) The median rate among the DSAs.
(2) For each assessment period, threshold rates will be established based on the organ transplantation or kidney transplantation rates during the 12-month period prior to the period being evaluated:
(i) The lowest rate among the top 25 percent; and
(ii) The median rate among the DSAs.
(3) The 95 percent confidence interval for each DSA's donation and organ transplantation rates will be calculated using a one-sided test.
(
printed page 69443)
(4) Tier 1—DSAs that have an upper limit of the one-sided 95 percent confidence interval for their donation and organ transplantation rates that are at or above the top 25 percent threshold rate established for their DSA will be identified at each assessment period.
(5) Tier 2—DSAs that have an upper limit of the one-sided 95 percent confidence interval for their donation and organ transplantation rates that are at or above the median threshold rate established for their DSA but are not in Tier 1 as described in paragraph (b)(4) of this section will be identified at each assessment period.
(6) Tier 3—DSAs that have an upper limit of the one-sided 95 percent confidence interval for their donation or organ transplantation rates that are below the median threshold rate established for their DSA will be identified at each assessment period. DSAs that have an upper limit of the one-sided 95 percent confidence interval for their donation and organ transplantation rates that are below the median threshold rate for their DSA are also included in Tier 3.
(7) For the DSA that includes the non-contiguous State of Hawaii and surrounding territories, the kidney transplantation rate will be used instead of the organ transplantation rate. The comparative performance and designation to a Tier will be the same as in paragraphs (b)(4) through (6) of this section except kidney transplantation rates will be used.
(c) CMS will evaluate OPO performance on the outcome measures at each assessment period.
(1) Performance on the outcome measures is based on an evaluation at least every 12 months, with the most recent 12 months of data available from the OPTN and State death certificates, beginning January 1 of the first year of the agreement cycle and ending December 31, prior to the end of the agreement cycle.
(2) An assessment period is the most recent 12 months prior to the evaluation of the outcome measures in which data is available.
(3) If an OPO takes over another OPO's DSA as a result of a change of control or ownership or service area, as specified at § 486.310, on a date later than January 1 of the first year of the agreement cycle so that 12 months of data are not available to evaluate the OPO's performance in its new DSA, the OPO will be held accountable for its performance on the outcome measures in the new area once 12 months of data are available.
(4) If an OPO takes over a new DSA as a result of a competition, as specified at § 486.316(d), or assignment by CMS as specified at § 486.308(a)(4) or § 486.316(e), on a date later than January 1 of the first year of the agreement cycle, we will hold the OPO accountable for its performance on the outcome measures in the new area:
(i) For the QAPI requirement, specified at § 486.348(d), once 12 months of outcome measure performance data are available.
(ii) For purposes of re-certification, as specified at § 486.316, in the final assessment period of the following agreement cycle.

Department of Health and Human Services
Office of the Secretary
45 CFR Part 84
RIN 0945-AA27
AGENCY:
Office for Civil Rights (OCR), Office of the Secretary, Department of Health and Human Services.
ACTION:
Final rule.
SUMMARY:
The Department of Health and Human Services (HHS or Department) issues this rule to revise the regulation implementing section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 (section 504) as it applies to recipients of HHS funding (entitled “Nondiscrimination on the Basis of Disability in Programs or Activities Receiving Federal Financial Assistance,” (“2024 Final Rule”)), published on May 9, 2024. This rule clarifies that the Department interprets the statutory exclusion of “gender identity disorders not resulting from physical impairments” from the terms “individual with a disability” and “disability” set forth in our regulations to encompass “gender dysphoria not resulting from a physical impairment” for purposes of the regulation. This clarification is necessary to resolve ambiguity introduced in the preamble to the 2024 Final Rule and to ensure compliance with the best reading of the governing statute.
DATES:
This rule is effective January 4, 2027.
FOR FURTHER INFORMATION CONTACT:
John Thompson, Office for Civil Rights, Department of Health and Human Services at (202) 545-4884 or (800) 537-7697 (TDD), or via email at
504@hhs.gov
.
SUPPLEMENTARY INFORMATION:
Table of Contents
I. Background
II. Overview of the Final Rule
III. Response to Public Comments on the Proposed Rule
IV.
Executive Order 12866
and Related Executive Orders on Regulatory Review
I. Background
Section 504 of the Rehabilitation Act of 1973 (section 504) prohibits discrimination on the basis of disability in programs and activities that receive Federal financial assistance as well as in programs and activities conducted by any Federal agency.
The Office for Civil Rights (OCR) in the United States Department of Health and Human Services (HHS or the Department) enforces section 504 as well as other statutes that prohibit discrimination on the basis of disability.
Congress passed the Rehabilitation Act in 1973, and what was then the U.S. Department of Health, Education, and Welfare issued regulations to implement section 504 in 1977. In the following decades, major legislative and judicial developments shifted the legal landscape of disability discrimination protections under section 504. Those developments include multiple statutory amendments to the Rehabilitation Act, the enactment of the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990 (ADA) and ADA Amendments Act of 2008 (ADAAA), passage of the Affordable Care Act (ACA), and Supreme Court and other significant court cases.
On May 9, 2024, the Department issued the 2024 Final Rule
[
1
]
to modernize and clarify its regulations implementing section 504 for recipients of HHS financial assistance mainly due to those developments. As relevant here, the preamble to the 2024 Final Rule discussed whether “gender dysphoria may constitute a disability under section 504.”
[
2
]
The 2024 Final Rule concluded, in its preamble, that “gender dysphoria does not fall with the statutory exclusions for gender identity disorders.”
[
3
]
The codified regulatory text defining the term “disability” cross-referenced the statutory exclusion in
29 U.S.C. 705(20)(F)
[
4
]
and was silent on whether gender dysphoria may be a disability under section 504.
[
5
]
In April of 2025, the Department published a clarification in the
Federal Register
,
90 FR 15412
(Apr. 11, 2025) (2025 Notice), regarding the 2024 Final Rule preamble language that addressed whether gender dysphoria may constitute a disability under section 504. The notice expressed the Department's concern that “there has been significant confusion about the preamble language referencing gender dysphoria in the” 2024 Final Rule.
[
6
]
The notice clarified that the 2024 Final Rule “does not say that gender dysphoria is a disability” and that the preamble language “does not have the force or effect of law” and “cannot be enforced.”
[
7
]
The Proposed Rule
On December 19, 2025, the Department published a proposed rule to amend
45 CFR part 84
, Nondiscrimination on the Basis of Disability in Programs or Activities Receiving Federal Financial Assistance.
[
8
]
The proposed rule sought to resolve the ambiguity that the Department's April 2025 Notice
(
printed page 69208)
identified by ensuring compliance with the best reading of section 504.
The rule proposed to clarify part of the regulatory definitions of “disability” and “individual with a disability” through the best reading of the relevant statutory provisions.
[
9
]
As defined in statute, the terms “individual with a disability” and “disability” exclude “transvestism, transsexualism, pedophilia, exhibitionism, voyeurism, gender identity disorders not resulting from physical impairments, or other sexual behavior disorders.
[
10
]
The proposed rule interpreted “gender identity disorders not resulting from physical impairments” to encompass “gender dysphoria not resulting from a physical impairment” for purposes of the 2024 Final Rule's definitions of “individual with a disability” and “disability.”
[
11
]
The proposed rule described the relevant statutory framework and history for the definition of disability in section 504.
[
12
]
The proposed rule explained that Congress amended the Rehabilitation Act more than once to align its key definitions with those in the ADA and subsequent amendments to the ADA.
[
13
]
The terms “disability” and “individual with a disability” in section 504 are such definitions that Congress aligned.
[
14
]
Congress enacted the exclusion of “gender identity disorders not resulting from physical impairments” in the ADA in 1990
[
15
]
and aligned that definition in the Rehabilitation Act in 1992.
[
16
]
Neither section 504 nor the ADA define “gender identity disorders” in the statutory exclusion from the terms “disability” and “individual with a disability.”
[
17
]
The proposed rule reasoned that “the term must be given the `ordinary meaning' it had at the time of its adoption.”
[
18
]
The proposed rule documented and summarized the relevant medical diagnostic history of the term “gender identity disorders” at the time Congress excluded “gender identity disorders not resulting from physical impairments”
[
19
]
from these definitions. The Department relied on the revised third edition of the American Psychiatric Association's Diagnostic and Statistical Manual (DSM-III-R) from 1987, which was the edition in effect during 1990 and 1992 when Congress enacted the statutory exclusions in the ADA and the Rehabilitation Act.
[
20
]
The proposed rule also documented and summarized the relevant medical diagnostic history of the term “gender identity disorders” in the fourth edition of the DSM (DSM-IV) released in 1994 and the term “gender dysphoria” in the fifth edition of the DSM released in 2013 (DSM-5).
[
21
]
The Department acknowledged that, while later editions of the DSM may be relevant, “evolving medical classifications of gender disorders cannot change the meaning of the statutory language.”
[
22
]
Overview of Public Comments
The Department sought comments on the proposed rule. The comment period was set to end on January 20, 2026. Due to technical issues and numerous commenters requesting a sixty (60) rather than thirty (30) day comment period, in part because the comment period overlapped with end of the year holidays and scheduled vacations, the Department extended the comment period to February 20, 2026.
The Department received over 380 comments in response to the proposed rule. A wide range of individuals and organizations submitted comments, including private citizens, health care workers and institutions, educators, disability advocacy organizations, faith-based organizations, professional associations, state Attorneys General, and members of Congress. These comments were divided in support for and opposition to the proposed rule, and the Department reviewed and analyzed all of the comments.
II. Overview of the Final Rule
The text of the final rule is unchanged from the proposed rule.
This rule clarifies that the Department interprets the statutory exclusion of “gender identity disorders not resulting from physical impairments” from the terms “individual with a disability” and “disability” set forth at
29 U.S.C. 705(9)
& (20)(F)(i), and
42 U.S.C. 12211(b)
, to encompass “gender dysphoria not resulting from a physical impairment” for purposes of part 84. This clarification is necessary to resolve ambiguity introduced in the preamble to the 2024 Final Rule and to ensure compliance with the best reading of the statute.
III. Response to Public Comments
The Department has summarized public comments and responses to those comments into 12 categories:
general comments;
comments on the Department's authority for this final rule;
comments on the interaction of the rule with other laws and legal principles;
comments on administrative procedure;
comments on regulatory history and caselaw;
comments on the need for the proposed rule;
comments on the definition of disability;
comments on the meaning of statutory language;
comments on reliance interests;
comments on the progression of definitions in the DSM;
comments on regulatory alternatives; and
comments on potential federalism implications.
General Comments
[
23
]
Comments:
Several commenters expressed support for the proposed rule because they believe that the rule will ensure that only people with “legitimate disabilities” receive legal protections under section 504. Some expressed their belief that gender dysphoria is “illegitimate” and based on an internal sense of psychological self rather than a “true disability.”
Response:
The Department notes that this rulemaking is based on an interpretation of the exclusions to the term “individual with a disability” at
29 U.S.C. 705(20)(F)
and
42 U.S.C. 12211(b)(1)
and does not make a judgment on whether gender dysphoria not resulting from physical impairments is “legitimate” or a “true disability.”
Comments:
A group of commenters expressed support for the proposed rule based on the belief that if gender dysphoria could be a disability under section 504, clinicians would be required to provide sex-rejecting procedures and counseling to patients to treat such gender dysphoria under the theory that preventing, limiting, or
(
printed page 69209)
interfering with such procedures may amount to disability discrimination. Some commenters also stated that if gender dysphoria is considered a disability under section 504, then the Department considers such gender dysphoria to amount to an immutable characteristic. Accordingly, clinicians may feel constrained from practicing medicine in a manner that aligns with their personal beliefs. Some commenters stated that clinicians with moral or religious beliefs concerning certain procedures would be faced with having to violate those beliefs if gender dysphoria not resulting from physical impairment was a protected disability under section 504.
Response:
As a threshold matter, the Department handles allegations of disability discrimination on a case-by-case basis and cannot opine on particular factual scenarios. The Department recognizes that clinicians may hold moral or religious beliefs about certain procedures that are used as treatments for gender dysphoria not resulting from physical impairments. In addition to enforcing section 504, the Office for Civil Rights also enforces conscience and religious freedom laws that may protect such clinicians and other health care workers in such situations.
[
24
]
Comments:
Multiple commenters stated that excluding gender dysphoria not resulting from physical impairments from coverage as a disability would significantly restrict discrimination protections for individuals who identify as transgender; would result in people with gender dysphoria being turned away from basic services; and would result in bias, prejudice, and mistreatment. They argue that these impacts would result in additional poor health outcomes for individuals who identify as transgender, such as depression, anxiety, and suicide. Commenters also allege that this rulemaking is based on an effort to harm individuals who identify as transgender for the express reason of political gain rather than the best reading of the statute or relevant scientific evidence.
Response:
This final rule is not based on an effort to harm a population for political gain. The rule reaffirms certain statutory exclusions from the definitions of “disability” and “individual with a disability.” As the proposed rule explained, this is the best reading of the statute, informed, in part, by the relevant medical diagnostic history of the term “gender identity disorders” in the DSM-III-R, which was in effect at the time Congress enacted the statutory exclusions.
[
25
]
To the extent applicable, individuals with gender dysphoria continue to be covered by Federal nondiscrimination laws that protect them from discrimination based on their race, color, and national origin,
[
26
]
biological sex,
[
27
]
age,
[
28
]
and disability.
[
29
]
This rule clarifies that individuals do not have a basis in section 504 to claim that gender dysphoria amounts to a physical or mental impairment that substantially limits one or more major life activities and entitles them to the disability rights protections of section 504.
Comments:
Many commenters asserted that this proposed rule ignores scientific and medical consensus and the perceived need for sex-rejecting procedures for individuals with gender dysphoria. These commenters note that there has been a shift in medical understanding that recognizes the need to treat the distress caused by association with the other gender, rather than a need to treat the association with the other gender itself.
These commenters claim that the proposed rule disregards scientific psychiatric consensus that gender dysphoria not resulting from physical impairment is a recognized disorder that is separate from gender identity disorder. They said that gender dysphoria not resulting from physical impairment is a well-researched medical condition that can cause clinically significant distress or impairment, and that the medical consensus, including that from the American Psychiatric Association, is that such gender dysphoria should be treated through their preferred methods.
[
30
]
They note that the DSM-5 no longer includes the term “gender identity disorder,” but instead uses the term “gender dysphoria.” They also note that if gender dysphoria not resulting from physical impairments is not considered a medical condition or disability under section 504, there may be significant effects on insurance coverage, potentially limiting access to certain treatments or procedures due to out-of-pocket cost.
Response:
It is beyond the scope of this final rule to regulate treatment methods or clinical standards of care for gender dysphoria not resulting from physical impairments. The scope of this rule is the best reading of the statutory exclusions from the terms “disability” and “individual with a disability,” including that “gender dysphoria not resulting from physical impairments” is included within the exclusion for “gender identity disorders not resulting from physical impairments.” The best reading of the statute is informed, in part, by the relevant medical diagnostic history of the term “gender identity disorders” in the DSM-III-R, which was in effect at the time Congress enacted the statutory exclusions using this term.
[
31
]
The proposed rule identified the following gender identity disorders in the third edition of the DSM that were associated with symptoms such as anxiety and depression.
[
32
]
“Gender Identity Disorder of Childhood” was marked by “persistent and intense distress in a child about his or her assigned sex and the desire to be, or insistence that he or she is, of the other sex.”
[
33
]
“Transsexualism”—An “essential feature[ ]” of “transsexualism” included “a persistent discomfort and sense of inappropriateness about one's assigned sex in a person who has reached puberty.”
[
34
]
“Gender Identify Disorder of Adolescence or Adulthood, Nontranssexual Type” included “a persistent or recurrent discomfort and sense of inappropriateness about one's assigned sex[.]”
[
35
]
“Gender Identity Disorder Not Otherwise Specified” served as a catch-all for “[d]isorders in gender identity that are not classifiable as a specific Gender Identity Disorder.”
[
36
]
The Department stands by its position in the proposed rule that, while later editions of the DSM may be relevant in some circumstances, evolving medical classifications of gender disorders cannot change the meaning of the statutory language.
[
37
]
(
printed page 69210)
Comments:
Many commenters asserted that rather than limiting confusion, as the Department intends, this rulemaking will cause additional confusion. Commenters contend that the confusion stems from multiple factors:
The Department's position in this final rule is at odds with a ruling from the Fourth Circuit, the only circuit court to rule on the merits of whether gender dysphoria may be a disability under section 504 and the ADA;
[
38
]
The Department appears to be reversing its position from 2024, which commenters said had reflected the Department's acknowledgement that gender dysphoria not caused by a physical impairment could satisfy the elements of the definition of a disability in certain circumstances;
Insufficient caselaw exists to justify the shift in legal conclusion; and
Many recipients may refer to the three-prong disability test at
45 CFR 84.4(a)(1)
, rather than a statutory exclusion, to determine whether gender dysphoria amounts to a disability.
Response:
The Department addressed the Fourth Circuit decision in the proposed rule and acknowledges that
Williams
is binding precedent within federal courts in Maryland, North Carolina, South Carolina, Virginia, and West Virginia.
[
39
]
The Fourth Circuit decision in
Williams
applies only to the Fourth Circuit and it diverges with the rulings of numerous other courts.
[
40
]
Additionally, the court in Williams noted that gender dysphoria amounts to a subset of gender identity disorders.
[
41
]
As the Department maintains throughout this rulemaking, because gender dysphoria amounts to a subset of gender identity disorders, statutory exclusions for gender identity disorders not resulting from physical impairments necessarily apply to gender dysphoria not resulting from physical impairments.
The Department accordingly disagrees that this rule will cause confusion. Because of the ambiguity introduced by the preamble discussion in the 2024 Final Rule, the Department is concerned that individuals and recipients may be under the misconception that individuals are entitled to disability protections under section 504 based on gender dysphoria not resulting from physical impairments. This rulemaking clarifies that ambiguity and follows the Department's 2025 Notice that stated that the regulatory text of the 2024 Final Rule “does not say that gender dysphoria is a disability” and that the preamble language “does not have the force and effect of law” and “cannot be enforced.”
[
42
]
This rulemaking will help recipients and individuals understand the correct interpretation of the law through amended regulatory text rather than the prior, misleading preamble language. The Department is confident that those determining whether a condition is appropriate as the basis for a disability under 84.4 will consider all applicable paragraphs within that section, including the three-prong test at 84.4(a)(1) and the exclusion at paragraph (g) of 84.4.
Comments:
Some commenters were concerned about the requirement that the term disability under section 504 only excludes gender identity disorder or gender dysphoria that does not result from physical impairments. They stated that this requirement will require clinicians to make medical determinations as to whether the disorder results from a physical impairment or not without clear guidelines from the Department on how to make that determination. They also stated that the distinction between whether gender dysphoria results from a physical impairment or not is arbitrary and should not determine whether it is a disability under section 504.
Response:
The requirement that gender identity disorders must not result from physical impairments in order to be excluded under
42 U.S.C. 12211(b)(1)
has existed since 1990 when it was written into the statute by Congress with the enactment of the ADA. The Department has not been made aware of any recent instances in which a clinician has been unable to determine whether a gender identity disorder (including gender dysphoria) has been the result of a physical impairment. The distinction is not arbitrary. The distinction meaningfully lies in the causation of the gender identity disorder as set forth in the statutory text. The Department does not have authority to circumvent the language of the statute and did not have such authority at the time of the preamble to the 2024 Final Rule that created confusion.
Comments:
Several commenters said that HHS does not have the authority to pick and choose what conditions will be covered as a disability under insurance plans. They stated that the Federal government cannot rewrite medical consensus, nor can it eliminate a valid medical diagnosis.
Response:
The Department agrees that it cannot pick and choose which conditions may be covered as a disability under insurance plans or may amount to disabilities under Federal civil rights laws when excluded disorders are included in statutory language. The Department's obligation is to faithfully apply statutory language to its regulations and enforcement activities, not to attempt to alter statutory language based on recent changes to medical classification of a specific disorder.
Comments:
Many commenters alleged that this rulemaking is not being undertaken for the Department's stated reasons. Rather, those commenters alleged that the Department wants to implement ideological agendas and limit civil rights protections for individuals who identify as transgender regardless of a statutory basis or caselaw. They point to the statements of the Secretary of the Department and other HHS officials
[
43
]
to contend that the reasons for this rulemaking are ideological only, tied to the Administration's advancement of its policy position that Federal law should only recognize an individual's sex and that individuals who identify as transgender should be denied civil rights protections. Commenters' observations and concerns are also described in this final rule's description of comments received on “General Administrative Procedure” matters.
Response:
As the Department has stated, this rulemaking advances the best interpretation of the statutory exclusion to the terms “disability” and “individual with a disability” as these terms are defined in statute for purposes
(
printed page 69211)
of section 504 by including the term “gender dysphoria” within the term “gender identity disorder.” The best understanding of the statute, as written, is not an ideological agenda or policy choice, but rather a mandate of the Supreme Court's interpretation of federal statutes.
[
44
]
Comments on the Department's Authority for This Rulemaking
Comments:
Many commenters stated that the Department is well within its authority to undertake rulemaking on this topic, mainly because the preamble to the 2024 Final Rule incorrectly suggested that gender dysphoria may be a disability under section 504. Those commenters expressed their belief that section 504 excludes gender dysphoria, gender identity disorders, and transsexualism from the definition of disability. Some commenters reasoned that the preamble language addressing gender dysphoria related to the 2024 Final Rule was an overstep by the Department, stating that the Department expanded on its delegated statutory authority rather than letting courts decide whether gender dysphoria could be a disability under section 504. Finally, some commenters asserted that this rulemaking correctly interprets the statutory text of
29 U.S.C. 705(20)(F)
and
42 U.S.C. 12211(b)(1)
, which reflects the intent of Congress, to exclude gender dysphoria not resulting from physical impairments from the definition of disability under section 504.
Response:
The Department agrees that this rulemaking is necessary to eliminate the confusion caused by the preamble language in the 2024 Final Rule that introduced ambiguity on whether gender dysphoria not resulting from physical impairments may amount to a disability. As discussed throughout the preamble of this final rule, the Department has set forth its reasoning that gender dysphoria is encompassed by the statutory exclusion of gender identity disorders not resulting from physical impairments at
29 U.S.C. 705(20)(F)
and
42 U.S.C. 12211(b)(1)
.
Comments:
Many commenters expressed that the current rulemaking oversteps the Department's authority by undermining the intent of Congress as expressed through statutory text. By adding language not explicitly included in the statute deciding that gender dysphoria not resulting from physical impairments falls within the exclusion, the commenters argue that the Department is undermining Congress' authority to shape section 504 in a manner not intended by Congress. Commenters also point to the 2008 ADAAA
[
45
]
passed by Congress to explain why this final rule is in conflict with the statutory authority for section 504. They note that the 2008 ADAAA stated that the definition of disability should be interpreted broadly and not require extensive analysis.
[
46
]
They also state that the term gender dysphoria was widely used within the medical community when the 2008 ADAAA was passed and Congress consciously chose not to update the statutory exclusion language at
29 U.S.C. 705(20)(F)
or
42 U.S.C. 12211(b)(1)
. They argue that this was a signal of Congressional intent that gender dysphoria should not be excluded from the definition of disability under the ADA or section 504. They believe that the Executive Branch is picking and choosing which conditions should be covered by section 504, regardless of actual statutory language and Congressional intent.
Response:
The Department appreciate these commenters' views but respectfully disagree with their conclusions. The Department agrees that the best method to interpret the intent of Congress is through the statutory text as it was understood at the time that the text was adopted.
[
47
]
While reasonable individuals may disagree over changes to the characterization of medical conditions or other circumstances over time, the statutory text of the law remains unchanged until it is formally changed by Congress. Here, the Department intends to respect the intent of Congress by clarifying in the regulations that existing statutory language referring to gender identity disorders not resulting from physical impairments includes gender dysphoria not resulting from physical impairments, consistent with the understanding of gender identity disorders at the time that Congress adopted the statutory exclusion through the ADA's enactment. The alternative, advancing the opinion that gender dysphoria not resulting from physical impairments might amount to a disability when gender identity disorders are clearly excluded by
29 U.S.C. 705(20)(F)
and
42 U.S.C. 12211(b)(1)
, would not be the best reading of statutory text and Congressional intent.
As noted, in 2008 Congress passed the ADAAA in an effort to ensure that the ADA was interpreted consistently with the intent of Congress as it was passed in 1990.
[
48
]
The ADAAA was silent on the exclusions at
29 U.S.C. 705(20)(F)
and
42 U.S.C. 12211(b)(1)
. In the absence of any statutory language suggesting that Congress intended to alter the excluded disorders listed at
29 U.S.C. 705(20)(F)
and
42 U.S.C. 12211(b)(1)
, the Department cannot rationalize any such changes. Additionally, Congress' decision not to update
29 U.S.C. 705(20)(F)
or
42 U.S.C. 12211(b)(1)
with additional disorders or change existing disorders does not suggest that Congress intended to keep gender dysphoria not resulting from physical impairments off the list of exclusions. Congress did not change
29 U.S.C. 705(20)(F)
or
42 U.S.C. 12211(b)(1)
, signaling only that it did not intend to update those exclusions.
Comments:
Many commenters stated that the regulatory language the Department intends to add to this rulemaking is not the best reading of the statute. They reason that altering statutory language should be undertaken by Congress and that the Department oversteps its authority under the ruling in
Loper Bright
[
49
]
when it attempts to alter statutory text. They also argue that at the time that the statutory exclusions were published, gender identity disorders and gender dysphoria were understood to be two separate conditions. They contend that the excluded conditions in the statute from 1990 were considered morally harmful, dangerous, or illegal at the time, and assert that now it is more commonly understood that gender dysphoria does not fall within such categories.
Response:
Whether gender identity disorders or gender dysphoria (when not resulting from physical impairments) are or were considered morally harmful, dangerous, or illegal, has no bearing on interpreting
29 U.S.C. 705(20)(F)
or
42 U.S.C. 12211(b)(1)
. Nothing in section 504 indicates that the excluded conditions are listed because they are “morally harmful, dangerous, or illegal.” Additionally, the Department is not persuaded that in 1990, when the ADA was enacted, gender identity disorders and gender dysphoria were both broadly accepted terms with different definitions within the medical community. The DSM-III-R, the chief diagnostic manual for
(
printed page 69212)
mental disorders in 1990, did not mention the term gender dysphoria. It was not until the publication of the DSM-5 in 2013 that the American Psychiatric Association (the publisher of the DSM-5) introduced the term gender dysphoria as a replacement for gender identity disorders.
[
50
]
The American Psychiatric Association's introduction of the any new term does not change the meaning of Congress' statute and the Department does not have the authority to circumvent the statutory language based on a later change by the American Psychiatric Association.
Concerning the language added by this rule, the Department does not intend to overstep the statutory text as written by Congress. Instead, the regulatory amendments at 84.4(g) clarify how gender dysphoria not resulting from physical impairments falls within an existing statutory exclusion.
In the 2024 Final Rule, the Department's preamble language created an ambiguity when it suggested that the definition of disability included a disorder excluded by Congress. This rulemaking intends to rectify that ambiguity. As stated in
Loper Bright,
“even if some judges might (or might not) consider the statute ambiguous, there is a best reading all the same—`the reading the court would have reached' if no agency were involved.”
[
51
]
The Department's process of statutory interpretation here sets forth this best reading.
Comments on the Interaction of the Rule With Other Laws and Legal Principles
Comments:
Some commenters expressed their opinion that the preamble regarding gender dysphoria to the 2024 Final Rule violated the major questions doctrine because the Department did not have a clear mandate from Congress to conduct rulemaking on the definition of disability. Those commenters stated that the Department overstepped its authority when it said that gender dysphoria could amount to a disability under certain circumstances in the 2024 Final Rule preamble, and that this rulemaking corrects that mistake by returning to the prior understanding of the definition of disability.
Response:
The Department has regulatory authority to adopt a definition of disability that reflects the best reading of section 504 as updated by the ADA and the ADAAA. The Department does not have the authority to expand that statutory definition or narrow a statutory exclusion. Through this rulemaking, the Department intends to eliminate any confusion caused by the 2024 Rule preamble language regarding whether gender dysphoria may be a disability under section 504.
Comments:
Many commenters asserted that this rulemaking and the premise that gender dysphoria cannot be considered a disability under section 504 contradict state laws finding the opposite. Some states have their own nondiscrimination laws that extend protections to people with gender dysphoria based on disability status, and these commenters believe that this rulemaking undermines those laws.
Response:
The Department's responsibility is to establish section 504 regulations consistent with the Federal statute. The fact that state law may be inconsistent with Federal regulations is irrelevant. Where there is a direct conflict, section 504 and similar Federal nondiscrimination laws will usually preempt conflicting state laws.
[
52
]
However, States may impose their own laws,
[
53
]
provided the State law does not serve as an obstacle to or frustrate the purpose of Federal law.
[
54
]
States cannot dictate the requirements or exclusions of Federal law or regulation.
Comments:
Many commenters expressed their belief that this rulemaking violates the Equal Protection Clause of the 14th Amendment of the United States Constitution. They state that the Department has determined, based on animus, that it does not want to extend disability protections to individuals who identify as transgender, and rewrote statutory exclusions to accomplish said goal.
Response:
HHS disagrees with comments that the rule violates the Equal Protection Clause of the 14th Amendment of the United States Constitution and rejects the contention that the Department is acting based on animus. Existing statutory language does not prohibit any individual from appropriately invoking the protection of section 504, it only prohibits certain disorders from being considered disabilities under the statute and certain individuals with those disorders from the definition of individuals with disabilities. This rulemaking corrects a previous misinterpretation of statutory language that was set out in the 2024 Final Rule preamble.
Comments:
Some commenters expressed concern that recipients covered by section 504 also include health programs and activities covered by section 1557 of the Affordable Care Act (ACA)
[
55
]
and public entities covered by ADA title II,
[
56
]
and that the exclusions from the section 504 definition of disability would put the definition of disability at odds with the definition of disability within section 1557 of the ACA and title II of the ADA. These commenters also assert a concern that a person with gender dysphoria could be considered an individual with a disability under title II of the ADA or section 1557 of the ADA but would not be considered a person with a disability under section 504.
Response:
The changes to the text in this rulemaking do not run counter to the text and requirements of section 1557 of the ACA or title II of the ADA. The only discussion in a rule of whether gender dysphoria not resulting from physical impairments may be considered a disability in prior Federal disability rights regulations occurs in the preamble of the 2024 Final Rule.
Comments on Administrative Procedure
Comments:
Some commenters agreed with the Department's decision to use a notice of proposed rulemaking (NPRM) that solicited public comments to correct what they consider to be the overreach of the preamble language to the 2024 Final Rule. They noted that this format of rulemaking allows the public to weigh in on the rulemaking and the Department to consider all comments when deciding on a final rule.
Response:
While the Department pursued notice and comment rulemaking for this regulatory amendment, the Department does have the authority, under
5 U.S.C. 553(a)(2)
, to promulgate rules under section 504 without notice and comment because section 504 governs recipients of Federal financial assistance, all types of which fall into one or more of the exceptions in section 553(a)(2).
Comments:
Many commenters disapproved of the Department using a comment period of 30 days for the rulemaking. They believed that due to the importance of the rulemaking and the fact that the comment period overlapped with December and January holidays, a time period of 60 days should be used.
(
printed page 69213)
Response:
While a 60-day comment period is not required for this rulemaking, the Department decided to extend the comment due date from January 20, 2026 to February 20, 2026, in part to give the public a longer opportunity to comment on the rulemaking.
[
57
]
Comments:
Many commenters argued that the rulemaking violates the Administrative Procedure Act (APA)
[
58
]
because it is allegedly arbitrary and capricious; that is, the rulemaking is based on misinformation, assumptions, and animus rather than the Department's stated goals of clarifying confusion and returning to the plain statutory language. In support of these assertions, the commenters point to public statements, which are described in the “general comments” section of this final rule, made by Department Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and then Deputy Secretary Jim O'Neil at a press conference that announced this and two other rulemakings that dealt broadly with gender identity.
[
59
]
Commenters claimed that the statements from these two Department leaders, which included assertions that there are only two sexes, assertions that the public figures invoked religion to support their views on these matters, and associated the proposed rule with other rulemakings released on the same day, prove that the Department is not motivated by clearing up confusion, statutory text, or the correct legal interpretation.
Response:
The Department is pursuing this rulemaking in an effort to better align its interpretation of the definition of disability with the statutory language at
29 U.S.C. 705(20)(F)
and
42 U.S.C. 12211(b)(1)
. Numerous Federal courts
[
60
]
have signaled interpretations of the law similar to the Department's current position that gender dysphoria not resulting from a physical impairment is excluded from the definition of disability because it constitutes a gender identity disorder not resulting from physical impairments. The Department is pursuing this rulemaking to rectify confusion caused by language in the preamble to the 2024 Final Rule. On December 18, 2025, the Secretary of HHS and the former Deputy Secretary delivered remarks on three rulemakings being pursued by the Department that dealt broadly with gender identity.
[
61
]
The two rulemakings published by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services (CMS) do not impact this rulemaking. Regardless of the general views expressed by the Secretary and the former Deputy Secretary at that event, this rulemaking is being pursued for the express reasons given here and in the preamble to the proposed rule and not any other alleged basis.
Comments:
